docs.title: Home
docs.text:
Homelab Wizard

Your household's photos, passwords, documents, money, music, and books, on a computer you own. A desktop app and a small CLI that install, connect, back up, update, and watch over 70+ self-hosted apps.

What it is · Tour · How it works · Get started · What it replaces · Everyday tasks · Questions · Apps · Docs · What's new

Note

Beta. Homelab Wizard runs a real household on a Mac, and it is now being tested on Windows and Linux machines too. The builds are not signed yet (no Apple Developer ID or Windows code-signing certificate), so each system asks once whether to trust them. Open problems are in Known Issues; what changed in each version is in the CHANGELOG.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Homelab Wizard turns a computer you already own (a Mac mini, a desktop PC, a Steam Machine) into your household's own private cloud. It installs free, open-source apps that do the jobs you pay subscriptions for, such as photo backup, a password manager, and streaming for the films and music you own. It connects them to each other, and then it looks after them:

  • A copy of everything, every night, encrypted before it leaves the house, and a monthly test that proves a restore works.
  • Updates while you sleep, each app's data copied first, with a one-click undo. An app that comes back unwell is put back by itself.
  • A watchdog every 15 minutes that restarts what hangs, and an alert on your phone when something needs you.
  • Nothing published to the internet. Your phones and computers reach the apps over Tailscale's private network, at home and away.

Two parts are its own: Finances, the household's money paycheck by paycheck, and Tidy Up, which keeps the music, films, and books you download sorted. No command line is needed: install the app, click Set it up for me, tick what you want, and it does the rest.

docs.title: Take the tour
docs.text: StatusEvery app on the computer, live: what runs, what needs a look, and one button to open or start each. An app's pageRestart it, read its log in plain words (explained by the AI on this computer), and undo an update. Choose appsTick what you want; each app says what it does and which subscription it can replace. The plan says what it will install before anything happens. BackupsEach app's newest copy, the encrypted off-site jobs, the last restore test, and a printable recovery kit. FinancesWhat each paycheck leaves once the bills are paid, and net worth month by month. Typed in by you, kept at home, no bank connection. Tidy UpDrop in a download and it's filed in the right library: music, films, shows, books, audiobooks. Undo for every change. SetupThe checklist for finishing up, checked live. Do the N I can do for you runs every step that's ready. On your iPhoneThe Homelab app: Status, each app's page, Backups, and Finances in your pocket, at home or away, behind Face ID.

docs.title: On your iPhone
docs.text:
The Homelab app for iPhone and iPad keeps the homelab in your pocket: Status with Start and Logs, each app's page, Backups, the household's Finances, alerts, and a widget, behind Face ID. A phone only looks until you let it make changes, and sees Finances only if you allow it. It's built with Xcode on your own Mac for now, not from the App Store (apple-client).

Every screen in more detail, with what each button does: the full tour.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
flowchart TB
  you(["<b>Your phones and computers</b><br/>at home and away"])
  subgraph home["The computer at home"]
    direction LR
    wizard["<b>Homelab Wizard</b><br/>the app, and its agent<br/>in the background"]
    apps["<b>Your apps</b><br/>Photos · Passwords · Documents<br/>Films · Music · Books · …<br/>each in its own container"]
    wizard -- "installs, connects,<br/>updates, restarts" --> apps
  end
  backup[("<b>Your backups</b><br/>a cloud drive's folder,<br/>or an external drive")]
  you -- "Tailscale: private,<br/>nothing on the internet" --> apps
  wizard -- "every night,<br/>an encrypted copy" --> backup

The apps are free, open-source projects (Immich, Vaultwarden, Paperless-ngx, Jellyfin, Navidrome, and 60-odd more), each running in its own container through Docker, or OrbStack on a Mac. Homelab Wizard is the part that picks them, sets them up with a strong password each, connects them to each other, and keeps them running, with an alert on your phone when something needs you. The traffic paths, the engine, and a night of jobs, drawn out: Architecture.

docs.title: Get started
docs.text:
You need a computer that stays on (a Mac, a Windows 10 or 11 PC, a Linux machine, or a Steam Machine; 8 GB of memory runs the Start here apps, 16 GB is comfortable), its container runtime (OrbStack on a Mac, Docker Desktop on Windows, Docker Engine on Linux), and a free Tailscale account. Within the first week, add somewhere for backups: a cloud drive's synced folder or an external drive. No domain and no router changes. Getting Started walks through every step with pictures.

  1. Install the app with one pasted line. On a Mac or Linux, in Terminal:
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Snooper42/homelab-wizard/main/install.sh | sh

On Windows, in PowerShell:

irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Snooper42/homelab-wizard/main/install.ps1 | iex

Both download the newest build from Releases, check it against GitHub's SHA-256 checksum, install it, and open it. The line is there because the builds aren't signed yet: a browser download gets blocked, a download from Terminal or PowerShell doesn't. Both scripts are short enough to read first (install.sh, install.ps1). 2. Open it and choose Set it up for me. It makes the homelab folder (~/Homelab), with a strong password for every app, and starts the essentials (updates, backups, alerts). 3. Pick what you want on Choose apps (Photos, Passwords, Movies and TV, Music, Files, or anything from the full list) and click Install. 4. Finish on Setup. Do the N I can do for you runs every step that is ready; the rest say in one line what they give you. Signing in to Tailscale and installing it on your phones is the part only you can do.

You are done when Setup leaves the sidebar (it comes back by itself if a step comes undone) and every app on Status has a green dot. Then put Tailscale, the Homelab app, and the apps' own phone apps on each phone (Getting Started › Set up each person's phone).

Every download, and the command line | Platform | Download | Install | |---|---|---| | macOS (Apple Silicon and Intel) | [Releases › Latest](https://github.com/Snooper42/homelab-wizard/releases/latest) › `Homelab-Wizard-macOS.dmg` | `install.sh` (above). Or open the download, drag the app to Applications, and clear the download flag once: `xattr -dr com.apple.quarantine "/Applications/Homelab Wizard.app"`. Later updates install themselves | | Windows 10 and 11, x64 or ARM | [Releases › Latest](https://github.com/Snooper42/homelab-wizard/releases/latest) › `Homelab-Wizard-Windows-Setup.exe` | `install.ps1` (above). Or run the download (SmartScreen: More info › Run anyway, while it's unsigned), or unzip the portable build. Later updates install themselves | | Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, Arch | Releases › Latest › `.deb`, `.rpm`, or `.pkg.tar.zst` | `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Snooper42/homelab-wizard/main/install.sh \| sh` picks the package and installs it; or `sudo apt install ./homelab-wizard_*.deb` (or `dnf install`, `pacman -U`). Later updates install themselves | | SteamOS, or Linux without WebKitGTK | Releases › Latest › `Homelab-Wizard-x86_64.AppImage` | The same `install.sh` line (on SteamOS it puts the AppImage in `~/Applications`), or `chmod +x` and open it; Settings › This machine › **Add to the app menu** | Every build carries the `homelab` CLI, so nothing else is needed. What each contains: [Releasing](docs/Releasing.md#each-platforms-build). Building it yourself: [app/README.md](https://github.com/Snooper42/homelab-wizard/blob/main/app/README.md). Prefer the command line? The same homelab from git, shown here on a Mac (on Linux, install Docker and Go from your package manager; on Windows, use `homelab.cmd`): 
brew install --cask orbstack     # then OrbStack › Settings › Start at login
brew install go                  # ./homelab builds itself on first run
git clone https://github.com/Snooper42/homelab-wizard.git ~/Homelab
cd ~/Homelab
./homelab doctor                 # checks the machine, the runtime, and the settings
./homelab up                     # makes .env with generated passwords, starts the essentials
./homelab setup                  # the same checklist as the app's Setup screen
The [runbook](docs/Runbooks.md#first-time-bring-up) has every setup step as commands.

docs.title: What it replaces
docs.text:
A small private cloud on a computer at home. It does the jobs you would otherwise pay monthly subscriptions for, but the apps run at home and the files stay yours.

When you want to… Open Instead of paying for Back up phone photos and find them by face, place, or thing Immich iCloud+ 2 TB Keep everyone's passwords Vaultwarden (with the Bitwarden apps) 1Password Families Scan and search receipts, letters, and paperwork Paperless-ngx Evernote See what each paycheck leaves after the bills, and your net worth Finances, a screen of Homelab Wizard itself a spreadsheet, or a budgeting app Sort and tag the music, films, shows, books, and audiobooks you download, and free the space they waste Tidy Up, a screen of Homelab Wizard itself a music tagger, a file-renaming app Plan the budget, and track investments MoneyMatter or Actual Budget, Ghostfolio YNAB, a portfolio tracker Watch your movies and shows Jellyfin Netflix and others, for what you own Listen to your music, audiobooks, and podcasts Navidrome, Audiobookshelf Spotify Family, Audible Recipes, groceries, chores, and to-dos Mealie, Grocy, Vikunja Plan to Eat, a list app, Todoist Run the lights, locks, sensors, and cameras Home Assistant, Frigate each device's own cloud app Reach everything while away, with ads blocked Tailscale, AdGuard Home a VPN, NextDNS

…and 60-odd more. The apps are free; Homelab Wizard is the part that sets them up, connects them, backs them up every night (and proves a restore works), updates them overnight with a one-click undo, restarts what hangs, alerts your phone, and gives each person in the household one sign-in. Used to the full, it can replace about $4,487 a year in subscriptions (what it saves).

docs.title: Everyday tasks
docs.text: Adding an app, opening one on a phone, fixing what's down, updating or undoing an update, backing up and testing a restore, adding a person, moving to a new computer: each one in the app and the same from a terminal, in Everyday tasks. Adding your own app, every command, and taking the homelab off a machine are there too.

docs.title: Questions
docs.text: Is it safe?  Nothing on the computer is opened to the internet. By default the apps answer only your own devices over Tailscale's private network. With an optional domain, the apps that work away from home go through a Cloudflare tunnel and past CrowdSec, which blocks known attackers. Passwords are stored encrypted, and backups are encrypted before they leave the house. The full review: [Security](docs/Security.md). Found a hole? Please report it privately: [SECURITY.md](SECURITY.md).   What if the computer breaks?  The nightly backup holds the settings, passwords, documents, databases, and photos, so everything can be rebuilt elsewhere: on a new machine, `./homelab rebuild ` brings the homelab back from the backups alone, each app on the version that wrote its data. Backups › **Recovery kit** prints where the backups and passphrases are. Movies and music on the media drive are not backed up (too large) and can be obtained again. [Disaster Recovery](docs/Disaster%20Recovery.md) has each case.   Do I need a domain?  No. Every new homelab starts in Home mode: each app gets an `https://` address on your tailnet, at home and away. A domain adds short names (`photos.example.com`) and lets chosen apps open without Tailscale; add one any time ([Getting Started](docs/Getting%20Started.md#later-a-domain-of-your-own)).   Will it fit on my computer?  The install plan adds up the memory the apps you picked need and warns before they would not fit beside the system and everyday apps. On 8 GB, the *Start here* picks fit; Immich's face and smart search is the one to add with care.   How does it stay up to date?  The app looks for updates every 15 minutes and when its window comes forward. A line at the top of the window then says *Homelab Wizard … is ready*: **What's new** shows the patch notes, **Update now** puts the homelab files and the new app in place and opens it again, keeping your settings, data, and own apps (`./homelab upgrade` in a terminal). The apps themselves update overnight, each with a fresh database dump first; an update that leaves an app unwell is rolled back by itself. [Upgrading](docs/Upgrading.md) says what each version asks of you, if anything.   Does anything leave the house?  From Homelab Wizard itself: the backups (encrypted, to the place you pick), the outside heartbeat if you set one up, and what it asks GitHub (homelab and app updates, and the release notes of the apps you run). **Explain this** uses the Ollama on this computer. The apps do what they always do online (image downloads, film and book details, CrowdSec's community blocklist), and Tailscale's coordination server knows your devices; your files, photos, and passwords stay home.   I already run some of these apps in Docker.  `./homelab detect` finds them, and `./homelab adopt ` (Status › **Move in**) moves each into the homelab with its data; `./homelab cleanup` removes the old containers once all is well ([Commands](docs/Commands.md)).   Which systems are proven?  It runs a real household on a Mac. Windows, Linux, and SteamOS are built, tested in CI every night, and being tried on real machines: [Host › The same on every system](docs/Host.md#the-same-on-every-system) shows what each system has shown so far, and [Known Issues](docs/Known%20Issues.md) what is open.

| Optional: `./homelab install home-assistant` | https://home.example.com | Homey Premium | | [Grocy](services/household/Grocy.md) | Groceries and household stock, chores, and shared to-dos | Optional: `./homelab install grocy` | https://grocy.example.com | AnyList Complete (household) | | [Homebox](services/household/Homebox.md) | What you own, where it is, and its receipts, serial numbers, and warranties | Optional: `./homelab install homebox` | https://inventory.example.com | | | [Tandoor](services/household/Tandoor.md) | Recipes with meal planning, shopping lists, and nutrition | Optional: `./homelab install tandoor` | https://recipes.example.com | Plan to Eat | 72 apps: 16 baseline (started by `./homelab up`), 54 optional, 2 native. Databases and caches that apps need start with them and are not listed.

docs.title: Getting help
docs.text: Fix it on Status (or ./homelab fix) puts right what usually goes wrong. Otherwise see Troubleshooting and Known Issues, then make a diagnostics report (Settings › This Mac › Make a diagnostics report, or ./homelab report; passwords and tokens are removed), read it, and attach it to a bug report. Never paste .env, a token, or a password. A security problem goes privately instead (SECURITY.md).

docs.title: Documentation
docs.text:
If you want to… Read Set it up, step by step, without code Getting Started Fix something Troubleshooting, Known Issues Run it day to day Everyday tasks, Runbooks, Backups, Monitoring, Automation, Tidy Up Recover from a lost machine, or move to a new one Disaster Recovery Look up an app, an address, or a setting Services, Inventory, Environment, Commands Understand how it works Architecture, Networking, Security, Storage, Host See what works on a phone, an iPhone, or an iPad What each device can do, apple-client Try a new build on a real machine Testing, Upgrading Change the code or add an app CONTRIBUTING, Contributing (services), Maintainer Guide, Decisions

Everything else is in the knowledge base index.

docs.title: Development
docs.text: make check before every commit (make help lists the rest); CONTRIBUTING says what to run for each kind of change. Patch notes: CHANGELOG. What comes next: Roadmap.

docs.title: License
docs.text: MIT. Each app the homelab runs keeps its own license.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
What changed in each version of Homelab Wizard, newest first. Each version's notes are also its release notes on GitHub, and what the app shows before an update.

Notes are grouped as New, Improved, and Fixed, one line each, in plain words. The pull requests behind a version hold the details. Versions before 0.9.0-beta were tagged afterwards, at the commit where each one ended.

docs.title: New
docs.text:
• Lock After in the Homelab app: back within 5 minutes (or 1 or 15, or Right Away, under Settings › This iPhone), the app opens as you left it, Finances' amounts shown or hidden included, without Face ID. Locking the screen still locks it, and a change still asks for Face ID first.
  • Finances reminders for private Finances: the Homelab can't read a household member's private Finances, so the Homelab app on her phone reminds her itself: a bill due tomorrow, a paycheck that leaves checking under her cushion, a yearly renewal, balances not updated for weeks, worked out on her phone with the computer's own code each time she opens them, and planned two weeks ahead.
  • Private Finances offline in the Homelab app: with no signal, or away from home, a household member's iPhone or iPad still opens her private Finances with Face ID, her passphrase or her recovery code, from the locked copy it keeps (only ever locked). A change she makes waits on the device, said in one line, and goes to the Homelab by itself once it answers; if another of her devices changed them meanwhile, the app says so plainly and shows the newest.
  • Private Finances open in the Homelab app: on a household member's iPhone or iPad, Make Them Private… under her Finances (her 16-word recovery code shown once, two of its words typed back, then a passphrase), or on her phone's page; once they're private, Finances shows them locked, and Open with Face ID, her passphrase or her recovery code opens them, on her phone only: they're read forward there with the computer's own Finances code, and saved locked again. After she opens them once with her passphrase or code, Face ID opens them on that device (its key kept in the Keychain behind Face ID, never synced). Lock, leaving Finances, or 5 minutes untouched closes them; what the household shares shows either way. Turn Privacy Off… keeps them plain on the Homelab again.
  • Private Finances offline, on a member's phone page: with no connection (away from home), her phone still opens her private Finances with Face ID or her recovery code, from the locked copy it keeps (only ever locked). A change she makes waits on the phone, said in one line, and goes to the homelab by itself when it answers; if another of her devices changed them meanwhile, the page says so plainly and shows the newest.
  • A household member's phone page shows what the household shares: a read-only Household card under her own Finances (the bills coming up, the subscriptions, this month's budgets), as the Homelab app has, and still there while her private Finances are locked. Turn privacy off… (once she confirms) keeps her Finances plain on the homelab again, receipts included.
  • Private Finances on a household member's phone: on her phone's page, Finances offers Make them private…. Her recovery code is shown once (16 words; she types two back), then Face ID (or a passphrase, where the phone's passkeys can't do it) locks them. From then on the homelab keeps them without being able to open them, the person who runs it included: her phone opens them, reads them forward with the computer's own Finances code, and saves them locked again. Lock (or leaving Finances, or 5 minutes untouched) closes them; Face ID, her passphrase or her recovery code opens them again. The page says its one limit: it comes from the homelab computer, so the Homelab app on her iPhone (next) is the stronger place for them.
  • Finances offline in the Homelab app: with no signal, or away from home, Face ID opens the last Finances your iPhone or iPad read, marked As of when, to look at. Changes wait until the Homelab answers, and then the newest Finances are read by themselves. They're kept locked with a key only that device holds, and go if the phone is unpaired or Finances are taken from it.
  • Add cards from the iPhone and iPad: in the Homelab app, Finances › Collection has Add a Card (and a card's page Edit): its name, set and number, its condition or grade, how many, what one cost and when, what one is worth now and Keep This Price, and a photo of your own, taken with Take a Photo or picked from Photos, shrunk and sent without its location; Remove Card takes it out. Each save asks for Face ID, on a phone allowed to change Finances.
  • The Collection in the Homelab app: on the iPhone and iPad, Finances has Collection: what your cards are worth and the gain on what you paid, each card with its picture (read from the computer), and a card's page with its price over time. Update Prices (on a phone allowed to change Finances, after Face ID) has the computer read the prices from TCGdex. Cards are added on the computer.
  • Update prices for your cards: in Finances › Net worth › Collection, Update prices reads each card's TCGplayer market price from TCGdex, a free card database, and, for a card with no picture yet, its picture, kept on the computer. Only a card's name is sent to find it (then the id TCGdex gives it), never what you paid, how many or anything else of Finances, and only when you press it. A card is matched by its number and set; it says which it couldn't find or couldn't tell apart. A card kept at your own price is never looked up. Each card's page draws its price over time.
  • Your own photo of a card: in a card's form in Finances › Net worth › Collection, Use my own photo takes a picture from your files (or the phone's camera on the phone's page), made small on that device, and the computer keeps it with the card: it shows in the list and large on the card's own page. The pictures are in data/finance-cards/, in the nightly backup; one no card uses any more goes after a day.
  • Your card collection in Finances: Finances › Net worth › Collection lists your cards (made for Pokémon cards, as the mockup drew it): what the collection is worth now, the gain on what you paid and a chart over time, then each card with its set and number, condition, what you paid, what it's worth and its gain. Add a card keeps them in their own Pokémon cards account, so they count in your net worth; a card opens its own page, large. Prices are the ones you type for now: Update prices, with each card's picture, comes next. The phone's page shows it too.
  • Send to my phone and Open on the Computer, in the Homelab app: a page the computer sends your iPhone or iPad shows at the bottom as From the Computer: Radarr with Open. On an app's More About page, Open on the Computer puts the computer's window on that app's page, from a phone allowed to change things (no Face ID, since it changes no data); the computer's window comes forward on it.
  • Send to my phone: right-click an app on Status, pick Send to my phone › and then one of your paired phones, and the page your phone's browser opens shows From the computer: Radarr at the bottom with Open. ⌘K sends the page you're on (Send Finances › Recurring to Sam's iPhone). A wall screen is never offered, Finances goes only to a phone allowed to see them, and a household member's phone only gets Status and their own apps. The Homelab app on the iPhone gets it next.
  • Transactions in columns: on a wide screen, Finances › Spending › Transactions lines each row up in columns (payee, category, account, amount) under a header you click to sort by: the date (newest or oldest first), payee, category or account (A to Z), or amount (most out first, click again for most in). Each device keeps its sort. A narrow window and the phone keep the list as before.
  • The Dashboard looks back: Finances' Dashboard has Checking, last 90 days: what checking held at the end of each day, from the balance you typed in through its transactions, as the account's own page draws it. Pick 30 days or a year, or another account; click a day to open it on the calendar, or the title for the account's page. On the phone's page too.
  • Arrange the Dashboard: on Finances' Dashboard, Arrange the Dashboard lets you move each card (drag its handle, or ▲ ▼), give it a third, half or the whole row, and hide the ones you don't use (they wait below to come back). Reset to the usual puts it back. Each computer keeps its own arrangement; the phone's page stacks its cards as before.
  • A loan's page on the iPhone and iPad: in the Homelab app, a loan's page says what it costs each month, the months left and when it's paid off, and lists the payments linked to it. Link a Payment links one, the same payee's next ones are offered with Link and Not This One, and one that paid more than the plan's payment asks whether to count all of it. Each asks Face ID first.
  • The Watchlist on the iPhone and iPad: the Homelab app's Investments page lists the tickers you follow, with their price and how much they've moved since you followed them; Follow a Ticker looks one up and follows it (after Face ID), and its menu unfollows it. The bar of each holding's share is gone there too.
  • A Watchlist in Investments: follow a ticker you don't own (Follow a ticker under your holdings), and it's listed with its price, a line of it, and how much it's moved since you followed it. Ghostfolio prices it each time it reads your investments. It never counts in your worth. Unfollow takes it off.
  • An account's page on the iPhone and iPad: in the Homelab app, tapping an account on Finances' Accounts page opens its page: what it holds (or owes) today, a chart of it over the last 30 or 90 days or a year, and its latest transactions, with Update Balance at the top. It typed the balance in before.
  • A loan's page, with the payments that pay it: a loan's page in Finances › Net worth says what it costs each month (and the whole payment, when only your share is in the plan), how many months are left and when it's paid off. Under it, Payments linked to this loan: link one with Link a payment… (a transfer to the person you share a mortgage with, say), and the same payee's next ones are offered to link by themselves. One that paid more than the plan's payment asks whether to count all of it.
  • Each account has its own page: in Finances › Net worth, clicking an account opens its page instead of the form to update it: what it holds (or owes) today with a chart over the last 30 or 90 days or a year, what came in and went out this month, and its latest transactions, with All of them in Transactions. Update balance and Edit are buttons there. The same on the phone's page.
  • Settings on the phone's page: the page your phone opens in a browser now has Settings too, as the Homelab app does: the settings a phone may change (never a password or token, nor what the phone connects through), saved from a phone allowed to make changes, and what the computer runs. A phone that only looks reads them; a wall screen doesn't show them.
  • Snooze from Every alert: an alert whose problem is still there now has Snooze… in Every alert, on the computer, the phone's page and the Homelab app, as the Watchdog card has: no alerts about it for an hour or a day, while the watchdog goes on checking. Phones snooze only where they're allowed changes.
  • What was done and Every Alert on the iPad and the Mac: in the iPad's and the Mac app's Homelab, an app's More About now opens beside the list, with Recently Done and Everything That Was Done, and Every Alert under Recent Alerts opens in the app's place until you pick an app again.
  • Links into the app on the iPad and the Mac: a homelab:// link, and with it a button on an alert (Restart, Show Logs, Start), now opens the iPad's and the Mac app's Homelab where it points, as it does on the iPhone: the screen it names in the sidebar, or the app's page beside the list with the action waiting for your tap. Siri's and Shortcuts' Open an App's Page, Restart and the rest do the same there. A link still never changes anything by itself.
  • The Dashboard by month: By month on the bar at the top of Finances' Dashboard steps through calendar months instead of paychecks. A month before this one shows what happened, from your transactions; this month shows what happened so far and what's still to come; a month ahead shows the plan: its paychecks and payments, what comes in and goes out, and checking at its end. Each device remembers which you picked.
  • Look back at a paycheck: on Finances' Dashboard, ‹ in the bar at the top now steps back before today, to the paychecks of the last half year. For each, What happened says what came in and went out, from your transactions (money moved between your own accounts counts as neither), and lists them, and Where it went shows that paycheck's spending by category.
  • Alerts from the Homelab app: Settings › Alerts From on the iPhone picks who notifies that phone: the ntfy app, as before, or the Homelab app, which shows new alerts as its own notifications while it's open. Each phone picks for itself. A locked phone still hears only from the ntfy app until the paid Apple program, so turn the ntfy app's notifications off only if you keep the Homelab app open.
  • Every alert on the iPhone: in the Homelab app, Every Alert under Recent Alerts lists the alerts your computer kept over the last 90 days, each with when its problem cleared or which phone snoozed it, until when.
  • Every alert, kept: the alerts the homelab sends are now kept on your computer for 90 days, not just the 12 hours the ntfy app holds them. Every alert… on Status's Recent alerts card lists them, on the computer and the phone's page, each with when its problem cleared (Cleared at 3:12 AM) or which phone snoozed it, until when. It keeps them whether or not phone alerts are set up. Finances' reminders and the weekly summary are kept only as a plain line, never with an amount.
  • Rules in Finances: fix a transaction once and tick Always do this for “…”: its new name and category go to its other transactions (the category only where they had none), and every import from then on brings that payee in the same way, before anything is guessed. Rules beside Import a file lists them, and Remove takes one away. They're kept in your plan, on your computer.
  • Back and Forward between screens: like a browser, the app now remembers where you've been. ⌘[ and ⌘] (Alt+← and Alt+→ on Windows and Linux), your mouse's back and forward buttons, or a two-finger swipe on a trackpad (right for Back, left for Forward) go back to the screen before, an app's page with its app, and forward again. A swipe over something that scrolls sideways (a wide table) scrolls it instead.
  • Status folds the same on the iPhone too: the Homelab app now shows the groups folded as the computer keeps them, and a group you fold or open on the phone (one allowed changes) folds or opens on the computer and the other phones.
  • Status folds the same everywhere: the groups you open or fold on Status (Media, Photos, Security…) are now kept by the computer, so the app and the phone's page show them the same way. Show every app stays each device's own, and Fold them again puts every device back to the usual (groups with a problem open, the rest folded). A phone that can only look keeps its own folds.
  • Home only: each app that can be on the internet (Paperless, Vaultwarden, Immich and the like) has Reach it away from home on its page, on the computer and in the iPhone app, once your domain has the Cloudflare tunnel. Off keeps it home only: it opens on your home Wi-Fi, and nobody outside can reach it, because its address comes off the tunnel and Cloudflare's DNS (only what the homelab put there; anything you added yourself stays). homelab away off paperless does the same. Apps you install from now on start home only; the ones you already have stay as they were.
  • What was done, on the iPhone: an app's More About page shows what was done to it lately, and Everything That Was Done searches the last 90 days, as on the computer.
  • Recently done, on each app's page: the last few things done to it (Restarted Vikunja, 2 hours ago, by the watchdog), and Everything that was done…, the last 90 days for every app, searchable by app, phone or word.
  • A record of what was done: every start, stop, restart, update, roll back and removal, the watchdog's restarts, settings saved and Finances changed are kept for 90 days, with who did it (this computer, which phone, the watchdog or the nightly update). homelab history lists them, --app immich or --search narrows them; the app and the iPhone show them next. It never keeps a setting's value or an amount of money.
  • The download apps rest when nothing is on the way: Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr, Prowlarr, Bazarr, FlareSolverr, qBittorrent and its VPN tunnel used to sit in memory all day. Now, with nothing downloading, queued or requested for 15 minutes, Tidy Up stops them, and starts them every 12 hours to look for new releases, at once when you request something in Seerr, and whenever Tidy Up needs them. A torrent still seeding keeps qBittorrent up. One you start yourself stays up until the next 12-hour wake. TIDY_ARR_REST=false in Settings keeps them running.
  • Buttons on alerts: an app down now reaches your phone with Restart and Show Logs (or Open Status when it's more than one), and an app stopped for restarting over and over with Show Logs and Start. A tap in the ntfy app opens the iPhone app on that app's page, where the action waits for your tap and Face ID: the button never changes anything by itself.
  • Links into the iPhone app: homelab://app/radarr opens Radarr's page, homelab://finances/budgets opens Budgets, and homelab://app/radarr?do=restart opens Radarr's page with Restart waiting for your tap. A link never changes anything by itself. They're for the buttons on alerts, coming next.
  • Away mode on the iPhone: when neither home nor the tunnel answers, the app no longer just says it can't reach the computer: it lists your apps that are on the internet (Immich, say), as it last saw them, each with whether it answers and a tap to open it.
  • The iPhone app away from home: once the computer is set up for it and the phone is paired again at home, the Homelab app shows Status, your apps, and the Finances it may see on cellular too, through your Cloudflare tunnel, sealed so that even Cloudflare can't read it. At home it goes straight to the computer as before. Away, it only looks: changes wait until you're home.
  • Reach Finances away from home: a Setup step that puts Cloudflare Access in front of the phone companion's own address (homelab-away.<your domain>), letting in only your household's phones, and publishes it through your tunnel, all with the Cloudflare token you already have (given two more permissions). Phones paired at home afterwards get what they need to reach it; the iPhone app's part comes next.
  • The iPhone app away from home, the computer's part: the phone companion can now answer the iPhone app through the Cloudflare tunnel, for looking only (Status, your apps, Finances it may see), behind Cloudflare Access's service token, Cloudflare's signed pass, the phone's own pairing, and a key the phone and the computer agree at home, so even Cloudflare can't read what passes. Nothing changes until Setup's Reach Finances away from home turns it on (next), and the iPhone app learns to use it after that.
  • Tdarr rests while it has nothing to do: Tdarr, which shrinks films and episodes, used to sit in memory all day. Now, with no video to shrink and nothing done for 15 minutes, Tidy Up stops it, and starts it again by itself when it has one (Shrink, a big download to file). The watchdog and the battery saver leave it resting; one you start yourself stays up until Tidy Up next uses it. TIDY_TDARR_REST=false in Settings keeps it running.
  • Packed downloads say so: a .rar or .7z dropped in a watched folder (or a download that's only .rar parts) no longer sits there unexplained: Needs a look lists it, says it's packed, and that what's inside is filed once you open it. Leave it stops it asking.
  • Look a film or show up: in the Inbox's Needs a look, It's a film… and It's an episode… now have Look it up: Radarr, Sonarr, or Jellyfin find what you typed, with its year, so you pick The Big Lebowski (1998) instead of typing the year. You can still type it yourself.
  • Name these songs: songs that don't say which artist or album they are no longer get filed into a folder with no name: they wait in the Inbox's Needs a look (with AcoustID set up, only the ones beets can't recognise by their sound). Name these songs… asks the album, and the artist if you know it, looks it up on MusicBrainz (Rumours · Fleetwood Mac · 1977 · 11 songs · Vinyl, US), and once you pick the one they are, writes its names onto them and files them in Music. Songs that don't fit the album you picked (a different count, or lengths far from its songs) stay, saying why.
  • Where should your libraries live?: the first time, Tidy Up shows your computer's disk and each drive plugged in, with its space and the libraries already on it, and where each library would go. Pick one (or another folder, such as a NAS), and Tidy Up keeps it and restarts the apps that read your libraries, after listing them. Nothing is moved or copied. Change where your libraries live… on the Inbox opens it again.
  • A loan read from its papers: give a loan the day its first payment was due and each payment (and, if you like, how many there are and the finance charge) and Finances works out what it owes each day, taking each payment off the day after it's due, with no balance to type. Its card on Net worth shows a ring of the payments made (3 of 36), what's paid down of what you borrowed, the next payment split into what pays it down and its interest, who pays it each month, when it's half and wholly paid off, and every payment in a table. With the finance charge, the first payment carries the days before it, so the 36 come to your papers to the cent.
  • Your last six months on Cash flow: under the Dashboard's typical month, a bar of money in beside money out for each of the last six months your transactions cover; pick a month for its transactions.
  • Spent this month on the Dashboard: beside your latest transactions, a ring of what your transactions spent since the 1st by category, largest first; pick a category for this month's transactions of it.
  • Latest transactions on the Dashboard: Finances' Dashboard lists your five newest transactions, each opening its own form, with See all for Transactions.
  • What a bill was paid lately: open a payment on Finances and its form lists its last few from your transactions, each with how much more or less it was than planned, and their average when they differ (Paid lately, $141.17 on average). An account's form likewise lists its balances lately, each with how it moved.
  • A running balance: pick one account on Finances › Transactions and each day says what it held after (or, for a card, what it owed), worked from the balance you last typed in through the transactions in and out of it.
  • Add on a calendar day: the day you pick on Finances › Calendar has Add a payment (a day ahead) or Add a transaction (today or before), its form starting on that day. T takes the calendar back to today.
  • A month in all, on the calendar: beside the day you pick, Finances › Calendar sums up the month shown: what its paychecks bring, what its bills take, the lowest checking gets and on which day (said when it's under your cushion), and what your transactions recorded so far. On a narrow window it comes first.
  • What happened, on the calendar: Finances › Calendar now shows the days before today too, each with its payees' logos and what it came to from your transactions; pick a day for the list, each opening its transaction, and go back a month for what it came to, as far back as your transactions go.
  • Needs a look: a download Tidy Up couldn't place (a video whose name says nothing, say) waits on the Inbox with why, instead of sitting in Downloads unexplained. Tell it It's a film… or It's an episode… and type the name: Tidy Up renames it and files it. Leave it stops it asking, and Show in Finder opens the folder. Something you put back with Undo shows here too.
  • What I did today: Tidy Up's Inbox lists each download it filed today in plain words, like Heat (1995) · Movies › Heat (1995) · too big, so Tdarr is shrinking it first or 12 songs, tags cleaned · lyrics added where found, newest first. Undo on one puts its files back where they came from, and Tidy Up leaves them there.
  • Drop anything here: Tidy Up opens on its new Inbox: the folders it watches for music, films, shows, books and audiobooks (Downloads to start; Add… a folder on your external drive too), when it tidies them (As things arrive, Once a day, 3 AM, or Only when I press it), and one Tidy up now button. A watched folder on a drive that's unplugged says so.
  • Add an account from the iPhone: Finances › Accounts › + adds one (its name, its kind, and what's in it or owed today), and a plan with none yet opens on Add an Account, so a household member can start their own Finances from their phone.
  • The iPhone app on a household member's phone: on a phone the computer gave to someone in the household (homelab phone person), Status shows only their apps, Finances is theirs ("My Finances"), with a Household card for the bills, subscriptions and budgets you share with them, to look at, and Settings is just their phone. Backups and Setup stay yours.
  • Month in Review on the iPhone: Finances › Month in Review tells each month back, one page each (swipe for the ones before): what you spent and how that compares with the month before, where it went, what came in and what was left, what grew and what shrank the most, and the biggest purchase.
  • Cash Flow on the iPhone: Finances › Cash Flow shows money in against money out for the last six months, as bars side by side, and what was left over each month. Tap a month for its figures.
  • Recurring as a calendar, and filters for Transactions: Recurring opens with this month as a calendar, a dot on each day a bill, subscription or paycheck lands; tap a day for what comes then. Transactions has a Filter menu: money in or out, one category, or only $100 or more.
  • Siri, Shortcuts and the Action button on the iPhone: "Is everything running in Homelab?" answers from the widget's line (how many apps need a look, never their names, and only once the iPhone is unlocked). "Restart an app in Homelab", or Start or Stop, opens Homelab at that app's page and asks as its button would: Face ID first, and Stop asks before it stops. "Open an app in Homelab" opens its page. With the widget built, it can also go on the Lock Screen: a tick or the count in a circle, or a line or two.
  • A phone for each person in the household: homelab phone person <phone> anna makes it Anna's. It shows only the apps she uses, starts or stops none, and its Finances are her own, kept apart from the household's, so she can keep her own money private. homelab person share anna bills,subscriptions,budgets lets her phone show those of the household's, to look at: names, amounts and days, never an account, a balance or a transaction. Nothing else of the homelab answers her phone.
  • Make a Calibre library from your books: when your books folder holds books (each in a folder of its own, as Calibre exports them) but no Calibre library, Tidy Up › Books offers Make a Calibre library…. It asks first, moves the books' folders aside on the same drive, has Calibre add each one with the title, author, series and cover beside it, and checks every book came in. The copy aside stays until you've looked. After it, the book review and Calibre-Web can read your books.
  • Spending on the iPhone: Finances › Spending shows a month's spending by category as a ring, with how it compares with the month before, the last six months as bars (tap one to see that month), and each category with its bar against its budget; a category opens its transactions. Money moved between your own accounts and money coming in aren't counted, and a refund counts against its category.
  • To Review on the iPhone: the transactions new since you looked, as an inbox: swipe right when one's right, or left to pick its category from buttons (it's marked reviewed either way). Finances' home links to it when there are new ones.
  • Recurring on the iPhone: Finances › Recurring lists every payment that repeats, with its logo, how often it comes, when next and what it costs, under about what your bills and subscriptions cost a month; money coming in, card payments and savings each have their own group. Tap one to change what it costs.
  • Put a buy right, or delete it: on Net worth's Investments card, open a holding to see its buys and sales as Ghostfolio keeps them. Change fixes the shares, what you paid, the day, or bought or sold; Delete (asked first) takes it out of Ghostfolio. The card reads Ghostfolio again after each, so its figures follow. A phone allowed to change Finances can do the same.
  • Investments' total adds up: the Total value on Net worth's Investments card is now what its rows add up to (each holding and the account's cash). Before, it took Ghostfolio's own figure for each account, which can lag a buy just put in, so a second holding was missing from the total.
  • Real logos from each company's website: Finances › Transactions › Logos lists every payee and account still showing initials, with its website guessed (fpl.com, fidelity.com); Get them all fetches each company's own icon from its site, shown before you save. A payee's, account's, or payment's logo picker has Get the real logo too. Your computer asks only the websites you click for, only then, and the logos are kept only in your plan.
  • Homelab on your iPhone, iPad and Mac: a native app, laid out as Homelab Wizard is: Status, Backups, Finances, Setup and Settings, each app with its logo, locked with Face ID or Touch ID. It pairs as the phone page does, and a phone allowed to make changes can change the everyday settings too; passwords, tokens and the settings a phone connects through stay on the computer. From a Mac with Xcode, apple-client/scripts/run-on-iphone.sh puts it on a plugged-in iPhone (apple-client/README.md).
  • Add investments from Finances: Add a holding on Net worth's Investments card records a buy or a sale without opening Ghostfolio. Pick the account (or make a new one, named the same in both), type a ticker or a name and pick it from what Ghostfolio finds, then the shares, what you paid, and the day. It goes into Ghostfolio on your homelab and the card reads it back. Only the ticker leaves the homelab, when Ghostfolio looks it up.
  • Investments from the iPhone app: a phone allowed to change Finances can now ask the computer to read Ghostfolio now, look up a ticker, and record a buy or a sale, just as the card on the computer does (over the secure link only). The iPhone app's screens for them come next.
  • Select transactions together: Finances › Transactions › Select picks rows with a click (Shift+click for a range), or every one shown with Select all (filter to an account or a month first to take a whole import), then Delete them, give them one category, or Move to… another account, for a file brought into the wrong one. Ctrl+A (⌘A on a Mac) selects every one shown, and Escape stops selecting. Undo (or ⌘Z) puts back what was deleted, moved or recategorized while its note shows.
  • Investments: Finances › Net worth has an Investments card that reads what each investment and retirement account holds from Ghostfolio, the investment tracker on your homelab: each fund and share, what you paid, what it's worth now, and the gain, with the total, the gain, and this month's change on top. Click a holding to see its worth at each read. Read now reads it again; after that, it reads once a day when Finances opens (a box turns that off). Only ticker symbols leave the homelab, when Ghostfolio looks prices up.
  • Money flow you can click: the Dashboard shows where a month's money came from and went: your pay and money in, through all of it, to taxes, each kind of spending, and each savings account (the rest kept as cash), with income, taxes, expenses and saved above it as shares of your income. ‹ › step through the months your transactions cover and a typical month from the plan, and Top 8 keeps the largest of each. Click any box to see the transactions or payments behind it.
  • A bill that changes, by its average: a bill marked as changing each time (electric, water), paid three times or more in six months, asks on the Dashboard when its average is off the plan: Electric has averaged $152.00 over 3 months, with Use $152.00 or Keep $140.00.
  • A bill not seen yet: a bill your transactions have paid before, with nothing for it three days after its day, is said on the Dashboard (Electric, due Oct 18, 12 days ago), so one that didn't go through is caught.
  • A subscription's new price: when a subscription is charged the same new amount twice in a row, the Dashboard asks: Netflix is now $17.99, was $15.49, with Update to $17.99 or Keep $15.49.
  • Money that comes in from someone: a payment can now come in, not only go out: Add a payment › Comes in from someone, say who sends it (a share of the mortgage, say), how much and when. It adds to checking on its day, without starting a pay period, and shows in the pay period, Recurring, the calendar, a typical month and the calendar feed. Their real transfer, in a bank's file, is linked to it.
  • Checking now, and after payday: Finances' Dashboard opens with two numbers: checking now, and checking once the next paycheck lands, before that day's bills. Rest on either (or tap it on a phone) to see how it adds up: the balance it starts from, each bill and paycheck in between, and the result, to hold next to your own sums.
  • Health in one line: every screen but Status now starts with one line: ✓ All well, or the one thing that needs you (Mealie: Stopped, 3 apps need a look: …, or a failing check of the watchdog's), with Open Status beside it.
  • Snooze an alert: beside a failing check on Status's Watchdog card, Snooze… stops its alerts for an hour or a day, for something you already know about. It's still checked and shown, its line says until when, and if it still fails when the snooze ends you get one alert then. homelab notify snooze <check> 1h does the same.
  • Devices on your tailnet: Settings › Phones lists every phone and computer that can reach the apps away from home, with whether it's online or when it was last seen. One not seen for a month is marked, in case it's lost, and Remove… opens it in Tailscale's admin console, where a device is removed.
  • Weekly integrity check: every Sunday morning, each off-site backup is checked with Duplicati's own Verify: a sample of its files where they are kept is downloaded and compared with what Duplicati recorded. If one is damaged, so that a version might not restore, the watchdog alerts, Status lists it, and Backups shows it in red beside the job until a check passes. Each job's hover on Backups says when it was last checked. homelab backup-check runs the check at any time.
  • Memory pressure alert: when the apps use 90% or more of the memory Docker has on two checks in a row (10 minutes or more), you get one alert, Homelab: memory nearly full, naming the three biggest apps and how much each uses. Status's Watchdog card lists them with Stop on each until memory comes down, and a second alert says when it has.
  • An update window per app: an app's page has Only on Sundays under Nightly updates, for an app you would rather not see change midweek; the other nights leave it alone. homelab updates days immich sat+sun picks any days.
  • Phones that expire: beside a phone in Settings › Phones, For a day, For a week, or For a month ends its changes and Finances then, and it only looks; its row says until when. For a guest's phone, or one lent for a while (homelab phone until <phone> 7d).
  • The last Status, offline: away from home with Tailscale off, the phone opens on the last Status it saw, with a line saying when (This is Status as it was at 7:42 AM), rather than an error. It needs the phone's address to be HTTPS (the domain, or the tailnet's).
  • A sheet of shortcuts: press ? on any screen, or pick Keyboard shortcuts in the command palette, for that screen's own shortcuts first (typing to filter Status, the calendar's keys on Finances), then those that work everywhere and each screen's key, as this computer writes them.
  • Quick actions on the phone: on a phone that may make changes, hold an app's row on Status for its menu: Open, Start, Restart, Stop, Stop for a while, and Logs. A phone that only looks, and a wall screen, have none.
  • A sheet for the fridge: each person's welcome page links to their apps on one printed page, each with its address, its phone app, and a code the phone's camera opens; the sheet never has their sign-in link or a password.
  • Suggestions from what you use: Choose stacks › Add more opens on the apps that go with ones you run, each with what it brings them: Beets with Navidrome, Bazarr and Prowlarr with Sonarr and Radarr, Paperless-AI with Paperless-ngx, Seerr and Tdarr with Jellyfin.
  • Quiet hours: from 10 PM to 7 AM alerts reach the phone without a sound, unless they are serious: the password vault not answering, or backups failing two nights running. Settings › Quiet hours picks other hours, or off.
  • Two apps that do the same job: Choose stacks says when you already run one that does it (Komga and Kavita, Mealie and Tandoor, Navidrome and Jellyfin's music), and why you might keep one or both.
  • What the apps have saved so far: on Status, hover (or Tab to) the figure under Replaces a year for what they have saved since the first nightly record, and month by month.
  • What changed since last night: on Backups, each app's copy shows the night before's size on hover, and beside it when it moved by a tenth; a copy less than half the night before's is marked in red, so an app that lost its data is noticed before the old copies age out.
  • What CrowdSec stopped: the proxy's page (and CrowdSec's) lists every address stopped since midnight, with where it came from, what it tried, the time, and whether it's still banned.
  • What happened overnight: in the morning, Status's first line sums up the night since 8 PM: Overnight: 4 apps updated, 1 rolled back, a backup of 2.1 GB, nothing needed you, or which app was down. Hide until tomorrow puts it away for the day.
  • A restart that keeps failing: an app Docker restarted 3 times within an hour is stopped instead of restarting forever, and the alert carries its last log lines. Its row on Status says so with a red dot until you start it again.
  • An update's notes: hover updates held on Status for why the app is held, how to put it back, and the first lines of its newest release, read from GitHub only when you look.
  • A backup's contents: on Backups, hover an off-site job's time (or Tab to it) for its last run and how long it took, what it holds of yours and in how many files, its size where it is kept and the versions to go back to, the folders it copies, and its next run.
  • Remember where you were: each screen keeps how far down you were and which of its sections were open, between visits and after quitting. Picking another screen opens it at its own place, no longer partway down where the last one was.
  • What changed since you looked: each app on Status that restarted, updated, stopped, or started since you were last there has a dot beside its name saying which, until you leave Status again.
  • Open, your way: on Status, Alt-click (⌥-click on a Mac) an app's address to copy it, and Shift-click (⇧-click) Open to use its address on this computer when the domain does not answer.
  • Pinned apps: right-click an app on Status and pick Pin to the top to keep the apps you open most in a Pinned group at the top, in the order you pinned them, and first in the menu bar's Open an app. homelab pin <app> does it from the Terminal.
  • Right-click the sidebar: a screen's own menu, without opening it first: Status's Check again and Update all; Backups' Back up now and Test a restore; Finances' Add a transaction, Update balances, and Hide amounts. Shift+F10 opens it from the keyboard.
  • Why an app restarted: hover up 9 minutes on Status for why it last started, and when: you, an update (yours or the nightly one), Fix it, the watchdog, the power coming back, its drive plugged in again, the end of a Stop for a while, or Docker after it stopped on its own.
  • A balance's accounts: rest the pointer on Cash, Investments, or another group in the sidebar for its accounts, each with its balance and how long since it was updated; one older than a month has a dot.
  • When an app was down this week: hover its 96.2% up this week on Status (or Tab to it, or tap it on a phone) for the week as a strip, with each time it was down, for how long, and why (Wed 3:15 AM, 45 minutes: nothing answers on its port).
  • Export your finances: Finances has Export: your whole plan as a JSON file to keep or take elsewhere, the year ahead as a spreadsheet (each payday and payment, with checking after each day), and this month or the next as a page that prints itself. Saved where you pick, readable only by you; on a phone, shared or downloaded, even one that may only look.
  • Tidy Up gets ffmpeg for you: without ffmpeg, Tidy Up's Overview has Install, with no Terminal and no password: it runs Homebrew (or winget on Windows) for you when it's there, and otherwise fetches ffmpeg for Tidy Up alone, checks it's exactly the build expected before it runs, and keeps it in its own folder. A scan that stopped for want of it offers Install ffmpeg, then carries on by itself. Calibre's row opens its download page, and coming back to the window checks again without a click.
  • Tidy Up: a screen for the libraries on the media drive. Music is matched, tagged into your 14 genres, and laid out as Artist/Album (Year)/01 Title on a hidden copy, swapped in with Navidrome paused and backed up, checked song by song, and only then is the old library put in the Trash. Books are reviewed in the app, before and after with their covers, each one yours to leave alone, then applied. Films and episodes in H.264, with lossless audio, or with other languages' tracks are shrunk through Tdarr to HEVC (or AV1), each checked before it replaces its original, its subtitles re-timed to the new copy. Audiobooks in dozens of MP3s become one .m4b each, with chapters and one cover. Every library's player is told about the one folder that changed, rather than scanning everything.
  • New downloads filed by themselves: whatever finishes downloading in Downloads (and the download apps' folder) is filed into its library a few minutes later: episodes and season packs, anime numbered from its first episode, films, albums, audiobooks, and loose books, .zip files unpacked first. A duplicate is kept only when it is the leaner copy, a bloated film goes through Tdarr before it is filed, and what a download leaves behind goes to the Trash. Sonarr, Radarr, and Lidarr can hand their renaming and importing over to it in one click.
  • Lyrics that scroll: time-synced lyrics from LRCLIB for every song, replacing plain ones when synced ones are found, instrumentals skipped; and a Navidrome smart playlist for each of your genres.
  • The nightly sweep: at 03:00, posters, .nfo and subtitle files whose film, episode, song, or book is gone, and empty folders, go to the Trash.
  • Tidy Up waits its turn: one job moves files at a time; while one does, the nightly update leaves the media apps for the next night and Duplicati waits, and the heavy jobs wait for power and pause when the laptop goes on battery. homelab media does it all from a terminal too, on a Mac, Windows (Docker Desktop, any drive letter), and Linux.
  • Type to find an app on Status: start typing an app's name anywhere on Status and the list keeps only the apps that have it, in a box beside the list that says how many; Return opens the first one's page, and Escape brings every app back.
  • Type a command: ⌘K (Ctrl+K on Windows and Linux) on any screen opens a box: type an app's name for its Open, page, Restart, Stop, or Logs, or stop media, back up now, update all, a screen, or hide amounts. The arrows pick and Return runs it; a stop asks for a second press, and Update all shows its list first, as their buttons do. On a Mac it is in View too.
  • Undo a stop: after Stop, Stop all, or Stop for a while, a note at the bottom of the window says what stopped ("Stopped 6 Media apps") with Undo, which starts them again. It stays 10 seconds, and longer while your pointer is on it; ⌘Z (Ctrl+Z on Windows and Linux) undoes too.

docs.title: Improved
docs.text:
• The Homelab app's buttons read clearly in dark mode: filled buttons (Back Up Now, Start, Unlock) keep the app's violet under their white words, and the lighter violet of links and bordered buttons (Test a Restore) is brighter, so each reads at 4.5:1 or more; light mode is unchanged.
  • Spending and Transactions in the Homelab app at larger text: Spending's legend shows names like Subscriptions whole, and its +$1,021 on Sep stays inside the ring; at the largest sizes Transactions puts 5 New under Latest Transactions instead of breaking the heading mid-word.
  • The Homelab app at the largest text sizes, and Setup's steps: Finances' big amounts (what's left, net worth, investments, bills a month) grow with the text as their titles do; Setup says Look for Problems lists what it would fix first, and nothing changes until Fix These under that list.
  • Transactions in the Homelab app: a transfer's line takes a second line when it needs one, so From Chase Checking · Oct 28 shows whole, and a transaction's Mark Reviewed shows its checkmark.
  • Status in the Homelab app, clearer: a group's menu says what it does (Start or Stop All, Start All or Restart or Stop All, by what the group's apps can do) instead of All of These; and at the largest text sizes, what needs a look puts Open Its Page under Start and Logs, so Start no longer breaks in two.
  • What's left comes first in the Homelab app's Finances: the first card reads Left until Nov 19, after the bills, what checking comes to once the next paycheck is in and its bills are paid, with Under your $500 cushion on Thu, Nov 5 when checking dips under it before then, and opens Bills. Checking after the paycheck now says it's before its bills.
  • Spending in the Homelab app says what its change is against: the month's ring reads +$1,021 on Sep, not a bare red +$1,021.
  • A transfer's line in the Homelab app's Transactions fits: it names the account the payee doesn't (From Main Checking under Roth IRA), instead of both accounts cut off after the first.
  • Times in the Homelab app in the phone's own clock: Settings shows quiet hours as 10 PM to 7 AM (not 22-7), and nightly updates as Every night at 4 AM (not Daily at 04:00), on the iPhone and iPad, in 12- or 24-hour time as the phone is set.
  • Add a payment by keyboard: Name and Amount come first, and the logos after them are one stop for Tab: the arrow keys move between them, and Space picks one. Tab used to pass every one of the 337 logos before reaching Name.
  • The period bar on a phone: back, the period's name and forward stay on one line, the name wrapping between them, at any width and text size.
  • Finances' first three things stay until they're done: with a checking account and no paycheck or payment yet, Start with three things stays on the Dashboard, the account ticked (✓ Example Checking), and Add a paycheck and Add a payment still there; it goes once all three are in.
  • Frigate says where its recordings go: picking it, the plan says Frigate's recordings go to /Volumes/Media/frigate, on a drive with 1.6 TB free, and Settings › Frigate has a Frigate recordings folder to pick another; once it's installed, Done says what to do next (add your camera). Any app can say the same with stores and next in its x-homelab.
  • Choose apps says what it installs, all of it: Connect the apps for me shows only when there are two apps to connect, one of them new, and names them; an app another one brings in (qBittorrent's VPN tunnel) shows ticked and greyed, Installed with qBittorrent, which needs it; Done names it too (With qBittorrent: Gluetun, the ProtonVPN tunnel…); and the plan says more apps they need rather than helpers.
  • Backups in plain words: a copy that's late says Out of date: Mealie, last copied 3 days ago rather than Stale; the restore test says 12 files checked, all the same as now rather than 12 of 12 sampled files identical; and Browse the backups opens the backup app's own page (was Open Duplicati).
  • Plain words, and the keyboard, in three more places: the watchdog's alerts name the setting that turns its restarts off as Settings does (Settings › Notifications › Restart an app that stops answering), never by its code name, and the words check refuses a code name on a screen; an app's page says At home and on your own private network; on Status a running app's dot stays on the line of its word at any width; qBittorrent's ProtonVPN key says it's needed (on a paid plan) and where to make it, not Optional; and Choose apps' Open and Settings beside an app are reached with Tab.
  • Settings › People in plain words: a sign-in with their phone's face or fingerprint (no "passkey"), the household's sign-in for Pocket ID, New music and films password in place of Reset password, Make a new sign-in link with a line on when each is needed, and the apps someone uses as All the apps or Only these rather than "none ticked: all of them".
  • After Add them, Settings › People says what happened and how to hand over the welcome page: Anna Smith is added, with Show their sign-in to scan (the welcome page opens on the computer, now with a code for their phone's camera beside the sign-in link) and Open the fridge sheet. It says the welcome page is for them alone, since it holds their sign-in link and their music and films password, and that the fridge sheet is the one to email. The welcome page no longer opens by itself.
  • Update apps says what it changed: once it's done, the sheet says Updated: Navidrome 0.53 → 0.54. Already up to date: Vikunja, Mealie. (or a newer build when an app's image doesn't say its version), above each app's row, and homelab update ends the same way. Show details reads (each step, as it ran) rather than (what Docker said).
  • Update apps says what it will do, in plain words, before you press Update: These 3 apps have updates: Navidrome, Vikunja, Mealie. Their data is copied first, so each update can be undone: Mealie., by the apps' names. The command and anything a terminal says stay folded under Show details until it runs (and homelab update --all says the same).
  • Settings › Phones is simpler to pair with: Pair a phone and Pair a wall screen are two buttons, each with its own QR code: a TV's has what makes it a wall screen in it already, so no link is edited by hand. The pairing says which link the QR code holds, and the home Wi-Fi link sits under If the phone can't open it, saying a phone paired with it only looks. Every phone's row has the same controls in the same places (what it may do, Finances, for how long, Remove), with no warning mark nothing explained, and the words are plain (no tailnet, key or kiosk).
  • Read now in Investments no longer asks you to match an empty Ghostfolio account: Ghostfolio's own My Account, made when you sign up, with nothing in it, isn't listed under In Ghostfolio but matched to no account here. One that holds something still is.
  • Tidy Up's own trash on a USB drive empties itself: on a drive with no Recycle Bin (a USB drive, an SD card, a network share), what Tidy Up set aside in its hidden .tidy-trash folder goes for good after 30 days, once Undo can no longer put it back.
  • A Dashboard card opens what it sums up: in Finances, click a card's title (or its ↗) to see what's behind it: Spent this month opens that month's transactions, Cash flow and Where it goes open Recurring, Renewing soon the subscriptions, Budgets to watch and Latest transactions Transactions, the checking chart the calendar, This paycheck Paychecks, and Net worth its tab. The phone's page does the same, a phone allowed only to look included.
  • Budgets keep their figures whole: on the Dashboard's Budgets to watch and Spending's Budgets, the line under a long category name now breaks between its parts, never inside $200.00 of $150.00; what's left a day reads $15.00 a day on one line (the end date is already under the name); and every bar ends in line with the others, on the computer and the phone.
  • Investments as a list: Finances' Investments card no longer has the bar of what each account holds. Each holding has its price and a line of its worth over the year (green up, orange down) beside what you paid, its worth and its gain, and a chart of all your investments' worth over the year is on top.
  • Tidy Up in the dark looks like Finances: a near-black background, with cards a step lighter and a thin line round each, instead of the grey the rest of the app uses. With more contrast asked for, it keeps the app's own colours.
  • Tidy Up lists sizes as Finances lists amounts: what a job freed is now on the right of its line in Recently done (Movies shrunk · 12 files replaced, and 412 GB on the right), in the same place and type as Finances' amounts, instead of at the end of its words; and Merge on Audiobooks says what it wins back, as Shrink does for films.
  • Tidy Up's rows say it shorter: the lyrics, Tdarr, Radarr and Sonarr rows, and Music's Lyrics row, now fit on one line in a window half your screen wide.
  • Tidy Up's cards line up as Finances' do: two cards side by side are the same height, and Genres picks which library it shows with the same switch Finances' cards use, not a drop-down.
  • Settings on the iPhone, plainer: the homelab's everyday settings come first, in plain words (nightly updates, quiet hours, restarting an app that stops answering, undoing an update that breaks one, alerts on the computer's screen), then this iPhone's own (Face ID, the widget, who sends alerts), and every other homelab setting is one tap down, under All homelab settings.
  • Backups on the iPhone, tidier: the top card is followed by three tiles (the restore test, the password export, and the second copy), then only the copies that need a look; the ones up to date fold to a row of their logos until you tap them, and Duplicati's jobs, the restore tests and where the backups go are one tap down, under More.
  • Tidy Up's Music and Books tabs say their space once: the Space card that only repeated the header's On the drive figure is gone, and Genres takes its row instead of sitting beside half an empty one.
  • One period picker for the Dashboard: the paycheck's ‹ ›, and Today, now sit in a bar at the top of Finances' Dashboard, with the period's name and days, and the cards under it follow what you pick.
  • Snooze from the phone: a phone allowed to make changes can now snooze a failing check's alerts on the phone's page (Snooze… on the watchdog's card, for an hour or a day), as on the computer, and so can the iPhone app (Snooze… under the check, behind Face ID). A phone that can only look still has no Snooze.
  • Finances tabs open where you left them: Spending and Plan now open again on the page you were last on (Reports, Recurring, Paychecks…), not always their first.
  • A bank's own categories on import: an American Express or Chase file's Category column ("Restaurant-Restaurant", "Merchandise & Supplies-Groceries", "Food & Drink") now gives a shop the matching category of yours (Eating out, Groceries, Travel, Gas…) when nothing better says. Your own choice for a payee, a rule, the bill it pays and a known brand still come first, and one the file calls Other is left for you to pick. A company's ending goes from a payee's name too: SUNSHINE DENTAL, INC. comes in as Sunshine Dental.
  • Rules that reach further: a rule can be for every payee starting with some words (Truly Nolen for Truly Nolen 80, 81 and 112): rename a payee to the start of its name and tick Always do this for…, and that's picked for you, or pick Only that name. Also change the N already in gives every matching transaction the name and category, replacing a category picked before. And in Rules each rule's words, starts with, name and category can be changed, not only removed.
  • Tidy Up's Undo holds up: Recently done finds the music swap's and the books' Undo by what was done, not by the words of its line, so rewording a line in a later update can't quietly take its Undo away.
  • Stop a Tidy Up job you didn't start here: a job the overnight agent or a Terminal started (say, collecting Tdarr's work) used to hold every button on Tidy Up until it ended. Its card now has Stop, which stops it at its next safe point, as Stop does for a job you started, and says Stopping… until it has.
  • Finances in four tabs: Dashboard, Spending (Transactions and Reports), Plan (Calendar, Recurring and Paychecks, which was Pay) and Net worth, instead of seven side by side. Spending and Plan show their pages in a second row and open on the first; everything that opened a page before (a Dashboard card, a report, the sidebar) still opens it.
  • A stopped app on the iPhone says what to do: its row in Status has a Start button when the phone may make changes, and a phone that can only look says Start it from the computer, on the row and the app's page, instead of nothing.
  • Games go where they belong: a game store's wording comes in as its brand, with its logo: WL *STEAM PURCHASE and STEAMGAMES.COM are Steam, MICROSOFT*XBOX is Xbox, and PlayStation, Nintendo, Epic Games, GameStop and Roblox read the same way. Each goes into your Gaming category (or Games, or Video games) when you keep one, and Shopping when you don't.
  • Cleaner American Express names: a card file's payees no longer keep Amex's own wording: AplPay STARBUCKS SEATTLE WA comes in as Starbucks, WWP*… and WL *… as the shop after them, and the town and state after a shop are left off, whether Amex spaced them into columns, ran them into a store number, or named them in the file's City/State column. The iPhone app cleans names the same way. To rename rows you brought in before, import the same file again.
  • Updates on Windows and Linux are checked against how they were built: before installing, the app checks GitHub's signed record that this project's own build made the file, and refuses one without it.
  • The iPhone app hides what the computer can't do yet: with Homelab Wizard on the computer older than the app, Start, Stop and Restart, Stop for a While and an app's settings aren't offered, and the app's page says to update the computer, with the version it has.
  • The iPhone app says when the computer needs updating: when the app is newer than Homelab Wizard on the computer, something the computer can't do yet says "Update Homelab Wizard on the computer to use this" (with the version it has), instead of failing with an error that explains nothing.
  • The iPhone app notices when you get home: once it has reached the computer through the tunnel, it goes that way for up to 5 minutes, but when the phone's network changes (Wi-Fi to cellular, back on the home Wi-Fi, a VPN on or off), it tries home first again straight away.
  • Status on the iPhone, trimmed: one line when all is well ("All 47 apps are running"), or one card for the app that needs a look, with what's wrong, its button and Open Its Page; then your apps by group. The ring, the four tiles, the Changed Since You Looked list and the cards under the apps are gone (an app that changed has a dot on its row; what your apps save is a line in Settings). The same on a household member's phone, with only their apps.
  • Imports link the bills a name doesn't give away: a payee you've linked to a planned payment once (an HOA paid as Sunset Palms Eas…) links to it again every month, and a bill of $100 or more to the cent links within two weeks of its day, not just five.
  • Checking on payday, as your spreadsheet counts it: the Dashboard's pay period card now also says what checking holds at the end of payday, once that day's own payments (savings, a card paid off) are out, beside where it ends the period. Step › to your second paycheck for a sheet's "2 paychecks".
  • Update balances by group: the accounts are listed under Cash, Credit cards, Investments, Home & Car and Loans, each heading in its colour.
  • Back from Transactions: opened from a report's row or a Dashboard card, Finances › Transactions has Back to Reports (or the Dashboard) beside its filters.
  • What went out, in the weekly summary: Homelab this week ends its Finances lines with what your transactions spent in the last seven days and where most of it went (Spent this week: $148.20 in 3 transactions, the most at Costco, $100.00).
  • Pay, a year at a time: each person on Finances › Pay says their take-home a year too (about $55,900 a year), and one with no gross typed in says what adding it shows, with Add them.
  • Find a charge by its amount or day: Finances › Transactions' search finds what a transaction came to (86.10, or 2,400 with its comma) and its day (Oct 28) too. A day with more than one transaction says what they came to together.
  • A day on the checking chart opens it: click a day on the Dashboard's Checking chart and the Calendar opens on it, with what comes and goes that day.
  • This month against last: Finances › Transactions' This month says how much more or less has gone out than by the same day last month ($293.05 more out than by Sep 30 last month ($200.00)).
  • Long ledgers stay quick: Finances › Transactions draws the newest 200 at a time, with Show more for the next, so a year of bank files opens about five times faster and the search keeps up as you type; counts, totals and Select all still take in every one.
  • What Update balances changes: as you type, a line by Save says how many balances differ from what was expected and what that does to your net worth (2 balances differ from what was expected: net worth +$444.05).
  • More paychecks to the right: Net worth's Accounts, paycheck by paycheck shades its right edge while more paychecks lie past it, so it's clear the table scrolls sideways even where the scroll bar hides.
  • Goals, easier to read: each goal says what it needs a paycheck first ($90.16 a paycheck ($274.91 a month) to be there by Jun 30, 2028), and under its bar what's saved and its pace lately ($889.78 a month lately: there by May 2027), in amber when that's late.
  • ⌘F on Transactions: on Finances › Transactions, ⌘F (Ctrl+F on Windows and Linux) goes to its search, as it does on Choose apps and Settings; the shortcuts sheet (?) lists it.
