Job Source Folder Schedule Homelab Photos /source/immich photos Daily 01:00 Homelab Databases /staging/databases, /staging/volumes databases Daily 05:00 (after the 03:30 dumps) Homelab Secrets /staging/secrets secrets Daily 05:00 Homelab AppData /source/appdata (without Duplicati's own folder) appdata Daily 05:30 Homelab Stack Data /source/homelab-appdata stack-data Daily 05:30 Homelab Infrastructure /source/stacks infrastructure Sundays 06:00 Homelab Jellyfin /source/jellyfin (without its cache, transcodes, and logs) jellyfin Sundays 02:00 Homelab Calibre /source/calibre calibre Sundays 03:00 Homelab Files /source/sync (Syncthing's synced folders, SYNC_ROOT) files Daily 05:45

./homelab duplicati jobs lists them with their last and next run, as the app's Backups screen does.

Failure alerts are set once for every job, as Duplicati default options: send-http-url is http://ntfy:80/duplicati-alerts?auth=<NTFY_PUBLISH_AUTH> and send-http-level is Warning,Error,Fatal. Set up the alert token (notify setup) and duplicati setup both set them; ntfy refuses anonymous posts, so they wait for the token. A job you make by hand gets them too.

docs.title: Alert topics (ntfy)
docs.text:
Topic Published by watchtower The nightly updates and rollbacks (named for Watchtower, which sent them before) duplicati-alerts Duplicati job failures and homelab backup failures uptime-kuma Uptime Kuma monitors tunnel-watchdog homelab watchdog, and the Sunday weekly summary reminders The apps you point at it (Wallos renewals, Changedetection.io changes)

ntfy refuses anonymous publishing. ./homelab notify setup gives the homelab user write-only access to exactly these topics and stores its token in .env; ./homelab notify test <topic> sends a test message with it. A new topic needs to be added to the list in internal/notify and notify setup run again, or its messages are refused.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
• Everything previews first and needs --apply (or a yes in a terminal) to change anything.
  • Every job checks its own result: a dump must end with Postgres's completion marker, a copy must hash identically, and a URL must actually answer.
  • Alerts fire when something changes state, not on every check.

docs.title: Backups
docs.text:
Every night the homelab copies its databases, then Duplicati encrypts and versions everything into the backup folder you picked in Setup (a cloud drive such as Proton Drive or iCloud Drive, or an external drive). Databases are dumped first, because copying a live database's files can produce a backup that will not restore.

In the app, Backups shows all of it: the last backup, each app's newest copy, the off-site jobs, and the last restore test, with Back up now, Test a restore, Recovery kit, and Moving to a new machine. You rarely need anything below unless something is red.

docs.title: How it fits together
docs.text:
03:30  homelab backup   → recovery-staging/databases/<db>/<db>-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.sql.gz
                        → recovery-staging/volumes/<volume>/<volume>-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.tar.gz
                        → recovery-staging/databases/images/images-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.json
                        → recovery-staging/secrets/homelab.env, and data/'s records in secrets/data
01:00–06:00 Duplicati → encrypted, deduplicated versions in BACKUP_DESTINATION
Property Value Software Duplicati (duplicati, http://localhost:8200) Destination BACKUP_DESTINATION in .env: a Homelab Backups folder Setup makes in a cloud drive's synced folder or on an external drive other than the media drive. Setup offers each one it finds: on a Mac Proton Drive, iCloud Drive, Google Drive, OneDrive, and Dropbox (in ~/Library/CloudStorage) and the drives in /Volumes; on Windows OneDrive, iCloud Drive, and Dropbox in your user folder and every drive letter but the system's (not Google Drive's own drive, which Docker Desktop does not see); on Linux ~/Dropbox, ~/OneDrive, and the drives mounted in /run/media/<you> or /media/<you>. The watchdog checks the free space on its disk; a cloud drive's own quota cannot be read from this machine, so keep an eye on it in the drive's app Encryption Duplicati AES-256. DUPLICATI_SECRETS_PASSPHRASE opens Homelab Secrets: keep it in Vaultwarden and on the recovery kit (Backups › Recovery kit, or ./homelab recovery-kit, prints a page with a line for it). DUPLICATI_PASSPHRASE opens the other jobs; it is in .env, which the Secrets job holds Database dumps and volume archives ./homelab backup, daily at 03:30 (a scheduled job), newest 7 kept A copy before anything risky Before an update, each app's databases are dumped and its own data copied (recovery-staging/before-update, Automation); a rollback with --data sets today's aside before it puts the copy back. Before an app starts again on changed settings (a domain or tailnet address, signing in with Pocket ID, or Fix it applying settings changed by hand), its databases are dumped too, beside the nightly dumps and rotated out with them (the newest 7). A dump that fails stops the change The versions that wrote them The same run notes each running app's image and the digest that pulls it again (recovery-staging/databases/images, newest 7 kept, off-site with the dumps). move in and rebuild start those versions, not the newest, then name them so homelab update can move them on. .env keeps the same for each app the nightly update moves forward (<APP>_DIGEST), so starting the homelab also brings them back Storage measured The same nightly run measures each app's folder in data/appdata and each person's photos in Immich (data/storage.json): Status › What the apps keep and Photos per person

docs.title: Duplicati mount mappings
docs.text:
Mac path Container path Mode ~/Homelab/data/appdata /source/appdata read-only ~/Homelab/appdata /source/homelab-appdata read-only ~/Homelab/stacks /source/stacks read-only JELLYFIN_DATA_DIR /source/jellyfin read-only IMMICH_UPLOAD_LOCATION /source/immich read-only MEDIA_ROOT/Books /source/calibre read-only SYNC_ROOT (default ~/Homelab/data/sync) /source/sync read-only ~/Homelab/recovery-staging /staging read-write BACKUP_DESTINATION /destination read-write

Job settings always use the container paths on the right. Sources are read-only, so a restore goes into /staging/... and is copied back by hand. This makes it impossible to overwrite live data by accident.

docs.title: What is covered
docs.text: Data How Core service settings (proxy, CrowdSec, Vaultwarden, Uptime Kuma, ntfy, media apps) Homelab AppData job (/source/appdata) The stacks' files (appdata/: Paperless documents, Karakeep's and Linkwarden's saved pages, Nextcloud's files, and the rest) Homelab Stack Data job (/source/homelab-appdata) Every PostgreSQL database (Immich, Paperless, MoneyMatter, and each optional stack's), and consistent copies of the SQLite apps homelab backup dumps → Homelab Databases job .env (every secret) homelab backup copy → Homelab Secrets job Compose files and local edits Git, plus the Homelab Infrastructure job Photos and videos Homelab Photos job (/source/immich) Jellyfin settings and metadata Homelab Jellyfin job (/source/jellyfin) Calibre library (metadata.db and books) Homelab Calibre job (/source/calibre) The synced Files (Syncthing's folders, SYNC_ROOT) Homelab Files job (/source/sync), made once the folder has something in it. Syncthing passes a deletion on to every device, so this is the copy a file deleted by mistake comes back from MoneyMatter attachments homelab backup archives the moneymatter-attachments volume → Homelab Databases job (/staging/volumes) Music, movies, TV, audiobooks, comics Not backed up (re-obtainable, and too large for most cloud drives) The homelab's own records in data/ (the household, paired phones, single sign-on settings, Finances with each balance's history, its receipts and the Collection's pictures, update history) homelab backup copies them into recovery-staging/secrets/data → Homelab Secrets job

docs.title: Database dumps
docs.text:
homelab backup runs pg_dumpall --clean --if-exists inside each database container, using the container's own POSTGRES_USER (so no password leaves the container). It gzips the output and keeps the file only if it ends with Postgres's completion marker. Databases are marked in the compose files with dump: postgres; a new database with that line is included automatically.

Apps that keep their data in SQLite (Vaultwarden, Nginx Proxy Manager, Uptime Kuma, ntfy's accounts, Navidrome, beets, Audiobookshelf, Calibre-Web, Komga, Kavita, Seerr, Mealie, Grocy, Homarr, Karakeep) are marked dump: sqlite:/path/in/the/container. Duplicati copies their files too, but a copy of a database file taken while the app writes can be torn. So homelab backup also:

  • takes a consistent copy with SQLite's online backup, through a small helper image it builds once (dockerfiles/sqlite), as the file's owner;
  • checks it with PRAGMA integrity_check;
  • keeps it gzipped as <app>-<stamp>.sqlite.gz.

An app with no database at that path yet (Uptime Kuma set up on MariaDB, say) is skipped.

An app that is installed but stopped, or runs outside the homelab, makes the backup fail with an alert, rather than leaving last night's dump as the newest. Each dump has two hours to finish.

Named volumes that hold files rather than a database (MoneyMatter's attachments) are listed under archive: in the owning service. homelab backup tars each one through a throwaway Alpine container and keeps the archive only if it reads back completely.

Restore one into a fresh, empty database container:

gunzip -c recovery-staging/databases/paperless-db/paperless-db-<stamp>.sql.gz \
  | ./homelab compose paperless exec -T paperless-db psql -U paperless -d postgres

Restore a SQLite copy with the app stopped, over its database file:

./homelab stop vaultwarden
gunzip -c recovery-staging/databases/vaultwarden/vaultwarden-<stamp>.sqlite.gz > data/appdata/vaultwarden/db.sqlite3
rm -f data/appdata/vaultwarden/db.sqlite3-wal data/appdata/vaultwarden/db.sqlite3-shm
./homelab start vaultwarden

Immich has extra rules (its own Postgres image, and a search-path fix). See Disaster Recovery.

docs.title: Restore testing
docs.text:
A backup counts only once a restore has been proven. Monthly, click Test a restore on the app's Backups screen, or:

./homelab restore-test --auto

It signs in to Duplicati with DUPLICATI_PASSWORD, picks a dozen files from data/appdata (spread across apps, unchanged for over a day so last night's backup holds them as they are, leaving out caches, logs, and live database side files), and asks Duplicati to restore them from the newest version of the Homelab AppData job into recovery-staging/restore-test. When the restore finishes it hashes each file against the live one, and removes the restore when they match. On a difference it fails and leaves the files there for a look. --job "<name>" tests another job whose source is /source/appdata.

With Kopia installed as the second engine, ./homelab restore-test --auto --engine kopia does the same from Kopia's newest snapshot of /source/appdata, signed in with KOPIA_SERVER_PASSWORD. Each engine's test is on record on its own, and each has its own monthly reminder. The Backups screen shows Kopia's line beside Duplicati's jobs (Second copy (Kopia): where its repository is and its last test), with Test Kopia's restore.

The manual way, for any job or a whole-job restore:

  1. In Duplicati, restore a job to /staging/restore-test, with restoring permissions turned off in the metadata step (the files only need their contents).
  2. Read the error and warning counts, not just the icon.
  3. Compare against the live files, then delete recovery-staging/restore-test:
./homelab restore-test recovery-staging/restore-test data/appdata

It hashes a sample of the restored files against the originals and fails on any difference. Files changed since the backup are listed, not failed.

Either way the test goes on record in scripts/logs/restore-test.json (the last 24, passed or failed): the restore drills. --auto times each one from asking Duplicati to the last file checked, so you know how long getting files back takes before you need it. The Backups screen shows the last pass and how long it took, a failure since in red, and the record when you hover the tile; the weekly summary and homelab report include them too. When the last pass is more than 30 days old, the nightly backup job sends a reminder to the duplicati-alerts topic, at most once a week until the next test.

docs.title: Password vault export
docs.text:
The Vaultwarden database dump restores the server, but it needs a working server to read. Once a month, also keep an export that opens anywhere:

  1. In the Bitwarden web vault: Tools › Export vault, format .json (Encrypted), type Password protected. Keep that password outside the vault (on paper, with the recovery kit). An account restricted export only opens in the same account, which is lost with the server.
  2. Save the file in recovery-staging/secrets in the homelab folder. The nightly Homelab Secrets job takes it off-site with .env.

The nightly backup looks there: when the newest bitwarden_encrypted_export_*.json is over 30 days old it sends a reminder to duplicati-alerts (at most weekly), and when a plain export (bitwarden_export_*, readable) is there it alerts every night until it is deleted. The app's Backups screen shows the same.

docs.title: Moving to a new machine
docs.text:
When the old machine still works, nothing needs restoring from Duplicati: Backups › Moving to a new machine carries everything over.

  1. On the old machine, Move out… asks where to save one file, takes a fresh backup, stops the apps, and packs the settings, the apps' data, and the newest database dumps into it (click twice to confirm).
  2. On the new machine, install Homelab Wizard and choose Set it up for me.
  3. Plug in the drive with the photos and media, and Move in… with that file.

Moving between kinds of computer (a Mac, Windows, Linux) works too: Move in sets this machine's account and network settings itself, and stops for any folder from the old machine (/Volumes/…, D:\…) until you pick its place here in Settings › Storage, then carries on. In Terminal: ./homelab move out --to <file> and ./homelab move in <file>. Disaster Recovery has the details.

docs.title: Rebuilding a lost machine
docs.text: When the machine is gone, ./homelab rebuild <backup folder> brings the homelab back from these backups alone, on a new machine with Homelab Wizard installed: it asks for DUPLICATI_SECRETS_PASSPHRASE, restores Homelab Secrets, then the databases, the apps' data, and the stacks' data, starts each app on the version that wrote its data, and makes the backup jobs again. The photos, the Jellyfin library, and the books come back with their own jobs. Disaster Recovery has the details, and the same by hand.

docs.title: Recovery order
docs.text:
1. Vaultwarden (every other credential is in it)
  2. .env from the Secrets job
  3. Addresses: Tailscale in Home mode; with a domain, Nginx Proxy Manager and CrowdSec
  4. Databases, then their apps
  5. Everything else, then monitoring

docs.title: Commands
docs.text: Everything runs from a terminal in the homelab folder: ./homelab on macOS and Linux, homelab.cmd on Windows. It builds itself the first time when Go is installed (brew install go on the Mac, winget install GoLang.Go on Windows); without Go it runs the copy the desktop app carries, so the app's buttons and the terminal both work without it. ./homelab help prints the full list.

docs.title: The main loop
docs.text:
./homelab               # an interactive menu (in a terminal)
./homelab status        # what runs, its health, and its addresses (--all: the helpers too)
./homelab status --timing   # how long each part of Status takes on this machine
./homelab doctor        # anything wrong with this machine, the runtime, disk space, drive health, or .env
./homelab runtime install --apply   # Linux and SteamOS: Docker in your home folder, run as you, kept across system updates
./homelab kit           # a folder the app made: which build of the homelab files it is
./homelab kit update homelab-kit.tar.gz   # bring such a folder up to a newer kit (never .env, data, or your own apps)
./homelab fix           # repair what usually goes wrong (the plan first): runtime, apps down or unwell, settings not yet applied, CrowdSec's bouncer, a full disk, jobs
./homelab migrate       # move apps from homelab_core into their category's project (backup first)
./homelab report        # a file to share when asking for help: secrets, tokens, your account name, and email addresses removed (--stdout: print it)
./homelab upgrade       # the newest homelab files from GitHub (fast-forward only), then up (the app's Update now)
./homelab homepage      # Homepage's list of apps, from what runs (also after each install)
./homelab version       # this CLI's version

docs.title: Picking apps
docs.text:
Every command that takes apps (install, plan, start, stop, restart, update, remove) takes any mix of these:

Write Selects sonarr radarr Apps by name (./homelab apps lists them) overseerr, money An alias (Seerr, MoneyMatter) '*-arr', 'son*' The whole *arr set (the bundle's alias), or a pattern over app names; quote it so the shell leaves the * alone @arr, arr, @household, @adblock A bundle (./homelab bundles lists them; the @ is optional, as PowerShell needs) stack:immich Everything in one stack folder cat:media A whole category (cat:network, cat:household, …) --exclude x Leave an app out of the rest

docs.title: Start, add, remove
docs.text:
./homelab up                     # start the baseline (preview, then confirm)
./homelab install sonarr radarr  # slot in optional apps
./homelab install '*-arr'        # the whole *arr set
./homelab plan qbittorrent       # what an install would do, nothing changed
./homelab stop|start|restart <app>
./homelab stop <app> --until 21:00  # stopped for a while (21:00, 1h, or a date and time); it starts again by itself then
./homelab pin|unpin <app>        # an app at the top of Status and the menu bar's Open an app, or back in its group
./homelab update <app>           # dump its databases, pull or rebuild, then recreate
./homelab update --all           # every app the nightly update would, now
./homelab db upgrade paperless-db  # a database to its next PostgreSQL major version (--to N), back by itself on failure
./homelab upgrade --back         # the homelab files as they were before the last upgrade, then up
./homelab rollback <app>         # back to the image before its last update (kept a week), with its data from just before; holds its updates
./homelab rollback <app> --image-only  # the earlier image on today's data
./homelab rollback <app> --data  # after a rollback that kept today's data: put back the copy from before the update
./homelab remove <app>           # remove the container; data stays
./homelab logs <app> -f
./homelab logs <app> --explain   # what its log says, from the Ollama on this machine
./homelab apps                   # the catalog (--category ID)
./homelab bundles                # the bundles, such as @arr and @adblock (the @ is optional: install adblock, as PowerShell needs)
./homelab detect                 # containers already running on this machine
./homelab adopt vaultwarden      # move an app from an older setup into the homelab

./homelab cleanup                # remove old containers whose apps now run in the homelab
./homelab cleanup --volumes      # ...and their volumes, when nothing else uses them
./homelab signups open           # Vaultwarden sign-ups for 10 minutes (--for 30m), then closed
./homelab signups close
./homelab updates                # whether the nightly updates run, and when
./homelab updates pause          # stop them until resumed (kept across up)
./homelab updates resume
./homelab updates hold <app>     # leave one app out of nightly updates
./homelab updates release <app>  # put it back (after a rollback too)
./homelab updates days immich sun  # update Immich on Sundays only (sat+sun, weekend; every: each night)
./homelab updates notes <app>    # what updating it brings: its newer releases' notes
./homelab wire                   # connect running apps: Prowlarr, FlareSolverr, qBittorrent, root folders, Bazarr, Seerr
./homelab move out --to /Volumes/Drive/homelab.tar   # moving machines: back up, stop, pack it into one file
./homelab move in /Volumes/Drive/homelab.tar         # on the new machine: unpack, load the databases, start what ran
./homelab rebuild ~/ProtonDrive/Homelab\ Backups      # the machine is lost: restore .env and the data from Duplicati's backups, start what ran
                                                     #   (--force: into a folder that already has apps' data)
./homelab uninstall              # take the homelab off this machine; the folder, data, and backups stay
./homelab uninstall --data       # ...and delete the apps' data too, and sign out of the tailnet (never the backups or the media drive)
./homelab uninstall --folder     # ...and the whole homelab folder, .env included (implies --data)
./homelab uninstall --backups    # ...and the backup folders on this machine (BACKUP_DESTINATION, KOPIA_REPOSITORY), never one in a cloud drive
./homelab uninstall --app        # ...and Homelab Wizard, its settings, and its downloads
./homelab uninstall --everything-else  # ...and every other container, image, volume, and network in the runtime, and the build cache

uninstall refuses --folder for a folder without compose.yaml and .env.example, a home folder, or a drive. A backup folder in a cloud drive's folder (or one named after a cloud drive: Proton Drive, Google Drive, My Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox, iCloud Drive, pCloud, MEGA, Nextcloud, Sync) is kept and named in the plan, as is one that holds the home folder, the homelab folder, or the media drive. --backups deletes only what the backups wrote: Duplicati's job folders (secrets, databases, …) and duplicati- files, and a Kopia repository (its folder, marked by kopia.repository.f, unless it is the top of a drive); anything else in a backup folder, such as the household's own files on a backup drive, stays and is named. --folder without --backups keeps the backups inside the homelab folder (./backups, ./backups-kopia by default) and any media folder there, and deletes the rest. In a terminal, --everything-else asks for delete everything typed out, and --folder or --backups for delete; --apply (scripts, and the app, which asks for its own) goes ahead without.

./homelab custom add wiki --image ghcr.io/requarks/wiki:2 --port 3000 --volume /wiki/data
./homelab custom                 # your own apps
./homelab custom remove wiki     # take one out; its data stays

custom add writes the app into stacks/custom/compose.yaml (optional, on the shared network, on a free port, its folders under data/appdata/<id>) and validates the catalog, putting everything back on any problem. The custom stack is yours alone, like .env: git ignores it and the generated docs leave it out, so git pull keeps working. --install starts it straight away; --env KEY=value passes settings.

adopt is for apps that status lists as elsewhere. It stops the old container (and, by name, its helpers such as moneymatter-db), copies each folder or volume the old container used to where the homelab keeps it (matched by the path inside the container; shared folders like the media drive stay put), carries the generated secrets the copied data depends on (a database password) into .env without printing them, and starts the app. It refuses to overwrite a folder that has files or a volume that exists, and to copy PostgreSQL data across major versions. The old container is only stopped; the last line says how to go back.

docs.title: Compose, without changing folders
docs.text:
./homelab compose immich ps
./homelab compose paperless exec paperless document_exporter ../export
./homelab compose media down      # a whole category's project (homelab_media)

The first argument is an app, a category (network, media, media-automation, …), or a stack folder (immich, paperless, budget-tracker, cloudflare).

docs.title: Domain
docs.text:
./homelab domain setup --dry-run   # preview
./homelab domain setup             # proxy hosts, AdGuard rewrite, tunnel hostnames
./homelab domain setup --ssl       # also the wildcard certificate (first time)
./homelab domain status
./homelab away on|off <app>        # a public app reached away from home through the tunnel, or (off) home only, nothing of it on the internet
./homelab domain resolver          # this machine finds every app by name, also with a VPN on (asks for the administrator's password once)
./homelab domain resolver --undo   # takes that back, and homelab's lines in the hosts file

domain resolver writes /etc/resolver/<domain> on macOS, a systemd-resolved drop-in (/etc/systemd/resolved.conf.d/homelab-<domain>.conf) on Linux, or a Name Resolution Policy Table rule on Windows, pointing at AdGuard Home on this machine's home-network address (--ip to name it). Outside a terminal it previews; --apply writes it. --undo removes it again (only what homelab wrote: a file it did not write, or a rule without its homelab comment, stays), and homelab's lines in the hosts file from domain setup --dns hosts; name the domain (--undo old.example.org) to take back one the homelab had before. uninstall leaves them, and says so.

Home mode (no domain), every app on the tailnet:

./homelab tailnet login            # sign Tailscale in through its page in the browser; no auth key needed
./homelab tailnet setup            # https://<TAILSCALE_HOST>:<port> for the running apps (signs in first when needed)

With TAILNET_ADMIN_APPS=false, the admin apps (the proxy, AdGuard Home, Duplicati, Dozzle) stay off the tailnet and open on this machine only.

Ad blocking (AdGuard Home), in either mode:

./homelab install @adblock         # AdGuard Home, and DNS on the tailnet address
./homelab adguard setup            # first-run wizard with a generated login; the tailnet DNS setting

The household (Pocket ID accounts):

./homelab person add "Anna Smith" --email anna@example.com   # account, first sign-in link, welcome page
./homelab person                   # who is in the household
./homelab person welcome anna      # a new sign-in link and welcome page
./homelab person password anna     # a new password in Jellyfin and Navidrome, on a fresh welcome page
./homelab person apps anna immich-server paperless mealie   # only these on their page and Homepage tab (--all: every app)
./homelab person share anna bills,budgets                    # what of the household's money her phone shows her, to look at (bills, subscriptions, budgets; none)
./homelab person remove anna       # sign-in off; their data stays in every app

Single sign-on with Pocket ID (needs a domain):

./homelab sso                      # which apps sign in with Pocket ID
./homelab sso setup                # connect the rest: their clients in Pocket ID, their settings

docs.title: Phones
docs.text:
./homelab phone pair --name "My iPhone"   # a one-time code and the links to open on the phone (--can-change: it may make changes;
                                          #   --finances view|edit: it sees Finances, or changes them too)
./homelab phone list                      # paired phones, what they may do, when last seen
./homelab phone allow <id>                # may start, stop, restart, and back up
./homelab phone read-only <id>
./homelab phone finances <id> view        # it sees Finances (edit: it may change them too; card: a wall screen's money card only; off: hidden again)
./homelab phone person <id> anna          # Anna's phone: only her apps (homelab person apps) and her own Finances, apart from the household's; none: yours again
./homelab phone until <id> 7d             # its changes and Finances end in a week (12h, 2w); then it only looks. never: no end
./homelab phone remove <id>               # its token stops working
./homelab serve                           # the companion itself (the serve job runs it)

A household member's phone (phone person) sees only the apps they use, and starts or stops none. Its Finances are their own, in data/members/<username>/ beside the household's, and of the household's money it shows only what person share names: bills in the next five weeks, subscriptions, budgets, with names, amounts and days, never an account, a balance or a transaction. Nothing else of the homelab answers it.

Finances go only to a phone paired with the https link (Tailscale, or https://homelab.example.com with a domain), never to one paired over plain home Wi-Fi, nor to a TV or wall screen in kiosk mode, whatever is picked for it.

The companion also serves Finances' calendar feed, /finances.ics?key=…: the paydays and bills ahead for a phone's calendar to subscribe to, made in Finances › Pay › Paydays and money, with amounts or without. Like Finances on a phone it goes only over the https link, and only for the plan's key: a new link, or Turn it off, stops the old one at once.

docs.title: Jobs
docs.text:
./homelab backup                   # preview; --apply to run
./homelab watchdog                 # the checks the watchdog job runs every 15 minutes
./homelab agent                    # the background agent itself, which runs the parts below (schedule install sets it up)
./homelab awake                    # hold off sleep while plugged in (the awake job runs it)
./homelab awake allow              # Linux: let the awake job hold off sleep (once, with the administrator's password); --undo takes it back
./homelab notify setup             # write grants for the alert topics
./homelab notify test duplicati-alerts
./homelab notify off vikunja        # checked, but no alerts about it (on: alerts again)
./homelab notify snooze "crowdsec bouncer" 1h  # one check not alerted about for an hour (1d: a day; off: now); alerted then if it still fails
./homelab digest                   # the weekly summary; --send sends it now
./homelab schedule install         # the startup, backup, watchdog, awake, and serve jobs
./homelab schedule status
./homelab schedule remove          # take the jobs out again
./homelab quit                     # stop the homelab until the next login: the agent (still installed), the tray item, every app
./homelab resume                   # start what quit stopped; opening the app or the next login does it too
./homelab duplicati destination    # BACKUP_DESTINATION: "Homelab Backups" in Proton Drive, or a folder you name
./homelab duplicati setup          # create the Duplicati backup jobs (preview, then confirm)
./homelab duplicati jobs           # each job's last and next run
./homelab kopia repository <folder>  # KOPIA_REPOSITORY: Kopia's second copy, never in Duplicati's folder; Kopia starts again there
./homelab backup-check             # Duplicati's own check of each backup (the agent runs it weekly, on Sundays)
./homelab restore-test --auto      # Duplicati restores a sample; checked against the live files
./homelab restore-test --auto --engine kopia   # the same from Kopia's newest snapshot, when it is installed
./homelab restore-test recovery-staging/restore-test data/appdata
./homelab recovery-kit             # recovery-kit.html to print: where the backups and passphrases are, how to restore
./homelab export                   # every app's data in open formats in export-<date>: tables as CSV, documents, albums
./homelab export --photos --to /Volumes/Drive/Export   # ...with the original photos, onto a drive with room

docs.title: Docs and checks
docs.text:
./homelab docs        # refresh the generated tables in docs/ and services/
./homelab docs --check   # fail if a generated table is out of date
./homelab validate    # compose metadata and docs (links, versions, lines left from a merge); CI runs this
make check            # gofmt, vet, tests, validate

docs.title: Global flags
docs.text: Flag Does --apply (or -y) Go ahead without asking; needed outside a terminal (scheduled jobs, scripts) --json One JSON object per line (below) --root DIR The homelab folder, when not run from it (HOMELAB_ROOT does the same) --no-color Plain output --set KEY=value, --set-stdin For install, plan, and up: write a setting to .env first, never echoed

docs.title: Driving the CLI from an app
docs.text:
The desktop app (and scripts) use --json: every line of output is one object, {"schema": 1, "type": ..., "data": ...}. schema changes only when a field a client may read is removed or changes meaning; new fields can appear at any time, so ignore the ones you do not know. The fields are the JSON types in internal/api (plus setup.Step and install.Event), and internal/api/testdata/contract.json is the list a test holds them to.

Command Lines homelab --json apps catalog: categories, apps (kind, dependencies, the .env inputs each needs), and presets (bundles like @arr, whole stacks like stack:immich) homelab --json plan <apps> plan: what would start, what was added as a dependency, skips, port and .env changes, problems homelab --json install <apps> --apply plan, then a progress pair (start, done) per step, then done with each started app's address; without --apply, plan then preview homelab --json status status: state, health, and address of every app homelab --json updates [pause\|resume] --apply updates: whether nightly updates are paused, and their schedule homelab --json setup setup: each first-time step with its state, detail, and the settings it needs homelab --json upgrade upgrade: the check only: changes waiting on GitHub, and whether the app or the settings changed homelab --json digest digest: the weekly summary's title, body, and what needs a look (problems) homelab --json duplicati jobs jobs: each backup job's last and next run homelab --json wire --apply wiring (the planned links), then a link line as each connection is made: done, already, manual (with what to do), or failed

Longer jobs (update, start, stop, restart, remove across several projects, fix, backup, and restore-test --auto) report their steps as step lines, {"n": 2, "total": 5, "text": "Updating vikunja"}; in a terminal they read [2/5] Updating vikunja, and HOMELAB_PROGRESS=json writes them as JSON lines without the rest of --json (the desktop app sets it to show a progress bar). Any failure ends with an error line and exit code 1; a command that only previewed (no --apply) ends with a preview line. Form values go in with --set KEY=value, or --set-stdin (KEY=value lines) to keep secrets out of the process list; plans mark them secret and never print them. Go code can call the same engine directly: internal/api holds the JSON types and install.ApplyWithProgress reports the steps.

docs.title: First-time setup
docs.text:
./homelab setup                  # the bring-up as a checklist, each step checked live

./homelab doctor also checks the network: the home-network address (a VPN's tunnel or a container bridge is never taken for it), whether a VPN carries all traffic (other devices may then not reach the homelab), whether this machine uses the home DNS, how much of the runtime's memory the containers use, the free space on each disk the homelab writes to (with what the runtime keeps in images, volumes, and build cache), and, with smartctl installed, each drive's own health report. With CrowdSec and the proxy running, it also says when the proxy's bouncer last pulled CrowdSec's decisions (bans are only enforced while it does).

Each step says what is missing, which .env settings it needs, and the command that does it. The app's Setup screen shows the same checklist with buttons, and its Settings screen edits .env.

docs.title: Rules of thumb
docs.text:
• Without --apply, a command only previews. In a terminal it asks first.
  • If an output looks wrong, stop and read it before applying anything.
  • Never docker volume prune or docker system prune --volumes: databases live in volumes.

docs.title: Contributing
docs.text: How to change the homelab safely, and how to slot in a new service.

docs.title: Principles
docs.text:
• Documentation is part of the change.
  • Every change can be undone: know the rollback before you start.
  • Prefer the simple solution.
  • Preview first; apply second; verify the result, not the exit code.

docs.title: Standard change workflow
docs.text:
1. Know what you are changing and why.
  2. Make sure a recent backup exists (./homelab backup, then the Duplicati jobs).
  3. Plan the rollback.
  4. Change the compose file or settings; run ./homelab plan or the command without --apply.
  5. Apply, then verify the app actually works (open it, check ./homelab status).
  6. Run ./homelab docs, update the hand-written parts of the affected notes, and add a line to CHANGELOG.md.
  7. Run make check and commit.

docs.title: One container
docs.text:
Add a block to its category's file in compose/ (for example compose/documents.yaml, the homelab_documents project; services that depend on each other must share a file). Keep x-homelab as the last key:

  myapp:
    <<: *service
    image: example/myapp:latest
    profiles: [optional]                 # remove to make it part of the baseline
    environment:
      TZ: ${TZ:-UTC}
    ports:
      - ${BIND_IP:-127.0.0.1}:${MYAPP_PORT:-8123}:8080
    volumes:
      - ./data/appdata/myapp:/config
    x-homelab:
      name: My App                       # display name; the note is services/<category>/My App.md
      category: documents                # network, security, system, cloud, documents, finance, media, media-automation, household
      description: One line on what it is for
      subdomain: myapp                   # https://myapp.<domain>
      web: 8080                          # container port of the UI, or false
      # local: true                      # no sign-in of its own: this computer only, no tailnet or domain address

docs.title: Several containers
docs.text:
Create stacks/<name>/compose.yaml with its own name: homelab_<name>. Databases stay on the stack's default network; the web service also joins the shared network:

name: homelab_myapp

networks:
  default:
  homelab:
    name: homelab
    external: true

services:
  myapp:
    image: example/myapp:latest
    networks: [default, homelab]
    depends_on: [myapp-db]
    x-homelab: { name: My App, category: documents, web: 8080, subdomain: myapp }
  myapp-db:
    image: postgres:17
    volumes: [myapp-pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data]
    x-homelab: { name: My App database, category: system, internal: true, dump: postgres }

volumes:
  myapp-pgdata:

Use ../../appdata/<name>/... for bind mounts so data sits next to the other stacks' data.

docs.title: x-homelab fields
docs.text:
Field Meaning name, category, description How the app is listed and where its note lives web Container port of the UI, or false subdomain Hostname label (defaults to the service name) path Path of the UI under its address (defaults to /) url The .env setting with the address the app is opened at, for apps that need to know it (sign-in, links). Empty means https://<subdomain>.<domain>; in Home mode homelab tailnet setup fills it with the tailnet address public: true Also publish through the Cloudflare Tunnel (refused for admin apps) admin: true Its pages manage the homelab, so it is never published; every Network and System app counts as admin already internal: true A helper (database, cache): no note, not listed, pulled in as a dependency aliases Other names that select it (overseerr → seerr) requires .env variables that must be set before it starts (for example a token) warning One line the install plan shows under Worth knowing (for example that its page has no password at first) stores The .env folder settings it fills, each with what it keeps there ({ FRIGATE_RECORDINGS: recordings }): the install plan says where that folder is and how much room its drive has next What to do once it's installed, shown under Ready to open (Frigate: add a camera) seed A repository folder of starter files copied into its data folder on install, never over existing files login .env variables the homelab set the app's sign-in up with, user then password; the app's page on Status shows them behind Sign-in details (the password is only copied) dump: postgres homelab backup dumps this database daily archive Named volumes homelab backup tars daily phone The phone app people use the app with, shown on each person's welcome page (homelab person add) version For a PostgreSQL database (dump: postgres): the .env setting with its major version, used in its image as postgres:${KEY:-N}; homelab db upgrade moves it on proxy_host Reach the UI through another container (qBittorrent through gluetun) conflicts Apps that cannot run alongside it goes_with Apps this one adds to, each with one line on what it brings them (navidrome: "Tags and sorts the music…"). Choose apps suggests it, under Suggested for what you run, to someone who runs one same_job Apps that do much the same, each with one line on why you might keep one or both (kavita: "Both read comics…"). Written on one side of a pair; Choose apps says it on both, beside the one you don't run yet doc A different note path releases The GitHub project (owner/name) the image's releases are published in, when the image does not say (no org.opencontainers.image.source label, not on ghcr.io): Update shows their notes pin Why the image is updated by hand rather than by the nightly updates (a database, a cache, and a locally built image are by hand already)

The catalog-wide blocks live in compose.yaml: x-homelab-format (the layout version), x-homelab-categories, x-homelab-small-baseline, x-homelab-bundles (name, description, apps, aliases, starter), and x-homelab-native for apps that run on the host (name, category, description, subdomain, port, install, install_linux, install_windows, public, doc, phone).

docs.title: Then
docs.text:
1. Add any new variables (ports, secrets as __REPLACE_ME__) to .env.example and Environment.
  2. ./homelab docs creates the note with its facts filled in; write Purpose, Setup, Backup, and Troubleshooting.
  3. make check.
  4. ./homelab install myapp. It gets its address by itself: on the tailnet in Home mode, or a proxy host once Set up the domain has run (AUTO_DOMAIN).
  5. Check the watchdog sees it (./homelab watchdog); add an Uptime Kuma monitor only for checks of your own (see Monitoring).

docs.title: Service acceptance checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] restart: unless-stopped (from <<: *service); an x-homelab pin with the reason if its image must not update nightly
  • [ ] App ports on ${BIND_IP}; data in data/appdata, appdata, or a named volume
  • [ ] Authentication on, with the password in Vaultwarden
  • [ ] Backup coverage (an existing Duplicati job, dump, or archive), or the gap written in the note
  • [ ] The watchdog checks it (a health check, or a web page it can open)
  • [ ] Note written, ./homelab validate passes
  • [ ] If it replaces a paid service, a row in Savings and an updated summary
  • [ ] CHANGELOG.md updated

docs.title: Code changes
docs.text: See the repository's CONTRIBUTING for the Go workflow.

docs.title: Decisions
docs.text:
Architecture decisions and why they were made.

ADR Title Status ADR-0001 A Mac as the only host Accepted ADR-0002 OrbStack as the container runtime Accepted ADR-0003 Cloudflare Tunnel for public access, through the proxy Accepted ADR-0004 Custom Nginx Proxy Manager image with the CrowdSec bouncer Accepted ADR-0005 No Cloudflare Access or WARP Accepted; narrowed by ADR-0023 for the phone companion's own hostname ADR-0006 Watchtower opt-in by label Superseded by ADR-0020 ADR-0007 Database dumps scheduled by launchd, not Duplicati scripts Accepted ADR-0008 compose files are the catalog; one CLI in Go Accepted ADR-0009 One shared Docker network; apps reached by name Accepted ADR-0010 Native Jellyfin Accepted ADR-0011 One .env for every project Accepted ADR-0012 Home mode (no domain) is the default Accepted ADR-0013 The app updates itself from a numbered build of main Accepted ADR-0014 One engine, followed live through a local socket Accepted ADR-0015 A typed Preact frontend, compiled and committed Accepted ADR-0016 The watchdog heals once, then leaves it to a person Accepted ADR-0017 CPU weights for background work, not throttling Accepted ADR-0018 Not now: Docker Go SDK, tsnet, several machines Accepted ADR-0019 Kopia as an optional second backup engine beside Duplicati Accepted ADR-0020 A rollback puts back the app's data with its image Accepted ADR-0021 Finances as a screen of the app, typed in by hand and kept on this machine Accepted ADR-0022 SQLite only for records that grow and are searched; small state stays in JSON Accepted ADR-0023 The iPhone app away from home: the companion through the tunnel, behind Access and sealed end to end Accepted

docs.title: ADR-0001: A Mac as the only host
docs.text: Context: The homelab needs one always-on machine at home. Decision: Run everything on one Mac with Apple Silicon (a Mac mini, or a MacBook kept plugged in), kept awake by the homelab's awake job. Trade-offs: One machine is a single point of failure, and with FileVault nothing starts after a reboot until someone logs in. Apple Silicon is quiet and efficient, and native Jellyfin can use its media engine.

docs.title: ADR-0002: OrbStack as the container runtime
docs.text: Context: Docker on macOS always runs in a Linux VM. Decision: OrbStack, with Start at login enabled. Rationale: Lighter and faster than Docker Desktop, fast bind mounts, Rosetta for the few Intel-only images. The CLI uses the plain docker CLI, so Docker Desktop still works.

docs.title: ADR-0003: Cloudflare Tunnel for public access, through the proxy
docs.text: Context: Family members use some apps from outside the home without extra software. The router must not open ports. Decision: One remotely managed tunnel. Each public hostname points at http://nginx-proxy-manager:80, not at the app. Rationale: No inbound ports. Routing through the proxy means CrowdSec reads and blocks tunnel traffic exactly like LAN traffic, which removes the need for a separate edge bouncer and its Workers KV limits. The visitor's real address arrives in CF-Connecting-IP; proxy hosts trust X-Forwarded-Proto, so there is no redirect loop. Trade-offs: The proxy becomes a dependency of public access. The watchdog checks it every 15 minutes.

docs.title: ADR-0004: Custom Nginx Proxy Manager image with the CrowdSec bouncer
docs.text: Context: CrowdSec detects attacks but needs an enforcement point. Decision: Build dockerfiles/npm-crowdsec from jc21/nginx-proxy-manager plus CrowdSec's Lua bouncer (lua-cs-bouncer) and lua-resty-http, following CrowdSec's own OpenResty reference build. The bouncer configuration comes from environment variables at start. Consequences: Never update it by pulling the upstream image (that silently drops the bouncer). Left out of the nightly updates; ./homelab update nginx-proxy-manager rebuilds it. With no bouncer key the bouncer turns itself off instead of stopping the proxy.

docs.title: ADR-0005: No Cloudflare Access or WARP
docs.text:
Status: Narrowed by ADR-0023 (November 2026): the phone companion's own hostname is behind Access with a service token, which the Homelab app sends itself. Every other app stays without Access, for the reasons below.

Context: Cloudflare Access could gate the public apps behind a login. Decision: Do not use Access or WARP. Rationale: The public apps are used through native apps (Bitwarden, Immich, Subsonic players, Audiobookshelf) that talk to APIs and cannot complete an Access login. WARP would mean installing software on every family device. Mitigation: Strong unique passwords, 2FA where offered, CrowdSec, Cloudflare's managed rules.

docs.title: ADR-0006: Watchtower opt-in by label
docs.text:
Status: Superseded by ADR-0020 (October 2026): Watchtower is gone; the agent runs the nightly updates, every app updates unless its x-homelab has a pin or it is a database or built locally.

Decision: WATCHTOWER_LABEL_ENABLE=true; every service states com.centurylinklabs.watchtower.enable explicitly. Rationale: Updates happen where they are safe. The proxy (built locally), databases (major versions are pinned), and MoneyMatter (pinned build) are excluded and updated deliberately. The maintained nickfedor/watchtower fork is used because it negotiates the Docker API version.

docs.title: ADR-0007: Database dumps scheduled by launchd
docs.text: Context: Duplicati runs in a container and cannot run host commands before a job. Decision: ./homelab backup dumps every database at 03:30 into recovery-staging, and the Duplicati jobs run afterwards. Rationale: LaunchAgents run as the user, in the session where OrbStack lives, and the same command works by hand. The Linux and Windows profiles do the same with a systemd user unit and the user's Run key (all three now start one background agent, homelab agent, which runs the backup at 03:30).

docs.title: ADR-0008: compose files are the catalog; one CLI in Go
docs.text: Context: Describing apps in several places (scripts, JSON, docs) let them drift apart. Decision: Every app is a service with an x-homelab block in compose/<category>.yaml (included by compose.yaml) or stacks/*/compose.yaml. One Go binary (./homelab) installs, proxies, publishes, backs up, monitors, and documents from that metadata. Facts in the notes are generated from it. Rationale: A single source cannot drift. Go builds a single small binary with no runtime to install, starts instantly, and has testing built in.

docs.title: ADR-0009: One shared Docker network
docs.text: Decision: Every project joins the external homelab network. Web services are reached by service name; databases stay on their stack's private network. Rationale: No hairpin through host.docker.internal, no published ports needed for the proxy or the tunnel, and a database can never be reached from another stack. Service names must therefore be unique across stacks; homelab validate enforces it.

docs.title: ADR-0010: Native Jellyfin
docs.text: Decision: Jellyfin runs as the macOS app, not a container. Rationale: Containers on macOS have no access to Apple's hardware video encoder; the native app does. The CLI still proxies it (host.docker.internal:8096), and Duplicati backs up its data folder.

docs.title: ADR-0011: One .env for every project
docs.text: Decision: All projects read ~/Homelab/.env (the CLI passes --env-file). Rationale: One file to protect (mode 0600), one file in the Secrets backup job, and secrets generated in one place. COMPOSE_PROJECT_NAME must never be set in it, or it would override each stack's project name.

docs.title: ADR-0012: Home mode (no domain) is the default
docs.text: Context: A domain means a Cloudflare account, an API token, AdGuard on every device, and a certificate: the steps where a new household got stuck. Decision: HOMELAB_DOMAIN is empty in .env.example, so every new homelab, git clones included, starts in Home mode: Tailscale Serve gives each app https://homelab.<tailnet>.ts.net:<port>, and homelab tailnet setup reruns after every install. An existing .env keeps its domain; setting one later switches to the proxy, AdGuard, and the tunnel. Trade-offs: Each device needs Tailscale, nothing is published to the internet, and single sign-on with Pocket ID needs a domain.

docs.title: ADR-0013: The app updates itself from a numbered build of main
docs.text: Context: Downloading a build, dragging it to Applications, and clearing the download flag is too much to ask for every change. Decision: Every push to main that touches the app or the engine publishes the builds as a numbered release, the repository's Latest: VERSION with the patch raised by the commits since VERSION changed (v0.9.4-beta), so each build has a version people can read without a commit to bump it. Builds carry their version, commit, and repository (-X main.version, main.commit, main.repo); internal/selfupdate compares the commit with the newest build (the Latest release, or the newest vX.Y.0 on the stable channel), checks the download against GitHub's SHA-256 digest, replaces the app, and reopens it. See Releasing. Trade-offs: Until the builds are signed, the update trusts GitHub's release and digest. A release for every build fills the releases page; the stable channel takes only vX.Y.0. Since then (October 2026): on Windows the update unpacks the portable zip with Windows' own PowerShell (as an administrator only in Program Files) instead of running the installer, which SmartScreen and Smart App Control blocked as an unsigned program; an update that does not go in place says why, from update.log, instead of being offered again. Since then (November 2026, the owner's call): each release is one more than the newest, not the commits since VERSION changed: 0.17.0, 0.17.1, … 0.17.10, then 0.18.0 by itself (internal/tools/nextversion). Numbers like 0.16.41 said nothing a person could use; one number per release reads as a count of releases, and a new minor every eleven gives the stable channel something to move to. VERSION is the floor, raised by hand for a bigger step.

docs.title: ADR-0014: One engine, followed live through a local socket
docs.text: Context: The app, the menu bar item, and the phone each polled the container runtime every 10 to 60 seconds, so a stopped app showed late and each asked the runtime on its own. Decision: The engine follows docker events (internal/engine), gathering a burst into one change. The agent serves it on a socket only your account can open (/v1/status, /v1/events as Server-Sent Events); the app and the menu bar item follow it, and homelab serve passes the changes on to paired phones. Without the agent, each follows the runtime itself. Trade-offs: One more long-running process to keep healthy; a client falls back to its own follower, so nothing depends on it. Since then (0.15): the events, the containers, and the commands run in them go through the engine's own API (internal/dockerapi), with the docker CLI behind it; each change on /v1/events carries the Status read after it, and /v1/cards serves Status's cards once for every window and phone.

docs.title: ADR-0015: A typed Preact frontend, compiled and committed
docs.text: Context: The frontend was one 2,000-line script building the page by hand: no types against the Go side, and every live change rebuilt whole screens (losing focus and typed values). Decision: TypeScript checked against types generated from the methods the app binds, and Preact components per screen, compiled by esbuild into web/dist/app.js. The built file is committed, so go build needs no Node; CI fails while it is out of date. Preact rather than React or a framework with its own build: 10 KB, the same model, and no runtime beyond the bundle. Trade-offs: A contributor changing the frontend needs Node for make frontend; Go-only work does not.

docs.title: ADR-0016: The watchdog heals once, then leaves it to a person
docs.text: Context: Docker restarts a container that stops, not one that hangs (running, but unhealthy or not answering), and those stayed down until someone clicked Fix it. Decision: The watchdog restarts an app whose check failed on two runs in a row, at most once in 6 hours (AUTO_HEAL), and says so. An app updated in the last 6 hours is left to the rollback, which now also counts a page that stopped answering; a crash loop is left to Docker. Settings that changed under a running container are shown, not applied by themselves: recreating is the user's call (Fix it). Trade-offs: A restart can hide a slow leak until the next one; the alert on every restart keeps it visible.

docs.title: ADR-0017: CPU weights for background work, not throttling
docs.text: Context: Backups, photo indexing, and downloads could slow the apps people were using. Decision: Background services and the backup's own containers run with cpu_shares: 256 (a quarter of Docker's default). Weights only count while the CPU is busy, so idle machines still give background work all of it. Trade-offs: Only between containers: native apps such as Jellyfin are outside it. Watching load and changing limits on the fly was left out as more moving parts for the same result.

docs.title: ADR-0018: Not now: Docker Go SDK, tsnet, several machines
docs.text: Decision: Left out for now: the Docker Go SDK in place of the docker CLI (its JSON is already typed, and the CLI resolves each system's socket, context, and Windows pipe, which could not be tested here); Tailscale built into the binary with tsnet (Tailscale Serve already gives every app its address); several machines as one, and moving apps between them by power (a different product, for a household with one computer); GitOps (a homelab folder that is a git checkout already updates with homelab upgrade). Revisit when: the CLI's output stops being enough, or a household runs the homelab on more than one machine. Since then (0.15): the Docker part is being revisited, as the 0.10 timings on Windows asked: a small client of the engine's API of the homelab's own (not the SDK) reads the containers and runs commands in them, found as the CLI finds the socket, with the CLI as its fallback (DOCKER_API). A new ADR replaces this part once the timings on each machine are in (Roadmap).

docs.title: ADR-0019: Kopia as an optional second backup engine beside Duplicati
docs.text:
Status: Accepted in October 2026, with the owner's answers below (Roadmap 0.13).

Context: Duplicati is the only engine. One engine is one way to fail: its local database can need a repair before a restore, a restore of a large job is slow, and a bug or a corrupted destination loses every copy at once. The 3-2-1 rule (three copies, two kinds of storage, one off-site) is easier to meet with a second, independent copy.

Proposal:

  • What it backs up: the same read-only sources as Duplicati (/source/appdata, /source/homelab-appdata, /source/stacks, /source/immich, /source/jellyfin, /source/calibre) and recovery-staging (the dumps and the secrets copy), as Kopia snapshots, one per source, so a restore can pick one app's folder.
  • Where: its own destination, never Duplicati's folder: KOPIA_REPOSITORY, a folder (a second drive, or a cloud drive's folder) or an S3-compatible bucket (Backblaze B2, Wasabi). The repository is encrypted with KOPIA_PASSWORD, kept with the recovery kit like DUPLICATI_SECRETS_PASSPHRASE.
  • How it runs: kopia/kopia (Docker Hub) as an optional app in compose/system.yaml, in server mode with its web page (admin only), on the same read-only mounts as Duplicati. Its own schedule runs after the nightly dumps (03:30), with cpu_shares like the other background work. Failures go to ntfy's duplicati-alerts topic through Kopia's webhook notifications, so one topic covers backups.
  • Restore test: homelab restore-test --auto gains --engine kopia. It picks the same sample of unchanged files from /source/appdata, restores them from the newest snapshot with kopia restore into recovery-staging/restore-test, and hashes them against the live files, exactly as for Duplicati. restore-test.json records the engine with each drill, and the 30-day reminder counts each engine. The nightly real-Docker run tests both.
  • The Backups screen: the off-site tile lists each engine with its last run and its last passed restore test; Test a restore asks which engine when both are set up. With Kopia not installed, nothing changes.
  • How someone chooses: Duplicati stays the default, set up by Setup. Kopia is in Choose apps › System as optional, described as "a second, independent copy somewhere else". Setup's backup step gains a line once it is installed: where its repository is, and whether its first snapshot and restore test passed.

Trade-offs: two engines are two passwords, two destinations, and two schedules to explain; the disk is read twice each night; Kopia's web page is plainer than Duplicati's.

Alternatives:

  • A second Duplicati job to another destination: no new engine, but the same software, so not independent of Duplicati's bugs or its database.
  • Restic with Backrest's web page instead of Kopia: similar design (content-addressed, encrypted, deduplicated); Kopia has its own web page and server mode in one image, Backrest is a separate project wrapping restic.
  • Kopia instead of Duplicati: fewer moving parts in the end, but it replaces a working, tested engine and every household's existing backups.

Decision (the owner, October 2026): the safest and simplest choice for a household, each time.

  1. Beside Duplicati, not replacing it: Duplicati stays the default and the off-site copy; Kopia is the second, independent one.
  2. Kopia, not restic with Backrest: one app with its own web page, so fewer moving parts.
  3. Setup offers it as an optional step once it is installed, defaulting to a second drive; it never writes into Duplicati's destination.
  4. Yes: the nightly run tests a restore from both engines.

docs.title: ADR-0020: A rollback puts back the app's data with its image
docs.text:
Status: Accepted in October 2026, with the owner's answers below (ISSUE-0022). Done after 0.14.0: the agent runs the nightly updates, and the owner chose to remove Watchtower altogether rather than keep it to pull and recreate, so no container holds Docker's socket to write to it.

Context: A rollback starts the earlier image on today's data. An app whose newer version migrated its data (ntfy 2.11 after 2.34: "version 17 is higher than current version 13") then refuses to start. homelab update dumps databases first, but Watchtower's nightly updates are not preceded by anything, the rollback restores nothing, and files outside a dump (ntfy's message cache, SQLite apps' side files, settings folders) are not kept at all.

Proposal:

  • A copy before every update. Watchtower stops updating by itself: the nightly updates are run by the agent as homelab update --all --nightly at the same hour, using Watchtower only to pull and recreate (its --run-once mode, for the apps that have a newer image). Before each app is updated, the homelab:
  • dumps its databases, as homelab update does today;
  • stops it and copies its own data: the bind-mounted folders inside the homelab folder and its named volumes (tarred, as archive: does), into recovery-staging/before-update/<app>/<time>/;
  • starts the update.
  • What is left out: folders outside the homelab folder (MEDIA_ROOT, IMMICH_UPLOAD_LOCATION, Jellyfin's data), and any folder over a size limit (UPDATE_COPY_LIMIT, 2 GB by default). Those apps' schemas live in their databases, which the dump covers. The update says which folders it did not copy.
  • The rollback (by hand, or the watchdog's after a failed update) stops the app; moves today's data aside to recovery-staging/rolled-back/<app>/<time>/ (never deleted by the rollback); puts the copy back; restores the dump into its database (PostgreSQL through pgexec, SQLite as a file); then starts the earlier image. It says what was put back and that changes made since the update are in the rolled-back folder.
  • Keeping copies: the newest copy per app, until the rollback window closes (a week, as for the earlier image); the backup's clean-up removes older ones.

Trade-offs: each update stops the app for the copy (seconds for most, a minute for a large settings folder); disk for one copy per updated app; and anything written between the update and the rollback is set aside, not merged.

Alternatives:

  • Keep Watchtower as it is and copy every app's data in the nightly backup before 4 AM: no change to how updates run, but a copy of every app every night, and up to a few hours of changes lost on rollback.
  • Restore only the dumps (no folder copies): smaller, but leaves ntfy's case, and every SQLite app's side files, unsolved.
  • Offer "restore the dump from before the update" as a separate step after a rollback: least work, but a person must know to do it, and the watchdog's automatic rollback still loops.

Decision (the owner, October 2026): the safest and simplest choice for a household, each time.

  1. The agent runs the nightly updates (this proposal): only the job that updates knows the moment before, and it copies just the apps it is about to update.
  2. 2 GB per folder by default (UPDATE_COPY_LIMIT), and the databases are always dumped whatever their size; a folder left out is named in the update's result.
  3. The watchdog puts the data back by itself only when nothing new can have been written since the update: the app never came up healthy after it. Otherwise it rolls back the image, alerts, and offers Restore data as one step, so photos or documents added since the update are never set aside without a person choosing it.

docs.title: ADR-0021: Finances as a screen of the app, typed in by hand and kept on this machine
docs.text:
Status: Accepted; built in October 2026 (#311, #323) and recorded afterwards from the code and the patch notes. The reasons below are what the design shows, not the owner's words: correct them here if they differ.

Context: The household wanted to see, paycheck by paycheck, what checking holds once the bills are paid, which paycheck covers each bill, and net worth with the home's and car's equity. The catalog's budget apps (MoneyMatter, Actual Budget, Firefly III) keep what was spent; none reads pay and bills forward, and each is a separate app with its own sign-in, database, and update.

Decision:

  • A screen of Homelab Wizard, not a catalog app. Finances is in the sidebar beside Status and Backups, drawn by the same frontend on the computer and the phone companion; internal/finance reads the plan forward (paydays moved before weekends and bank holidays, interest a day at a time, cards paying what is charged to them).
  • Typed in by hand, no bank connection. Nothing about the household's money leaves the machine, and no bank credentials or aggregator are involved.
  • One file in the homelab folder: data/finance.json, written 0600 and whole (a failed write leaves the last one), each balance kept by the day it was typed in for net worth over time. The nightly backup copies it with the household's other records into the encrypted Homelab Secrets job.
  • Phones by permission: off for every phone until picked (Sees Finances or Changes Finances, apart from Can make changes), only over an encrypted connection, never to a kiosk screen.
  • No lost saves: each read carries the file's version, and a save made after another device's is refused with the latest shown and the form kept.

Trade-offs: balances go stale unless someone types them in (the heading says when they are a week old, and Update balances starts each at what is expected); no transaction history, categories, or imports, which stay the budget apps' job; and one more screen the app itself must keep working, outside the catalog's per-app proof (its checks are in the click-through and internal/finance's tests).

docs.title: ADR-0022: SQLite only for records that grow and are searched; small state stays in JSON
docs.text:
Status: Accepted, November 2026, from the maintenance order (the owner's call). First used by the record of what was done (internal/history, November 2026), then the alerts the homelab sent (internal/history's alerts table: 90 days, at most 5,000, Nov 11).

Context: The homelab keeps its own records as small JSON files in data/ (what is stopped, pinned, held, the watchdog's state, Setup's ticks), each changed whole under a lock beside it (internal/lockedfile, internal/applist) and copied by the nightly Secrets backup. That suits a record of a few kilobytes that is read whole. Two planned features are different: the Memory screen needs a day of samples taken every minute or so, and a record of what the homelab did needs months of entries that a screen filters and searches. As JSON, each would be read and rewritten whole on every change, and a search would read everything.

Decision:

  • SQLite, in pure Go: modernc.org/sqlite, no cgo, so the same build works on a Mac, Windows, and Linux without a C toolchain, as every other part of the CLI does.
  • One database file in data/ (data/homelab.db), this account's alone (0600), opened in WAL mode so the app, the agent, and a phone's requests read while one writes. The nightly backup copies it through SQLite's own backup, as it already does for the apps' SQLite databases, never as a file copied mid-write.
  • Only for data that grows and is searched: the Memory screen's samples, the action record and the alert record. Each table keeps a limit (by age or by count) from the day it is added, so nothing in it only grows (see the maintenance order's Memory and growth).
  • Small state stays in JSON files: a record read whole and changed a few times a day keeps its file, its lock, and its whole write. Nothing moves into the database for being a record alone.

Trade-offs: a dependency of some size (the pure-Go SQLite is a translation of SQLite's C, and grows the binary), a schema to migrate between versions, and a file that, unlike the JSON records, a person cannot read or fix in a text editor. In return the two growing records stay fast and bounded, and the rest of data/ stays as simple as it is.

Alternatives: JSON lines files with rotation (simple, but every search reads them all, and a day of samples is rewritten to trim it); bbolt or another key-value store (pure Go too, but no queries, so each screen would grow its own index); the cgo SQLite driver (the original C, but a C toolchain on every build machine and harder cross-builds).

docs.title: ADR-0023: The iPhone app away from home: the companion through the tunnel, behind Access and sealed end to end
docs.text:
Status: Accepted, November 2026 (the owner's call, Nov 9). The computer's side is built; the Setup step that makes the Access application and the iPhone's side follow.

Context: The phone companion (homelab serve) answered only at home and on the tailnet, and refused anything with Cloudflare's headers, so on cellular the iPhone app showed nothing. The owner doesn't use Tailscale and won't add an app to every device; they use the Cloudflare tunnel, with Proton VPN's DNS. The companion holds Finances, so putting it on the internet as the other apps are (ADR-0005: their own sign-in, CrowdSec, Cloudflare's rules) is not enough.

Decision: the companion gets one address through the tunnel, /api/tunnel, behind four locks, any one of which stops someone who got past the rest:

  1. Cloudflare Access with a service token on the companion's own hostname only. A request without the household's token is stopped at Cloudflare and never reaches the house. This narrows ADR-0005: the Homelab app sends the token itself (CF-Access-Client-Id and -Secret), so nobody completes a login, and no other app goes behind Access. The token reaches a phone only when it pairs at home, kept in its Keychain.
  2. Access's signed pass, checked by the companion (Cf-Access-Jwt-Assertion): RS256 by one of the team's keys (fetched from https://<team>.cloudflareaccess.com/cdn-cgi/access/certs, the team's name checked as one DNS label, cached an hour), for this application's audience, by the team's issuer, for the household's service token (common_name), and not expired. Anything else with Cloudflare's headers is refused, as before.
  3. The phone's own pairing: its device token, inside the sealed message, so a phone unpaired on the computer is cut off at once.
  4. Sealed end to end: at pairing, at home over an encrypted link, the phone and the computer agree a key (X25519, HKDF-SHA256 with the phone's ID), and every request and answer through the tunnel is sealed with it (AES-256-GCM; a request bound to its phone, an answer to its request). Cloudflare opens the tunnel's TLS, so without this it could read Finances; with it, it sees which phone, and nothing more. A request carries its time (within 2 minutes) and is taken once.

Through the tunnel the phone only looks: a method that changes anything (Finances' edits included), the household's settings, a stream, pairing, and the frontend are never served there. Ten wrong attempts lock an address, or a phone, out for 10 minutes. A wall screen, and a phone paired over plain home Wi-Fi, get no key, so never go out.

Trade-offs: the companion is reachable from the internet at all, where it wasn't; the locks are why that is acceptable, and each is tested (internal/companion/tunnel_test.go). The key lives in data/phones.json (0600) beside the hashed tokens, since a sealing key can't be kept as a hash; whoever can read that file can already read data/finance.json. Phones paired before this pair again once, at home. Cloudflare outages leave the phone with only what it last saw.

Alternatives: Tailscale (encrypted, no Access needed, but the owner won't install it); Access with a person's login (the app can't complete one, as ADR-0005 says); Access alone without sealing (Cloudflare could read every answer); a VPN server at home (another app on every device, and a port to open).

docs.title: Disaster Recovery
docs.text: What to do when the machine or an app is lost. Home mode (no domain, apps on your tailnet) is the default; steps marked with a domain apply only when HOMELAB_DOMAIN is set. If the old machine still works, use moving to a new machine instead of a restore.

docs.title: Recovery priorities
docs.text:
1. The machine, its container runtime (OrbStack on a Mac), and the homelab folder
  2. Secrets: Vaultwarden and .env
  3. Addresses: Tailscale in Home mode; with a domain, AdGuard Home, Nginx Proxy Manager, and CrowdSec
  4. Databases, then the apps that use them
  5. Monitoring, and with a domain public access (the tunnel)

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• The backup folder (the cloud drive account, or the external drive) and DUPLICATI_SECRETS_PASSPHRASE (in Vaultwarden, with an offline copy of it and of the Vaultwarden master password on the recovery kit: Backups › Recovery kit). It opens Homelab Secrets, whose homelab.env holds DUPLICATI_PASSPHRASE for every other job
  • Homelab Wizard (it carries the homelab files), or the GitHub repository
  • This documentation

docs.title: Scenario: full Mac rebuild
docs.text:
The machine is lost (stolen, dead disk) and the backup folder is all that is left. On the new Mac, install OrbStack (brew install --cask orbstack, with Start at login) and Homelab Wizard, make the homelab folder (Setup › Set it up for me, or git clone the repository to ~/Homelab), let the cloud drive finish syncing the backup folder, then:

cd ~/Homelab
./homelab rebuild "$HOME/Library/CloudStorage/ProtonDrive-you@proton.me-folder/Homelab Backups"

It asks for DUPLICATI_SECRETS_PASSPHRASE (from Vaultwarden or the recovery kit; the typing does not show), and with Duplicati's own command line in a throwaway container restores Homelab Secrets (.env and the household's records: the people, the paired phones, the sign-in settings, Finances), then, with the passphrase .env holds, the database copies and volumes, the apps' data, the stacks' data, and your own apps. Then it does what move in does: checks this Mac's folders (it stops, saying which, when the media drive is not plugged in; plug it in and run the same command again to carry on), starts each app on the version that wrote its data, loads each database from its copy, starts the apps that ran, installs the jobs, and makes Duplicati's jobs again from their backups. The photos, the Jellyfin library, and the books live on their own drives and are not restored by it; its list of what is left says how, for any that is missing. Then do steps 7 (Jellyfin), 8 (addresses and alerts), and 10 below. The nightly run does this against real Docker on a wiped machine, and its summary page has how long it took.

It shows what it will do and asks first (outside a terminal, add --apply). It refuses a homelab folder that already has apps' data (data/appdata), so a working homelab is never overwritten: rebuild into a new folder, or add --force to replace it. While it runs it keeps data/homelab-rebuild.json, so running it again after a stop (the media drive, say) carries on without restoring the files a second time.

The same by hand, in Duplicati's own window, when the command cannot be used:

  1. Install OrbStack (brew install --cask orbstack) and turn on Start at login.
  2. Install Homelab Wizard and choose Setup › Set it up for me (it makes ~/Homelab), or git clone the repository to ~/Homelab (that way needs Go: brew install go).
  3. Install Duplicati temporarily (or start only the duplicati service). In its UI: Restore › Direct restore from backup files, the folder secrets in the backup folder, and DUPLICATI_SECRETS_PASSPHRASE from Vaultwarden or the recovery kit. That gives homelab.env: copy it to ~/Homelab/.env and chmod 600 .env. It holds DUPLICATI_PASSPHRASE for every other job. Copy the files in its data folder (the household, paired phones, Finances, and the apps' sign-in settings) into ~/Homelab/data.
  4. The same way (Direct restore from backup files, with DUPLICATI_PASSPHRASE), restore the appdata folder to data/appdata, stack-data to appdata, and databases to recovery-staging.
  5. ./homelab up and watch it start the baseline (databases start empty).
  6. Restore each database from its dump (see below), then restart its app.
  7. Install Jellyfin (brew install --cask jellyfin), quit it, restore Homelab Jellyfin to its data folder, and start it.
  8. Addresses: in Home mode, Setup › Addresses on your tailnet (./homelab tailnet setup; it opens Tailscale's sign-in page when needed, no auth key required). With a domain, ./homelab domain setup. Then ./homelab notify setup and ./homelab schedule install.
  9. ./homelab duplicati setup (Setup › Create the backup jobs) makes the jobs again with the passphrases from the restored .env. Each job whose folder already holds its backup gets its database rebuilt from it (a repair) instead of a first run. Without that, Duplicati refuses to back up into the folder.
  10. Check everything: ./homelab status, ./homelab watchdog, ./homelab doctor, and open a few apps from a phone on mobile data (with Tailscale on in Home mode; with a domain, every public app).

docs.title: Scenario: moving to a new machine
docs.text:
When the old machine still works (a new Mac, say), there is nothing to restore from Duplicati. In the app: Backups › Moving to a new machine › Move out… on the old machine, and Move in… with that file on the new one. In Terminal, on the old machine:

cd ~/Homelab
./homelab move out --to /Volumes/Drive/homelab-move.tar

It backs up, stops the apps, packs .env, the apps' data, your own apps, and the newest database dumps into that one file, and removes the scheduled jobs, so the old machine stays stopped. Move the drive with the photos and media over. On the new machine, install the runtime and Homelab Wizard, make the homelab folder (Setup › Set it up for me, or git clone), then:

./homelab move in /Volumes/Drive/homelab-move.tar

It unpacks everything, stops if a folder in .env (the media drive, the photos) is not on this machine yet (fix it in Settings, then run ./homelab move in again to carry on), starts each app on the image it ran when the backup was made (by its digest, from recovery-staging/databases/images), loads each database from its dump, starts the apps that ran before, and installs the jobs. Its list of what is left names the apps on an older version than the newest: ./homelab update <app> moves each on once all is well, with a copy of its data first.
