docs.title: Next
docs.text:
The first batch, chosen because each makes the group menu safer or quicker. A loop builds this page in order, one pull request per feature (its prompt):

  1. Right-click an app's row (Everyday control): Built
  2. Stopped on purpose (Everyday control): Built
  3. Stop for a while (Memory): Built
  4. Undo (Everyday control): Built

docs.title: Everyday control
docs.text:
The things you do many times a day, made one click shorter.

  • Right-click an app's row (M, Built, #369): Open, Open on a phone, Copy address, Restart, Stop, Logs, Back up now, Tell me if it stops. Everything on the app's page, without opening it. A right-click on a group's heading opens its menu.
  • Stopped on purpose (M, Built, #367): an app you stop from the menu stays stopped. Start them all, the watchdog, and plugging in skip it, and its row says "Stopped by you" with Start beside it. The wait for a drive skips it too.
  • Undo (S, Built, #375): after Stop, Stop all, or Stop for a while, a note for 10 seconds: "Stopped 6 Media apps · Undo", and ⌘Z. Restart all has none (nothing to take back).
  • Right-click the sidebar (S, Built, #413): Status: Check again, Update all. Backups: Back up now, Test a restore. Finances: Add a transaction, Update balances.
  • Command palette (M, Built, #395): ⌘K (Ctrl+K elsewhere), then type "immich" for Open, Restart, or Logs, or type "stop media", "back up now", "update all".
  • Type to filter Status (S, Built, #385): start typing an app's name on Status and the list narrows, as Finder does; Escape clears it, and Return opens the first one's page.
  • A quick peek (M, Idea): Space on a selected row shows its last log lines, memory, uptime, and its address's QR code, without leaving Status.
  • Pinned apps (S, Built, #414): pin the apps you open most to the top of Status and of the menu bar item's Open an app.
  • Open, your way (S, Built, #415): ⌥-click (Alt-click) an address to copy it; ⇧-click Open to use the address on this computer instead of the domain.
  • What changed since you looked (S, Built, #416): a dot on each row whose state changed since you last opened Status (restarted, updated, stopped), cleared once seen.
  • Remember where you were (S, Built, #417): each screen keeps its scroll position and open sections between visits and restarts.
  • Drop files onto an app (M, Idea): drop a PDF on Paperless's row and it goes into its import folder; an album folder on beets lands in its downloads; photos on Immich go to an album named for the day.

docs.title: Answers on hover
docs.text:
Questions the screen can answer without a click.

  • Why it restarted (S, Built, #411): hover "up 9 minutes" for the reason: an update, a crash, the battery saver, the watchdog, or you, with the time.
  • The week's outages (S, Built, #406): hover "94% up this week" for a strip of the week with each time it was down, and why.
  • A balance opens its own group (S, Built, #379): clicking Cash or Investments in the sidebar opens Net worth on that group's accounts, not the whole page; each account opens its own history.
  • A balance's accounts (S, Built, #409): hover a group in the sidebar's Accounts for its accounts and how long since each was updated; a dot marks one older than a month.
  • A backup's contents (S, Built, #418): hover a backup's time on Backups for its size, what it holds, and how long it took.
  • An update's notes (S, Built, #419; "updates held" only, as Status has no per-app update waiting yet): hover "updates held" or an update waiting for the release's first lines.

docs.title: Memory and performance
docs.text:
So a laptop or a small machine stays responsive, and you can see why when it does not.

  • A Memory screen (L, Mocked up): what OrbStack (or Docker Desktop) uses of the machine's memory, split into the apps, the runtime and its cache, and what is free; today's peak; a chart of the day with its spikes named (the nightly updates, Immich reading photos); every group and app with its memory now and its peak; and Ways to free memory. Needs a day of samples kept by the agent, and the runtime's own total.
  • An app's Memory tab (M, Mocked up): each part of an app (its server, its database, its machine learning) with its line over the day, its peak, and how often it was stopped for memory.
  • Stop for a while (S, Built, #367): Stop for an hour, until tonight, or until tomorrow, then it starts again by itself; from the group menu and an app's page, and later from a row's right-click and the Memory screen.
  • Memory limits (M, Mocked up): a limit for an app or one part of it, suggested from its peak; reaching it restarts that part, and the watchdog says so.
  • Stop when idle (L, Mocked up): stop Immich's machine learning after an hour with no new photos and start it when a phone uploads; the same for other apps with a clear sign of work.
  • Ways to free memory (M, Mocked up): suggestions from what the apps actually do: one idle for hours, two that do the same job (Komga and Kavita), one not opened in a month, and the runtime's limit set higher than the apps need.
  • Memory pressure alert (S, Built, #458): an alert when the apps stay above 90% of the memory Docker has for 10 minutes or more (two watchdog runs in a row), naming the three biggest; Status's Watchdog card lists them, each with Stop, until it comes down.
  • Quiet hours for heavy work (M, Idea): Tdarr, Immich's jobs, and the downloads run at night, or while the machine is idle and plugged in, and pause when you use it.
  • Disk space ahead (M, Idea): at today's rate, when each drive fills (photos, downloads, backups), and which app grows fastest.

docs.title: Reliability and self-healing
docs.text:
The homelab looks after itself, and says what it did.

  • Start in order (M, Idea): Start all and Restart all start databases and VPNs first (Gluetun before qBittorrent), from each app's dependencies.
  • One app at a time (M, Idea): the nightly update updates one app, waits for it to answer, then the next; the first that stays unwell is rolled back and the rest are held until morning.
  • An update window per app (S, Built, #457): update Immich only on Sundays (an app's page › Only on Sundays, or homelab updates days immich sun for any days). Still an idea: Vaultwarden at once when a security release comes out.
  • A restart that keeps failing (S, Built, #427): an app Docker restarted three times in an hour is stopped and flagged, with its last log lines, instead of restarting forever.
  • After sleep (S, Built, #422): when the machine wakes, every app is checked at once rather than at the watchdog's next run.
  • A drive comes back (S, Built, #423): when an unplugged drive returns, the apps waiting for it start within a minute, as the battery saver now does for power. On Linux, where Docker made an empty folder in the drive's place and started the app on it, the library folders now wait for the drive too (#428).
  • What happened overnight (S, Built, #420): Status's first line in the morning: "Overnight: 4 apps updated, 1 rolled back, a backup of 2.1 GB, nothing needed you."

docs.title: Security and privacy
docs.text:
Safe by default, and easy to check.

  • Hide amounts (S, Built, #368): one shortcut (⌘⇧H) and a menu item blur every money figure, the sidebar's balances included, for screen sharing or someone at your shoulder (Finances' Hide amounts and a wall-screen card).
  • Lock with Touch ID or Windows Hello (M, Idea): Finances, sign-in details, and the recovery kit ask for the system's own unlock after the app has been idle.
  • What is reachable from the internet (M, Idea): a check from outside, through the tunnel, that lists every address it can reach and flags anything admin that answers.
  • A log of what was done (M, Idea): every start, stop, update, restore, and settings change, by whom (this computer, or which phone), kept for 90 days and searchable.
  • Phones that expire (S, Built, #455): a phone's access to Finances or to changes ends after a time you choose, and Settings › Phones shows when each was last seen.
  • Tailnet devices (S, Built, #465): every device on the household's tailnet in Settings › Phones, online or when it was last seen (a month unseen is marked), and Remove for a lost phone, in Tailscale's admin console where it is done.
  • Rotate a secret (M, Idea): a new database password or API key put in .env and into the app, then the app restarted, in one step; old ones flagged after a year.
  • Images with known holes (M, Idea): each running image checked against the public vulnerability lists weekly; one with a critical finding is named with its fix version.
  • What CrowdSec stopped (S, Built, #430): the addresses banned today, where from, and what they tried, on the proxy's page (and CrowdSec's): Status › Nginx Proxy Manager.
  • Two-step sign-in, nudged (S, Idea): Setup and the weekly summary name each admin app without a second factor until it has one.

docs.title: Backups and data
docs.text:
Confidence that what matters can come back.

  • Restore one file (M, Idea): browse a backup by app and date and bring back one document, photo, or setting without restoring the whole app.
  • Yesterday's version of an app (M, Idea): Restore to last night on an app's page: its data and its image as they were, the current ones kept aside in case.
  • A copy before anything risky (S, Built, #461): a database dump just before an update (with the app's own data, kept for the week a rollback can use it), before a restore (rollback --data sets today's aside), and now before an app starts again on changed settings (a new address, signing in with Pocket ID, settings changed by hand), kept with the nightly dumps.
  • What changed since last night (S, Built, #435): each backup's size beside the night before's, with a warning when an app's data shrinks sharply (under half of a copy of 1 MB or more).
  • Weekly integrity check (S, Built, #463): Duplicati's own Verify of each job on Sundays (homelab backup-check, a sample of its files against the hashes it recorded); a damaged file is a failing check on Status and a red line on Backups until a check passes again.

docs.title: Notifications and alerts
docs.text:
Few, clear, and useful when they come.

  • Buttons on alerts (M, Built, Nov 2026): "Radarr stopped" on the phone with Restart and Show logs: ntfy's view buttons, as links into the iPhone app (homelab://), which open the app's page with the action waiting for a tap and Face ID; more than one app down gets Open Status.
  • Quiet hours (S, Built, #439): no sound overnight unless it is serious (backups failing for days, the vault unreachable). QUIET_HOURS=22-7 by default; Settings › Quiet hours.
  • One alert for many (S, Idea): three apps stopping together is one alert, "3 apps stopped: the drive was unplugged", not three.
  • Snooze an alert (S, Built, #469): snooze one failing check for an hour or a day beside it on Status's Watchdog card (or homelab notify snooze): still checked, not alerted about until it wakes, and alerted then if it still fails. Not from the phone's alert itself: ntfy's buttons would need a way in to the computer from the notification.
  • Who hears what (S, Idea): each person picks the alerts they get; the household's other members get only the ones about their apps.

docs.title: The household
docs.text:
The homelab as something a family uses, not one person.

  • Guest access (M, Idea): a guest's sign-in to chosen apps (Jellyfin, an Immich album) that ends on a date.
  • A printable welcome sheet (S, Built, #446): each person's apps, addresses, and QR codes on one page for the fridge, linked from their welcome page, with no sign-in link or password on it.
  • Each person's apps (S, Built): a person's welcome page lists only the apps they use, with their phone app for each (homelab person apps <name> <app>…).
  • What's new for the family (S, Idea): a short page in plain words when an app they use gains something (a new player in Navidrome), not the technical notes.

docs.title: Apps and the catalog
docs.text:
Picking, trying, and using apps.

  • Import music on a button (M, Idea): beets' import from Status, with the albums it is unsure of asked in the app instead of Terminal. The Roadmap has the library work in order.
  • Try an app for a day (M, Idea): install an app on trial; tomorrow the app asks to keep it or removes it with its data.
  • Suggestions from what you use (S, Built, #445): with Navidrome, beets; with Sonarr, Bazarr; each with one line on why. Thirteen, in each app's goes_with, under Choose apps › Add more › Suggested for what you run.
  • Two apps that do the same job (S, Built, #438): Choose apps says when you already run one that does it (Komga and Kavita, Navidrome and Jellyfin's music), and why you might want both. Eight pairs, in each app's same_job.
  • Quick settings on an app's page (M, Idea): the two or three settings people change most (Navidrome's scan interval, Immich's machine learning on or off) as switches, without opening the app.

docs.title: The desktop and the menu bar
docs.text:
The app at home on each system.

  • A Dock menu (M, Idea): right-click the Dock icon for Open an app ▸, Back up now, Pause updates. Likely needs native code beyond the app's framework; the Windows taskbar's jump list and a Linux desktop file's actions are the same idea.
  • An app's submenu in the menu bar (S, Idea): Open an app ▸ Immich ▸ Open, Restart, Logs.
  • ⌥-click the menu bar item (S, Idea): Option-click (as with Wi-Fi) for more: each app's memory, the runtime's version, Restart the runtime.
  • A global shortcut (S, Idea): one key anywhere opens the command palette over whatever you are doing.
  • Shortcuts and Siri (L, Idea): actions for the Shortcuts app: back up now, stop an app, the homelab's state.
  • Widgets (L, Idea): Status and net worth on the desktop and the phone's home screen, once signing is in place (the Roadmap has the iOS app).

docs.title: The phone companion
docs.text:
The household's phones as a second screen.

  • The last Status, offline (S, Built, #453): away from home with no tailnet, it shows the last Status it saw and when, rather than an error. The page itself is kept on the phone too (a service worker), where it's served over HTTPS.
  • Add to Home Screen, done right (S, Built, #452): an icon, a name, and a splash screen, so it opens like an app: PNG icons an iPhone takes (and a maskable one for Android), a splash in the app's own background, and the bar above it light or dark with the phone.
  • Quick actions (S, Built, #447): long-press an app for Open, Restart, Stop for a while, on a phone that may make changes (also Start, Stop, and Logs).

docs.title: Media library cleanup
docs.text:
Begun by the owner on Nov 3, 2026, with the two scripts and a wider brief (films, TV, audiobooks, the Downloads inbox, lyrics, a nightly sweep, and space reclaimed by itself): built as Tidy Up. The plan below was its starting point; where the brief changed it (reports in reports/media; Windows too; duplicates and verified backups to the Trash by themselves rather than kept for review), Tidy Up's page says how it works now.

  • Library cleanup (L, Built, #376): the owner's tested engine, two stdlib Python scripts added unchanged at tools/media/ (music_organizer.py: init, status, scan, run, finalize, verify, undo, delete-backup; books_organizer.py: init, status, review, apply, undo), wrapped, not rewritten. The plan, agreed in outline:
  • Settings from the homelab: homelab media writes data/homelab_media.json before each run (libraries from MEDIA_ROOT, pause_containers as the containers that mount each library, the beets container's image, engine: container) and always passes --config.
  • CLI: homelab media music|books <action> [flags] runs the script with --events json, prints the events as ordinary CLI lines, forwards flags, and never adds --yes itself.
  • Background and lock: --background runs the job detached (it outlives the window and the app), holding data/media.lock (pid, script, action, start) and writing logs/media/<job>.jsonl; one media job at a time; a stale lock (its process gone) offers to run the same action again, which the scripts resume.
  • A Library cleanup page from the Media group's menu and Navidrome's and Calibre-Web's pages: status --json; Scan → Run → Finalize → Verify → Delete backup, Undo after Finalize; Books: Review → Apply → Undo; live progress, a summary from the result event, and buttons for the album report CSV, the planned changes CSV, the books review page, and Music - Needs Attention.
  • Confirmations: a native dialog before each step that changes anything, and only then --yes; Delete backup in an in-app sheet that needs DELETE typed (Wails' dialogs take no text).
  • Battery: no music run on battery; Start when plugged in, picked up by the awake job within a minute of power.
  • Updates: while the lock is held, nightly updates and Update apps postpone every app whose container mounts a media library (Navidrome, beets, Calibre-Web, Komga, Kavita), and say so; updating one alone is refused; homelab up at login leaves them too, so nothing starts Navidrome mid-swap.
  • Backups: nothing backs up the music library today (Duplicati and Kopia have no music source), so the guard is a doctor and Needs a look warning for any job, the owner's own included, that covers the music folder without excluding .music-cleanup, and the exclusion built in should a music job ever be added.
  • Needs a look, from what the wrapper records after each step (data/media.json), so Status runs no Python: verify exit 2; built but not swapped; the originals' backup still there 14 days after finalize (Verify, then Delete backup); a books review that flagged misfiled books.
  • Preflight with plain fixes: python3 on the Mac (checked without macOS's install prompt), the library drive mounted, OrbStack running, the beets image pulled (offer to pull it), calibredb installed.
  • Tests with no Docker or Python: a stub python3 replays recorded event fixtures and exit codes; event parsing, settings generation, the lock, battery, nightly and single updates, up, and each Needs a look case.

Never delete ~/.music-cleanup or <library>/.music-cleanup/original (the original library's backup and the scripts' saved progress); only the script's own delete-backup, after DELETE is typed. Don't change the scripts' genre lists or matching rules; any other change to them small, in its own commit, with why. Four PRs: the CLI, settings, and lock; the page, dialogs, and progress; battery, updates, up, and backups; Needs a look and preflight.

Still to decide with the owner: where reports go (<homelab>/reports/media rather than ~/Downloads, proposed); after a crash or restart, a Resume button (proposed) or resuming a stopped Run at login; Mac and Linux only (proposed; the scripts and Calibre's paths are Mac and Linux); Needs a look as a line in its tile plus a note atop Status opening the page (proposed).

docs.title: Finances
docs.text:
The Finances loop's unfinished items, built by the features loop now, with their numbers from its backlog. The rest of its backlog (items 1 to 15, 22 to 24, and the MoneyMatter list) is in the app.

  • Hide amounts and a wall-screen card (S, Built, #368; F16): every money figure as $••• on ⌘⇧H, View › Hide Amounts, or the eye on Finances, kept in the plan so the phones follow; and a money card with the next payday, what is left after it, and the next 3 bills, on a wall screen allowed it in Settings › Phones.
  • The calendar, further ahead (S, Built, #373; F20): a payment past the chart's 93 days, such as a yearly renewal, shows in its month a year ahead, without a balance.
  • Card charges on the calendar (S, Built, #380; F21): a bill charged to a card shows on its day, marked "on Chase Freedom", with the card's due day.
  • Finances on the phone (M, Built, #381; F17): the phone's Dashboard opens with Coming up (the next two weeks of bills, card charges on their cards) and the goals; the calendar (a list of days), Renewing soon, and Update balances (one sheet, every account) were already there.
  • Export (S, Built, #405; F18): the plan and its projection as CSV and JSON, and a printable month.
  • Polish, all along (S, Idea; F19): empty states for a new plan, alignment, 860px and phone widths, contrast themes, focus order, labels; a little in each Finances round.

docs.title: Accessibility and polish
docs.text:
Details that make it feel finished.

  • Status read aloud (S, Built, #451): VoiceOver and Narrator announce a job's progress and a row's change, not only the result: Vikunja: Restarting…, then Vikunja: Running, and apps that go down together in one line.
  • A sheet of shortcuts (S, Built, #450): press ? (or Keyboard shortcuts in ⌘K) for the shortcuts of the screen you are on, then those that work everywhere and each screen's key.
  • Shapes as well as colours (S, Built, #449): each state's dot also has a shape (a circle when up, a triangle when stopped or it needs a look, a cross when down), for colour-blind eyes, small screens, and contrast themes.
  • Every menu by keyboard (S, Built, #369, #413): right-click menus open with the context-menu key and Shift+F10, and work like More… (arrows, Escape): an app's row, a group's heading, and the sidebar.

docs.title: Insight
docs.text:
What the homelab did for you, in numbers you can trust.

  • A monthly report (M, Idea): uptime, backups and restore tests, updates, memory, and what the apps replaced in money, as a page and a PDF.
  • Health in one line (S, Built, #470): "All well", or the one thing that needs you (an app in its row's words, several in one line, or a failing check that is no app's), at the top of every screen but Status, with Open Status.
  • Savings over time (S, Built, #437): what the apps have saved since the homelab started, month by month, from Savings: hover Instead of subscriptions on Status.

docs.title: Getting Started
docs.text:
From an empty computer to a homelab the whole household uses, without reading any code. Set aside an afternoon; most of it is waiting for downloads. The steps below show a Mac; on Windows, Linux, or a Steam Machine only the first section differs.

Tip

The desktop app's Setup screen walks through the same steps with a live check for each one, and does the technical ones for you. This page explains what each step is for and what to have ready.

docs.title: What you need
docs.text: Why Cost A computer that stays on Every app runs on it: a Mac (a Mac mini, or a MacBook kept plugged in), a Windows 10 or 11 PC, a Linux machine, or a Steam Machine. 16 GB of memory is comfortable; 8 GB runs the Start here apps. Already owned A free Tailscale account Gives every app a private https:// address that opens on your own phones and computers, at home and away. Nothing is published to the internet. Free A cloud folder for backups Encrypted copies of everything leave the house every night. Proton Drive is what this homelab uses. An existing plan An external drive (optional) Movies, music, books, and photos that do not fit on the computer. Already owned A domain on Cloudflare (optional, later) Short addresses such as photos.example.com, and photos, passwords, documents, and music open away from home without Tailscale. It also needs the router's admin page, to give the computer an address that never changes. See Later: a domain of your own. About $11 a year

docs.title: 1. Install the basics
docs.text:
On a Mac:

  1. Install OrbStack, the engine the apps run in: download it from orbstack.dev (Apple Silicon), open the download, drag OrbStack to Applications, and open it; it asks for the Mac's password once to finish. (Homelab Wizard's Setup screen links to the same page with Download OrbStack.) With Homebrew instead:
brew install --cask orbstack

Open OrbStack once and turn on Start at login in its settings. Optional, with Homebrew: brew install smartmontools lets the homelab read each drive's health and warn before one fails; everything else works without it.

  1. Install Homelab Wizard. The app isn't signed with an Apple Developer ID yet, so macOS stops it the first time. Either way below takes about a minute, and you do it once; after that the app keeps itself current (Update now on the line at the top of the window).

With Terminal (one line, no warning, because macOS doesn't stop downloads made from Terminal):

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Snooper42/homelab-wizard/main/install.sh | sh

It downloads the newest build from Releases › Latest, checks it against GitHub's SHA-256 checksum, copies it to Applications, and opens it.

Without Terminal (the browser):

  1. On GitHub › Releases › Latest, download Homelab-Wizard-macOS.dmg and open it.
  2. Drag Homelab Wizard onto Applications, then open it from Applications.
  3. macOS says it cannot verify the app: click Done (not Move to Trash).
  4. Open the Apple menu › System Settings › Privacy & Security, scroll to Security, and click Open Anyway beside “Homelab Wizard” was blocked.

  5. Enter the Mac's password, then click Open Anyway once more. It opens like any other app from then on.

  6. Open Homelab Wizard. On a new Mac it offers Set it up for me: it makes ~/Homelab from the homelab files it carries, with no git or Terminal needed. Later, Update now on the line at the top of the window brings both the homelab files and the app up to date, keeping your settings, data, and own apps, and saving a copy of any file you changed as .local.

To work on the homelab itself instead, clone it (the first time, macOS offers to install its command line tools; accept), and brew install go for the ./homelab commands:

git clone git@github.com:Snooper42/homelab-wizard.git ~/Homelab

Either way, Homelab Wizard finds ~/Homelab on its own and opens on Setup. Every new homelab starts in Home mode: no domain, and every app at an address on your tailnet.

docs.title: On Windows, Linux, or a Steam Machine
docs.text:
The steps are the same with each system's pieces (Host has the details):

Windows 10 or 11 Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, Arch Steam Machine (SteamOS, desktop mode) The engine Docker Desktop with WSL 2 (winget install Docker.DockerDesktop), started at sign-in Docker Engine and its compose plugin; your user in the docker group Setup › Set up Docker for me puts Docker in your home folder, where SteamOS updates leave it alone The files Set it up for me in the app, or git clone into your user folder, outside OneDrive Set it up for me, or git clone into ~/Homelab Set it up for me, or git clone into ~/Homelab The app In PowerShell: irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Snooper42/homelab-wizard/main/install.ps1 \| iex, or GitHub › Releases › Latest › Homelab-Wizard-Windows-Setup.exe (until the builds are signed, SmartScreen asks once: More info › Run anyway) curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Snooper42/homelab-wizard/main/install.sh \| sh, or Releases › Latest › the .deb, .rpm, or Arch package The same install.sh line (it puts the AppImage in ~/Applications), or Releases › Latest › the AppImage: chmod +x, open it, then Setup › Add to the app menu (right-click it there › Add to Steam to open it in Game Mode) Terminal commands homelab.cmd instead of ./homelab ./homelab ./homelab

Each app build carries the homelab CLI and the homelab files, so Setup's buttons work without Go or git. Update now brings the homelab files up to date and replaces the app with its newest build, as on a Mac. Settings › This PC (This machine) can start the tray icon at login, and the AppImage can add itself to the app menu; both follow it if you move it or swap in a newer one.

docs.title: 2. Work down the Setup screen
docs.text:
The steps are grouped as Needs you, Can wait, and Done.

  • Each step says first what it gives you, then what to do. One with more to know right now has a chevron that opens it.
  • A step that didn't work says why under it, and what to press once that is put right.
  • A step moves to Done when its check passes. Check again runs every check again.
  • Backups and Alerts when this machine is down sit under Can wait for the first week: get the apps going, then do them within the week. After that they count as left to do again, and the Setup tab's number says so.
  • Do the N I can do for you runs every step that is ready, one after another. It stops at the first that fails, or when what is left needs you: a setting, a choice, or something only a person can do.
Step What it gives you What you do OrbStack is running (Docker Desktop or Docker on Windows and Linux) The engine for every app. Nothing, once it's open. This laptop stays plugged in and open (MacBooks only) The apps stay reachable: plugged in, the homelab keeps the Mac awake (it never does on battery). Keep it on the charger with the lid open: closed, a MacBook sleeps unless a display is connected. The homelab is started The homelab's own apps running (updates, backups, alerts), and a settings file with a strong, unique password for each one. Click Start the homelab. The first start downloads every app and takes a while. Addresses on your tailnet (Tailscale) An https:// address for every app that opens on your own phones and computers, at home and away, with nothing published to the internet. Click Set up the addresses and sign in to Tailscale in the browser window it opens (make a free account there if you have none). In the Tailscale admin console › DNS, turn on HTTPS Certificates. No auth key is needed. This Mac opens the tailnet addresses The addresses in Status open on this Mac too, not only on your phones. Install the Tailscale app on the Mac and sign in with the same account. Password manager account Vaultwarden, used through the Bitwarden apps, for everyone's passwords. Shown once Passwords is installed. Click Open sign-ups for 10 minutes, create an account for each person at the passwords address, and let the window close. Two-step sign-in A stolen password alone opens neither the vault nor the homelab's settings. In each Vaultwarden account turn on two-step login with an authenticator app (keep the recovery code with the recovery kit). In Nginx Proxy Manager add a personal administrator and turn on Two-Factor Auth for it, then tick Done. The homelab's own proxy account (NPM_API_EMAIL) keeps it off, because the homelab signs in with it. Backups leave this machine Somewhere safe for the nightly encrypted backups: a cloud drive survives fire and theft, an external drive restores faster. Click the button for where they should go: Use Proton Drive, Use iCloud Drive (or Google Drive, OneDrive, Dropbox, whichever syncs on this Mac), or Use the … drive for an external drive. Each makes a Homelab Backups folder there. Any other folder: Settings › BACKUP_DESTINATION › Choose…. Backup jobs in Duplicati Settings, databases, and photos encrypted into the backup folder every night, so a dead disk loses nothing. Click Create the backup jobs. Then, in Settings, Copy DUPLICATI_SECRETS_PASSPHRASE into Vaultwarden and write it on paper: it is the one key to every backup. Alerts on the phone A message on the phone when an app, a backup, or the connection fails. Click Set up the alert token. In the ntfy app on your phone, add the ntfy address with user phone and the password from Settings › NTFY_PHONE_PASSWORD › Copy, then subscribe to the alert topics. Scheduled jobs The homelab starts again after a restart, backs up at night, and checks itself every 15 minutes. Click Install the jobs. Alerts when this machine is down An email when the Mac itself stops, which the homelab cannot report on its own. Create a free check at healthchecks.io (15-minute period and grace) and put its ping address in Settings. Tailscale on phones and computers The apps open on each device, at home and away. Install the Tailscale app on each phone and computer, sign in with the same account, then tick Done. Ad blocking on every device Ads and trackers blocked on every device signed in to Tailscale, with no router change. Shown once Ad blocking is installed from Choose apps. Click Set up ad blocking, then in the Tailscale admin console › DNS add the address it shows as a custom nameserver and turn on Override DNS servers.

If a step does not turn green, open Settings › This Mac (This PC, This machine) and click Make a diagnostics report. It writes one file with every check and log, with all passwords and tokens removed, that you can share when asking for help.

Once every step is done, Setup leaves the sidebar. It comes back by itself, with a count, if a step comes undone (a token runs out, the backup drive goes away) or the homelab has an update; ⌘4 (Ctrl+4) opens it any time. The machine's details stay in Settings › This Mac, and Status keeps a line on how this machine looks after the homelab.

docs.title: Later: a domain of your own
docs.text:
Home mode needs no domain. When you want short addresses such as photos.example.com, or want some apps (photos, passwords, documents, music) to open on a phone without Tailscale, put your domain in Settings › HOMELAB_DOMAIN and Save. Setup then swaps the tailnet step for these:

Step What it gives you What you do This machine keeps its address The app names keep pointing at the Mac at home. In the router's app, reserve the Mac's current address (the step shows it), then tick Done. Home DNS answers (AdGuard Home) The home network learns the apps' names, and ads are blocked for every device that uses it. Click Set up AdGuard: it answers AdGuard's first-run wizard with a new login. Cloudflare API token Lets the homelab get the padlock certificate and publish addresses. Create a token with the three permissions the step lists, and paste it in Settings. Never paste it anywhere else. Addresses and certificate https:// addresses for every app, on the Mac and on phones at home. Click Set up the domain. The first certificate takes a few minutes. Apps you install afterwards get their addresses by themselves. This Mac finds its apps by name The addresses open on this Mac too, also with a VPN on, and for apps added later. Click Find the apps on this Mac and enter the Mac's password once. Access away from home (Cloudflare Tunnel) Photos, passwords, documents, and music work on mobile data, with no ports opened on the router. Create a tunnel in Cloudflare Zero Trust, paste its token in Settings, and click Start the tunnel. Phones and computers use the home DNS Ads are blocked on every device at home. The app names already work at home without it, with a VPN on too: Set up the domain points them at this Mac in Cloudflare's DNS. On each device, set the Wi-Fi DNS server to the Mac's address, then tick Done. With a VPN app on a device, turn on its Allow LAN connections instead.

docs.title: 3. Choose more apps
docs.text:
Open Choose apps.

  1. Start here has the five things most homes want first: Photos, Passwords, Movies and TV, Music, and Files. Click the ones you want.
  2. Every other app is under Add more, where each says what it does and which subscription it can replace. Tick what you want, or pick a preset such as Household (smart home, groceries, to-dos, saved links, and a start page) or Media automation (the *arr apps, Seerr for requests, and qBittorrent behind a VPN).
  3. Read the plan on the right. It says in one line how many apps it installs and lists the ones you picked; helpers, port moves, and settings written wait under Details. When an app needs a setting first (the VPN key for qBittorrent, for example), the plan names it and the field to fill in appears below, with where to find it.
  4. Click Install.

If the apps would need more memory than the Mac has room for beside macOS and everyday apps, the plan says so and names the heaviest to leave out. On an 8 GB Mac the Start here picks fit; Immich's face and smart search (machine learning) is the one to add with care.

docs.title: 4. Set up each person's phone
docs.text:
In Home mode, first install the Tailscale app on the phone and sign in with the same account as the Mac: the apps' addresses open only on devices in your tailnet.

Install To Sign in at Tailscale Reach the apps at home and away (Home mode) your Tailscale account Bitwarden Use the shared password manager the passwords address, with the account from step 2 Immich Back up photos and browse them by face, place, or thing the photos address The Homelab app (iPhone and iPad) See Status, Backups, and Finances, and start or restart an app, behind Face ID pair it with the QR code in Settings › Phones (below); built with Xcode on your Mac for now (apple-client) ntfy Get the homelab's alerts (the person who looks after it) the ntfy address, as user phone Jellyfin or Infuse Watch the movies and shows you own the Jellyfin address Any Subsonic music app, or Feishin in a browser Listen to your music the music address

To open an app on a phone without typing its address, click its row in Status and then Open on a phone on its page: it shows the address as a QR code for the phone's camera, with what the phone needs (home Wi-Fi or Tailscale) and the app's phone app. Everything else opens in a web browser. Install Homepage from Choose apps for one start page with every app on it, kept up to date by the homelab; the Inventory lists every address too.

Each person can have their own sign-in, through Pocket ID, the household's sign-in app (without it, the card offers Set up the household's sign-in first):

  1. In Settings › People, click Add a person.
  2. Give their name, email, and the apps they use (All the apps, or Only these), and click Add them.
  3. The homelab makes their account and says so, with two ways to hand it over: Show their sign-in to scan opens their welcome page on the computer (a one-time link to sign in with their phone's face or fingerprint, as a code for its camera too, the apps they use, and their own tab on the start page); Open the fridge sheet opens a page with just their apps. The welcome page holds their sign-in link and their films and music password, so keep it for them: the fridge sheet is the one to email or hang up.

Later, Make a new sign-in link makes a fresh link (the old one stops working), and Remove turns their sign-in off and keeps their data.

Jellyfin and Navidrome have a password of their own, so that Infuse, the TV apps, and music apps such as Arpeggi can sign in. With JELLYFIN_API_KEY and a Navidrome administrator's login in Settings, adding someone makes those accounts too (one password for both, on their welcome page and nowhere else); New music and films password gives them a new one, and Remove turns them off. With a domain, ./homelab sso setup then lets Karakeep, Paperless-ngx, Mealie, Vikunja, and Open WebUI sign in with Pocket ID.

For the person who looks after the homelab: Settings › Phones › Pair a phone shows a QR code. Scan it from the Homelab app on an iPhone or iPad, and the app shows Status, each app's page, and Backups, at home or over Tailscale. A phone without the app (Android, a visitor's) scans it with its camera instead, and gets the same screens in its browser (Share › Add to Home Screen keeps it as an app). Your partner's phone pairs the same way; beside each phone, Sees Finances or Changes Finances adds the household's Finances to it (only for a phone paired with the https link).

docs.title: 5. Day to day
docs.text:
• Status shows every app with a coloured dot. A category where everything runs folds into one line; what needs a look stays open at the top. Each row has one button, Open (or Start when stopped); a click on the row opens the app's page, where it can be restarted, updated, stopped, or removed, its log read, and its nightly updates and alerts switched off. Sign-in details on the page of each app the homelab made a login for (the proxy, AdGuard, Duplicati, Kopia, PsiTransfer, Beszel, Nextcloud) shows the user and copies the password. When something is down, Fix it shows a plan and puts it right. The menu bar icon shows the same at a glance.
  • This week on Status is the Sunday summary at any time: apps, backups, the restore test, attacks caught, and disk space, with what needs a look marked. What the apps keep shows the largest app folders, and an app that was down part of the week says so (for example 96.2% up this week).
  • Updates to the apps install themselves at night. Pause them with Pause on Status's Nightly updates tile, or from the menu bar, before something important. If an update breaks an app, Roll back on its page puts the previous version back (kept for a week), and an app that stays unwell after an update is put back by itself.
  • Updates to the homelab itself show by themselves as one line at the top of the window (and Update to … in the menu bar): the app looks every 15 minutes and downloads what it finds. Update now puts the homelab files in place, then the newest Homelab Wizard, checked, and opens it again (on Windows, asking for an administrator's approval only when the app is in Program Files; on Linux, when it was installed from a package). If it cannot go in place, the line says why, with the release page to install it by hand.
  • Finances in the sidebar is the household's money, typed in by hand and kept on this computer: who gets paid and when, the accounts and cards, and the payments that repeat. Its dashboard shows checking over the next month, which paycheck covers each bill, and every account after each paycheck; Net worth draws it month by month, with your home's and car's equity. Nothing connects to a bank, and the file goes off-site with the nightly backup, encrypted.
  • Tidy Up in the sidebar keeps the music, films, shows, books, and audiobooks on the media drive in order. Drop a download into a folder it watches (Downloads, to start) and it works out what it is, cleans it up, and files it into the right library; What I did today lists each one with Undo, and each library's tab has its own clean-up. Anything it throws away goes to the Trash (Tidy Up).
  • Backups run at night. The Backups screen shows each app's newest copy and when a restore was last proven; once a month, click Test a restore to prove they work (Backups), and the homelab reminds you.
  • When something breaks, an alert arrives on the phone. Open Status and click Fix it, or read the app's log and restart it; with Ollama on this computer, Explain this under the log says in plain words what it shows. If that does not help, make a diagnostics report.
  • Text too small? Cmd and + or − (Ctrl on Windows and Linux) makes the whole app bigger or smaller, and Cmd and 0 goes back.

docs.title: Where to go next
docs.text:
• Troubleshooting: symptoms and their usual fixes.
  • Testing: the checklist for trying a new build.
  • Runbooks: step-by-step procedures, such as making an app public or updating the proxy.
  • Disaster Recovery: moving to a new machine (Backups › Moving to a new machine), rebuilding a lost one from the backups in one command (./homelab rebuild), and the printable recovery kit.
  • Upgrading: what each update asks of you.
  • Savings: what each app can replace, and what that is worth.

docs.title: Homelab Context
docs.text: The facts this project is designed around. Read this before suggesting a change. Addresses and names are examples: example.com for the domain, 192.168.1.10 for the Mac.

docs.title: Who and what
docs.text:
• A private homelab for one household. One person administers it; family members use a handful of apps from their phones.
  • The goal is to own photos, documents, passwords, music, and books, with little maintenance.
  • Uptime matters for passwords, photos, and documents; everything else can wait a day.

docs.title: The host
docs.text:
• One Mac with Apple Silicon (a Mac mini, or a MacBook kept plugged in), kept awake by the homelab's awake job. See Host. Linux and Windows profiles exist too.
  • OrbStack runs the containers. Jellyfin runs as a native app for hardware transcoding.
  • Media is on an external drive (MEDIA_ROOT, /Volumes/Media by default).
  • The homelab folder lives at ~/Homelab, outside folders that macOS syncs or protects.

docs.title: The network
docs.text:
• A home router with the Mac's address reserved (192.168.1.10 in these docs).
  • Many ISP routers cannot hand out a custom DNS server, so either each device points at the Mac by hand, or Tailscale's DNS setting does it for every Tailscale device.
  • No ports are open on the router.
  • Home mode is the default for a new homelab: with no domain (HOMELAB_DOMAIN empty), every app gets a private https address on the tailnet through Tailscale Serve.
  • With a domain on Cloudflare, apps get https://<name>.example.com through Nginx Proxy Manager, and public apps go through a Cloudflare Tunnel.

docs.title: Constraints that shape every decision
docs.text: Constraint Consequence One machine as the only host Single point of failure; backups must leave the Mac (Proton Drive or another synced folder) Containers run in a Linux VM No hardware video encoding in containers; paths must be shared with OrbStack FileVault Nothing starts after a reboot until someone logs in A consumer cloud drive as the off-site target Large media is not backed up; photos, documents, and settings are Family uses native apps No login gateway (Cloudflare Access) in front of public apps One administrator Prefer boring, documented, automated solutions over clever ones

docs.title: What runs by default
docs.text: In a git checkout, ./homelab up starts the full baseline: the proxy, DNS, security, backups, monitoring, passwords, photos, documents, budget, music, audiobooks, books, and comics. A folder the desktop app makes starts the small baseline instead (updates, backups, and alerts; HOMELAB_BASELINE=small), and the household picks the rest in Choose apps. Everything else is defined, documented, and one command away (./homelab install <app>). See Service Organization.

docs.title: The project
docs.text:
• Public on GitHub as Snooper42/homelab-wizard; the Go module is github.com/Snooper42/homelab-wizard.
  • One engine with three ways in: the homelab CLI (cmd/homelab), the Wails desktop app (app/, with its frontend in web/src, built into web/dist), and the phone companion (homelab serve), all on the packages in internal/. The phone companion is reached from a phone's browser or from the native iPhone and iPad app (apple-client/). Tidy Up's engines are Python scripts in tools/media. The Maintainer Guide lists each package.
  • The catalog is the compose files: compose.yaml, compose/<category>.yaml, and stacks/<name>/compose.yaml.
  • Every push to main that changes the app or the engine publishes a numbered release with builds for macOS, Windows, and Linux as the latest build (Releases › Latest), which the app updates itself from (Releasing).

docs.title: Mission
docs.text: Run the household's private services on hardware we own, securely and reliably, with as little upkeep as possible.

docs.title: Values
docs.text:
1. Data first. Photos, documents, and passwords are irreplaceable. Nothing else matters if they are lost.
  2. Secure by default. No open ports, no default passwords, least privilege everywhere.
  3. Boring is good. Prefer the simple, well-trodden solution to the clever one.
  4. One source of truth. The compose files describe the apps; the notes are generated from them; nothing is described twice.
  5. Reversible changes. Preview, back up, change, verify.
  6. Written down. If it is not in the docs, it does not exist.

docs.title: Rules
docs.text:
• No change without a backup and a rollback plan.
  • No secret in git, a note, a chat, a command line, or a log.
  • No public hostname without authentication in the app and CrowdSec in front of it.
  • No container gets the raw Docker socket to change the engine: read-only users go through the socket proxy, and the nightly updates run outside any container. The one exception is the optional Beszel agent, which runs on the host's network and reads the socket mounted read-only.
  • No app is added without a note, a backup decision, and a monitor (Contributing).
  • The baseline holds only what the household needs every day. Everything else is optional.

docs.title: Definition of healthy
docs.text:
• ./homelab status shows every baseline app running and healthy.
  • ./homelab watchdog passes.
  • Last night's backup jobs succeeded, and a restore test passed this month.
  • No unread alerts in ntfy.

docs.title: Hardware and system
docs.text: Property Value Model A Mac with Apple Silicon (a Mac mini, or a MacBook kept plugged in) OS macOS (current release) LAN address 192.168.1.10, reserved in the router Power Always on charger; the homelab's awake job keeps it from sleeping (KEEP_AWAKE) Container runtime OrbStack, Start at login on Native apps Jellyfin, Proton Drive, and the phone companion (homelab serve, a scheduled job) Homelab folder ~/Homelab (a git checkout, or a folder the desktop app made) Media /Volumes/Media (external drive)

docs.title: macOS settings
docs.text: Setting Value Why The awake job Installed with the other jobs (Setup › Install the jobs); it holds a caffeinate assertion while on power. The Mac must never sleep System Settings › Battery › Options "Prevent automatic sleeping on power adapter when the display is off" on Belt and braces with the awake job System Settings › General › Login Items OrbStack, Proton Drive, Jellyfin, Homelab Wizard (its menu bar item) Everything comes back after a login Automatic login Not available with FileVault on; after a restart someone must log in Accepted trade-off (see Known Issues) AirPlay Receiver Leave on or off; no homelab app uses ports 5000 or 7000 Kavita is published on 5500 for this reason Firewall On, with OrbStack allowed incoming connections The proxy and DNS must accept LAN traffic Software updates Install manually during a maintenance window An unattended restart leaves everything stopped until login

docs.title: OrbStack settings
docs.text: Setting Value Start at login On Memory limit At least 8 GB (Immich's machine learning and Paperless's OCR are the heaviest) Rosetta On (MoneyMatter's images are Intel-only) File access Allow access to /Volumes and to the Proton Drive folder when macOS asks

docs.title: Mac-specific behaviour
docs.text:
• Paths: every path a container uses must be under /Users, /Volumes, or /private/tmp; OrbStack shares these.
  • Media drive: the startup job waits up to 15 minutes for /Volumes/Media before starting. If the drive is unplugged while apps run, unplug it only after ./homelab stop on the media apps.
  • Privacy prompts: the first time a container reads /Volumes/Media or the Proton Drive folder, macOS may ask OrbStack for permission. Allow it, or grant Full Disk Access to OrbStack.
  • Address changes: the proxy and DNS listen on all addresses, so switching between Wi-Fi and Ethernet keeps them working. The router reservation must follow the interface in use.
  • Sleep: if the Mac sleeps, the tunnel drops and the watchdog alerts on wake. ./homelab doctor reads the Mac's sleep setting and warns when the apps would sleep with it (on Linux GNOME's, on Windows the power plan's).
  • Names with a domain: ./homelab domain resolver writes /etc/resolver/<domain>, so the Mac looks up its apps in AdGuard Home even with a VPN on (Networking).
  • Updates of the app: Update now (the line at the top of the window) replaces the running Homelab Wizard with the newest build (the Latest release, numbered v0.9.4-beta and on, or the newest vX.Y.0 release with UPDATE_CHANNEL=stable) after checking its SHA-256 checksum, and opens it again.

docs.title: SteamOS
docs.text:
SteamOS keeps its system folders read-only and replaces them with every update, so nothing is installed with its package manager. The homelab runs from the AppImage (install.sh puts it in ~/Applications), in desktop mode.

How Container runtime Setup › Set up Docker for me (homelab runtime install --apply): Docker's own static build and the Compose plugin, checked against their checksums, in ~/.local/share/homelab-wizard/docker, run as you (Docker's rootless mode) as a service of yours (systemctl --user docker). It asks for your password once, to give your account the ID ranges containers use (/etc/subuid, /etc/subgid) and the ports from 53 up (/etc/sysctl.d/90-homelab-ports.conf); the home folder and /etc are kept across SteamOS updates Starting at boot loginctl enable-linger (the same setup does it), so Docker and the agent run without a login The apps' files A container's root is you, so .env has PUID=0 and PGID=0, and DOCKER_SOCKET is your own socket This machine's own apps The phone companion and Ollama are reached at this machine's address (HOST_GATEWAY), since Docker run as you cannot reach its loopback Its look KDE Plasma's Breeze, its accent, and the app's icon count in the taskbar Game Mode The app is a desktop-mode app; the homelab keeps running in Game Mode. The AppImage's menu entry has Add to Steam to open it from there

Needs from the system (SteamOS has them): newuidmap and newgidmap, the ip command, /dev/net/tun, and systemd for the user; homelab runtime install says which is missing. Status: ISSUE-0012.

docs.title: The same on every system
docs.text:
The parity audit of October 2026 (Roadmap, Goal 1): every feature on each system, read from the code (the runtime.GOOS switches and the *_darwin, *_windows, *_linux, and *_other files). Each cell is works, works differently (and how), missing (and what), or can't (and why). Linux means GNOME and KDE Plasma on a desktop distribution; SteamOS is Plasma in desktop mode, with Docker run as you.

Proven by says what shows it today. "Unit tests" run on all three systems' runners on every pull request (CI's check and test jobs) but against fakes of the system's tools; "click-through" is make app-smoke, which draws the app as each system on Ubuntu's Chromium. "The real-Docker run" is test/realdocker against a real Docker Engine on Ubuntu, every night and on each pull request that changes the catalog. No cell is proven on a real machine yet; those steps are in Testing › Waiting for real hardware, and on the machine names them (M for the Mac, W for the Windows PC, S for the Steam Machine). A row without it is shown by CI on each system already (free space, the jobs' logs, the homelab files), or has nothing to show yet (signed builds).

Each on the machine step is marked in Testing › Waiting for real hardware. On the Mac, M1–M4, M6, M8, M9, and M12–M17 passed on Nov 3, 2026; M5, M7, M10, M11, and M18 are still to run. None of the Windows PC's or the Steam Machine's has been run one by one yet.

docs.title: What the audit turned into
docs.text:
A works differently cell that a person would notice says so on the screen where it shows: its row's Proven by names that screen (said on screen), and the click-through draws it as that system. The rest are not seen on a screen: the time zone, Ollama's step (already in each system's words), the native app after a restart, Jellyfin as a container on SteamOS (it is listed as Jellyfin in a container), a drive's health (homelab doctor says what it needs), and the signed builds, whose question comes before the app opens, so Getting Started says how to answer it.

Each missing cell is an item of 0.12; the ones with a fix that a runner can prove come first (done: keeping awake only on power on Windows and Linux, Plasma's sleep setting, the memory and the time zone on Windows, smartctl found on Windows and the SteamOS hint): the startup asking Docker Desktop to open, a toast Windows shows, undoing the names (domain resolver --undo), and the wording. Jellyfin on SteamOS is now a container (jellyfin-container, which install jellyfin gives there). The jobs without a sign-in on macOS and Windows stay as they are until a route exists.

docs.title: Taking it off this machine
docs.text: ./homelab move out packs the homelab into one file for a new machine, and ./homelab move in <file> unpacks it there (Commands). ./homelab uninstall removes the containers, images (the update undo copies and the backup's helper too), jobs, the menu bar item at login, and the homelab network; the folder, .env, the data, and the backups stay (--data also deletes the apps' data, never the backups or the media drive). --folder, --backups, --app, and --everything-else take the rest (Commands). --app removes the app in each system's way: to the Trash on a Mac; on Windows its uninstaller, started a few seconds after the app and its tray icon quit, as an administrator (the portable build's folder is deleted instead); on Linux the AppImage file, and the app menu entry it added, or the package command (sudo apt remove homelab-wizard, dnf, or pacman -R) to run. Each takes the app's own folders too: its settings (~/Library/Application Support/Homelab Wizard, %APPDATA%\Homelab Wizard, ~/.config/Homelab Wizard), its downloads and the agent's socket (the cache folder), and on Windows the jobs' scripts (%LOCALAPPDATA%\Homelab). The container runtime stays: each system's way to remove it is the last line (RemoveRuntime in internal/host).
