docs.title: ISSUE-0001: Custom proxy image not yet built on the Mac
docs.text:
The image in dockerfiles/npm-crowdsec follows CrowdSec's OpenResty reference build, but has not been built and run on Apple Silicon yet.

Verify:

  1. ./homelab up builds it; ./homelab logs nginx-proxy-manager shows no Lua errors.
  2. ./homelab compose crowdsec exec crowdsec cscli bouncers list shows nginx_proxy_manager with a recent last pull.
  3. Status › Protection says bans are enforced, and the ban test in Runbooks returns 403.

Progress (October 2026): on Linux, the nightly workflow's proxy job builds this image and runs it with CrowdSec: the bouncer is registered and pulling (cscli bouncers list, and the watchdog's check), and a banned address gets 403 through the proxy until the ban is lifted. Still to verify: the build and run on Apple Silicon.

If it fails: the proxy still serves traffic with the bouncer off (empty CROWDSEC_BOUNCER_KEY). Detection keeps working; only enforcement is missing. A bouncer that worked and then stopped (stale or revoked, often after CrowdSec restarted) is a different case: Protection's Fix (./homelab fix) reconnects it.

docs.title: ISSUE-0002: Client addresses for LAN requests through OrbStack
docs.text:
Requests from other LAN devices reach the proxy through OrbStack's port forwarding. Whether the proxy logs the device's real address or OrbStack's gateway address is to be confirmed.

Impact: low. CrowdSec never bans private addresses (its default whitelist), so LAN devices cannot be locked out either way. Tunnel traffic carries the visitor's address in CF-Connecting-IP, which the proxy uses.

Verify: open any app from a phone on Wi-Fi, then look at the address in the newest access log line:

./homelab compose nginx-proxy-manager exec nginx-proxy-manager sh -c 'tail -n 1 /data/logs/proxy-host-*_access.log'

docs.title: ISSUE-0003: Duplicati writing into the Proton Drive folder
docs.text:
Proton Drive on macOS stores its folder under ~/Library/CloudStorage (a File Provider folder). Duplicati writes there through OrbStack's file sharing. This combination is to be verified.

Verify: run the Homelab Secrets job, confirm the files appear in the Proton Drive web app, then restore one file to /staging/restore.

If it fails: point BACKUP_DESTINATION at a plain local folder and use the Proton Drive app's folder sync, or use Duplicati's own remote destination.

docs.title: ISSUE-0004: Domain automation not yet run against the live services
docs.text:
Only with a domain; Home mode does not use it. ./homelab domain setup is tested against fakes of the Nginx Proxy Manager, AdGuard Home, and Cloudflare APIs.

Verify: run ./homelab domain setup --dry-run, then for real, and check each proxy host, the AdGuard rewrite, the tunnel's public hostnames, and the CNAME records in Cloudflare.

Progress (October 2026): the nightly workflow's domain job runs domain setup example.test --dns adguard --ip 127.0.0.1 --no-tunnel against the real Nginx Proxy Manager (the homelab's own image) and AdGuard Home. It reads each proxy host and the *.example.test rewrite back through their APIs, asks AdGuard's DNS for ntfy's name, and gets ntfy's health through the proxy by that name. Still to verify: everything through Cloudflare (the certificate, the tunnel's public hostnames, the CNAME records), which needs a real account.

docs.title: ISSUE-0005: Scheduled jobs not yet run under launchd
docs.text: Verify: after ./homelab schedule install, log out and back in, then check ./homelab schedule status and the logs in scripts/logs. The next morning, confirm a new dump in recovery-staging/databases.

docs.title: ISSUE-0006: No alert when OrbStack itself is down
docs.text:
The watchdog notices that OrbStack is down, but ntfy runs inside OrbStack, so the alert cannot be delivered. The failure is written to scripts/logs/watchdog.log.

Fix (0.3.0): the watchdog pings HEARTBEAT_URL (healthchecks.io) every run, and /fail when something is down; the outside monitor alerts when the pings stop (Monitoring). Verify: set it up, then quit OrbStack and wait for the alert.

docs.title: ISSUE-0007: Nothing starts after a restart until someone logs in
docs.text:
FileVault prevents automatic login. OrbStack and the jobs run in the login session.

Mitigation: install macOS updates by hand, then log in straight away. The startup job brings the baseline back.

docs.title: ISSUE-0008: With a domain, each device's DNS is set by hand
docs.text: Home mode (the default) is not affected: devices find the apps through Tailscale. With a domain, many ISP gateways cannot hand out a custom DNS server, so devices that do not use 192.168.1.10 cannot resolve *.example.com on the LAN; public apps still work through Cloudflare. On the Mac itself, Setup › This Mac finds its apps by name (./homelab domain resolver --apply) covers it, also with a VPN on.

docs.title: ISSUE-0009: MoneyMatter runs Intel-only images under Rosetta
docs.text:
The first start takes several minutes (the health checks allow 300 seconds). The images are pinned and left out of the nightly updates.

Native option: the frontend and backend build for arm64 from MoneyMatter's own Dockerfiles at the pinned commit; its note has the two build commands and the three settings that switch to them (and back). The exchange-rate service stays on Intel because its source is not public. Not yet tried on the Mac. The lasting fix is upstream publishing multi-arch images, which its release workflow already anticipates.

docs.title: ISSUE-0010: Immich machine learning runs on the CPU
docs.text: Containers on macOS have no GPU. The first face and smart-search indexing of a large library takes hours; afterwards new photos are processed quickly.

docs.title: ISSUE-0011: Alerts reach the phone only on the home network
docs.text:
Applies with a domain; in Home mode the phone reaches ntfy over Tailscale. ntfy was LAN-only: its publishers (Duplicati, Uptime Kuma, the watchdog) use anonymous write grants, which must not be reachable from the internet. Away from home the phone cannot fetch messages.

Fix (0.3.0): ./homelab notify setup gives the publishers an access token and removes the anonymous grants; ntfy is marked public, and domain setup publishes it only once the token exists. Verify: after notify setup, the token in Uptime Kuma and Duplicati, and domain setup, send ./homelab notify test with the phone on mobile data.

docs.title: ISSUE-0012: Linux host profile not yet run on the Steam Machine
docs.text:
The Linux profile (Docker Engine, systemd user units) is tested only with fakes in CI. On SteamOS, whose root filesystem is read-only, Docker runs in the home folder as the user (homelab runtime install, Host). That route was run on a Linux machine in October 2026: the downloads and their checksums, the administrator's script, Docker 29.9.2 started as an ordinary user, and Compose publishing port 80 without root; Docker's setup tool making the user service was not (no systemd for the user there).

Verify: on the Steam Machine, Setup › Set up Docker for me (or homelab runtime install --apply), a reboot, and docker info shows rootless; then ./homelab doctor, ./homelab up, then ./homelab schedule install, loginctl enable-linger $USER, a reboot, and ./homelab schedule status. MoneyMatter's Intel-only images run natively on x86, so ISSUE-0009 does not apply there.

Also check, from the October 2026 changes that could not be run here: as a normal user (not root), ./homelab plan adguard-home nginx-proxy-manager keeps ports 53, 80, and 443 (only a real holder moves them); on a desktop with systemd-resolved, a new .env sets ADGUARD_DNS_BIND_IP to the machine's address and AdGuard Home starts; doctor reads GNOME's Automatic suspend; Setup's backup step offers an external drive mounted in /media/<you>; and Status's Start for a stopped Jellyfin asks for the password and starts jellyfin.service.

Also check, the native feel: in KDE's System Settings › Colors & Themes, an accent other than the default blue: the app's links, buttons, and selected sidebar item take it (after Setup › Check again, or reopening the app). On GNOME 47 or later, the same with Settings › Appearance › Style › Accent colour.

Also check, KDE's look: in desktop mode on the Steam Machine, the app looks like Plasma's own apps (System Settings, Dolphin): Noto Sans, bordered buttons, and the selected sidebar item tinted blue with a blue edge, on Breeze and Breeze Dark.

docs.title: ISSUE-0013: Windows host profile not yet run on the Windows PC
docs.text:
The Windows profile (Docker Desktop, Task Scheduler, homelab.cmd) is tested only with fakes and a cross-compile in CI. Expected rough edge: bind mounts from Windows folders into containers are slower than from WSL 2.

The app is a GUI program, so each command it starts (docker for Status every few seconds, git, the CLI) would get a console window of its own; they start hidden instead. The one background job, the agent (it starts the apps, keeps the PC awake on power, runs the watchdog every 15 minutes and the nightly backup), starts at sign-in from the user's Run key (HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run, value homelab-agent) through homelab-run.exe (installed beside the CLI, and built by homelab.cmd), a windowless program, so signing in shows no window; without homelab-run.exe it is a script in the Startup folder. Installing it removes the separate Task Scheduler jobs older versions made.

Verify: on the Windows PC, homelab.cmd doctor, homelab.cmd up, homelab.cmd schedule install, sign out and back in, then homelab.cmd schedule status (the agent runs at sign-in) and the logs. Task Manager › Startup apps lists homelab-agent, signing in opens no window, and Task Scheduler has no Homelab folder left from an older version.

Also check, from the October 2026 changes: doctor reads the power plan's Sleep after (with no console window flashing from the app); Setup's backup step offers OneDrive and the other drive letters, and leaves out Google Drive's own drive; with a domain, This PC finds its apps by name shows in the app and its button asks for approval once; Status's Start for a stopped Jellyfin starts the JellyfinServer service or its tray app; and an account outside docker-users gets the group hint, not "Docker Desktop is not running".

Also check, the native feel: with an accent other than blue in Settings › Personalization › Colors, the app's links, buttons, and the selected sidebar item take it on light and on dark (after Check again on Setup, or reopening the app).

Also check, high contrast: Settings › Accessibility › Contrast themes › Night sky, Apply: the selected screen is outlined, buttons have borders, links are the theme's link colour, and Status's dots and Setup's bars still show.

docs.title: ISSUE-0014: Release builds not yet opened on a Mac, a Windows PC, or SteamOS
docs.text:
release.yml runs green without secrets and builds, for each platform, the app with its tray and the homelab CLI: the macOS universal DMG (signed ad hoc), the Windows installer (x64 and ARM64) and portable zips, the Linux .deb, .rpm, Arch package, and tarball, and an AppImage for SteamOS. The AppImage carries WebKitGTK; each run starts it with the system's copy moved away and checks the window comes up on its own (a screenshot is kept with the run).

Still unproven: opening each on its real machine (step 2 of Testing for the Mac), and signing, notarization, and the signed installer rebuild, which run once the secrets are added (docs/Releasing.md). The AppImage is built on Ubuntu 22.04, so it needs that release's glibc (2.35) or newer: ldd --version on the Steam Machine shows its own.

Verify: on the Mac, the DMG as in Testing step 2. On the Steam Machine (desktop mode), download the AppImage, chmod +x Homelab-Wizard-x86_64.AppImage, open it, check Settings › This machine shows the machine and the tray icon appears; with the homelab folder chosen, Install the jobs and confirm systemctl --user list-timers points at bin/homelab in the folder. On a Windows PC, run the installer and check homelab.exe sits beside the app in its folder.

Progress (October 2026): every run of release.yml now opens what it built on that system's runner, and keeps a screenshot: the DMG mounted, the app dragged to Applications and started (macOS 15); the installer run silently and the app started with its window, the CLI beside it (Windows Server 2022); the AppImage started without the system's WebKitGTK (Ubuntu 22.04). Still to verify: each on a real machine, with a person's account and screen, and the signed builds.

docs.title: ISSUE-0015: App wiring and the menu bar item not yet run against real apps
docs.text:
homelab wire is tested against fake Prowlarr and Sonarr APIs only; the field names it fills come from each app's own templates, but a version that renames one fails that link with a clear message. The macOS menu bar helper (Objective-C for hiding its Dock icon) has not been compiled yet; the release workflow is the first place it builds.

Verify: install @arr and qBittorrent with "Connect the apps for me", set QBITTORRENT_PASSWORD, run homelab wire --apply again, and check Prowlarr › Settings › Apps and Sonarr › Settings › Download Clients. On each machine, check the menu bar or tray item appears once, its links open, and Back up now writes a new dump.

Progress (October 2026): the nightly workflow's wire job runs homelab wire --apply against the real Prowlarr, Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr, and FlareSolverr: Prowlarr's own API then lists Sonarr, Radarr, and Lidarr as applications at their container addresses and FlareSolverr as its indexer proxy, and a second run finds each link already made. Still to verify: qBittorrent as each app's download client (it waits for Gluetun's VPN key, which needs an account), the menu bar or tray item on each machine.

docs.title: ISSUE-0016: Duplicati jobs, restores, and repairs through its API not yet run against the real image
docs.text:
homelab duplicati setup creates jobs (POST /api/v1/backups), runs and repairs them, and sets the alert URL as a default option (PATCH /api/v1/serversettings). restore-test --auto restores a sample, and Backups reads each job's next run from the proposed schedule in /api/v1/serverstate. All of this was written against Duplicati's current source and tested against fakes. The image is lscr.io/linuxserver/duplicati:latest, which may be an older 2.1 release with small API differences. A refused request fails with Duplicati's own message. Each job is created whole or not at all, and running the step again creates only the jobs still missing.

Verify: Setup › Create the backup jobs: Duplicati's UI lists the jobs with the right sources, the /destination/<folder> targets, AES, and smart retention; Settings › Default options shows send-http-url; the first runs finish (Backups › Off-site jobs), and each job shows "next in N hours" matching Duplicati's own Next scheduled task. Then Backups › Test a restore passes and its tile says how long it took.

Progress (October 2026): the nightly run against real Docker (lscr.io/linuxserver/duplicati:latest) now does most of this. It gives Duplicati a backup folder and runs duplicati setup --apply, then reads each job back through Duplicati's own API: its sources, its /destination/<folder> target, AES, smart retention, and its schedule. It checks that send-http-url is a default option once the alert token exists, and that Backups (homelab duplicati jobs) knows each job's next run. Once Homelab AppData's first run finishes, restore-test --auto restores a sample and passes. After the move, the run plays a new machine: the jobs are taken out of Duplicati (their backups stay), duplicati setup --apply makes them again and rebuilds each one's database from its backup, and Homelab AppData then backs up into its old folder without an error. Beside it, the nightly rebuild job runs every job into a folder, wipes the homelab, and restores each one from its backup files alone with Duplicati's own command line (homelab rebuild), then makes the jobs again from their backups. Still to verify: the same on the Mac with Proton Drive (ISSUE-0003).

docs.title: ISSUE-0017: Updates from the app not yet run on the Mac
docs.text:
Update now (the line at the top of the window) moves the homelab files forward, then on a Mac downloads the newest Homelab Wizard (the latest build, or the newest v* release with UPDATE_CHANNEL=stable), checks it against GitHub's SHA-256 checksum, replaces the running app, and opens it again. For a git checkout, the update check runs git fetch as the user, with prompts turned off (GIT_TERMINAL_PROMPT=0, ssh -o BatchMode=yes), and moving forward is a fast-forward to the newest release tag whose build provenance names the commit it points at, followed by up. An app opened from Finder relies on the macOS SSH agent (or the keychain) for the GitHub key; without it the check says GitHub could not be reached and uses the last fetch. A folder the app made (Set it up for me) moves forward from the files inside the newer app instead.

Verify: within 15 minutes of a build of a merged change (or on bringing the window forward), the line at the top says the update is ready, with no Check again; Update now brings the files in and runs up, then replaces the app and opens the new one, which says Updated to …; the menu bar's Update to … goes away. When only the app is behind, Update now does the app alone. With a build from the release workflow, the version row shows build <commit>.

docs.title: ISSUE-0018: Disk space readings not yet compared on the Mac
docs.text:
Settings › This Mac › Storage, homelab doctor, and the watchdog read free space with statfs, as df does: the space free right now. Finder's Available also counts purgeable space (caches and iCloud copies macOS deletes when room is needed), so on the Mac the homelab's number can be lower than Finder's, and a disk could read low while Finder still shows room. That errs on the side of warning early. On Windows the reading comes from GetDiskFreeSpaceEx. Disks are grouped by device, so folders on the Mac's disk (the homelab folder, the Proton Drive folder) share one line, and the media drive gets its own.

Verify: Settings › This Mac › Storage shows two lines, the Mac's disk and the media drive, with free space matching df -h ~ /Volumes/Media. With the drive unplugged, its line goes away instead of showing the Mac's disk under its name.

docs.title: ISSUE-0019: A cloud drive's own quota cannot be read
docs.text:
The watchdog, doctor, and Settings › This Mac › Storage read the free space on the disk that holds BACKUP_DESTINATION. A cloud drive's folder (Proton Drive, iCloud Drive, and the like) sits on the Mac's own disk, and the account's storage limit is not visible from the Mac, so a full cloud account is not warned about ahead of time. The off-site jobs then fail, and the watchdog alerts once a job fails or has not succeeded for a week.

Mitigation: check the space left in the cloud drive's own app or website now and then (the monthly checks in Monitoring).

docs.title: ISSUE-0020: Vaultwarden web vault shows a black screen in LibreWolf
docs.text:
In LibreWolf, Vaultwarden's web vault can load as a black screen. The server and the Bitwarden apps are not affected.

Workaround: open the web vault in Safari or another browser.

docs.title: ISSUE-0021: Installing and updating the app on Windows and Linux not yet run everywhere
docs.text:
install.sh was run on Ubuntu 24.04: it installed the .deb with apt, and with HOMELAB_APPIMAGE=1 put the AppImage in ~/Applications. The self-update code (Stage and Swap, run from a test harness) replaced an AppImage with the live release's. The silent installer runs on the Windows runner in every release.yml run (ISSUE-0014's progress). Still unproven: install.ps1 on Windows (the agent and tray stopped and started again around the installer), the portable zip's update, a package update through pkexec, and the .rpm and Arch package paths.

Found on a Windows PC (October 2026): updating went round in a loop (the app closed, opened again, still the old version), because SmartScreen or Smart App Control blocked the unsigned installer the update ran as an administrator. Since then the update unpacks the new files with Windows' own PowerShell, as an administrator only when the app is in Program Files, and a build that does not go in place says why when the app opens again instead of offering the same update. Each attempt's steps are in %LOCALAPPDATA%\Homelab Wizard\update.log. A PC already in the loop needs this build installed by hand once (Upgrading).

Verify: on Windows, run irm https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Snooper42/homelab-wizard/main/install.ps1 | iex; the app opens, and after the next change to main the line's Update now brings the new build (one approval prompt for Program Files, and no SmartScreen), with the tray item and homelab-agent running again after, and update.log ending with done (Testing W21, W22). On Fedora or Arch, install.sh, then the same update from the line (pkexec asks for the password).

docs.title: ISSUE-0022: A rollback brings back the image, not the data the newer version changed
docs.text:
Found by the nightly run against real Docker (October 2026). homelab rollback (and the watchdog's automatic rollback of an update that leaves an app unwell) starts the image the app ran before its update, on the data as it is now. An app that changes its own data when a newer version starts (a database schema moved on) can then refuse it: ntfy 2.11 rolled back from 2.34 stopped with "unexpected schema version: version 17 is higher than current version 13" and restarted in a loop. The update dumps the app's databases first, but the rollback does not put them back, and not every file an app migrates is dumped (ntfy's message cache is not).

Workaround: restore the dump the update took (recovery-staging/databases/<app>, the newest before the update's time) as Disaster Recovery describes for that app, or update again (homelab updates release <app>, then homelab update <app>).

Progress (October 2026): homelab update now stops each app whose image changed, copies its folders and named volumes and keeps its dumps (recovery-staging/before-update), then starts the new image; homelab rollback sets today's data aside and puts that copy back with the earlier image. The watchdog's rollback puts the copy back by itself only when the app was never well after the update; otherwise it keeps today's data and its alert names homelab rollback <app> --data. Resolved: the nightly updates are run by the agent (homelab update --all --nightly), so they are copied too, and Watchtower is gone. The nightly run now proves it across a schema change: it starts on ntfy v2.25.0 (its cache database at schema 15, its users at 8), which refuses the newer ntfy's migrated databases; after the update to the newest (17 and 9), both homelab rollback and the watchdog put it back on v2.25.0 with its data from before, and its tokens from then still publish and read.

Fix (decided in ADR-0020, October 2026; Roadmap): before an update, keep a copy of the app's data folders and named volumes as well as its dumps, and have the rollback put that copy back with the older image. Large data (photo libraries, media) stays where it is; the apps that keep those (Immich) keep their schema in the database, which the dump covers. homelab update and homelab rollback do this since 0.13.0 (Progress, above), and since Watchtower went the nightly updates are homelab update --all --nightly, so they do it too.

Resolved (after 0.14.0): every update, the nightly ones included, copies the app's data first, and a rollback puts it back.

docs.title: ISSUE-0023: Nextcloud's default port is the phone companion's
docs.text:
NEXTCLOUD_PORT defaulted to 8099, the port the phone companion (homelab serve) always listens on, so Nextcloud could take it while the companion was not running.

Fixed (October 2026): the install plan never hands a container the fixed port of an app that runs on the machine itself (the phone companion's 8099, Jellyfin's 8096), whether or not that app runs now; a .env that still says 8099 gets Nextcloud moved to a free port, and says why. A new .env starts Nextcloud on 8089. Jellyfin in a container still takes 8096, the port it stands in for.

docs.title: ISSUE-0024: The homelab's own records in data/ were not in the off-site backup
docs.text:
Duplicati's jobs read data/appdata, not the files beside it in data/: the household (people.json and the welcome pages), the paired phones (phones.json), the apps' single sign-on settings (data/sso), the update history, Setup's ticked steps, and the savings history. A rebuild from the backups lost them.

Fixed (October 2026): the nightly backup copies data/*.json, data/people, and data/sso into recovery-staging/secrets/data, which the encrypted Homelab Secrets job takes off-site with .env. A restore puts them back with .env (Disaster Recovery, step 3).

docs.title: Maintainer Guide
docs.text: The facts, code layout, and rules for anyone changing this repository.

docs.title: Critical facts
docs.text: Fact Detail The catalog is the compose files compose/<category>.yaml and stacks/*/compose.yaml (one project each), with the categories, presets, and native apps in compose.yaml. Each service's x-homelab block is read by the CLI. Never describe an app that is not in them. Baseline vs optional Services without profiles start with ./homelab up. Services with profiles: [optional] start only when named (./homelab install sonarr). Nginx Proxy Manager is a custom image Built from dockerfiles/npm-crowdsec with the CrowdSec Lua bouncer. Left out of the nightly updates. Update with ./homelab update nginx-proxy-manager (rebuilds). Pulling jc21/nginx-proxy-manager silently removes CrowdSec. One shared network Every project joins the external homelab network. NPM, cloudflared, and Uptime Kuma reach apps by service name. Service names must be unique across all stacks. Tunnel goes through the proxy Public hostnames point at http://nginx-proxy-manager:80, so CrowdSec sees and blocks tunnel traffic. Proxy hosts trust X-Forwarded-Proto; the real visitor address comes from CF-Connecting-IP. Duplicati uses container paths /source/appdata, /source/homelab-appdata, /source/stacks, /source/jellyfin, /source/immich, /source/calibre, /staging, /destination. Never Mac paths in job settings. Two appdata folders data/appdata/<service> holds core services; appdata/<stack> holds stack apps. They are different folders. Databases live in named volumes Not in bind mounts. ./homelab backup dumps them to recovery-staging/databases. Never run docker volume prune or docker system prune --volumes. Immich needs its own Postgres image A restore must use ghcr.io/immich-app/postgres with the same vectorchord/pgvecto.rs tag; a stock Postgres image will not work. MoneyMatter signs in at one address Only at MONEYMATTER_URL (https://money.example.com by default), not localhost. Budget tracker folder stacks/budget-tracker, project homelab_budget_tracker. Not "money". NPM admin http://localhost:8181 on the Mac only. The CLI's NPM account must not have 2FA. ntfy denies by default New alert topics need a write grant: add them to notify.Topics and run ./homelab notify setup. host.docker.internal The Mac itself, from inside a container. Used only for native apps (Jellyfin). 127.0.0.1 inside a container is the container. .env and data/ hold the state .env: ports, secrets, settings, and the version each app runs (<APP>_DIGEST). data/*.json: the homelab's own records (the household, paired phones, Finances, update history, Setup's answers). Never print or commit their values. Home mode is the default HOMELAB_DOMAIN is empty in .env.example, so a new homelab gives every app a tailnet address through Tailscale Serve (homelab tailnet setup). The proxy hosts, AdGuard rewrites, and the tunnel apply only once a domain is set. Repository and module Public as Snooper42/homelab-wizard; the Go module is github.com/Snooper42/homelab-wizard. Use placeholders in docs and tests: example.com, 192.168.1.10, /Volumes/Media. --json is a contract Every line carries "schema": 1. The recorded fields are in internal/api/testdata/contract.json, and TestJSONContract fails when one disappears or is renamed. A new field is fine (UPDATE_CONTRACT=1 go test ./internal/api records it); removing or renaming one, or changing what it means, needs a new schema number and a note in Commands.

docs.title: Code layout
docs.text: Where What cmd/homelab The CLI: one file per command group, all on top of internal/ cmd/homelab-run Windows only: starts the scheduled jobs without a console window cmd/financewasm Finances' projection as WebAssembly, for the phone's page when a household member keeps her Finances sealed app/ The Wails desktop app (app.go binds the engine to the frontend), app/tray and app/cmd/homelab-tray for the menu bar item, app/packaging for the Linux packages and AppImage, app/preview for make screenshots web/src The frontend: app.ts (which screen shows, the keyboard, and starting up), screens/*.ts (each screen's data, kept in a store, and its commands), core.ts and jobs.ts (what they share), and a folder of Preact components per screen, compiled by web/build.mjs (esbuild) into web/dist/app.js web/dist The frontend as served (app.js, built and committed; companion.js for the phone, style.css), shared by the desktop app and homelab serve web/types The frontend's TypeScript types for the Go side: backend.d.ts (generated by TestBindings in app/) and window.d.ts compose.yaml, compose/, stacks/ The catalog (see above) internal/ The engine, one package per job (below) mobile/finance The same projection for the phone (WebAssembly and an iOS framework, gomobile bind), outside internal/ so the phone can import it tools/media Tidy Up's engines in Python (music and books organizers, vendored; films, TV, audiobooks, the inbox, the nightly sweep), run by internal/media apple-client/ The native iPhone and iPad app (SwiftUI), a client of the phone companion; its own README says how to build it Package What it does adopt, detect Find apps already running outside the homelab and move them in awake, battery, sysmem Keeping the machine awake on power (Linux's permission for it), the battery saver, and this machine's memory for install plans api The structured view programs read (--json, the app, the phone), with its contract test appicon Each app's own icon for its page, asked of the app on this machine and kept in data/icons backup, duplicati, recovery Nightly dumps into recovery-staging (with the homelab's own records from data/ and each app's image digest), Duplicati's API (jobs, repairs, restore test), and the printable recovery kit. homelab rebuild (in cmd/homelab/rebuild.go) restores with Duplicati's own command line in a throwaway container catalog, compose, selector Read the compose files and their x-homelab blocks; resolve selections (sonarr, @arr, cat:media) companion homelab serve: the phone companion and its pairing board The cards beside Status (the watchdog, alerts, storage, usage, the week, protection) read side by side for one answer that fills in as each is read; the agent serves them at /v1/cards crash What a crash of the app, the menu bar item, or the agent leaves for the next start and the diagnostics report core What the desktop app and its menu bar item share crowdsec, npm, domain, tailnet The proxy's bouncer, Nginx Proxy Manager's API, domain setup, and Home mode's tailnet addresses custom, install, ports, wiring Your own apps, install plans, host port conflicts, and connecting apps to each other digest, health, notify, diskspace, diskhealth The weekly summary, the watchdog's checks (with Days and Week for the last 7 days), ntfy, free space, and SMART docker, dockerapi, pgexec, procattr, host The container runtime (the docker CLI, with the reads it makes all the time and commands run in containers going to the engine's own API over its socket, or Docker Desktop's named pipe; DOCKER_API=off keeps the CLI), psql in a database container as its own user, windowless commands on Windows, and the host profile (macOS, Linux, Windows) docs, savings Generated note blocks, link checks, and the prices in Savings engine The engine as something to follow: its events gathered into changes, each sent with the Status read after it, and the agent's local socket (/v1/status, /v1/events, /v1/cards) explain, releases Explain this (an app's log) through the Ollama on this machine, and the release notes an update brings envfile, settings, setup .env edits, the Settings screen's fields, and the first-time checklist export, move Open-format export, and move out / move in homepage, people, sso Homepage's start page, the household, and Pocket ID sign-in kopia Kopia's server API for its restore test kit, upgrade, updates, selfupdate The homelab files a build carries, homelab upgrade, pausing and holding the nightly updates, and the app's own update (the latest build or the newest v* release, checked against GitHub's SHA-256 digest) progress, transfer Compose's progress read into a row per app, and a download counted as it comes in, for the bars rootless Docker in the home folder, run as you (homelab runtime install, SteamOS) schedule The background agent and its jobs: launchd, a systemd user unit, or the Run key and Task Scheduler on Windows accounts Jellyfin's and Navidrome's own accounts for each person (Settings › People), for the apps that can't sign in with Pocket ID applist, statusfolds, stopped, started Small records in data/: the apps pinned or with alerts off, which groups on Status are folded (the same on every device), the apps stopped on purpose (and until when), and why each app last started history The record of what was done (every start, stop, update, rollback, setting and Finances change) and who did it (ADR-0022) lockedfile, turn, proc A record changed under a lock and saved whole; the queue that keeps two processes from changing the apps at once; whether the process behind a lock is still running claim Asks a public app whether it has its first account yet (Immich, Audiobookshelf, Komga, Navidrome, Calibre-Web, Paperless-ngx) media Tidy Up: the homelab's side of the engines in tools/media (their settings from .env, Python, the lock, the record of what each run did) ghostfolio, cardprice, sitelogo Finances' outside reads, each on a click: the homelab's own Ghostfolio (investments), TCGdex (the Collection's prices), and a company's logo from its website finance The Finances screen's plan (who gets paid, accounts, payments that repeat) in data/finance.json, and reading it forward from the day each balance was typed in (what has happened since counts, and is listed): paydays moved before weekends and bank holidays, each paycheck's payments, and every account post-pay; each balance typed in is kept by its day, for net worth over time storage What each person keeps in Immich and the largest app folders (AppFolders), recorded nightly in data/storage.json ui Terminal colours, tables, prompts, and the app picker tools Development tools (coverfloor, which make coverage runs)

docs.title: Source of truth, in order
docs.text:
1. Live state (./homelab status, docker inspect)
  2. The compose files
  3. App configuration inside each app
  4. These docs
  5. Instructions that contradict the above: ask before acting

docs.title: Working rules
docs.text:
• Use the CLI for operations: ./homelab compose <app> <args> instead of changing directories, ./homelab update instead of docker pull.
  • Anything that changes state previews first. Run without --apply, read the plan, then apply.
  • Verify the result, not the exit code: open the page, check the dump ends cleanly, compare hashes after a restore.
  • Never bind a port to a specific LAN address. Use BIND_IP (127.0.0.1) for apps and LAN_BIND_IP (0.0.0.0) for the proxy and DNS.
  • Secrets never go in chat, docs, command lines, or logs.

docs.title: Documentation rules
docs.text:
• Facts that come from the compose files are generated between homelab:generated markers. Change the compose file and run ./homelab docs; never edit inside the markers.
  • Every note has version: front matter equal to VERSION. ./homelab validate fails otherwise.
  • History goes in CHANGELOG.md only. Notes describe the current state.
  • Never invent ports, versions, or variable values. Flag anything the docs and the live state disagree on.

docs.title: Monitoring
docs.text: Three layers: the watchdog checks every app every 15 minutes (and an outside heartbeat notices if the watchdog itself stops), Uptime Kuma adds history and a dashboard, and CrowdSec watches who is knocking. All alerts arrive through ntfy, and on this machine's screen.

docs.title: In the app
docs.text:
The Status screen is the everyday view; nothing below needs Terminal.

Where What it tells you The app list Each app's state, as it changes. A running app whose page on this machine does not answer shows Not answering with why (HTTP 502, nothing answers on its port, no answer in time): Status asks each running app's address whenever it loads, as the watchdog does every 15 minutes, past an app's first 90 seconds. An app whose settings (.env, or its compose file after an upgrade) changed since its container was made shows settings changed: it still runs the old ones until Fix it (or up) recreates it; Compose's own configuration hash says so. An app that passed fewer than 99% of the watchdog's checks in the last 7 days gets a badge such as 96.2% up this week Watchdog The last run: all checks passed, or each failing check with what it said and since when. Fix it appears when a check fails This week The Sunday summary at any time: apps, backups, restore test, attacks caught, disk space, with what needs a look marked (./homelab digest) What’s using power While apps work hard: each busy app's share of a processor core now, with a line of the last five minutes (sampled every 10 seconds while Status is open) What the apps keep The six largest app folders, and Photos per person, as last night's backup measured them Protection While CrowdSec and the proxy run: bans enforced or not, attacks caught this week, addresses banned now. When bans are not enforced, Fix reconnects the proxy to CrowdSec Recent alerts The last 12 hours of alerts from ntfy, each line of an alert on its own, less those whose problem has cleared: a watchdog alert once a later run passed every check it named, a backup's once each app it skipped runs again. Check again reads them now

The cards come in the same answer as Status, each drawn the moment it is read, so a slow one (the week asks several apps) holds up none of the rest. While the background agent runs, it reads them once for the window and the phone companion together.

Fix it (./homelab fix) shows its plan first, then starts the runtime if it is stopped, starts or restarts apps that are down or unwell, recreates apps whose settings changed since they started, frees disk space when a disk is low, installs missing scheduled jobs, and reconnects the proxy to CrowdSec when bans are not enforced.

docs.title: Uptime Kuma
docs.text:
Uptime Kuma runs with the baseline, but setting up its monitors is optional: the watchdog already alerts on every app, so Uptime Kuma is for history graphs and a status page. Its monitors are set up by hand (it has no API for creating them).

Add monitors only for the apps you have installed. Uptime Kuma is on the homelab network, so monitors use service names and container ports, not localhost addresses.

Monitor Type Target Nginx Proxy Manager HTTP http://nginx-proxy-manager:81 AdGuard Home HTTP http://adguard-home:80 AdGuard DNS DNS npm.example.com, resolver 192.168.1.10, port 53 CrowdSec TCP port crowdsec, port 8080 Duplicati HTTP http://duplicati:8200 Vaultwarden HTTP http://vaultwarden:80/alive ntfy HTTP http://ntfy:80/v1/health Navidrome HTTP http://navidrome:4533/ping Feishin HTTP http://feishin:9180 Audiobookshelf HTTP http://audiobookshelf:80/healthcheck Calibre-Web HTTP http://calibre-web:8083 Komga HTTP http://komga:25600 Immich HTTP http://immich-server:2283/api/server/ping Paperless-ngx HTTP http://paperless:8000 MoneyMatter HTTP http://moneymatter-frontend:80 Jellyfin HTTP http://host.docker.internal:8096/health

Add one for each optional app you install (http://<service>:<container port>; the port is the web value in its note's table).

Notifications: Settings › Notifications › Setup Notification › ntfy. Server URL http://ntfy:80, topic uptime-kuma, priority 4, authentication method Access token with NTFY_PUBLISH_TOKEN from .env (after ./homelab notify setup). Apply it to every monitor.

These monitors check that each app answers on the Docker network. They do not prove the public path works; that is the watchdog's job.

docs.title: Watchdog
docs.text:
./homelab watchdog runs every 15 minutes (a part of the background agent; Automation) and checks:

  • that the container runtime (OrbStack on a Mac) is running;
  • every app the homelab runs: a container that is unhealthy or keeps restarting (Docker counts one waiting to be restarted as running, so this is checked apart), a baseline app that is not running, and, for apps without a health check, whether the web page answers on this Mac. Optional apps that are stopped and the tunnel before it has a token are left alone;
  • with a domain, every public hostname, resolved through public DNS (Cloudflare 1.1.1.1), so the request takes the same path as a visitor's;
  • each running app's newest database dump, which fails when it is over 26 hours old (backups that quietly stopped);
  • each Duplicati job, with DUPLICATI_PASSWORD set: one whose last run failed, or with no successful run for over a week (jobs never run yet are left alone), and one whose last weekly check (homelab backup-check) found a damaged file, until a check passes again;
  • the proxy's CrowdSec bouncer, while CrowdSec and the proxy run: missing, revoked, or without a pull for over 5 minutes means bans are not enforced (it pulls every 10 seconds). It reads every entry CrowdSec keeps for the proxy, nginx_proxy_manager and the nginx_proxy_manager@<address> it adds when the proxy comes back with a new address;
  • free space on each disk the homelab writes to: the homelab folder's, and those under IMMICH_UPLOAD_LOCATION, MEDIA_ROOT, DOWNLOADS_ROOT, BACKUP_DESTINATION, JELLYFIN_DATA_DIR, and SYNC_ROOT that are connected. A disk fails under 5% free, at least 10 GB and at most 50 GB (a full disk stops databases, downloads, and the container runtime, whose disk image lives on the Mac's own disk). This check runs even while the runtime is down. homelab doctor and Settings › This Mac › Storage show the same;
  • each drive's own health report (SMART), when smartctl is installed (brew install smartmontools): a drive that says it is failing fails the check. Containers cannot read a Mac's disks, which is why this runs on the host rather than as an app like Scrutiny. Many USB enclosures do not pass the report through; those drives are listed by homelab doctor as having no report and are left alone. doctor also warns about early signs on a passing drive: reallocated or pending sectors, media errors, or an SSD past 90% of its rated wear.
  • the apps' memory, against what Docker has (the whole machine on Linux; Docker Desktop's or OrbStack's share on a Mac or Windows): above 90% on two runs in a row at least 10 minutes apart, it alerts once, Homelab: memory nearly full, with the three biggest apps and how much each uses, and Status's Watchdog card lists them, each with Stop, until it comes down (then memory is back to normal, once). A moment's peak, such as an import, says nothing.

A failing check you already know of can be snoozed: Status › Watchdog › Snooze… beside it (for an hour or a day), or ./homelab notify snooze <check> 1h|1d. The watchdog still checks it and shows it, but sends no alert about it until the snooze ends; if it still fails then, it alerts once. Alert again now in the same menu, or off, ends it early.

At night (QUIET_HOURS, 22:00 to 07:00 by default) every alert still reaches the phone, but at ntfy's low priority, without a sound or a vibration, except the serious ones: the vault (Vaultwarden) not answering, and a backup that has failed two nights running. Those sound at any hour. QUIET_HOURS=off sounds every alert; 13-15 picks other hours.

An app whose container runs but is unhealthy, or whose page does not answer, on two runs in a row (15 to 30 minutes) is restarted: Docker restarts a container that stops, but not one that hangs. Each app is restarted once in 6 hours at most, so one a restart does not help is left for a person, and an app updated in the last 6 hours is left to the rollback. An alert on tunnel-watchdog says which app was restarted and why; AUTO_HEAL=false in Settings makes the watchdog only alert. An app whose container is gone (removed outside the homelab, or by a prune) is made again on the same terms, if the watchdog saw it running in the last week. When it last restarted each app is kept in data/healed.json.

An app that stopped by itself and stays stopped (one whose restart policy is off, or that Docker couldn't start) is not stopped on purpose: Status's row and its page say when it stopped and, when Docker knows, why: Stopped at 3:12 AM: it ran out of memory, it quit with an error, another program is using its port 9925, or Docker couldn't start it, with a red dot, and Needs a look and the menu bar count it. One stopped cleanly (by docker stop, or a shutdown) says only when, with a yellow dot. homelab status puts the why in its HEALTH column. The watchdog counts one that stopped by itself as a failing check (mealie: stopped: it ran out of memory), so the phone hears of it; it alerts, and doesn't restart it. Any other stopped app it doesn't check, and Status's Watchdog line names it (Not checked while stopped: Mealie). Its page says under its name what to do: Start, or what to put right first; on a phone that can only look, to start it from the computer.

An app that keeps stopping on its own is restarted by Docker, forever. When Docker restarted one 3 times within an hour and it is still not settled (between restarts, unhealthy, or up less than a minute), the watchdog stops it instead and alerts tunnel-watchdog with its last 10 log lines, secrets taken out. It is kept as stopped by the watchdog in data/stopped.json, so nothing starts it by itself: Status's row says Stopped: it restarted 5 times in an hour with a red dot, Needs a look counts it, and the menu bar lists it. Starting it again (its row's Start, or homelab start) forgets that. One that restarted a few times while its database started and has run since is left, and so is one updated in the last 6 hours (the rollback decides). The counts it compares are kept in data/restarts.json; AUTO_HEAL=false leaves it to Docker.

It alerts the tunnel-watchdog topic when a check starts failing and again when it recovers, not on every run. State is kept in scripts/logs/watchdog-state.json, with the last run's time, how many checks ran, what each failing check said, and a count of passed and failed runs per check for each of the last 7 days (days; the % up this week badges come from it): the app's Status screen shows it under Watchdog, and homelab report includes it. An app's page says its week under This week: the share of checks passed and, from the outages kept beside it, the last time it was down, for how long, and why (Last down Tue at 3:10 AM for 45 minutes: HTTP 502 · 2 outages), or Down since … while it is. Checks it missed that passed the next time say so; an older agent with no outages says how many checks it didn't answer, and on which days.

docs.title: Weekly summary
docs.text:
On Sundays the nightly backup also sends Homelab this week to the tunnel-watchdog topic: the apps (all healthy, or which need a look), the watchdog (still running every 15 minutes, and any other check it alerted about, such as a public address or the CrowdSec bouncer), the database copies, the off-site jobs, the last restore test, a due or readable vault export, the free space on each disk (or which is low), each drive's health (passing, wearing, or failing), homelab updates waiting on GitHub, how many attacks CrowdSec caught, the yearly savings, and, once Finances has a plan, what the next paycheck leaves, the biggest bills before it, net worth with its change since last week, and, from the transactions, what went out in the last seven days and where most of it went. A good week arrives quietly (low priority) as all well; otherwise the title counts the things that need a look. Status › This week shows the same summary at any time; ./homelab digest prints it, and --send sends it now. Sending waits until Set up the alert token has run.

The nightly backup also sends Finances' reminders to the same topic, each on its one day: a bill or card due tomorrow, three days before a paycheck that will leave checking under the cushion, a week before a yearly payment renews, and each week the balances go without an update. Finances › Pay › Paydays and money turns each off.

docs.title: External heartbeat
docs.text: When OrbStack (or the whole Mac) is down, ntfy is down too, so it cannot say so. With HEARTBEAT_URL set, every watchdog run also pings an outside monitor: the URL when all checks pass, <URL>/fail with the failures otherwise. Create a free check at healthchecks.io with a 15-minute period and a 15-minute grace, give it your phone's or email alerts, and put its ping URL in HEARTBEAT_URL (the app's Settings screen, or .env). If the pings stop, because the Mac is off, asleep, or offline, or launchd stopped running the watchdog, healthchecks.io alerts you.

docs.title: On this machine's screen
docs.text: Every alert the homelab's own jobs send (the watchdog, backups, the weekly summary) also shows as a notification on the machine running the homelab: Notification Center on a Mac, the desktop's notifications on Linux, a toast on Windows. So alerts reach someone before the phone is set up, and while ntfy itself is down. DESKTOP_ALERTS=false in Settings sends them to the phone only. Until Set up the alert token has run, the screen is the only place they go.

docs.title: ntfy
docs.text:
ntfy denies everything by default. ./homelab notify setup creates the homelab user that every alert source publishes as, gives it write-only access to the topics below, saves its access token in .env (NTFY_PUBLISH_TOKEN, and the same as an ?auth= parameter in NTFY_PUBLISH_AUTH), and removes anonymous write access. The watchdog uses it automatically; Duplicati gets it as a default option for every job (by notify setup itself, and by duplicati setup), and Uptime Kuma as described above. In Home mode the phone reaches ntfy over Tailscale, at home and away. With a domain, once the token exists, ./homelab domain setup publishes ntfy through the tunnel, so the phone gets alerts away from home too.

It also creates homelab-reader, with read-only access to the same topics, and keeps its token in NTFY_READ_TOKEN. The desktop app uses it to show the last 12 hours of alerts on Status (ntfy keeps 12 hours), and the menu bar shows the newest one. Re-running notify setup on an existing homelab adds the reader and keeps the publisher's token.

And it creates phone, the account the phone subscribes with: read-only on the same topics, with a generated password kept in .env as NTFY_PHONE_PASSWORD. The password reaches ntfy through docker's environment, never a command line; an account named phone made by hand before gets the generated password. In the ntfy app on the phone: Settings › Users › add ntfy's address as the server (its tailnet address from Status in Home mode; with a domain, https://ntfy.example.com), user phone, and the password from the desktop app's Settings › NTFY_PHONE_PASSWORD › Copy (Universal Clipboard pastes it on an iPhone signed in to the same Apple ID). Then subscribe to the topics below on that server.

Topic Expect watchtower A summary after each night's updates, and each rollback (the agent sends it; the name is from Watchtower) duplicati-alerts Only failures uptime-kuma Down and up messages tunnel-watchdog Down and recovered messages reminders From the apps you set up for it: Wallos renewals, Changedetection.io changes

./homelab notify test <topic> sends a test message.

docs.title: CrowdSec
docs.text:
./homelab compose crowdsec exec crowdsec cscli metrics            # what is parsed, per source
./homelab compose crowdsec exec crowdsec cscli alerts list        # recent detections
./homelab compose crowdsec exec crowdsec cscli decisions list     # active bans
./homelab compose crowdsec exec crowdsec cscli bouncers list      # the proxy's bouncer and its last pull

./homelab doctor and the watchdog read the bouncer list themselves: doctor says how long ago the proxy pulled decisions, and the watchdog alerts when it stops. The app's Status screen shows Protection: bans enforced or not, the attacks caught this week (cscli alerts list --since 168h, the community blocklist left out), how many addresses are banned now, and the latest three. The weekly summary counts the week's attacks too.

When bans are not enforced (the bouncer is missing, revoked, or stale, often after CrowdSec restarted), Protection's Fix button, Fix it, or ./homelab fix removes the proxy's old bouncer entries (the @<address> ones too), restarts CrowdSec (which registers it again), and restarts the proxy.

The proxy's bouncer also asks CrowdSec's AppSec component about each request. It loads only the virtual-patching rules (exploits of known vulnerabilities in common apps; config/crowdsec/appsec.yaml), and lets requests through when AppSec is down.

cscli metrics should show lines read from /var/log/npm/*.log and parsed by the nginx-proxy-manager parser. If it reads nothing, check the npm-logs volume and config/crowdsec/acquis.yaml.

Optionally enroll the engine in the CrowdSec console (CROWDSEC_ENROLL_KEY) for a web view of alerts.

docs.title: Daily and weekly checks
docs.text: When Check Daily, glance No unread alerts in ntfy Weekly Status › This week (or the Sunday alert); Backups › Off-site jobs Monthly Backups › Test a restore (Backups); ./homelab doctor; disk space on the media drive and in the cloud drive's own app

docs.title: LAN
docs.text: Property Value Gateway The ISP's router, 192.168.1.1 (an example; use your own network's addresses) Subnet 192.168.1.0/24 Homelab host 192.168.1.10 (DHCP reservation for the interface in use) VLANs None Port forwards None

docs.title: Home mode (the default)
docs.text:
Every new homelab starts with HOMELAB_DOMAIN empty. Tailscale serves every app at https://<TAILSCALE_HOST>:<port> with its own certificate, on every device in the tailnet, at home and away, through Tailscale Serve. See Tailscale.

  • No auth key is needed: ./homelab tailnet login opens Tailscale's sign-in page in the browser (TAILSCALE_AUTHKEY still works, for signing in without it).
  • ./homelab tailnet setup writes the serve config for the running apps and saves TAILSCALE_HOST; every install runs it again.
  • TAILNET_ADMIN_APPS=false keeps the admin apps (the proxy, AdGuard Home, Duplicati, Dozzle) off the tailnet, so they open on this machine only; the household's apps stay on it.
  • Ad blocking works here too: @adblock installs AdGuard Home and tailnet-dns, which passes DNS sent to this machine's tailnet address on to AdGuard, so the tailnet's DNS setting can point at it.

The DNS rewrite, reverse proxy, and Cloudflare sections below apply only once a domain is set (Settings, or Setup › Set up the domain).

docs.title: DNS (with a domain)
docs.text:
AdGuard Home on this machine (port 53) answers for the LAN.

Setting Value Rewrite *.example.com → 192.168.1.10 (added by ./homelab domain setup) Upstream Encrypted DNS of your choice, for example https://dns.quad9.net/dns-query and https://cloudflare-dns.com/dns-query Bootstrap 9.9.9.9, 1.1.1.1 Clients Each device's DNS is set to 192.168.1.10 by hand (when the router cannot hand it out), or Tailscale's DNS setting does it for every Tailscale device

Because of the wildcard rewrite, every hostname, public or not, resolves to this machine on the LAN, and LAN traffic never leaves the house. Outside the house only the public hostnames exist, as CNAME records to the tunnel.

docs.title: The home record (any DNS server)
docs.text:
With CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN, ./homelab domain setup also writes one DNS-only record in Cloudflare: *.example.com → 192.168.1.10, commented managed by homelab. Any DNS server then answers the apps' names with this machine's address at home, so they open on a phone or laptop at home whose DNS is a VPN's (Proton VPN, with Allow LAN connections on) or the router's, with no per-device DNS setting. The tunnel's public hostnames keep their own CNAME records, which take precedence over the wildcard, so they still work away from home. Elsewhere 192.168.1.10 is some other network's address or none: the apps do not open there, and HTTPS keeps a device from sending anything to a stranger at that address, since only this machine has the certificate.

data/home-address.json keeps the address it wrote. When the router gives this machine another address on the same network, the watchdog moves the Cloudflare record and AdGuard's rewrite within 15 minutes and sends an alert; an address on another network (a laptop away from home, or a new router) leaves them, and Set up the domain writes them again. A * record the homelab did not write is left as it is (another kind of record, a public address, or another machine at home such as a NAS), unless it already points at this machine. --no-home-record leaves Cloudflare's DNS without it.

For the machine itself, Setup › This Mac finds its apps by name (This PC on Windows, This machine on Linux; ./homelab domain resolver) writes /etc/resolver/<domain> (on Linux a systemd-resolved drop-in, on Windows a Name Resolution Policy Table rule): macOS then looks up every name under the domain in AdGuard Home, whatever DNS the network or a VPN sets (Proton VPN included, with Allow LAN connections on), and for apps added later too. The rest of its lookups are untouched. Without AdGuard, ./homelab domain setup --dns hosts writes the hostnames into /etc/hosts on this machine instead.

docs.title: Reverse proxy
docs.text:
Nginx Proxy Manager listens on 80 and 443 on every address of this machine.

Setting (every proxy host) Value Forward to http://<service>:<container port> on the homelab network; host.docker.internal:8096 for Jellyfin Certificate Wildcard *.example.com from Let's Encrypt, DNS challenge through Cloudflare Force SSL, HTTP/2 On Block common exploits On Websockets On Trust forwarded proto On (requests from the tunnel arrive as HTTP with X-Forwarded-Proto: https)

./homelab domain setup creates and updates these; it matches hosts by name and changes only what differs. Hand-made proxy hosts are left alone. After it has run once, every install does the same for the apps it starts (domain setup --auto, AUTO_DOMAIN=true): their proxy hosts with the wildcard certificate, with no prompt. With /etc/hosts instead of AdGuard, run Set up the domain after an install to add the new names there (it asks for your password).

These automatic addresses are LAN only: an install adds proxy hosts, never tunnel hostnames. Publishing an app to the internet stays a deliberate Set up the domain (./homelab domain setup --apply), which also adds the public apps' tunnel hostnames.

Each proxy host includes /data/nginx/custom/server_proxy.conf, which sets real_ip_header CF-Connecting-IP so tunnel visitors are logged (and judged by CrowdSec) by their real address, and set_real_ip_from 198.18.89.2, cloudflared's fixed address on the tunnel's own network (homelab-tunnel, 198.18.89.0/29, which the CLI makes before any app starts). That line replaces Proxy Manager's own list (every private network), so a device at home or another container sending the header is seen as itself. cloudflared is on homelab-tunnel alone and reaches only the proxy; a file the household edited is kept, with a note in the proxy's log to add the line.

Nextcloud, Firefly III and its importer believe the visitor's address (and https, and the host name) the proxy hands them, so they are on a network of their own, homelab-front (198.18.89.16/28, made before any app starts), and not on homelab. The proxy is at 198.18.89.18 there and Tailscale at 198.18.89.19, and those two addresses are all the apps trust (TRUSTED_PROXIES). A device at home on an app's own port, or another app, is seen as itself.

docs.title: Docker network
docs.text:
Network Members homelab (external, shared) Every core service, cloudflared, and the web service of each stack homelab_immich_default Immich's server, machine learning, Redis, and database homelab_paperless_default Paperless and its database and broker homelab_budget_tracker_default MoneyMatter's five containers homelab_<stack>_default for each optional stack (Karakeep, RomM, Ghostfolio, Docmost, Dawarich, Beszel, Firefly III, Frigate, Linkwarden, Nextcloud, Tandoor) That stack's app and its helpers (database, search, cache)

Each category file (compose/<category>.yaml) is its own Compose project (homelab_network, homelab_media, …), but all of them join the one homelab network, so apps reach each other by service name.

qBittorrent has no network of its own: it uses Gluetun's (network_mode: service:gluetun), so its traffic can only leave through ProtonVPN, and its web UI is reached as gluetun:8082.

docs.title: Cloudflare
docs.text:
Item Setting Zone example.com SSL/TLS mode Full (strict) Always Use HTTPS On Minimum TLS 1.2 Tunnel One remotely managed tunnel; connector is the cloudflared container Public hostnames One per app marked public: true, each to http://nginx-proxy-manager:80, written by ./homelab domain setup DNS records A proxied CNAME per public hostname to <tunnel id>.cfargotunnel.com Access / WARP Not used (Decisions, ADR-0005)

The API token in CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN needs Zone:Read and DNS:Edit on the zone, and Cloudflare Tunnel:Edit on the account.

docs.title: Traffic paths
docs.text:
Home mode: device (in the tailnet) ─HTTPS→ <TAILSCALE_HOST>:<port> → Tailscale Serve → service

LAN:       device ─DNS→ AdGuard (*.example.com = 192.168.1.10)
           device ─HTTPS→ 192.168.1.10:443 → Proxy Manager (+CrowdSec) → service:port

Internet:  visitor ─HTTPS→ Cloudflare edge → tunnel → cloudflared
           cloudflared ─HTTP→ nginx-proxy-manager:80 (+CrowdSec, CF-Connecting-IP) → service:port

docs.title: What each device can do
docs.text:
One page that says what works on each device, and why something doesn't. It was read from the code on Nov 11, 2026: the computer's screens (web/src/screens), what a phone may call (phoneMethods in cmd/homelab/serve.go), what the phone's page hides (html.companion and .can-change in web/dist/style.css), and the Apple app's views (apple-client/Shared/Views). Where a description elsewhere disagreed with the code, the code won, and the row says so.

Keep it true: a pull request that adds or changes a feature changes its row here. TestParityNamesEveryPhoneCall (cmd/homelab/contract_test.go) fails until every call a phone may make is named on this page, in backticks, in the row of the feature it serves.

docs.title: The devices
docs.text:
• Computer: Homelab Wizard, the desktop app on the machine that runs the homelab. It is the same on a Mac, Windows and Linux except where Host › The same on every system says otherwise; that table has every difference by system, so this page only points to it.
  • Phone's page: the phone companion (homelab serve) in a phone's browser. It is the computer's own screens (the same bundle, drawn under html.companion), with only the calls in phoneMethods. Any phone works: Android, a partner's, a visitor's.
  • iPhone: the Homelab app (apple-client), on an iPhone.
  • iPad: the same app on an iPad, in a split view with a sidebar.

What a phone may do also depends on how it was paired, on every phone (the phone's page and the app alike):

  • Allowed changes (Change: true calls): start, stop, back up, settings and the like. The iPhone and iPad app ask Face ID first, except a fold, which only changes what shows open.
  • Look only: sees everything a phone may see, changes nothing.
  • Wall screen (#kiosk): Status only, look-only for good, and never names which phone did something.
  • A household member's phone (homelab phone person): only their apps, their own Finances, and what the owner shares with them; no Backups, Setup or homelab settings.
  • Away from home (through the Cloudflare tunnel, ADR-0023): looks only, on the iPhone app; changes wait until home.
  • Offline (the iPhone and iPad app, Nov 13): with the Homelab not answering (no signal, or away without the tunnel), Finances shows the last Finances read on this device, "As of" when, to look at only; they're kept sealed with this device's own key, only at the view or edit level, and go when Finances is taken away or the phone is unpaired. Once it answers, the newest are read by themselves.

docs.title: What the cells say
docs.text:
• yes: it's there and does the same job.
  • partly: it's there, and the cell says what's missing.
  • on purpose: it's left out, and the cell says why. Most are one of three: a phone can't install apps or move files on the computer; a wall screen only looks; away from home only looks.
  • gap: it could be there and isn't yet. Each gap is a candidate to close (Gaps, at the bottom).

docs.title: Private Finances
docs.text: A household member can keep her own Finances private, so that only she can open them, on her own phone. That includes the person who runs the homelab. This page says what that means, in plain words, for her and for whoever runs the computer.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
Everyone in Settings › People whose phone is theirs (Settings › Phones) already has Finances of their own on that phone: their accounts, bills, budgets, transactions and receipts, apart from the household's. Until they're private, the computer keeps them as ordinary files, and whoever runs it could open those files.

Make them private… (in Finances on her phone, in the Homelab app or on the phone's page) locks them on her phone before they reach the computer. From then on:

  • The computer keeps one locked file for her, finance.sealed, and her receipts locked beside it. It can't open them. Neither can anyone at the computer, nor anything it runs.
  • Her phone opens them, reads them forward with the computer's own Finances code built into the phone, and saves them locked again.
  • What the household shares with her (homelab person share: bills, subscriptions, budgets) still shows, as before. It's the household's money, not hers, so it isn't locked.

docs.title: How she opens them
docs.text:
• Her recovery code: 16 words, shown once when she turns privacy on. She writes them down and types two of them back. The code opens her Finances anywhere, a new phone included.
  • Face ID:
  • On the phone's page, a passkey made for them. It works at the address it was made on; another address (the homelab reached a different way) asks for the code instead.
  • In the Homelab app, Face ID opens them on any device where she opened them once with her passphrase or code. The key is then kept in that device's Keychain behind Face ID: never synced, never backed up, gone when the phone is unpaired. (The app can't use the page's passkey: that needs Apple's servers to reach the homelab's own address, and a homelab at home isn't on the internet.)
  • A passphrase (12 characters or more), where Face ID's passkey can't lock them, and always when she turns privacy on in the app.

They lock again when she leaves Finances, after 5 minutes untouched, and when the page is hidden or the app goes to the background.

docs.title: Away from home
docs.text: Her phone keeps the locked copy it last read (only ever locked, never her key). With no signal, Face ID, her passphrase or her code still opens them. A change she makes then waits on her phone, locked, and goes to the homelab by itself once it answers. If another of her devices changed them meanwhile, her phone says so plainly and shows the newest; the change made away isn't kept, and she makes it again.

docs.title: If she loses them
docs.text:
• Her phone: Remove it on the computer (Settings › Phones) as usual. Her Finances stay locked. She pairs her new phone and opens them with her recovery code (or, in the app, her passphrase).
  • Her recovery code and her passphrase, and her passkey: no one can open her private Finances, ever. The app and the page say so before she turns privacy on.

docs.title: What the person who runs the homelab can and can't do
docs.text:
• Can't: open them, read them, or see any amount, account, payee or receipt of hers, on the computer, in a backup, a log or the record of who changed what.
  • Can see: that she keeps them private, and when they were last saved (Settings › People, and homelab person list).
  • Can delete them: removing her from the household (homelab person remove) asks whether to keep her Finances, and keeps them unless told otherwise (--delete-finances). Deleting them can't be undone.
  • No longer does for her: the nightly Finances reminders, the Finances calendar feed, and the money card on a wall screen. The computer can't read her Finances to make them. The Homelab app on her phone gives her the same reminders itself (a bill due tomorrow, a paycheck that leaves checking under her cushion, a yearly renewal, balances not updated for weeks), worked out on her phone with the computer's own code each time she opens her Finances, and planned two weeks ahead.

docs.title: The phone's page has one limit
docs.text: The phone's page is served by the homelab computer. Someone who changed the homelab's own code could make the page send them her key the next time she opens her Finances there. The Homelab app comes from Apple, not from the computer, so it doesn't have this limit: it's the stronger home for private Finances. The page says this where she turns privacy on.

docs.title: Turning it off
docs.text: Turn privacy off… (on her phone, once she confirms) keeps her Finances plain on the homelab again, receipts included. The locked file and her recovery code stop mattering; whoever runs the computer could read her Finances again.

docs.title: Backups
docs.text: Her locked file is in the nightly backup of the homelab's records (the encrypted Homelab Secrets job), as the rest of data/members/ is. The copies of her plain Finances from before she turned privacy on are in the last 7 nights' backups, and age out on their own.

docs.title: For the curious
docs.text: How it's built: the format and the steps are in .claude/prompts/private-finances.md. In short, a random key locks her Finances with AES-256-GCM on her phone; that key is itself locked by her recovery code (stretched with scrypt) and by her passkey or passphrase. The computer stores only what's locked (internal/finance/sealed.go) and checks its shape and size, never what's in it. The security review is in Security.

docs.title: Releasing
docs.text: .github/workflows/release.yml builds the desktop app and the CLI for macOS, Windows, and Linux, signs what it has certificates for, and drafts a GitHub release for each v* tag. Every change to main that touches the app or the engine also publishes a numbered release with the builds for every system as the latest build (Releases › Latest).

docs.title: Version numbers
docs.text: Every build of main is a release of its own, numbered one more than the newest release: 0.17.0, 0.17.1, … 0.17.10, then 0.18.0 by itself, and so on (the release workflow's version job, internal/tools/nextversion; the owner's call of November 2026, after builds numbered by their commits reached 0.16.41). VERSION is the floor: a newer minor or major there makes the next build that, and a re-run of a released commit keeps its number. Before 0.17.0, a build's patch was the commits since VERSION changed. Versions carry no -beta from 0.11.0 on (October 2026, the owner's call); 0.9.0-beta to 0.10.0-beta kept it. Nothing needs committing for a build to get its number. A push that changes none of the built paths (docs alone) builds nothing, so the numbers can skip.

docs.title: A new minor or major version
docs.text:
Each minor after its .10 starts by itself; set one by hand only to jump ahead (a big change, or 1.0.0).

  1. Set VERSION (0.12.0, 1.0.0), the version: front matter of every note to match (./homelab validate checks it), and move the [Unreleased] notes in CHANGELOG.md under a new ## [0.12.0] - <date> heading, with a bold one-line summary of the version.
  2. Push to main. That build is v0.12.0, which the stable channel moves to, and its release notes are that version's section of the CHANGELOG; the builds after it are v0.12.1 to v0.12.10, then v0.13.0.
  3. If this version changed the shape of a file the homelab folder keeps (.env, data/*.json, scripts/logs/*.json), add its folder to the upgrade set once it is tagged: testdata/upgrades/make.sh v0.12.0, then commit testdata/upgrades/v0.12.0. TestEachReleasesFolderUpgrades then opens it with every later build.

docs.title: Release notes
docs.text:
CHANGELOG.md is the patch notes: each version's New, Improved, and Fixed, one plain line each (CONTRIBUTING.md says how to write one). The publish job makes each build's notes from it: the version's own section for the first build of a version, then the CHANGELOG lines added since the release before (each commit's first line when a build added none). The app shows them before an update.

The versions before numbered releases (0.2.0 to 0.9.0-beta) were tagged afterwards at the commit where each ended, and their releases published by hand from their CHANGELOG sections. They have notes and no builds, so the stable channel skips them. A workflow could not publish them: its token may not tag a commit whose .github/workflows differ from main's.

A tag made with your own login (gh release create, git push --tags) starts a tag build of that commit, as a tag pushed by hand does. For a notes-only release of an old commit, cancel those runs in Actions: one that finishes attaches its build to the release, and the stable channel would then offer that old build.

A tag pushed by hand (git tag v0.10.0 && git push origin v0.10.0) still builds a draft release with checksums and build provenance, to check for "unsigned" notes and publish yourself.

To get the files without a release (for testing the pipeline), run the workflow by hand: Actions › Release › Run workflow. It builds the Mac app unless you pick all (or Windows or Linux) under Which builds to make, and the files stay attached to the run for 3 days; a tagged build keeps them 14 days, and the release keeps its own copies.

If a run fails with Artifact storage quota has been hit, older runs' files fill the account's storage: run Actions › Clean up artifacts (it keeps the newest run's files and deletes the rest), wait for GitHub to recount (up to 12 hours), and run the release again.

docs.title: The latest build
docs.text:
Every push to main that changes app/, web/, cmd/, internal/, go.mod, go.sum, VERSION, or the workflow runs the macos, windows, and linux jobs, then the publish job makes the numbered release ("Homelab Wizard 0.14.3", tag v0.14.3 on that commit, with its release notes from the CHANGELOG) the repository's Latest, with every build that worked (the Mac build must; a failed Windows or Linux build is left out until the next push). A newer push cancels a build still running. The same files also replace the nightly pre-release, which apps from before numbered releases look for; their next update brings a build that follows the numbered releases.

Each build carries where it came from: -ldflags set main.version, main.commit, and main.repo for the app, and Commit and Repo in app/tray for the menu bar item (the CLI gets main.version). The app's update (internal/selfupdate, Update now on the line at the top of the window) reads the newest build for the update channel (the Latest release on testing, the newest vX.Y.0 release with builds on stable), compares its commit with the running build's, downloads the file for how it was installed (the Mac's DMG, the Windows portable zip for the PC's processor, whether the app came from the installer or the zip, with the installer only for a release that has no zip; the AppImage; or the .deb, .rpm, or Arch package), checks it against the SHA-256 digest GitHub records for the asset (and stops if they differ), swaps itself for the new build, and reopens. On Windows a hidden PowerShell script puts the zip's files in place once the app has quit, as an administrator (one approval) only where the account cannot write the folder (Program Files), so SmartScreen and Smart App Control, which blocked the unsigned installer, are not in the way. Each attempt's steps go in update.log in the user's cache folder; a build that did not go in place says why when the app opens on the old one, with the release page, and the same update is not offered again. A homelab folder the app made then follows by itself (homelab upgrade, Finishing the update…), on every system. The app looks every 15 minutes and when its window comes forward; with the window closed, the menu bar item looks on the same schedule and says Update to ….
