  3. On the new machine: install the runtime and Homelab Wizard, Setup › Set it up for me, then Backups › Move in… with the file (./homelab move in <file>).
  4. Follow the steps it lists, then ./homelab uninstall on the old machine.

Check: Status shows every app green, and a photo, a password, and a document open. Disaster Recovery has the details.

docs.title: Rebuild a lost machine from the backups
docs.text:
When the old machine is gone and only the backup folder is left.

  1. On the new machine: install the runtime and Homelab Wizard, Setup › Set it up for me, and let the cloud drive finish syncing the backup folder (or plug in the backup drive).
  2. ./homelab rebuild <backup folder> and type DUPLICATI_SECRETS_PASSPHRASE (from Vaultwarden or the recovery kit).
  3. If it stops for a folder this machine does not have (the media drive), plug it in or set it in Settings › Storage, then run the same command again: it carries on.
  4. Install Jellyfin and restore Homelab Jellyfin into it, if you had it; then the addresses (Setup › Addresses on your tailnet, or Set up the domain).

Check: Status shows every app green, Settings › People and Phones list the household, Finances shows the plan, and a photo, a password, and a document open. Disaster Recovery has the details and the same by hand.

docs.title: Let a phone see Finances
docs.text:
1. Pair it with the https link (Tailscale, or the domain): Settings › Phones › Pair a phone. A phone paired with the http: link never gets Finances: Remove it and pair it again.
  2. Beside the phone, pick Sees Finances (look only) or Changes Finances (./homelab phone finances <id> view, or edit).

Check: Finances is in the phone's tab bar; with Sees Finances, view only under its heading and no Edit. No Finances (off) takes it away again.

For a guest's phone, or one lent for a while, pick For a day, For a week, or For a month beside it (./homelab phone until <id> 7d): its row says until when, and then it only looks, with no Finances, without anyone remembering to take them back. A wall screen keeps its money card.

docs.title: Restart the Mac safely
docs.text:
1. Close nothing; the containers stop with OrbStack.
  2. Restart, then log in straight away (FileVault).
  3. Within a few minutes the startup job runs homelab up.

Check: ./homelab status and ./homelab watchdog.

docs.title: Rotate a secret
docs.text:
1. Change it in the app (or generate a new value).
  2. Update .env and the Vaultwarden entry.
  3. Recreate the containers that read it: ./homelab update <app> (or ./homelab compose <stack> up -d).
  4. ./homelab backup --apply so the Secrets job picks up the new .env.

Database passwords live inside the database too: change them with ALTER USER first, then in .env.

docs.title: Monthly restore test
docs.text: In the app, Backups › Test a restore; in a terminal, ./homelab restore-test --auto. Each test goes on record with its result and how long it took: the Backups tile, the weekly summary, and ./homelab report show it (Backups, Restore testing). A failed test leaves the restored files in recovery-staging/restore-test; Troubleshooting has the usual causes, and one that repeats belongs in Known Issues.

docs.title: Savings
docs.text:
What the homelab could replace if the household used it to the full: every paid service each app can stand in for, with its monthly and annual price, organised by stack (the same categories as services/).

This is the full-replacement picture. Each saving is tagged with what it takes to get it, so you can see how much is automatic and how much depends on owning the media.

Kind What it means Services Annual plan Direct The app does the same job; the saving is real as soon as you switch 15 $1,376.39 Library Needs media you own (films, music, books); the app replaces the service's player and catalogue 12 $2,027.96 Equivalent A paid product with the same function that a household may not otherwise buy 12 $1,082.73

How to read the numbers

  • Monthly: the month-to-month price. Marked † where the service only bills yearly; the figure is the annual price ÷ 12.
  • Annual plan: the cheapest way to pay for a year (an annual plan where one exists, otherwise 12 × monthly). The headline totals use this column.
  • Paid monthly for a year: 12 × Monthly, what a year costs without an annual commitment.
  • Runs: Baseline apps start with ./homelab up; Optional apps need ./homelab install <app> first; Native is Jellyfin, installed on the computer itself rather than in a container.

docs.title: Posture
docs.text: Area Control Inbound No router ports. Public apps go through the Cloudflare Tunnel, which only connects outward Edge Cloudflare proxy with the free managed ruleset, Full (strict) TLS Ingress Every request, LAN or tunnel, passes Nginx Proxy Manager with the CrowdSec bouncer Detection CrowdSec reads the proxy's logs, bans attackers, pulls the community blocklist, and checks requests against virtual-patching rules (AppSec) App ports Bound to 127.0.0.1; only 53, 80, and 443 listen on the LAN Containers no-new-privileges, no container that can change Docker, read-only mounts where possible Databases Only reachable from their own stack's private network Secrets .env (0600, never committed) and Vaultwarden Backups Encrypted by Duplicati before they leave the Mac Alerts ntfy with deny-all access; only the alert topics are writable Tidy Up's lookups Only for music, and only what a lookup needs: LRCLIB (lrclib.net) gets a song's title, artist, album and length, for songs without time-synced lyrics, from Add lyrics or new music (TIDY_LYRICS_NEW_MUSIC=off stops the second); MusicBrainz gets an album's tags (beets' matching) or the release picked; AcoustID gets a song's sound fingerprint and length, only when fpcalc is installed; a music cleanup also asks Cover Art Archive, iTunes, Amazon and AlbumArt.org for an album's cover (beets' fetchart) and Last.fm for its genre (lastgenre), by artist and album; the books review asks the metadata sources enabled in Calibre's own preferences (fetch-ebook-metadata) by a book's title and first author, and its ISBN for a cover. No file, path, account or key of the household's goes with them

docs.title: Public apps
docs.text:
App Hostname Authentication Vaultwarden passwords Master password, 2FA required for every account Immich photos Immich accounts Paperless-ngx docs Paperless accounts, 2FA available Navidrome navidrome Navidrome accounts Feishin music Signs in to Navidrome Audiobookshelf audiobooks Audiobookshelf accounts Calibre-Web books Calibre-Web accounts (change the default admin first) Komga comics Komga accounts ntfy ntfy Deny-all; only the alert tokens and the phone's login (published once notify setup has made the token) Nextcloud (optional) cloud Nextcloud accounts, 2FA available

Any of these can be kept home only (data/home-only.json): an app's page › Reach it away from home off, or homelab away off <app>, takes it off the internet, removing only what the homelab put there (its tunnel rule, its service in the proxy, and the CNAME when it points at this tunnel; the household's own rules and records are left and named). A public app installed new starts home only until the switch is turned on; apps installed before stay as they were. The switch shows once the domain has the Cloudflare tunnel. The generated list of public hostnames is in Inventory. Everything else is LAN-only: its hostname is not in public DNS and not in the tunnel. Making an app public is one line (public: true) and must meet the Contributing checklist first. Admin apps are never public: homelab validate (and CI) refuses public: true on an infrastructure app (the proxy, AdGuard, Duplicati, Dozzle, and the like) or one marked admin: true (Uptime Kuma). Publishing one would first need Cloudflare Access in front of it, signing in at Cloudflare before the page loads.

docs.title: CrowdSec
docs.text:
Part Detail Engine crowdsec container, collections crowdsecurity/nginx-proxy-manager and crowdsecurity/appsec-virtual-patching Log source npm-logs volume, read-only, via config/crowdsec/acquis.yaml Bouncer Lua bouncer inside the proxy image, stream mode, refreshed every 10 seconds Bouncer key CROWDSEC_BOUNCER_KEY, registered by the engine at start Whitelist Private addresses are never banned (CrowdSec's default) AppSec The bouncer sends each request to CrowdSec's AppSec listener (crowdsec:7422, config/crowdsec/appsec.yaml) and blocks those matching a virtual-patching rule: exploits of known vulnerabilities in common apps. Generic rules are not loaded, to keep normal traffic untouched Failure mode If CrowdSec is down, the proxy keeps serving from its last list, and requests skip AppSec (fails open)

Test it with the ban runbook in Runbooks.

Bans only hold while the proxy's bouncer pulls them, so ./homelab doctor says when it last did, and the watchdog alerts when it stops (missing, revoked, or no pull for 5 minutes). The app's Status screen shows Protection: bans enforced or not, and what CrowdSec caught this week.

docs.title: Accounts and secrets
docs.text:
• Every password is 40 random characters, generated by Vaultwarden, unique per app.
  • Turn on 2FA wherever an app offers it (Vaultwarden, Paperless, the personal Nginx Proxy Manager admin). Setup's Two-step sign-in step walks through Vaultwarden and the proxy.
  • The Proxy Manager automation account (NPM_API_EMAIL) cannot use 2FA because the CLI signs in with it. Keep a separate personal admin with 2FA.
  • Close Vaultwarden sign-ups (VAULTWARDEN_SIGNUPS_ALLOWED=false) once accounts exist.
  • Secrets never go into git, notes, chats, command arguments, or logs. The CLI reads them from .env and sends them only to the service they belong to.
  • Keep an offline copy of the Vaultwarden master password and DUPLICATI_SECRETS_PASSPHRASE (the Homelab Secrets job's passphrase, from .env). Without them, nothing can be restored.

docs.title: Docker socket
docs.text: Consumer Access Homarr, Dozzle (optional) docker-socket-proxy, read-only: container list, logs, and engine info Beszel agent (optional) The socket mounted read-only: it runs on the host's network, where it cannot reach the socket proxy by name. A read-only mount does not limit what Docker's API allows, so treat it like the raw socket; pinned (BESZEL_AGENT_VERSION) and updated by hand, as the socket proxy is (N18) Everything else None

docs.title: Updates
docs.text:
• The background agent updates the apps nightly, outside any container, copying each first; the proxy, databases, MoneyMatter, docker-socket-proxy, and the Beszel agent (both hold Docker's socket) are updated by hand.
  • ./homelab update nginx-proxy-manager rebuilds the proxy on the newest NPM_VERSION you set.
  • macOS and OrbStack: install updates by hand, then log in straight away.

docs.title: Review (October 2026)
docs.text:
Everything reachable from outside this machine, what guards it, and what is left. Reviewed against the code, not only the docs; re-run it before each release.

Surface Who can reach it Controls What is left Public apps through the Cloudflare Tunnel Anyone on the internet Outbound-only tunnel; Cloudflare's managed rules; the proxy with CrowdSec bans and AppSec virtual patching; each app's own sign-in (2FA on Vaultwarden); validate refuses public: true on admin apps; new public installs start home only, and homelab away off (an app's Reach it away from home) takes one off the tunnel and DNS A flaw in a public app before its patch: nightly updates and virtual patching narrow the window, they do not close it. Away from home, a public app's pages pass Cloudflare decrypted. Keep the public list short: turn off what isn't needed away ntfy (public, for phone alerts) Anyone on the internet Deny-all by default; publishing and reading need tokens (NTFY_PUBLISH_TOKEN, NTFY_READ_TOKEN, the phone's login); only published once the token exists A leaked phone login reads the alerts (which name apps, never secrets): rotate it with homelab notify setup The proxy and DNS on the LAN (80, 443, 53) Every device on the home network TLS with the wildcard certificate; app ports bound to 127.0.0.1 (BIND_IP); the same per-app sign-in CrowdSec never bans private addresses, so a compromised device at home is not stopped by it; admin apps (the proxy, AdGuard, Duplicati) are reachable from the LAN behind their own passwords Home mode: Tailscale Serve Devices signed in to your tailnet Tailnet only: Funnel is never turned on, so nothing is on the internet; WireGuard end to end Every device in the tailnet reaches every app, admin apps included. Share the tailnet only with the household, set TAILNET_ADMIN_APPS=false to keep the admin apps on this machine only, or limit the homelab machine with Tailscale's access controls Phone companion (homelab serve, 8099) Home network and tailnet; through the tunnel, the iPhone app looking only (ADR-0023) Refuses public addresses; through Cloudflare (Cf-Ray/Cf-Connecting-Ip) only /api/tunnel, and only with Access's signed pass for the household's service token (RS256 against the team's keys, audience, issuer, common_name, expiry), sealed end to end with the key the phone agreed when it paired at home (X25519, AES-256-GCM, 2 minutes' skew, each message once), carrying its device token, for a method that only looks (no change, Settings, stream, pairing, or page); 10 wrong attempts lock an address or a phone out for 10 minutes; without Access set up, nothing through Cloudflare; one-time pairing codes (8 characters, 10 minutes, 10 wrong codes lock pairing for 10 minutes); device tokens stored as SHA-256 hashes and compared in constant time; read-only unless allowed, and allowed only to a phone paired over an encrypted link (M5); Finances (the household's money) only to a phone picked for them, only over an encrypted connection, never to a kiosk screen, and changed only by one picked for Changes Finances; Settings (.env) only over an encrypted connection and never to a kiosk screen, a secret only as set or not, and only everyday ones changed by a phone allowed changes: secrets and the settings a phone connects through (the companion, its bind addresses, the domain and proxy key, the proxy's ports, AdGuard's DNS address, Tailscale) are changed on the computer only; strict CSP and no framing Anyone on the home Wi-Fi can try to pair, at the rate limit; a phone that is lost needs Remove in Settings › Phones (or No Finances at least) The desktop app This machine only Opens no port; secrets are copied to the clipboard (cleared after 90 seconds) and never sent to the page; Finances (data/finance.json), the household, and the paired phones are written 0600 and go off-site only inside the encrypted Secrets job Anything running as you on this Mac can read .env and Finances, as with any local secret store Self-update (the latest build or a v* release) Whoever controls the GitHub repository HTTPS from GitHub; the download is checked against GitHub's SHA-256 of it before it is opened; the old app is kept until the new one is in place; on Windows an administrator's approval is asked only when the app is in Program Files; build provenance attestations for tagged releases Builds are unsigned until the Apple Developer ID is in place, so a compromised repository or GitHub account could ship a bad build. Signing and notarisation (1.0) close this; until then, keep 2FA on the GitHub account Release workflow Pushes to main and tags contents: read by default; write only in the nightly and release jobs; no secrets in pull-request runs The nightly job replaces the nightly release on every app change to main: review what merges Diagnostics reports Whoever you send one to Passwords, tokens, emails, your account name, and the home folder are redacted (homelab report) Read it before sending; app logs can still name hosts and IPs

Findings that changed code in this review: none needed. Follow-ups: signed builds (1.0), and a second person's review of this table before 1.0.

docs.title: The app's own code
docs.text:
The review above covers what can be reached from outside. This part covers the homelab's own code: the homelab CLI, the desktop app, and the frontend. make security runs three scanners, and CI runs it on every pull request (the security job):

Scanner What it looks for Where govulncheck Known vulnerabilities in the Go standard library and the Go packages the code uses, counted only when the code can reach the flawed function The CLI for macOS, Linux, and Windows; the app for Linux and Windows (its Mac build needs a Mac to compile, so its Mac-only Wails code is not scanned) gosec Risky patterns in the Go code: weak randomness, unsafe conversions, hard-coded secrets, unbounded decompression Both Go modules npm audit Known vulnerabilities in the frontend's packages Fails on any advisory in what is bundled into the app (Preact), and on high or critical ones in the build tools (esbuild, TypeScript)

The builds use a current Go (toolchain in go.mod and app/go.mod), so fixes to Go itself reach the app. Until October 2026 the release builds were made with Go 1.25.0, which no longer gets security fixes.

gosec rules left out, because the homelab does these on purpose, as the person running it, with paths and commands it builds itself:

Rule What it flags Why it is left out G204, G702 Running a program named by a variable Running Docker, Compose, and the system's own tools is the homelab's job. Arguments go as a list. The few places that build a shell or PowerShell script from values are checked one by one in the threat review G304, G703 Opening a file whose path is a variable The paths are inside the homelab folder or the user's own settings. Unpacking an archive made elsewhere (a move file, a kit) is checked in the threat review G301, G302, G306 Folders and files readable by other users (0755, 0644) Logs, schedules, and generated pages are meant to be readable; .env, backups, and anything holding a secret are written 0600 G104 An error not checked Low severity; the unchecked ones are best-effort clean-up (removing a temporary file, closing a window)

The 14 other places gosec flagged were checked and marked in the code with #nosec and the reason (a percentage that cannot overflow, the names of settings mistaken for passwords, random numbers that only pick which backed-up files to test).

When the security job turns red without a change of yours, a new advisory was published. govulncheck names the package and the fixed version: update it (go get <package>@<version>, then go mod tidy; for Go itself, the toolchain line), or for npm, npm update <package>. If no fix exists yet, write it up in Known Issues with why it does or does not reach the homelab.

docs.title: Threat review of the app (October 2026)
docs.text:
Every way into the homelab's own code: what can reach it, what guards it, and what was found. Read against the code in October 2026 (0.6.0); the review above covers the apps and the network around them. Each finding is fixed in its own pull request, highest risk first, and ticked here when merged.

Result: no high findings. Six medium, five low, and the rest fine as they are.

docs.title: What was looked at
docs.text: Way in Who can reach it What guards it Phone companion (homelab serve, port 8099) Anything on the same network as the computer (home Wi-Fi, or a café's), and the tailnet Private addresses only, nothing through Cloudflare; one-time 8-character codes, 10 wrong codes lock pairing for 10 minutes; device tokens stored hashed, compared in constant time; a fixed list of methods, read-only unless allowed, and allowed only to a phone paired over an encrypted link (M5); Finances only to a phone picked for them and only over an encrypted connection, never to a kiosk screen; Settings only over an encrypted connection, never to a kiosk screen, secrets never sent, and a phone changes only everyday settings (never a secret, nor what it connects through); strict CSP, no framing; tokens are sent as a header, never a cookie, so another website cannot act for a phone Kiosk mode (&kiosk on the pairing link) Anyone standing at the TV or wall screen A screen paired in kiosk mode is read-only on the computer's side (M4), so showing the buttons again changes nothing The engine's local socket Programs running as you on this computer Owner-only folder and socket; read-only (/v1/status, /v1/status/last, /v1/events, /v1/cards) The desktop app's page Only the app's own frontend, bundled into the app Opens no port; outside text (release notes, logs, the model's answer) is shown as text, never as HTML; the only raw HTML is the app's own icons Docker Whatever can use Docker's socket No container can change Docker (Watchtower, which could, is gone); the optional Beszel agent reads the socket mounted read-only; Homarr and Dozzle go through docker-socket-proxy, which allows no changes. On a Mac, Docker (OrbStack or Docker Desktop) can open the files in your home folder, so control of Docker is control of your files Update downloads Whoever controls the GitHub repository or its release workflow HTTPS; the download checked against GitHub's SHA-256; opt-in install on quit. Unsigned until the Developer ID (1.0) GitHub release notes Each app's GitHub project, which writes its own notes Shown as plain text; size-capped; cached 6 hours Explain this (Ollama) The model on this machine Passwords and tokens taken out of the log first; the answer is shown as advice, nothing it says is run Input from the page and the phone The app's page; paired phones .env values with line breaks are refused; app names are checked against the catalog before any command; phone actions are a fixed list

docs.title: Findings
docs.text:
# Risk Finding Fix M1 Medium The release workflow uses actions by movable tags, one of them third-party (softprops/action-gh-release) with write access to releases. A hijacked action could swap the builds that every copy's Update installs, and the checksum the app checks would come from the same release Fixed: every action is pinned to a commit, and Dependabot proposes updates once a month; TestWorkflowActionsArePinned (November 2026) fails on any step that is not M2 Medium Unpacking a move file follows links: a crafted move file can put a link to a folder outside the homelab, then write through it (into ~/Library/LaunchAgents, say, which runs at login). Needs you to move in a file someone else made Fixed: unpacked through os.Root, which cannot leave the folder, with a test of such a file M3 Medium Any paired device reads raw app logs, a read-only phone or a kiosk TV included, and logs can hold passwords and tokens Fixed: a log sent to a phone has .env's secrets and anything shaped like a password or token taken out, as in a diagnostics report M4 Medium Kiosk mode is only a look: a TV paired with Can make changes keeps that power, and #kiosk=off brings the buttons back Fixed: a screen paired in kiosk mode is made read-only on the computer, whatever its code allowed M5 Medium The phone companion uses plain HTTP on the home network: the pairing code and the device's token cross the Wi-Fi unencrypted, so someone on the same Wi-Fi who knows its password could copy a token. The tailnet link is encrypted (WireGuard) Fixed: a phone paired over plain HTTP from the home network may only look, for good; changes need an encrypted link (Tailscale, the domain's https, or this computer), and a change sent over plain HTTP is refused M6 Medium The two containers that control Docker update themselves from :latest every night (Watchtower, docker-socket-proxy). Whoever controls those images controls the computer Fixed: both pinned and updated by hand after reading their notes, like the proxy and the databases; since then Watchtower is gone, and docker-socket-proxy stays pinned (SOCKET_PROXY_VERSION) L1 Low docker-socket-proxy lets dashboards read each container's details, its settings from .env included, and Dozzle (optional) has no sign-in on the home network and tailnet Fixed: Dozzle is kept to this computer: no tailnet or domain address (local: true), and domain setup removes the logs. proxy host an earlier setup made. The socket proxy itself has no published port; only the homelab's own containers reach it L2 Low HOMELAB_DOMAIN reaches an administrator prompt unchecked: an elevated PowerShell script on Windows, a file path under /etc/resolver on the Mac. Only someone who can already edit .env could abuse it Fixed: the domain and the address are checked before any prompt, and anything else is refused L3 Low The app's Open opens any address its page asks for, not only web links. Needs another bug in the page first Fixed: only http, https, and mailto addresses are opened L4 Low An update without GitHub's checksum is installed unchecked (GitHub now gives one for every release file) Fixed: a download without GitHub's checksum is refused L5 Low On Linux, the Ollama note says to listen on 0.0.0.0, which opens Ollama (no password) to the home network Fixed with Docker Engine: Ollama listens on Docker's own address (docker0, 172.17.0.1), which the containers reach and the home network does not, and the homelab's Explain, doctor, and Setup find it there. On SteamOS, Docker run as you reaches the computer only through its home-network address, so Ollama stays open to the home network there, as its note says

Fine as they are: the engine's socket (yours only, read-only); another website pointing its name at this computer (DNS rebinding: without a code or a token it gets only the page); guessing a pairing code (31⁸ codes, 10 tries per 10 minutes, and only while one is waiting); the companion answering on a café's Wi-Fi (the page and pairing only); Explain with OLLAMA_HOST set to another computer (the log then leaves this one, with secrets taken out); the menu bar item's lock port (another program could keep it from starting, nothing more).

docs.title: Threat review (November 2026)
docs.text: What was added since the 0.6.0 review, read against the code by the security audit loop (.claude/prompts/audit-loop.md), one way in per round. Each finding is fixed in its own commit, with a test that fails without the fix, and ticked here when merged.

docs.title: Findings
docs.text: # Risk Finding Fix N1 Low The phone companion trusts X-Forwarded-Proto: https from anyone when it decides whether a request was encrypted. Checked against the M5 attacker (someone on the home Wi-Fi who copied a token): a phone paired over plain HTTP is made look-only and without Finances when it pairs (MarkUnencrypted), and SetCanChange and SetFinances refuse it later, so a copied token with a forged header gets nothing it did not have. A phone paired over an encrypted link keeps its token per address, so that token never crosses plain HTTP. The per-request check is a second layer, not the guard Fine as it is, now tested: TestAForgedHTTPSHeaderGivesACopiedTokenNothingMore, which fails if pairing stops marking such a phone (checked by removing that step) N3 Low Two generated secrets were not taken out of reports and phones' logs: HOMEBOX_API_KEY_PEPPER and GHOSTFOLIO_ACCESS_TOKEN_SALT are secret by their placeholder in .env.example, not by their name, and the redaction behind a diagnostics report and a log sent to a phone (M3) went by the name alone; their values are plain text that no token pattern catches. It needs an app's log or the report to print one Fixed: what is secret is read as Settings reads it, by the name or by .env.example (settings.SecretKeys); TestEverySecretIsRedacted puts a value in every secret .env.example names and fails if any is left in a report or a phone's log (it named both before the fix) N4 Low The Windows update unpacks as an administrator from a file in your account's folder. Between the checksum check and the approval prompt, a program already running as you could swap the zip, and it would be unpacked into Program Files with the administrator's approval. The script itself is fixed text with the paths as parameters, and the one command built from text (the elevated unpack) quotes both paths (' doubled) and is passed encoded Fine as it is: it needs a program already running as you, which can already do anything you can; Windows does not hold its approval prompt to be a security boundary. Signed builds (1.0) let the app check the file again as the administrator N5 Low Set up the domain could move the household's own * record to this machine. The home record (0.16.6) took over any *.domain A record at a private address, though the homelab never wrote one without its comment before: one a household made by hand for another machine (a NAS) was pointed here, and the watchdog would keep it here Fixed: a record without the homelab's comment becomes the homelab's only when it already points at this machine; any other is left as it is and Set up the domain says so (TestHomeRecord, which moved a NAS's record before) N6 Low Explain took out only what looks like a token before sending an app's log to the model, not the secrets in .env themselves; with OLLAMA_HOST on another computer, a secret an app printed plainly (a generated pepper looks like nothing) would leave this one, though the review above said secrets are taken out Fixed: the log loses every secret value in .env first (settings.Hide, settings.SecretValues, which reports and phones' logs now share), then anything shaped like a token; TestExplainSendsNoSecret failed before (a password in the log reached the model's text) N7 — What a pull request from a fork can do in the workflows: CI and Nightly run on pull_request (never pull_request_target or workflow_run), read-only and without secrets; Release runs only on pushes to main, tags, and by hand; no step puts a pull request's title, branch, or text into a script Fine as it is, now tested: TestWorkflowsGiveAPullRequestNothing fails on either trigger, on a workflow without top-level permissions, or on such text in a step (checked by adding both to ci.yml) N8 — The agent's socket since 0.6.0 (/v1/cards added): it serves Status and its cards, the same as the window shows, read-only, to whoever can open it; it lives in your own runtime or cache folder, 0600 in a 0700 folder Fine as it is, now tested: TestTheSocketIsYoursAlone fails if the socket or its folder is open to others (checked with 0666) N9 — The homelab's own records in data/ (Finances' plan, ledger, and receipts; people's welcome pages; sso; the paired phones): each written 0600, and off-site only inside the encrypted Secrets job (copied into its staging each night); Duplicati's other jobs read only data/appdata and appdata. home-address.json is 0644 and holds only this machine's address at home Fine as it is, now tested: TestNoOtherJobReadsTheRecords fails if another job's source would take data/ (checked by mounting ./data) N2 Low Any paired device can make a diagnostics report (Report, up to 3 minutes of work each), a look-only phone or a wall screen included, and several at once Fine as it is: the report has every secret taken out (as a phone's logs, M3), it is how a household member sends one to their helper, and it changes nothing; a paired device is the household's N10 Low The record of apps stopped on purpose could lose a stop, or be read half-written (data/stopped.json, 0.17). Three writers change it (the awake job each minute, homelab stop, and a phone's StopUntil), each by reading it, changing it, and writing it whole in place with no lock. The awake job held its copy through the seconds a compose start takes and saved it over a stop made meanwhile, and a reader in that moment could see an empty file: either way the watchdog, the battery saver, or a drive coming back started an app the household had stopped. docs.title: Review: the phone companion through the tunnel (November 2026)
docs.text:
The owner asked for the iPhone app away from home without Tailscale (ADR-0023). This puts one address of the companion, which holds Finances, on the internet, so it was reviewed before it merged, against someone on the internet, Cloudflare itself, someone who stole a phone, and someone who copied a pass or a message.

What is exposed: https://<the companion's hostname>/api/tunnel, POST only, behind Cloudflare Access. Nothing else of the companion answers through the tunnel: the page, pairing, /api/call, /api/me, /api/events and the calendar are refused there before anything is read (TestTheTunnel).

Who What they try What stops them Test Anyone on the internet Reach the companion Access stops a request without the household's service token at Cloudflare. If Access were turned off or the hostname set up by mistake, the companion still needs Access's signed pass, and its sealed message TestTheTunnelNeedsAccesssPass Anyone with a pass of their own Another Cloudflare team's pass, another application's, a person's login, or one signed by a key that isn't the team's The pass is checked against the team's own keys, the application's audience, the team's issuer, the household's service token (common_name), and its expiry TestTheTunnelNeedsAccesssPass Cloudflare, or whoever reads the tunnel Read Finances, or change a request Every request and answer is sealed end to end (AES-256-GCM) with a key agreed at home (X25519); Cloudflare sees which phone and the size, nothing more. A changed box doesn't open TestTheTunnel (answers don't show their contents), TestTheTunnelNeedsThePhone Someone who copied a sealed request Send it again A request carries its time (2 minutes either way) and each is taken once TestTheTunnelNeedsThePhone Someone with the service token, or a valid pass Ask without the phone The message must be sealed with that phone's key and carry its device token TestTheTunnelNeedsThePhone Whoever has a lost or stolen phone Keep using it Unpair on the computer cuts it off at once (its key and token go); Face ID on the phone, as at home; only looking, never a change TestTheTunnelNeedsThePhone Someone guessing Many tries 10 wrong attempts lock the address, or the phone, out for 10 minutes TestTheTunnelLocksOutAfterWrongAttempts Someone on the home Wi-Fi Catch the key at pairing The key is agreed (X25519), never sent; and only for a pairing over an encrypted link, never plain Wi-Fi, never a wall screen TestTheTunnelKeyIsGivenOnlyWhereItIsSafe

What a phone may do through the tunnel: look only. A method that changes anything (Method.Change), anything at the Finances edit level (N31), the household's settings (Private), streams, and anything a phone may not do at home are refused, sealed, with words saying it waits until home. Finances go only to a phone already allowed to see them.

Left as it is: - Cloudflare learns that a phone is in use, when, and how much it sends, but not what. - The sealing key is in data/phones.json (0600), since it can't be kept as a hash. Whoever can read that file can already read data/finance.json beside it. - The team's keys are fetched from Cloudflare; the address is made from a team name checked as one DNS label, so it can't be pointed elsewhere. - Lockouts are kept in memory: restarting homelab serve clears them. Cloudflare's own rate limits stand in front.

docs.title: Review: the record of what was done (November 2026)
docs.text:
internal/history keeps what was done in data/homelab.db, the homelab's first SQLite file (ADR-0022).

  • What it stores: one line per thing done (Restarted Immich, Changed settings: QUIET_HOURS, Changed Finances' transactions), its kind, the app's id, when, and who did it: this computer, a phone by the name it paired with, the watchdog, or the nightly update. Never a setting's value, a secret, or an amount of money: settings are named only, and Finances says only what kind of thing changed. A household member's own Finances are never recorded. Lines are cut at 500 characters and kept to one line without control characters.
  • Who can read it: this account (the file and its -wal and -shm files are 0600, made so before SQLite opens them); homelab history; the desktop app (History); and the owner's paired phones through the companion's look-only History call, every line through phoneLog's redaction of .env's secrets and anything shaped like a token. A member's phone and a wall screen can't call it (N34).
  • The alert record (alerts, Nov 11): each alert the homelab sent, when it cleared, and who snoozed it. It never holds an amount of money: Finances' reminders and the weekly summary are kept only as a plain line (notify.Message.Kept; TestAlertIsKept reads the database's files for the amounts). The owner's phones read it through the look-only AlertLog, every line through phoneLog's redaction (TestAlertLogFromAPhone); a wall screen gets it without which phone snoozed one; a member's phone can't call it.
  • How long: 90 days, and at most 20,000 entries (the newest), trimmed on every write.
  • Backups: the nightly Secrets backup takes a copy made through SQLite (VACUUM INTO), encrypted with .env and the other records, never the file copied mid-write.
  • Who it names: a phone's own name, as its owner gave it at pairing, and reached from the companion's verified caller (companion.Caller), passed to the command it runs (HOMELAB_ACTOR). A terminal user can set that variable by hand, which only changes the line they write about themselves.

docs.title: Independent review of #544 to #560 (November 2026)
docs.text:
Everything merged from #544 to #560 was read again by a session that wrote none of it. What was found is N31 to N34 above; what was checked and holds:

  • Home only can't remove the household's own work (#559): Unpublish drops only a tunnel rule for the app's exact hostname that sends it to the proxy (as Publish writes it), and a CNAME only when it points at this tunnel; a rule for another service, a wildcard, the catch-all, and a record of another kind or pointing elsewhere are left and named (TestUnpublish, TestAwayOffKeepsAnAppHomeOnly).
  • Who can publish an app (#559, #560): SetAppSetting is Change, so a phone that only looks is refused, a member's phone is refused (not Member), a wall screen has no changes, and the tunnel refuses it; on the iPhone it asks for Face ID first. The app id must be in the catalog and the hostname is made from the catalog's subdomain, so nothing a phone sends reaches Cloudflare's API but a known app; DNS names and record ids are escaped.
  • The tunnel's locks (#544 to #548): Access's pass is checked for RS256, the team's own keys (2048-bit or more, fetched only from <team>.cloudflareaccess.com), audience, issuer, the service token and expiry; a sealed request is AES-256-GCM bound to its phone, its time within 2 minutes, each taken once (kept 4 minutes, past the window); an answer is bound to its request; wrong attempts lock out. A header that claims Cloudflare only makes a request stricter.
  • Links and alert buttons (#549, #550): homelab:// carries no secret and changes nothing by itself: an action waits in a dialog for a tap, then goes through the button's own path (Face ID, and Stop asks again), only on a phone allowed changes. The computer sends only links it built from a valid app id and a known action.
  • /api/me's computer info (#551 to #553): only to a paired device; the version, the call names and the features, the same for every device and already in the public source.
  • The *arr apps resting (#554): it stops nothing while a job holds the lock, each stop is noted in data/stopped.json so the watchdog leaves it, and the apps' keys are read from their own config and sent only to them, at home.
  • The record of what was done (#555): every query is parameterised (a search's % and _ escaped); settings are named, never their values; Finances only by kind, never a member's; the files are 0600.
  • Databases (backlog item 60): every database in the catalog (19 today: Postgres, Valkey, Redis, Meilisearch) is on its own stack's network, none on homelab; TestDatabasesStayOffTheSharedNetwork keeps it so.
  • CrowdSec's API on the shared network (backlog item 59): any app on homelab reaches crowdsec:8080 and the AppSec listener on 7422, but reading decisions and asking AppSec both need the bouncer key, and adding or removing a ban needs a machine login: a new machine stays pending until cscli machines validate inside the container, as the homelab never turns on auto-registration. An app could only knock.
  • A hand-kept catch-all in the tunnel (backlog item 65): covered by N33: when such a rule and a wildcard record would carry a home-only app, Set up the domain and homelab away off say so.
  • N21, fixed after its test: the tunnel's network is made by every start, not just install, so an existing install gets it from its next update; cloudflared alone is on it, at an address Docker never hands out, so the danger (every visitor one address CrowdSec could ban) cannot come from a restart; and the proxy job's real-Docker run now checks who can name a visitor.
  • Vaultwarden on a public name (backlog item 61): sign-ups are closed by default (VAULTWARDEN_SIGNUPS_ALLOWED=false) and no ADMIN_TOKEN is ever set, so its /admin page is off.
  • Uptime Kuma's pages (backlog item 62): it is admin: true, which homelab validate refuses to make public, so its status pages and push URLs are on the home network only.
  • Homarr's SECRET_ENCRYPTION_KEY (backlog item 63): 32 random bytes from the system's generator (envfile.NewSecret), kept in .env (0600), redacted from reports and phones' logs as a secret by its placeholder (N3), and carried only by the encrypted Secrets backup.
  • The app's link to the agent on Windows (backlog item 64): a Unix socket in the account's own folder (%LocalAppData%\homelab-wizard\engine.sock on Windows, which only the account, SYSTEM and administrators may open; $XDG_RUNTIME_DIR or the cache folder, 0700, elsewhere, the socket 0600), serving only reads (/v1/hello, /v1/status, /v1/events, /v1/cards): nothing on it changes anything, and another account can't reach it.
  • The database dumps in the backup's staging folder (backlog item 73): each dump and volume archive is written to a hidden .partial file in a folder made 0700, removed if the dump fails or is incomplete, and set 0600 before it is renamed into place (internal/backup; the 0600 is tested). Another account on the computer cannot read them between runs, and a failed run leaves none behind.
  • The ntfy token in Duplicati's alert URL (backlog item 74): it is the publisher account's token, write-only on the five alert topics and nothing else (homelab notify setup). Someone who can see Duplicati's job settings could publish a false alert to the household's phones. But seeing those settings means having Duplicati itself, which reads every backup, so the token adds nothing to that.
  • Beszel's agent on the host network (backlog item 75): it listens on every interface (BESZEL_AGENT_PORT), but it answers only a hub that holds the private key matching KEY, so a device at home gets nothing from it. On Docker Desktop and OrbStack the host network is the runtime's VM. Beszel's own same-machine option, a Unix socket in a shared volume, would close the port too, but every existing hub would have to add its system again: worth doing at a fresh install, not by surprise.
  • Kopia's server (backlog item 76): --insecure means no TLS on its own port, which is this machine's alone (BIND_IP). People reach it through the proxy (HTTPS) or Tailscale (HTTPS), and the plain hop is container to container. Its password (KOPIA_SERVER_PASSWORD) is made random in .env and redacted from reports.
  • Sign-ups left open after the first account (backlog item 70): every public app is closed to strangers after its first account. Immich, Navidrome, Audiobookshelf and Komga have no self sign-up (the admin makes accounts), Calibre-Web's public registration is off by default, Paperless's ACCOUNT_ALLOW_SIGNUPS is off once it has a user, and Vaultwarden's sign-ups are off. The apps that keep sign-up open (Linkwarden, Karakeep, Memos, Wallos, Homebox) are not public, so it reaches the home network and the tailnet only, where the family makes its accounts. Each one's page says how to close it.
  • Every app that reads the client's address (backlog item 69): through the proxy, N21 makes the proxy set both X-Real-IP and X-Forwarded-For to the one address it settled on (the tunnel's visitor, or the device itself), so whichever header an app reads (Vaultwarden X-Real-IP, Nextcloud and Firefly III X-Forwarded-For, Pocket ID TRUST_PROXY, Immich, Paperless), it is told the truth; the proxy job's echo app checks the header. What is left is an app's own port, item 68.
  • CSV a spreadsheet would run (backlog item 77): the two CSVs made to be opened in a spreadsheet, Finances' Reports and its money ahead, put an apostrophe before any cell that starts with =, +, -, @, a tab or a return (cell in web/src/finances/reportData.ts and exportData.ts). Amounts stay numbers, so a payee or a bank reference someone else wrote is never run as a formula. The data export (internal/export) writes every database's tables as they are, for another service to import, so changing a cell there would corrupt the copy. It is not offered as a spreadsheet.
  • Investments (#558): no new network call, log line or alert: Ghostfolio's counts are compared with its own buys and sales on the machine, and the tests use made-up numbers.

docs.title: Finances' one outside source: card prices (November 2026)
docs.text:
Finances reads nothing from the internet but this, which the owner asked for (Nov 13): Update prices on the Collection reads TCGplayer's prices and the cards' pictures from TCGdex (internal/cardprice).

  • Only on the click that asks, from the computer (or a phone allowed to change Finances, through the computer). Nothing reads on its own.
  • What is sent: a card's name, to find it (api.tcgdex.net/v2/en/cards?name=eq:…), then the id TCGdex gave it. Never what was paid, how many, a grade, an account, a balance or any other part of the plan; a card's number and set narrow the answer on the computer, not in the question. TestUpdatePrices checks what goes out.
  • A picture comes only from assets.tcgdex.net over https (a redirect, for a picture or a question, only to TCGdex's own hosts over https: N75), at most 2 MB, a JPEG, PNG or WebP by its own bytes and at most 2,048 pixels on a side; it is saved on the computer (data/finance-cards/) and every screen shows it from there.
  • An answer is read up to 4 MB; a price over $10 million is not one. A failure to reach TCGdex changes nothing.

docs.title: Incident response
docs.text:
1. Look: cscli alerts list, the proxy logs, the app's logs.
  2. Contain: stop the app (./homelab stop <app>), or remove its public hostname by setting public: false and rerunning ./homelab domain setup (the tunnel route stays until removed in Cloudflare; delete it there too).
  3. Ban by hand if needed: ./homelab compose crowdsec exec crowdsec cscli decisions add --ip <address> --duration 24h.
  4. Rotate any secret that might have leaked (the app, .env, Vaultwarden).
  5. Write it up in Known Issues.

docs.title: Categories
docs.text:
Every app belongs to one category, declared in x-homelab-categories in compose.yaml. The category decides the folder its note lives in.

Category Folder What belongs here Network services/network Proxy, DNS, ad blocking on the tailnet, the tunnel, Tailscale, connection checks Security services/security Passwords, sign-in (Pocket ID), threat blocking, monitoring, alerts System services/system Backups, updates, logs, start pages, the phone companion, and the helpers (databases, caches) other apps need Cloud & Files services/cloud and files Photos, file sync and sharing, calendars and contacts, location history Documents services/documents Paperwork, PDFs, saved links, feeds, notes, the wiki, page watching, the AI assistant Finance services/finance Budgets, investments, subscriptions (the app's own Finances screen is part of Homelab Wizard, not an app in the catalog) Media services/media Video, music, audiobooks, books, comics, games Media Automation services/media automation Indexers, the *arr apps, requests, downloads Household services/household The smart home, groceries and chores, recipes, to-dos, home inventory

Network and System apps manage the homelab, so validate refuses to publish them. Categories from before 0.9.0 (infrastructure, productivity, home) still work for your own apps: they count as System, Documents, and Household.

docs.title: Baseline and optional
docs.text:
Baseline Optional In compose No profiles profiles: [optional] Started by ./homelab up, and the startup job after every login ./homelab install <app> or Choose apps; after that its restart policy brings it back with OrbStack Purpose What the household needs every day Ready to slot in, fully configured and documented

Baseline today: Nginx Proxy Manager, AdGuard Home, CrowdSec, Duplicati, Cloudflare Tunnel, Vaultwarden, Uptime Kuma, ntfy, Immich, Paperless-ngx, MoneyMatter, Navidrome, Feishin, Audiobookshelf, Calibre-Web, and Komga, plus Jellyfin and the phone companion natively.

Small baseline: a folder the desktop app makes (or any with HOMELAB_BASELINE=small) starts only Duplicati, ntfy, and Uptime Kuma (x-homelab-small-baseline in compose.yaml); the household picks every other app, the baseline ones included, in Choose apps.

Optional: every other app. ./homelab apps lists each one as baseline, optional, or native, and Inventory has their addresses.

Moving an app between the two is one line: add or remove profiles: [optional].

docs.title: Projects
docs.text: Where When to use it compose/<category>.yaml (homelab_<category>: homelab_network, homelab_media, …) A single container, or a small app whose helpers are not shared. Each category is its own Compose project, run from the homelab folder, so OrbStack groups the containers by category. Services that depend on each other share a file (Gluetun sits with qBittorrent, the Docker socket proxy with Homarr and Dozzle) stacks/<name>/compose.yaml (homelab_<name>) Several containers, especially with a database; can be stopped, updated, and restored on its own. Today: beszel, budget-tracker (MoneyMatter), cloudflare, dawarich, docmost, firefly-iii, frigate, ghostfolio, immich, karakeep, linkwarden, nextcloud, paperless, romm, tandoor, and custom once you add your own app

docs.title: Bundles and selection
docs.text:
Bundles name a set of apps, declared in x-homelab-bundles. The ones marked starter: true are the Start here cards in Choose apps.

Bundle Apps Select with photos (starter) Immich @photos passwords (starter) Vaultwarden @passwords movies (starter) Jellyfin @movies music (starter) Navidrome, Feishin, beets @music files (starter) File Browser, Syncthing @files arr Prowlarr, Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr, Bazarr, FlareSolverr, qBittorrent (with Gluetun), Seerr @arr, '*-arr', arrs household Home Assistant, Grocy, Vikunja, Karakeep, Homepage @household adblock AdGuard Home, tailnet-dns @adblock remote Tailscale @remote

Each stack folder is a preset too (stack:<name>).

Apps can also be selected by alias (overseerr → Seerr, money → MoneyMatter) or by category (cat:media), so ./homelab stop cat:media-automation or ./homelab start cat:media acts on a whole group.

docs.title: Naming
docs.text: Thing Rule Example Service name Lowercase, hyphenated, unique across all files uptime-kuma, immich-server Display name The product's own name Uptime Kuma Note services/<category folder>/<Display name>.md services/security/Uptime Kuma.md Hostname <subdomain>.example.com; short and obvious to family photos, docs, passwords Helper services <app>-db, <app>-redis, <app>-broker paperless-db Data folder data/appdata/<service> (core) or appdata/<stack> (stacks) data/appdata/navidrome Named volume <app>-<purpose> immich-pgdata Vaultwarden entry homelab - <service> <credential> homelab - paperless db password

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
One note per app, grouped by category. Each note starts with a generated table of facts (image, address, data, backups, updates), followed by hand-written sections: Purpose and Setup; how it works, where things live, everyday use, what it connects to, ideas to try, useful commands, and its API where it has one; links to learn more; then Backup and Troubleshooting.

Databases and caches are not listed separately: they appear as Helpers in the note of the app that uses them. See PostgreSQL and Redis and Valkey for how they are run.

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
• The repository has one version, in VERSION, following Semantic Versioning. Every build of main adds a patch number to it (0.9.5-beta); Releasing says how.
  • Every note in docs/ and services/ carries the same version in its front matter. ./homelab validate fails if one differs.
  • A release bumps VERSION, every front matter version, and adds a section to CHANGELOG.md. Notes carry no change history of their own.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Front matter with version, then a title that matches the file name.
  • Facts that come from the compose files (image, ports, addresses, data, backups, updates) live only in the generated block; never edit inside the markers.
  • Service notes have hand-written sections after the generated block: Purpose, Setup, How it works, Where things live, Everyday use, Connects to, Tinkering ideas, Useful commands, API (where the app has one), Learn more, Backup, Troubleshooting.
  • Write for the person fixing it at 2 AM: commands they can paste, expected results, and what to do if the result differs.
  • Links use the [Name](Relative%20Path.md) form so spaces work in both GitHub and Obsidian.
  • No secrets, public IP addresses, or MAC addresses in any note. The repository is public: use placeholders (example.com, 192.168.1.10, /Volumes/Media), never a real household's names or data.

docs.title: Compose
docs.text:
• One service block per container, with <<: *service (restart, no-new-privileges, log rotation).
  • The image tag says what you mean: latest for apps the nightly updates keep current, an exact version or digest for anything pinned.
  • A service whose image must not update nightly says why in its x-homelab pin.
  • Ports: ${BIND_IP:-127.0.0.1}:${<APP>_PORT:-<default>}:<container port>. Only the proxy and DNS use LAN_BIND_IP.
  • Settings come from .env with a sensible default (${TZ:-UTC}); secrets have no default.
  • x-homelab is always the last key of a service.
  • Databases and caches use named volumes; user files use bind mounts under data/appdata, appdata, or the media drive.

docs.title: Code
docs.text:
• Go, formatted with gofmt, checked with go vet; make check must pass before a commit.
  • Commands that change something preview first and need --apply (or a yes in a terminal).
  • Secrets are read from .env at the moment they are needed and never printed.
  • New behaviour comes with a test. End-to-end tests run the real CLI against a fake docker.
  • --json output is a contract: every line carries "schema": 1, and TestJSONContract holds each type to the fields recorded in internal/api/testdata/contract.json. Adding a field is fine (UPDATE_CONTRACT=1 go test ./internal/api records it); removing or renaming one, or changing what it means, bumps the schema.

docs.title: Commits
docs.text:
• Small, focused commits with a message that says why.
  • CHANGELOG.md gets a line for every change someone running the homelab would notice.
  • CI runs make check, a docker compose config of every file, cross-builds of the CLI for macOS, Linux, and Windows, the desktop app's build and tests, and make frontend-check on every push.

docs.title: Repository layout
docs.text:

docs.title: The homelab's own records
docs.text:
File Written by Holds data/storage.json the nightly backup Photos per person (Immich, read from its database) and the size of each app folder in data/appdata and appdata, largest first; Status shows them data/updates.json the watchdog, homelab rollback The image each app ran before its update, kept a week (homelab-rollback/<app>:previous); its data from just before is in recovery-staging/before-update data/people.json, data/people/<name>.html homelab person The household, and each person's welcome page data/sso/<app>.env homelab sso setup An app's Pocket ID sign-in settings data/phones.json homelab phone Paired phones, with what each may do (make changes, see or change Finances) data/members/<username>/data/ a household member's phone Her own Finances, apart from the household's: finance.json, finance-ledger.json and finance-receipts/ while plain; once she keeps them private (Private Finances), only finance.sealed (one locked file the computer can't open, 0600) and her receipts locked as finance-receipts/<hash>.sealed. In the nightly backup of the homelab's records data/finance-card-prices.json Finances › Collection's Update prices Each card's price on each day it was read (TCGplayer's, from TCGdex), a year and a month at most, by the card's id: its page's chart. A card removed takes its prices with it data/finance-cards/ Finances › Collection (a card's form, on the computer or a phone allowed to change Finances) Each card's picture, by its content's name: a photo of your own made small on the device it was picked on. One no card uses goes a day after the plan is next saved data/phone-sent/ Send to my phone (an app's row menu, ⌘K) A page sent to one paired phone, a small file each, until the phone companion passes it on (within a second) and removes it; one left over two minutes is dropped. Safe to delete data/finance.json Finances (the app, and phones allowed to change them) The household's money plan: who gets paid, the accounts with each balance typed in kept by its day (for net worth over time), the payments that repeat, the currency and bank holidays data/homelab-rebuild.json homelab rebuild Which backup folder a rebuild restored from, while it runs, so running it again carries on; homelab-rebuild-done.json once it is done data/icons/<app> the app's page The app's own icon (its home screen icon or favicon, asked of the app on this machine once a week; empty when it has none) data/setup.json Setup Steps marked done by hand data/alerts-off.json homelab notify off\|on <app> (an app's page › Tell me if it stops, or a phone) The apps the watchdog still checks and shows on Status but does not alert about. It used to be ALERTS_OFF in .env: the first install or homelab notify after an upgrade moves it here and takes the key out data/home-only.json homelab away off\|on <app> (an app's page › Reach it away from home, or a phone); a new install of a public app adds it The public apps kept off the internet: Set up the domain leaves them out of the tunnel and Cloudflare's DNS, and homelab away off removes the tunnel rule and DNS record the homelab made for one. Never a .env key data/alerts-snoozed.json homelab notify snooze <check> 1h\|1d\|off, or Status › Watchdog › Snooze… beside a failing check Each snoozed check and when it wakes: the watchdog still checks it but does not alert about it until then, and alerts then if it still fails. Safe to delete (every check alerts again) data/pinned.json homelab pin\|unpin <app> (a row's right-click › Pin to the top, or a phone) The apps at the top of Status and of the menu bar's Open an app, in the order pinned. It used to be APPS_PINNED in .env: the first install or homelab pin after an upgrade moves it here and takes the key out data/savings-history.json the nightly backup The yearly savings over time data/upgrade/ homelab upgrade Where the folder was before the last upgrade (previous.json; for a folder the app made, a copy of its files), for upgrade --back data/homelab-move.json homelab move in Where the bundle came from and what ran there, until the move is done data/appdata/tailscale/serve.json homelab tailnet setup Home mode: the app addresses Tailscale Serve answers scripts/logs/watchdog-state.json the watchdog Its last run, failing checks, and per-check pass and run counts for each of the last 7 days (days) scripts/logs/restore-test.json homelab restore-test The last 24 restore tests scripts/logs/digest.json the nightly backup When the weekly summary was last sent scripts/logs/<part>.log, <part>.1.log the background agent Each part's output (the watchdog, the backup, startup, …); at 5 MB the older half moves to <part>.1.log, replacing the one before scripts/logs/crash-<date>.log the app, the menu bar item, the background agent What a part was doing when it stopped unexpectedly, a file a day; kept 90 days scripts/logs/media/<kind>-<action>-<time>.jsonl, background.log Tidy Up Each job's events, a file a job (kept 30 days); the jobs run in the background write background.log, which at 5 MB moves its older half to background.1.log data/media-trash.jsonl Tidy Up's jobs What each run put in the Trash, for Undo. A line stays while Tidy Up still offers Undo for its run (Recent activity, or an action's last run), and at least 30 days

The nightly backup copies the .json files here, data/people, and data/sso into recovery-staging/secrets/data, which the Homelab Secrets job takes off-site with .env; the rest of data/ is in data/appdata (the AppData job) or rebuilt by itself.

Keep the repository at ~/Homelab. Inside ~/Desktop, ~/Documents, ~/Downloads, or a cloud-synced folder, macOS privacy controls and file syncing interfere with containers (./homelab doctor warns).

docs.title: recovery-staging
docs.text: Folder Written by Read by databases/<service>/ homelab backup (gzipped pg_dumpall, newest 7) Homelab Databases job (/staging/databases) volumes/<volume>/ homelab backup (tar.gz, newest 7) Homelab Databases job (/staging/volumes) secrets/homelab.env homelab backup (copy of .env, mode 0600) Homelab Secrets job (/staging/secrets) secrets/data/ homelab backup (the homelab's own records from data/, mode 0600) Homelab Secrets job (/staging/secrets) restore/, restore-test/ Duplicati restores You, and homelab restore-test before-update/<app>/<time>/ homelab update, just before an app moves to a newer image: a tar.gz of each folder in the homelab folder and named volume it writes to (up to UPDATE_COPY_LIMIT each), its databases' dumps, and copy.json saying what is in it. The newest per app, for a week homelab rollback rolled-back/<app>/<time>/ homelab rollback: the app's data as it was when its copy was put back, and its databases' dumps. Never deleted by the homelab You

docs.title: Named volumes
docs.text:
Databases and caches use named volumes inside the container runtime (OrbStack's VM on a Mac): faster than bind mounts on macOS, and safe from Finder and Spotlight. Their contents reach backups only through homelab backup.

Volume Holds Backed up homelab_immich_immich-pgdata Immich database Daily dump homelab_immich_immich-model-cache Machine-learning models No (downloaded again) homelab_paperless_paperless-pgdata Paperless database Daily dump homelab_paperless_paperless-redisdata Paperless task queue No homelab_budget_tracker_moneymatter-db MoneyMatter database Daily dump homelab_budget_tracker_moneymatter-attachments MoneyMatter attachments Daily archive homelab_budget_tracker_moneymatter-redis, -rates Cache, exchange rates No (rebuilt) homelab_karakeep_karakeep-meilisearch Karakeep's search index No (rebuilds itself) homelab_<stack>_<app>-pgdata (RomM, Ghostfolio, Docmost, Dawarich, Firefly III, Linkwarden, Nextcloud, Tandoor) Each optional stack's database Daily dump homelab_romm_romm-redis, homelab_dawarich_dawarich-public Cache, generated files No homelab_core_npm-logs Proxy logs, shared with CrowdSec (kept its homelab_core name after the category split) No homelab_core_adguard-work AdGuard query log and statistics No

Never run docker volume prune or docker system prune --volumes.

docs.title: Media drive
docs.text:
/Volumes/Media, an external drive.

Folder Used by music Navidrome (read-only, same path inside the container), Lidarr, beets audiobooks, podcasts Audiobookshelf Books Calibre-Web (the Calibre library), Kavita, LazyLibrarian comics Komga, Kavita (read-only) movies, tv Jellyfin, Radarr, Sonarr, Bazarr photos Immich (IMMICH_UPLOAD_LOCATION) downloads qBittorrent and the *arr apps; beets imports music from it

The startup job waits up to 15 minutes for the drive. Photos and the Calibre library are backed up by their own Duplicati jobs; other media is not (see Backups).
