  • LazyLibrarian on GitLab
  • LinuxServer image and its docs

docs.title: Backup
docs.text: data/appdata/lazylibrarian (database, settings) is in the Homelab AppData job.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: If books are downloaded but not imported, check Logs and that the download directory is /downloads in both LazyLibrarian and qBittorrent.

docs.title: Lidarr
docs.text:
Music automation: follows artists and files new albums into the music library, where Navidrome picks them up.

Service lidarr in compose/media-automation.yaml (project homelab_media_automation) Image lscr.io/linuxserver/lidarr:latest Category Media Automation Starts with ./homelab up No: optional, ./homelab install lidarr Address https://lidarr.example.com (LAN, through Nginx Proxy Manager) On this machine http://localhost:8686 (LIDARR_PORT) Data data/appdata/lidarr → /config/Volumes/Media/music → /music/Volumes/Media/downloads → /downloads Updates Nightly at 4 AM, with a copy of its data first

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: New albums by followed artists arrive in /Volumes/Media/music.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. Open https://<TAILSCALE_HOST>:8686 in Home mode, or https://lidarr.example.com with a domain, and set up authentication.
  2. Settings › Media Management: root folder /music.
  3. Settings › Download Clients: qBittorrent, host gluetun, port 8082. Category music.
  4. Indexers come from Prowlarr.

./homelab wire --apply (or Status › More… › Connect apps) does steps 2, 3, and 4 for you once Prowlarr and qBittorrent run (the root folder needs only the app and the media drive) (Prowlarr).

Navidrome sees new albums at its next hourly scan.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Lidarr comes from the same code base as Sonarr: a .NET (C#) server with a React web UI, a SQLite database (lidarr.db), and config.xml for the port, authentication, and API key.
  • Artist and album data comes from Lidarr's metadata service, which is built on MusicBrainz, so artists and releases match MusicBrainz entries.
  • Two kinds of profile decide what it wants: quality profiles (lossless or lossy formats) and metadata profiles (which release types count: albums, EPs, singles, live, compilations).
  • Indexers come from Prowlarr; grabs go to qBittorrent at gluetun:8082. Finished albums are imported from /downloads into /music/<Artist>/<Album>/.
  • Its API is version 1 (/api/v1), unlike Sonarr's and Radarr's /api/v3.

docs.title: Where things live
docs.text:
What Where Settings and API key data/appdata/lidarr/config.xml (/config/config.xml) Database data/appdata/lidarr/lidarr.db (/config/lidarr.db) Logs data/appdata/lidarr/logs/ (/config/logs/lidarr.txt) Scheduled app backups data/appdata/lidarr/Backups/ (/config/Backups) Music library ${MEDIA_ROOT}/music, default /Volumes/Media/music → /music Downloads DOWNLOADS_ROOT, default /Volumes/Media/downloads → /downloads

/music and /downloads are separate mounts, so imports are copies, not hard links; Sonarr explains the folder layout for the whole set.

docs.title: Everyday use
docs.text:
• Library › Add New: search for an artist, choose root folder /music, a quality profile, a metadata profile, and which albums to monitor.
  • An artist's page lists their albums; monitor or search one album at a time, or use Interactive Search to pick a release.
  • Calendar: upcoming releases by followed artists. Activity › Queue: downloads and imports.
  • Wanted › Missing and Wanted › Cutoff Unmet: albums still to get or to upgrade.
  • Library › Unmapped Files: files Lidarr found in /music but could not match to an album.
  • On Android, nzb360 works with Lidarr through its API key.

docs.title: Connects to
docs.text:
• Prowlarr adds and updates the indexers, using Lidarr's API key.
  • qBittorrent is the download client: host gluetun, port 8082.
  • Navidrome reads the same folder, read-only, at /Volumes/Media/music and scans it every hour; Feishin plays it from Navidrome.
  • ./homelab wire adds Lidarr to Prowlarr and qBittorrent to Lidarr (category music). See Prowlarr.
  • .env: LIDARR_PORT, MEDIA_ROOT, DOWNLOADS_ROOT, PUID, PGID, TZ.

docs.title: Tinkering ideas
docs.text:
• Settings › Profiles: trim the metadata profile to studio albums only, so artists do not pull in every single and live bootleg.
  • Settings › Import Lists: follow artists from Last.fm or Spotify playlists automatically.
  • Settings › Metadata: have Lidarr write tags into the files, so Navidrome shows the same artist and album names.
  • Settings › Media Management: turn on Rename Tracks and pick a track naming format.
  • Settings › Connect › ntfy: import notifications to ntfy at http://ntfy.

docs.title: Useful commands
docs.text:
Follow the log, restart, check the mounts, and read the API key.

./homelab logs lidarr -f
./homelab compose lidarr restart lidarr
./homelab compose lidarr exec lidarr df -h /music /downloads
grep -o '<ApiKey>[^<]*' data/appdata/lidarr/config.xml | cut -d'>' -f2

docs.title: API
docs.text:
The key is in Settings › General › Security, or <ApiKey> in data/appdata/lidarr/config.xml. The base URL is http://localhost:8686/api/v1/ (http://lidarr:8686/api/v1/ from other containers), with the key in the X-Api-Key header. This lists the followed artists:

curl -s -H "X-Api-Key: $(grep -o '<ApiKey>[^<]*' data/appdata/lidarr/config.xml | cut -d'>' -f2)" http://localhost:8686/api/v1/artist

Reference: Lidarr API docs.

docs.text:
• Lidarr

  • Lidarr on GitHub
  • LinuxServer image

docs.text: data/appdata/lidarr (database, settings, history) is in the Homelab AppData job. The app also writes its own scheduled backups into data/appdata/lidarr/Backups (System › Backup).

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: See Sonarr; the same fixes apply with /music.

docs.title: Prowlarr
docs.text:
The indexer manager for the *arr apps: add each indexer once here, and Prowlarr keeps Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr, and LazyLibrarian in sync.

Service prowlarr in compose/media-automation.yaml (project homelab_media_automation) Image lscr.io/linuxserver/prowlarr:latest Category Media Automation Starts with ./homelab up No: optional, ./homelab install prowlarr Address https://prowlarr.example.com (LAN, through Nginx Proxy Manager) On this machine http://localhost:9696 (PROWLARR_PORT) Data data/appdata/prowlarr → /config Updates Nightly at 4 AM, with a copy of its data first

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: One place to manage indexers, their credentials, and their health.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. ./homelab install @arr (Choose apps › Media automation) installs Prowlarr with Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr, Bazarr, FlareSolverr, qBittorrent with Gluetun (once PROTONVPN_WIREGUARD_PRIVATE_KEY is set), and Seerr.
  2. Open https://<TAILSCALE_HOST>:9696 in Home mode, or https://prowlarr.example.com with a domain, and set up authentication (Forms, with a username and password).
  3. Settings › Apps: add each app by service name and its API key (from the app's Settings › General):
  4. Sonarr http://sonarr:8989, Radarr http://radarr:7878, Lidarr http://lidarr:8686, LazyLibrarian http://lazylibrarian:5299
  5. Prowlarr server: http://prowlarr:9696
  6. Settings › Indexers: add FlareSolverr (FlareSolverr).
  7. Add indexers; they appear in the apps automatically.

./homelab wire --apply (or Status › More… › Connect apps) does steps 3 and 4 for Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr, and FlareSolverr (Connects to, below).

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Prowlarr comes from the same code base as Sonarr: a .NET (C#) server with a React web UI, a SQLite database (prowlarr.db), and config.xml for the port, authentication, and API key.
  • Most indexers are described by definition files (Cardigann YAML) that Prowlarr downloads and keeps up to date in /config/Definitions; a few have built-in code.
  • For each app under Settings › Apps, Prowlarr uses that app's API key to create one indexer entry per Prowlarr indexer. Each entry points back at Prowlarr (http://prowlarr:9696/<indexer id>/), so the app's searches run through Prowlarr, which translates them for the site.
  • With sync level Full Sync, adding, changing, or removing an indexer here does the same in every app.
  • Indexers tagged flaresolverr send their requests through FlareSolverr at http://flaresolverr:8191, which opens the page in a headless browser.
  • It checks each indexer's health, backs off from failing ones for a while, and records every query and grab under History.

docs.title: Where things live
docs.text:
What Where Settings and API key data/appdata/prowlarr/config.xml (/config/config.xml) Database (indexers, apps, history) data/appdata/prowlarr/prowlarr.db (/config/prowlarr.db) Indexer definitions data/appdata/prowlarr/Definitions/ (/config/Definitions) Logs data/appdata/prowlarr/logs/ (/config/logs/prowlarr.txt) Scheduled app backups data/appdata/prowlarr/Backups/ (/config/Backups)

Prowlarr has no media or download folders.

docs.title: Everyday use
docs.text:
• Indexers › Add Indexer: search the list, fill in the site's credentials, Test, Save. Add the flaresolverr tag for sites behind Cloudflare.
  • Indexers: the status column shows failing indexers; Indexers › Stats compares their response times and grabs.
  • Search: a manual search across every indexer. With a download client set under Settings › Download Clients, you can grab straight from here.
  • History: every query the apps made and what came back.
  • Settings › Apps › Sync App Indexers: push all indexers to the apps now instead of waiting.
  • System › Status: health warnings, such as an app that cannot be reached.

docs.title: Connects to
docs.text:
• Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr, and LazyLibrarian receive the indexers. Prowlarr needs each app's API key; the apps never need Prowlarr's.
  • FlareSolverr is an indexer proxy, used only by indexers that share its tag.
  • qBittorrent is optional here (host gluetun, port 8082), for grabbing from Prowlarr's own Search page.
  • .env: PROWLARR_PORT, PUID, PGID, TZ.

./homelab wire (or Connect apps in the desktop app) makes these links through the apps' APIs. It lists the links for the apps that are running and asks before making them (without a terminal it only previews); ./homelab wire --apply makes them without asking:

  • It reads each *arr's API key from data/appdata/<app>/config.xml and waits up to three minutes for the app's API to answer.
  • In Prowlarr › Settings › Apps it adds Sonarr, Radarr, and Lidarr, each with Prowlarr server http://prowlarr:9696, the app's address (http://sonarr:8989, http://radarr:7878, http://lidarr:8686), its API key, and Full Sync. LazyLibrarian is not added; add it by hand.
  • When FlareSolverr runs, it creates the flaresolverr tag and adds the FlareSolverr indexer proxy at http://flaresolverr:8191/ with that tag. You still tag the indexers yourself.
  • When qBittorrent runs, it adds qBittorrent as the download client in Sonarr, Radarr, and Lidarr: host gluetun, port 8082, user QBITTORRENT_USER (default admin), password QBITTORRENT_PASSWORD. Without that password in .env it stops with a next step instead. It files each app's downloads under its own category: tv, movies, and music. A download client that already exists keeps its category.
  • If an entry already exists with a different address, it corrects the address and keeps everything else. Running it again only adds what is missing.
  • It makes each app's root folder on the media drive: /tv in Sonarr, /movies in Radarr, /music in Lidarr (with Lidarr's first quality and metadata profiles as its defaults). It fails with a note when the media drive is not connected.
  • When Bazarr runs, it turns on Sonarr and Radarr in Bazarr at sonarr:8989 and radarr:7878 with their keys, read from Bazarr's own key in data/appdata/bazarr/config/config.yaml. Languages and providers stay your choice.
  • When Seerr runs and someone has signed in to it with Jellyfin, it adds Sonarr and Radarr in Seerr › Settings › Services as the default servers (by service name, with their keys, the HD-1080p profile or the first, and /tv and /movies), with Seerr's key from data/appdata/seerr/settings.json. Before that sign-in it prints it as the next step.

docs.title: Tinkering ideas
docs.text:
• Tags on an app and on indexers: send some indexers only to some apps (for example, music-only sites only to Lidarr).
  • Settings › Apps: change an app's sync level to Add and Remove Only if you want to tune indexer settings inside that app.
  • Settings › Notifications › ntfy: indexer health alerts to ntfy at http://ntfy.
  • Settings › Download Clients: add qBittorrent (gluetun, 8082) to grab from Prowlarr's Search page.
  • Indexers › Stats: find slow or failing indexers worth removing.
  • An indexer's settings: raise or lower its priority so the apps prefer it when releases tie.

docs.title: Useful commands
docs.text:
Follow the log, restart, check that Prowlarr can reach FlareSolverr and Sonarr over the Docker network, and preview or make the links.

./homelab logs prowlarr -f
./homelab compose prowlarr restart prowlarr
./homelab compose prowlarr exec prowlarr curl -s http://flaresolverr:8191/
./homelab compose prowlarr exec prowlarr curl -s http://sonarr:8989/ping
./homelab wire
./homelab wire --apply

docs.title: API
docs.text:
The key is in Settings › General › Security, or <ApiKey> in data/appdata/prowlarr/config.xml. The base URL is http://localhost:9696/api/v1/, with the key in the X-Api-Key header. This shows the health warnings:

curl -s -H "X-Api-Key: $(grep -o '<ApiKey>[^<]*' data/appdata/prowlarr/config.xml | cut -d'>' -f2)" http://localhost:9696/api/v1/health

Reference: Prowlarr API docs.

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• Prowlarr
  • Servarr wiki: Prowlarr
  • Prowlarr on GitHub
  • LinuxServer image

docs.title: Backup
docs.text: data/appdata/prowlarr (database, settings, history) is in the Homelab AppData job. The app also writes its own scheduled backups into data/appdata/prowlarr/Backups (System › Backup).

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: If an app shows no indexers, check Settings › Apps › Test, and that the address uses the service name, not localhost.

docs.title: Radarr
docs.text:
Movie automation: like Sonarr, for films.

Service radarr in compose/media-automation.yaml (project homelab_media_automation) Image lscr.io/linuxserver/radarr:latest Category Media Automation Starts with ./homelab up No: optional, ./homelab install radarr Address https://radarr.example.com (LAN, through Nginx Proxy Manager) On this machine http://localhost:7878 (RADARR_PORT) Data data/appdata/radarr → /config/Volumes/Media/movies → /movies/Volumes/Media/downloads → /downloads Updates Nightly at 4 AM, with a copy of its data first

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Wanted movies arrive in /Volumes/Media/movies, named and organised for Jellyfin.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. Open https://<TAILSCALE_HOST>:7878 in Home mode, or https://radarr.example.com with a domain, and set up authentication.
  2. Settings › Media Management: root folder /movies.
  3. Settings › Download Clients: qBittorrent, host gluetun, port 8082. Category movies.
  4. Indexers come from Prowlarr.

./homelab wire --apply (or Status › More… › Connect apps) does steps 2, 3, and 4 for you once Prowlarr and qBittorrent run (the root folder needs only the app and the media drive) (Prowlarr).

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Radarr is a fork of Sonarr and works the same way: a .NET (C#) server with a React web UI, a SQLite database (radarr.db), and config.xml for the port, authentication, and API key.
  • Film metadata comes from Radarr's own metadata service, which is based on TMDb.
  • An RSS sync (every 15 minutes by default) grabs new releases for monitored films that are not yet in the library or below the profile's target quality.
  • Indexers come from Prowlarr; grabs go to qBittorrent at gluetun:8082. When a torrent finishes, Radarr imports the file from /downloads into /movies/<Title (Year)>/.
  • It reaches the other containers by service name on the shared homelab Docker network.

docs.title: Where things live
docs.text:
What Where Settings and API key data/appdata/radarr/config.xml (/config/config.xml) Database data/appdata/radarr/radarr.db (/config/radarr.db) Logs data/appdata/radarr/logs/ (/config/logs/radarr.txt) Scheduled app backups data/appdata/radarr/Backups/ (/config/Backups) Poster and fan-art cache data/appdata/radarr/MediaCover/ (/config/MediaCover) Film library ${MEDIA_ROOT}/movies, default /Volumes/Media/movies → /movies Downloads DOWNLOADS_ROOT, default /Volumes/Media/downloads → /downloads

/movies and /downloads are separate mounts, so imports are copies, not hard links; Sonarr explains the folder layout for the whole set.

docs.title: Everyday use
docs.text:
• Movies › Add New: search for a film, choose root folder /movies, a quality profile, and whether to search straight away.
  • Movies › Discover: popular and upcoming films, and recommendations based on the library.
  • Collections: film series (all the films in a franchise), with one switch to monitor the whole collection.
  • Calendar: cinema, digital, and physical release dates. Activity › Queue: what is downloading or waiting to import.
  • Wanted › Missing and Wanted › Cutoff Unmet: films still to get or to upgrade.
  • On a film's page, Search Movie looks automatically; Interactive Search lists every release so you pick one.
  • On phones, nzb360 (Android) and Ruddarr (iOS) work with Radarr through its API key.

docs.title: Connects to
docs.text:
• Prowlarr adds and updates the indexers, using Radarr's API key.
  • qBittorrent is the download client: host gluetun, port 8082.
  • Seerr sends approved film requests here; Bazarr adds subtitles. Both use Radarr's API key (Settings › General › Security) with the address http://radarr:7878.
  • Jellyfin reads the same library at /Volumes/Media/movies.
  • ./homelab wire adds Radarr to Prowlarr and qBittorrent to Radarr (category movies). See Prowlarr.
  • .env: RADARR_PORT, MEDIA_ROOT, DOWNLOADS_ROOT, PUID, PGID, TZ.

docs.title: Tinkering ideas
docs.text:
• Settings › Import Lists: add films automatically from TMDb, Trakt, or IMDb lists.
  • Collections: monitor a whole franchise so new entries are added when announced.
  • Settings › Custom Formats and Settings › Profiles: prefer the releases you want; the TRaSH Guides have tested profiles.
  • Settings › Connect › Emby / Jellyfin: refresh Jellyfin as soon as a film is imported (host host.docker.internal, port 8096).
  • Settings › Connect › ntfy: notifications to ntfy at http://ntfy.
  • Settings › Media Management: turn on Rename Movies and choose a folder and file format Jellyfin matches well.
  • Calendar › iCal Link: release dates in Apple Calendar.

docs.title: Useful commands
docs.text:
Follow the log, restart, check the mounts, and read the API key.

./homelab logs radarr -f
./homelab compose radarr restart radarr
./homelab compose radarr exec radarr df -h /movies /downloads
grep -o '<ApiKey>[^<]*' data/appdata/radarr/config.xml | cut -d'>' -f2

docs.title: API
docs.text:
The key is in Settings › General › Security, or <ApiKey> in data/appdata/radarr/config.xml. The base URL is http://localhost:7878/api/v3/ (http://radarr:7878/api/v3/ from other containers), with the key in the X-Api-Key header. This lists the films in the library:

curl -s -H "X-Api-Key: $(grep -o '<ApiKey>[^<]*' data/appdata/radarr/config.xml | cut -d'>' -f2)" http://localhost:7878/api/v3/movie

Reference: Radarr API docs.

docs.text:
• Radarr
  • Servarr wiki: Radarr
  • Radarr on GitHub
  • LinuxServer image
  • TRaSH Guides

docs.title: Backup
docs.text: data/appdata/radarr (database, settings, history) is in the Homelab AppData job. The app also writes its own scheduled backups into data/appdata/radarr/Backups (System › Backup).

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: See Sonarr; the same fixes apply with /movies.

docs.title: Seerr
docs.text:
Media requests for Jellyfin: family members ask for a film or show, and once approved it goes to Radarr or Sonarr. Seerr is the merged successor to Overseerr and Jellyseerr.

Service seerr in compose/media-automation.yaml (project homelab_media_automation) Image ghcr.io/seerr-team/seerr:latest Category Media Automation Starts with ./homelab up No: optional, ./homelab install seerr Address https://seerr.example.com (LAN, through Nginx Proxy Manager) On this machine http://localhost:5055 (SEERR_PORT) Data data/appdata/seerr → /app/config Database dump Daily by ./homelab backup into recovery-staging/databases/seerr Updates Nightly at 4 AM, with a copy of its data first Also known as overseerr, jellyseerr

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: A friendly request page, so nobody has to use the *arr apps directly.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. ./homelab install seerr (or the whole Media automation bundle, ./homelab install @arr); with a domain, then ./homelab domain setup.
  2. Open https://<TAILSCALE_HOST>:5055 in Home mode, or https://seerr.example.com with a domain, and choose Jellyfin. Server: host.docker.internal, port 8096, with a Jellyfin admin login.
  3. Services: Radarr radarr:7878 and Sonarr sonarr:8989 with their API keys, quality profiles, and root folders (/movies, /tv).
  4. Import Jellyfin users; set who may request and who must be approved.

Step 2 is yours: Seerr has no administrator until someone signs in with Jellyfin. After it, ./homelab wire --apply (or Status › More… › Connect apps) does step 3: Radarr and Sonarr as the default servers, by service name, with their keys, the HD-1080p profile (or the first), and /movies and /tv. Running it again corrects an address or key that changed and adds nothing twice.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Seerr is a Node.js app written in TypeScript (a Next.js front end and an API server in one process). It keeps users, requests, and media status in a SQLite database and its settings in settings.json.
  • Film and show information, posters, and the Discover pages come from TMDB through Seerr itself; you do not need your own TMDB key.
  • People sign in with their Jellyfin accounts. Seerr checks the login against Jellyfin, which runs as a native app on this Mac and is reached from the container at host.docker.internal:8096.
  • An approved request goes to Radarr or Sonarr through their APIs, with the quality profile and root folder chosen under Settings › Services.
  • Background jobs (Settings › Jobs & Cache) scan Jellyfin's libraries and the Sonarr and Radarr queues, so a request moves from Requested to Processing to Available on its own.

docs.title: Where things live
docs.text: What Where Settings (Jellyfin, services, notifications, API key) data/appdata/seerr/settings.json (/app/config/settings.json) Database data/appdata/seerr/db/db.sqlite3 (/app/config/db/db.sqlite3) Logs data/appdata/seerr/logs/ (/app/config/logs) Daily database dump recovery-staging/databases/seerr (by ./homelab backup)

docs.title: Everyday use
docs.text:
• Discover: trending, popular, and upcoming films and shows; the search bar finds any title.
  • A title's page: Request (a show lets you choose seasons), or see whether it is already available.
  • Requests: approve or decline pending requests, and see what is processing.
  • Settings › Users: each person's permissions, auto-approve, and request limits.
  • Issues: household members report a problem with a film or episode (wrong audio, bad subtitles), and you see it in one list.
  • On phones, open the same address and add it to the home screen; it works as a web app.

docs.title: Connects to
docs.text:
• Jellyfin at host.docker.internal, port 8096: sign-in, users, and library scans.
  • Radarr at radarr:7878 and Sonarr at sonarr:8989, each with its API key (Settings › General › Security in that app).
  • ./homelab wire does not connect Seerr, because it needs your Jellyfin sign-in; it prints the steps instead.
  • .env: SEERR_PORT, TZ.

docs.title: Tinkering ideas
docs.text:
• Settings › Users: give trusted people auto-approve and set request limits (so many requests per number of days) for everyone else.
  • Settings › Notifications: tell people when their request is available, by email or through a webhook or chat service.
  • Settings › General: change the Discover region and the original language filter to suit the household.
  • Discover: add, remove, or reorder the sliders on the home page.
  • Settings › Jellyfin: choose which Jellyfin libraries Seerr scans for availability.

docs.title: Useful commands
docs.text:
Follow the log, restart, list its data, check its status, and check that it can reach Sonarr.

./homelab logs seerr -f
./homelab compose seerr restart seerr
./homelab compose seerr exec seerr ls /app/config /app/config/db
./homelab compose seerr exec seerr wget -qO- http://sonarr:8989/ping
curl -s http://localhost:5055/api/v1/status

docs.title: API
docs.text:
The key is under Settings › General (API Key). The base URL is http://localhost:5055/api/v1/, with the key in the X-Api-Key header. The interactive API reference is served by Seerr itself at http://localhost:5055/api-docs. This lists the latest requests:

curl -s -H "X-Api-Key: YOUR_KEY" 'http://localhost:5055/api/v1/request?take=10'

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text: • Seerr on GitHub (code, image, and links to the documentation)

docs.title: Backup
docs.text: data/appdata/seerr (settings, users, requests) is in the Homelab AppData job.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: If availability is not updated, Settings › Jobs: run the Jellyfin library scan.

docs.title: Sonarr
docs.text:
TV automation: follows series, picks releases from the indexers, sends them to qBittorrent, and files finished episodes into the TV library.

Service sonarr in compose/media-automation.yaml (project homelab_media_automation) Image lscr.io/linuxserver/sonarr:latest Category Media Automation Starts with ./homelab up No: optional, ./homelab install sonarr Address https://sonarr.example.com (LAN, through Nginx Proxy Manager) On this machine http://localhost:8989 (SONARR_PORT) Data data/appdata/sonarr → /config/Volumes/Media/tv → /tv/Volumes/Media/downloads → /downloads Updates Nightly at 4 AM, with a copy of its data first

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: New episodes of followed shows arrive in /Volumes/Media/tv, named and organised for Jellyfin.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. Open https://<TAILSCALE_HOST>:8989 in Home mode, or https://sonarr.example.com with a domain, and set up authentication.
  2. Settings › Media Management: root folder /tv.
  3. Settings › Download Clients: qBittorrent, host gluetun, port 8082, with qBittorrent's login. Category tv.
  4. Indexers come from Prowlarr.

./homelab wire --apply (or Status › More… › Connect apps) does steps 2, 3, and 4 for you once Prowlarr and qBittorrent run (the root folder needs only the app and the media drive) (Prowlarr).

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Sonarr is a .NET (C#) server with a React web UI. Series, episodes, history, and most settings live in a SQLite database (sonarr.db); the port, authentication, and API key live in config.xml.
  • Series and air dates come from Sonarr's own metadata service, which is based on TheTVDB.
  • An RSS sync (every 15 minutes by default, Settings › Indexers) asks each indexer for new releases and grabs those that match a monitored episode and its quality profile. Searches for missing episodes go to every indexer.
  • Indexers are created and kept up to date by Prowlarr; Sonarr's searches go through Prowlarr's address, http://prowlarr:9696.
  • Grabs go to qBittorrent with a category. Completed Download Handling watches qBittorrent's queue and, when a torrent finishes, imports the file from /downloads into /tv/<Series>/Season NN/.
  • It reaches the other containers by service name on the shared homelab Docker network.

docs.title: Where things live
docs.text:
What Where Settings and API key data/appdata/sonarr/config.xml (/config/config.xml) Database data/appdata/sonarr/sonarr.db (/config/sonarr.db) Logs data/appdata/sonarr/logs/ (/config/logs/sonarr.txt) Scheduled app backups data/appdata/sonarr/Backups/ (/config/Backups) Poster and fan-art cache data/appdata/sonarr/MediaCover/ (/config/MediaCover) TV library ${MEDIA_ROOT}/tv, default /Volumes/Media/tv → /tv Downloads DOWNLOADS_ROOT, default /Volumes/Media/downloads → /downloads

The download and library folders for the whole *arr set, from compose/media-automation.yaml:

In the container On this machine (defaults from .env) Mounted in /downloads DOWNLOADS_ROOT = /Volumes/Media/downloads qBittorrent, Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr, LazyLibrarian /tv ${MEDIA_ROOT}/tv = /Volumes/Media/tv Sonarr, Bazarr /movies ${MEDIA_ROOT}/movies = /Volumes/Media/movies Radarr, Bazarr /music ${MEDIA_ROOT}/music = /Volumes/Media/music Lidarr /books ${MEDIA_ROOT}/Books = /Volumes/Media/Books LazyLibrarian

Every app that imports from qBittorrent sees the downloads at the same path, /downloads, so the path qBittorrent reports is the path Sonarr opens and no remote path mapping is needed.

The layout is not hardlink-friendly. /downloads and /tv are two separate bind mounts, and a hard link or instant move cannot cross from one mount to another inside a container, even though both folders are on the same drive by default. Sonarr therefore copies each finished file into /tv while the torrent keeps seeding from /downloads, so an episode takes twice the space until the torrent is removed. The Remove Completed option in Sonarr's qBittorrent download client deletes the torrent and its files once qBittorrent has stopped seeding it.

docs.title: Everyday use
docs.text:
• Series › Add New: search for a show, choose root folder /tv, a quality profile, and what to monitor, and tick the box to start the search for missing episodes.
  • Calendar: what airs this week. Activity › Queue: what is downloading or waiting to import.
  • Wanted › Missing and Wanted › Cutoff Unmet: episodes still to get, or still below the profile's target quality.
  • On a series page, the search buttons look for a whole season or one episode automatically; Interactive Search lists every release so you pick one.
  • Activity › Queue: removing an item with its release blocklisted means it is never grabbed again (Activity › Blocklist).
  • System › Status shows health warnings; System › Tasks shows and runs the scheduled jobs; System › Logs has the log files.
  • On phones, nzb360 (Android) and Ruddarr (iOS) work with Sonarr through its API key.

docs.title: Connects to
docs.text:
• Prowlarr adds and updates the indexers, using Sonarr's API key.
  • qBittorrent is the download client: host gluetun, port 8082, with qBittorrent's Web UI login. qBittorrent shares Gluetun's network, so qbittorrent is not a valid host.
  • Bazarr and Seerr use Sonarr's API key (Settings › General › Security) with the address http://sonarr:8989.
  • Jellyfin reads the same library at /Volumes/Media/tv.
  • ./homelab wire adds Sonarr to Prowlarr and qBittorrent to Sonarr, reading Sonarr's key from data/appdata/sonarr/config.xml. The download client gets the category tv. See Prowlarr for everything it does.
  • .env: SONARR_PORT, MEDIA_ROOT, DOWNLOADS_ROOT, PUID and PGID (owner of the files it writes), TZ.

docs.title: Tinkering ideas
docs.text:
• Settings › Profiles and Settings › Custom Formats: decide which releases win; the TRaSH Guides have tested profiles to copy.
  • Settings › Import Lists: add shows automatically from a Trakt or IMDb list.
  • Settings › Connect › Emby / Jellyfin: refresh Jellyfin as soon as an episode is imported (host host.docker.internal, port 8096, an API key from Jellyfin's dashboard). Jellyfin sees the library at /Volumes/Media/tv, not /tv.
  • Settings › Connect › ntfy: import and health notifications to ntfy at http://ntfy.
  • Calendar › iCal Link: subscribe to the airing calendar in Apple Calendar.
  • Settings › Media Management: turn on Rename Episodes and adjust the naming format (Show Advanced reveals more options).
  • Hardlinks: mounting the drive once as /data in qBittorrent and every *arr (downloads in /data/downloads, the library in /data/tv) would make imports instant and free. It means editing compose/media-automation.yaml and every app's paths, and the drive must support hard links (APFS does, exFAT does not); it is untested here.

docs.title: Useful commands
docs.text:
Follow the log, restart, check both mounts from inside the container, read the API key, and connect the apps again.

./homelab logs sonarr -f
./homelab compose sonarr restart sonarr
./homelab compose sonarr exec sonarr df -h /tv /downloads
./homelab compose sonarr exec sonarr ls /downloads
grep -o '<ApiKey>[^<]*' data/appdata/sonarr/config.xml | cut -d'>' -f2
./homelab wire --apply

docs.title: API
docs.text:
The key is in Settings › General › Security, or <ApiKey> in data/appdata/sonarr/config.xml. The base URL is http://localhost:8989/api/v3/ from this Mac and http://sonarr:8989/api/v3/ from other containers; send the key in the X-Api-Key header. This lists the download queue:

curl -s -H "X-Api-Key: $(grep -o '<ApiKey>[^<]*' data/appdata/sonarr/config.xml | cut -d'>' -f2)" http://localhost:8989/api/v3/queue

Reference: Sonarr API docs.

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• Sonarr
  • Servarr wiki: Sonarr
  • Sonarr on GitHub
  • LinuxServer image and its docs
  • TRaSH Guides

docs.title: Backup
docs.text: data/appdata/sonarr (database, settings, history) is in the Homelab AppData job. The app also writes its own scheduled backups into data/appdata/sonarr/Backups (System › Backup).

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Fix Download client unreachable qBittorrent is reached through Gluetun: host gluetun, not qbittorrent Imports are slow copies /tv and /downloads are separate mounts, so files are copied rather than moved. Acceptable for this library's size "Path does not exist" on import qBittorrent and Sonarr must both see downloads at /downloads

docs.title: Tdarr
docs.text:
Shrinks the media library by converting films and shows to a smaller format.

Service tdarr in compose/media-automation.yaml (project homelab_media_automation) Image docker.io/haveagitgat/tdarr:latest Category Media Automation Starts with ./homelab up No: optional, ./homelab install tdarr Address https://tdarr.example.com (LAN, through Nginx Proxy Manager) On this machine http://localhost:8265 (TDARR_PORT) Data data/appdata/tdarr/server → /app/serverdata/appdata/tdarr/configs → /app/configsdata/appdata/tdarr/logs → /app/logs/Volumes/Media/tv → /media/tv/Volumes/Media/movies → /media/movies/Volumes/Media/tdarr-cache → /temp Database dump Daily by ./homelab backup into recovery-staging/databases/tdarr Updates Nightly at 4 AM, with a copy of its data first

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Goes through the film and TV folders and converts each file to a smaller format (usually H.265, also called HEVC), so the same library takes much less of the media drive, often half. It can also tidy files on the way: drop subtitle and audio tracks in languages nobody watches, or move every file to the same container. Jellyfin plays the converted files as before.

It is heavy and optional: converting means decoding and encoding every frame, so it keeps the processor busy for hours at a time. Install it when the drive is filling up, not by default.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. ./homelab install tdarr (a 1.6 GB download).
  2. Open it and create your account: the first account made is the only one, and sign-up closes after it.
  3. Libraries › Library +: name it, set Source to /media/movies (or /media/tv) and Transcode Cache to /temp. Under Transcode options, keep the classic plugins it suggests, or pick a Flow.
  4. Nodes (on its home page): the node homelab is this machine. Give it workers: Transcode CPU 1 to start with, and Health check CPU 1. It does nothing until it has workers.
  5. Keep it to the night (below), then Scan (Find new) on the library.

Try it on a copy of a few files first, in a folder of their own: a converted file replaces the original once it passes the size check.

docs.title: How much it takes, and keeping it to the night
docs.text:
• Processor: converting on the processor uses every core it is given, for roughly as long as the film runs, and longer on an older machine. A library of a few hundred films is weeks of nights. Each Transcode CPU worker is one file at a time; one worker is enough on a machine that also runs the other apps.
  • Memory: about 100 MB idle, and a gigabyte or more while a file converts.
  • Disk: a converted file is written in full to the cache (tdarr-cache on the media drive) before it replaces the original, so leave free space the size of the largest film. A file Tdarr was stopped part-way through (on battery, by an update or a restart) leaves its copy there; Tidy Up clears such a work folder once nothing has written to it for two hours, whenever Tdarr isn't converting a file (on Shrink, and each time it collects Tdarr's work).
  • At night only: in the library's Schedule tab, untick the daytime hours (for example 07:00 to 23:00 every day); outside the ticked hours it starts nothing new. The homelab also pauses it while a laptop is on battery.
  • On each system: on the Mac, containers cannot use Apple's video encoder, so it converts on the processor. On Linux and SteamOS, an Intel or AMD graphics chip can do the work (see Tinkering ideas). On Windows, only an NVIDIA graphics card can, through WSL 2.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• One container holds the Tdarr server (the web page, the library database, the schedule) and a node of its own named homelab that does the work with FFmpeg and HandBrake.
  • The server scans the libraries, decides with the plugins or a Flow what each file needs, and hands files to the node's workers. Results replace the originals in place.
  • Libraries, settings, and the file history are in a SQLite database under data/appdata/tdarr/server.
  • Other computers can join as extra nodes (Tinkering ideas); the server's node port (8266) stays inside the container unless you publish it.

docs.title: Where things live
docs.text: What Where Libraries, settings, history, account data/appdata/tdarr/server (SQLite in Tdarr/DB2/SQL) Node settings data/appdata/tdarr/configs Logs data/appdata/tdarr/logs Films and shows it converts <MEDIA_ROOT>/movies, <MEDIA_ROOT>/tv (as /media/movies, /media/tv) Files being converted <MEDIA_ROOT>/tdarr-cache (as /temp)

docs.title: Everyday use
docs.text:
• Progress: the home page shows each worker's file and percentage, and Stats the space saved so far.
  • A file that failed: Libraries › Transcode: Error/Cancelled lists them with the reason; Requeue tries again.
  • Pause: the node's worker counts at 0, or stop it: ./homelab compose media-automation stop tdarr.

docs.title: Connects to
docs.text:
• Sonarr and Radarr put the files in the folders it converts; it is best to let them finish importing before Tdarr picks a file up (a library's Folder Watch, or the nightly schedule).
  • Jellyfin plays the converted files; Jellyfin finds the changes on its next library scan.
  • .env: TDARR_PORT (default 8265).

docs.title: Tinkering ideas
docs.text:
• Graphics chip on Linux and SteamOS: add devices: ["/dev/dri:/dev/dri"] to tdarr in compose/media-automation.yaml, ./homelab up, and pick a plugin or Flow that encodes with VAAPI or QSV. On an NVIDIA card instead, install NVIDIA's container toolkit and add gpus: all.
  • Another computer as a node: publish the server port (${BIND_IP:-127.0.0.1}:8266:8266, with BIND_IP this machine's address) and run Tdarr's node there with serverIP set to this machine.
  • Flows: Tdarr's visual pipelines (Flows) do more than the classic plugins, such as keeping only the languages you speak.

docs.title: Useful commands
docs.text:
./homelab logs tdarr -f
./homelab compose media-automation restart tdarr
curl -s http://localhost:8265/api/v2/status

docs.title: API
docs.text:
• Token: POST /api/v2/public/auth/login with {"username":…,"password":…} (its token), or an API key from its API Keys settings sent as x-api-key.
  • Base URL: http://localhost:8265/api/v2 on this machine, https://tdarr.example.com/api/v2 on the LAN, with Authorization: Bearer <token>.
  • Nodes: GET /api/v2/get-nodes. Libraries: POST /api/v2/cruddb with {"data":{"collection":"LibrarySettingsJSONDB","mode":"getAll"}}.
  • The reference is its own page at /api/v2/public/api-docs.

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• tdarr.io and its documentation
  • Tdarr is free, with a paid Pro tier (its site says what Pro adds); this homelab uses the free tier.

docs.title: Backup
docs.text: ./homelab backup copies its database nightly into recovery-staging/databases/tdarr, and Duplicati takes it off-site with the rest. The films themselves are backed up with the media drive, if at all; Tdarr changes them in place, so a backup of the drive made before a conversion is the only way back to an original.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Nothing happens: the node has no workers (step 4), the library's schedule has no ticked hour now, or Scan was never run.
  • Every file errors: open one in Transcode: Error/Cancelled and read its log; a full cache drive or a plugin that does not suit the file are the usual causes.
  • The machine is slow while it runs: fewer workers, or a schedule kept to the night.

docs.title: qBittorrent
docs.text:
The torrent client for the *arr apps. It has no network of its own: it runs inside Gluetun's network, so every byte goes through ProtonVPN, and nothing leaves if the VPN is down.

Service qbittorrent in compose/media-automation.yaml (project homelab_media_automation) Image lscr.io/linuxserver/qbittorrent:latest Category Media Automation Starts with ./homelab up No: optional, ./homelab install qbittorrent Address https://qbittorrent.example.com (LAN, through Nginx Proxy Manager) On this machine http://localhost:8082 (QBITTORRENT_PORT) Depends on gluetun Data data/appdata/qbittorrent → /config/Volumes/Media/downloads → /downloads Updates Nightly at 4 AM, with a copy of its data first

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Downloads for Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr, and LazyLibrarian, only ever through the VPN.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. Set PROTONVPN_WIREGUARD_PRIVATE_KEY (Gluetun), then ./homelab install qbittorrent (it also comes with the Media automation bundle, ./homelab install @arr); with a domain, also ./homelab domain setup.
  2. The first start prints a temporary password: ./homelab logs qbittorrent. Sign in at the address Status shows (https://<TAILSCALE_HOST>:8082 in Home mode, https://qbittorrent.example.com with a domain) as admin and set a permanent password (Tools › Options › Web UI).
  3. Options › Downloads: default save path /downloads.
  4. Options › Connection: listening port = Gluetun's forwarded port.
  5. Options › Advanced: network interface tun0, so it cannot use any other route even by mistake.

The *arr apps reach it at host gluetun, port 8082.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• qBittorrent is a C++ and Qt program built on the libtorrent library; this image runs it without a desktop window (qbittorrent-nox), so you use the Web UI. WEBUI_PORT: "8082" sets that port.
  • Its settings live in qBittorrent.conf; each torrent's state (resume data and the .torrent file) lives in BT_backup, which is how it picks up where it left off after a restart.
  • It runs inside Gluetun's network (network_mode: service:gluetun), so it has no address of its own. Peers reach it through the ProtonVPN forwarded port; you and the *arr apps reach it at gluetun:8082.
  • The *arr apps add torrents through its Web API with a category, poll the API for progress, and import the finished files from /downloads.
  • With Options › Downloads › Default Torrent Management Mode set to Automatic, each category is saved in its own subfolder of /downloads (for example /downloads/tv); in Manual mode everything goes to the default save path.

docs.title: Where things live
docs.text:
What Where Settings data/appdata/qbittorrent/qBittorrent/qBittorrent.conf (/config/qBittorrent/qBittorrent.conf) Torrent list and resume data data/appdata/qbittorrent/qBittorrent/BT_backup/ Logs data/appdata/qbittorrent/qBittorrent/logs/qbittorrent.log Downloads DOWNLOADS_ROOT, default /Volumes/Media/downloads → /downloads

Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr, and LazyLibrarian mount the same folder at the same /downloads path, so no remote path mapping is needed. The libraries are separate mounts in those apps, so imports are copies rather than hard links; Sonarr has the whole layout.

docs.title: Everyday use
docs.text:
• The sidebar filters by status (Downloading, Seeding, Stalled) and by category (tv, movies, music, and so on).
  • Right-click a torrent to pause or resume it, force a recheck, change its category, or delete it with or without its files.
  • The speed icons at the bottom switch to the alternative speed limits, for example while you are on a video call.
  • Tools › Options › Speed and Options › BitTorrent: global speed limits and seeding limits.
  • View › Log: the execution log, with connection and listening-port messages.
  • On Android, nzb360 works with qBittorrent's Web API.

docs.title: Connects to
docs.text:
• Gluetun is its only way out; when Gluetun is recreated, restart qBittorrent.
  • Sonarr, Radarr, Lidarr, and LazyLibrarian use it as their download client with host gluetun, port 8082, and the Web UI login. Prowlarr can too.
  • ./homelab wire adds it to Sonarr, Radarr, and Lidarr. It needs the permanent Web UI password: add QBITTORRENT_PASSWORD (and QBITTORRENT_USER if it is not admin) to .env, then run ./homelab wire --apply. See Prowlarr.
  • Nginx Proxy Manager proxies https://qbittorrent.example.com to gluetun:8082.
  • .env: QBITTORRENT_PORT (published on Gluetun), DOWNLOADS_ROOT, PUID, PGID, TZ, and QBITTORRENT_USER and QBITTORRENT_PASSWORD for ./homelab wire.

docs.title: Tinkering ideas
docs.text:
• Options › BitTorrent: seeding limits (a ratio or a time) that stop the torrent when reached, so the *arr apps' Remove Completed option can clean up the downloads.
  • Options › Downloads: set Default Torrent Management Mode to Automatic, so each category gets its own folder under /downloads.
  • Options › Downloads: Keep incomplete torrents in /downloads/incomplete, so half-finished files never sit next to finished ones.
  • Options › Speed: schedule the alternative speed limits for the hours the household needs the bandwidth.
  • Options › Web UI: turn on Use alternative WebUI, or add the VueTorrent mod to the LinuxServer image (DOCKER_MODS, a compose change), for a friendlier, phone-sized UI.

docs.title: Useful commands
docs.text:
Follow the log, check that qBittorrent's own traffic leaves through ProtonVPN, look at the downloads folder, and restart it after Gluetun.

./homelab logs qbittorrent -f
./homelab compose qbittorrent exec qbittorrent curl -s https://ipinfo.io/ip
./homelab compose qbittorrent exec qbittorrent ls /downloads
./homelab compose qbittorrent restart qbittorrent

docs.title: API
docs.text:
The Web API is at http://localhost:8082/api/v2/ (http://gluetun:8082/api/v2/ from other containers). It uses the Web UI login: sign in once to get a session cookie, then send it with each call. This signs in and lists the torrents that are downloading:

curl -s -c /tmp/qbt.cookie --data-urlencode 'username=admin' --data-urlencode 'password=YOUR_PASSWORD' http://localhost:8082/api/v2/auth/login
curl -s -b /tmp/qbt.cookie 'http://localhost:8082/api/v2/torrents/info?filter=downloading'

The Web API reference is linked from the qBittorrent wiki.

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• qBittorrent
  • qBittorrent on GitHub and its wiki
  • LinuxServer image and its docs

docs.title: Backup
docs.text: data/appdata/qbittorrent (settings, torrent list) is in the Homelab AppData job. Downloads are not backed up.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Fix Web UI unreachable Gluetun is down or was recreated. ./homelab restart gluetun qbittorrent "Unauthorized" through the proxy Options › Web UI: turn off Host header validation, or add qbittorrent.example.com to the allowed domains Slow or no peers The listening port does not match Gluetun's forwarded port

docs.title: Ad blocking on the tailnet
docs.text:
Sends DNS from your Tailscale devices to AdGuard Home, so ads are blocked at home and away.

Service tailnet-dns in compose/network.yaml (project homelab_network) Image alpine/socat:latest Category Network Starts with ./homelab up No: optional, ./homelab install tailnet-dns Depends on tailscale, adguard-home Updates Nightly at 4 AM, with a copy of its data first

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Ad and tracker blocking on every phone and computer signed in to Tailscale, at home and away, without touching the router or each device's Wi-Fi settings. It is a small forwarder: DNS sent to this machine's tailnet address goes on to AdGuard Home, which does the blocking. The tailnet's DNS setting then points every device at that address.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. Home mode working first (Tailscale: Setup › Addresses on your tailnet, signing in when it opens Tailscale's page).
  2. Choose apps › Ad blocking › Install (or ./homelab install @adblock). That brings AdGuard Home with it, and the install runs ./homelab adguard setup: it answers AdGuard's first-run wizard with a generated login (saved as ADGUARD_USER and ADGUARD_PASSWORD) and shows this machine's tailnet address (100.x.y.z).
  3. In the Tailscale admin console › DNS › Nameservers › Add nameserver › Custom: that address, then Save. Turn on Override DNS servers.
  4. On the phone, with Tailscale on and Wi-Fi off, an ad-heavy page loads without its ads, and AdGuard's dashboard counts the queries.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• The container is socat in Tailscale's network namespace (network_mode: service:tailscale). Tailscale runs in userspace mode, where a connection to its own tailnet address is handed to 127.0.0.1 inside that namespace; socat listens there on port 53 (UDP and TCP) and passes each query to adguard-home:53 on the homelab network.
  • With Override DNS servers on, the Tailscale app on each device sends every lookup to that nameserver through the tailnet, so blocking works on mobile data too. MagicDNS names (*.ts.net) are still answered by Tailscale itself.
  • AdGuard sees every tailnet query as coming from the Tailscale container, so its per-device statistics lump them together.
  • When Tailscale restarts it gets a new network, and this container would be left on the old one. So it checks every 10 seconds that adguard-home still resolves; after 30 seconds without, it exits, and Docker starts it again inside Tailscale's new network. A health check makes the same test, so Status shows it as needing a look meanwhile (or while AdGuard is down).

docs.title: Where things live
docs.text: What Where The forwarding commands compose/network.yaml › tailnet-dns › command Blocklists, rules, query log AdGuard Home (its note) The nameserver setting Tailscale admin console › DNS (not on this machine)

docs.title: Everyday use
docs.text:
• Nothing to do day to day. Blocked and allowed lookups show in AdGuard Home's Query Log.
  • A site broken by blocking: AdGuard › Query Log › find the request › Unblock.
  • While this machine is off, devices with Tailscale on cannot look up any name. Turn Tailscale off on them until it is back, or turn off Override DNS servers for a longer outage. The watchdog and the heartbeat (Monitoring) tell you when it is down.

docs.title: Connects to
docs.text:
• Tailscale: shares its network and its tailnet address; it starts after Tailscale.
  • AdGuard Home: every query goes there.
  • ./homelab adguard setup: sets up AdGuard and prints the address for the admin console.

docs.title: Tinkering ideas
docs.text:
• Add a second nameserver in Tailscale (for example 9.9.9.9) so lookups still work while this machine is off; some will then skip AdGuard, so blocking becomes partial.
  • Restrict the nameserver to a few domains (split DNS) instead of overriding all DNS, to use AdGuard's rewrites only.
  • Give a child's phone stricter rules in AdGuard: Settings › Client settings, by its tailnet name.

docs.title: AdGuard Home
docs.text:
DNS for the house. It blocks ads and trackers and answers every *.example.com name with the Mac's address, so LAN traffic goes straight to the proxy. That is for a homelab with a domain; in Home mode (no domain, the default) it is optional and only blocks ads, through Ad blocking on the tailnet.

Service adguard-home in compose/network.yaml (project homelab_network) Image adguard/adguardhome:latest Category Network Starts with ./homelab up Yes (./homelab up) Address https://ads.example.com (LAN, through Nginx Proxy Manager) On this machine http://localhost:3003 (ADGUARD_PORT) Data data/appdata/adguard-home/conf → /opt/adguardhome/confadguard-work (volume) → /opt/adguardhome/work Updates Nightly at 4 AM, with a copy of its data first

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
• LAN DNS server on port 53 of the Mac (192.168.1.10).
  • One rewrite, *.example.com → 192.168.1.10, so every hostname works at home without a trip through Cloudflare.
  • Network-wide ad and tracker blocking.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. Setup › Set up AdGuard (or ./homelab adguard setup) answers the first-run wizard: admin pages on port 80 and DNS on 53 (the container maps them to 3003 and 53 on the Mac), with a generated login saved as ADGUARD_USER and ADGUARD_PASSWORD. By hand instead: the wizard at http://localhost:3002 with those two ports, then put the login you made in Settings. Afterwards, Sign-in details on its page in Status shows the user name and copies the password.
  2. Settings › DNS settings: set the upstream servers and bootstrap servers (Networking).
  3. ./homelab domain setup adds the rewrite (Filters › DNS rewrites).
  4. Point each device's DNS at 192.168.1.10, or, for every Tailscale device at home and away, install Ad blocking on the tailnet.
  5. On the Mac itself: ./homelab domain resolver (Setup › This Mac finds its apps by name) makes it look up every *.example.com name here, also with a VPN on. It asks for the Mac password once.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• One Go program is both the DNS server (port 53, TCP and UDP) and the web admin (container port 80, 3003 on this Mac). There is no database server: settings are one YAML file, and the query log and statistics are files in the work folder.
  • Each query is checked against the DNS rewrites, your custom rules, and the blocklists (downloaded and refreshed on a timer). A rewrite answers with its address, a blocked name gets an empty answer (0.0.0.0 in the default mode), and everything else goes to the upstream servers and is cached.
  • Every device whose DNS is 192.168.1.10 uses it. The wildcard rewrite is how *.example.com reaches Nginx Proxy Manager without leaving the house.
  • The CLI talks to its HTTP API (/control/...) with ADGUARD_USER and ADGUARD_PASSWORD to add and update the rewrite.

docs.title: Where things live
docs.text: What Where Settings, upstreams, rewrites, filter lists, users data/appdata/adguard-home/conf/AdGuardHome.yaml → /opt/adguardhome/conf/AdGuardHome.yaml Query log adguard-work volume → /opt/adguardhome/work/data/querylog.json Statistics /opt/adguardhome/work/data/stats.db Downloaded blocklists /opt/adguardhome/work/data/filters/ Web sign-in sessions /opt/adguardhome/work/data/sessions.db

docs.title: Everyday use
docs.text:
• Dashboard: queries, the blocked share, and the top clients and domains. How long statistics are kept is under Settings › General settings.
  • Query Log: what a device looked up and why it was blocked or allowed. Each row has buttons to block or unblock that domain.
  • Filters › DNS blocklists: add lists (Add blocklist › Choose from the list) and check for updates.
  • Filters › Custom filtering rules: one-off rules, such as @@||example.com^ to allow a domain or ||ads.example.com^ to block one.
  • Filters › DNS rewrites: the *.example.com rewrite lives here. Add your own for LAN devices, such as a printer.
  • Settings › Client settings: name devices by address, so the log shows "Kitchen iPad" instead of 192.168.1.x.
  • Setup guide: how to point each kind of device at it.

docs.title: Connects to
docs.text:
• Sends every *.example.com name to Nginx Proxy Manager on this Mac.
  • Ad blocking on the tailnet passes it the lookups of every Tailscale device, once the tailnet's DNS setting points at this machine's tailnet address. In Home mode that is the only way devices use it: no address depends on it, so it is an optional pick (Ad blocking).
  • Tailscale uses it as the split-DNS nameserver for example.com, so the names work away from home.
  • ./homelab domain setup writes the rewrite through its API with ADGUARD_USER and ADGUARD_PASSWORD. ADGUARD_PORT (3003) and ADGUARD_SETUP_PORT (3002) are its ports on this Mac; HOMELAB_DOMAIN is the rewritten name.
  • Uptime Kuma checks both its web page and a real lookup (Monitoring).
  • Without it, ./homelab domain setup --dns hosts writes the names into /etc/hosts instead (Networking).

docs.title: Tinkering ideas
docs.text:
• Settings › Client settings: give a child's device its own client with blocked services (Filters › Blocked services lists them), Safe Search, or parental control, leaving everyone else alone.
  • Filters › DNS blocklists › Add blocklist › Choose from the list: add a malware or tracker list and watch the blocked share on the dashboard.
  • Settings › DNS settings: compare the upstream modes (load balancing, parallel requests, fastest IP address) by the average processing time on the dashboard.
  • Settings › DNS settings: turn on DNSSEC validation.
  • Custom filtering rules with $client, such as ||youtube.com^$client=192.168.1.42, to block a domain for one device only.
  • Query Log: filter by one device for a day to see how chatty it is.

docs.title: Useful commands
docs.text:
The API takes the admin login from .env (ADGUARD_USER, ADGUARD_PASSWORD). dig against 192.168.1.10 asks AdGuard directly; a blocked name answers 0.0.0.0.

./homelab logs adguard-home -f
./homelab compose adguard-home restart adguard-home
dig npm.example.com @192.168.1.10
dig doubleclick.net @192.168.1.10
curl -s -u admin:<password> http://localhost:3003/control/status
curl -s -u admin:<password> http://localhost:3003/control/rewrite/list
curl -s -u admin:<password> "http://localhost:3003/control/querylog?limit=20"

docs.title: API
docs.text:
• Sign-in: HTTP basic auth with the admin login (ADGUARD_USER, ADGUARD_PASSWORD).
  • Base URL: http://localhost:3003/control on this Mac.
  • Example: curl -s -u admin:<password> http://localhost:3003/control/stats.
  • Reference: the OpenAPI file in the openapi folder of the source repo.

Turn it off Admin page unreachable after the wizard The admin port was set to something other than 80. docs.title: Cloudflare Tunnel
docs.text:
Publishes the public apps on the internet without opening a single router port. cloudflared connects out to Cloudflare, and Cloudflare sends visitors back through that connection to Nginx Proxy Manager.

Service cloudflared in stacks/cloudflare/compose.yaml (project homelab_cloudflare) Image cloudflare/cloudflared:latest Category Network Starts with ./homelab up Yes, once TUNNEL_TOKEN is set in .env Updates Nightly at 4 AM, with a copy of its data first Needs in .env TUNNEL_TOKEN

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
• Remote access for the family to the public apps from anywhere, with nothing to install.
  • Every public hostname goes to http://nginx-proxy-manager:80, so CrowdSec checks tunnel traffic exactly like LAN traffic.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. Cloudflare dashboard › Zero Trust › Networks › Tunnels › Create a tunnel › Cloudflared. Name it homelab.
  2. Under the Docker install instructions, copy the token (the long value after --token) into TUNNEL_TOKEN in .env.
  3. ./homelab up starts cloudflared; the tunnel shows Healthy in the dashboard.
  4. ./homelab domain setup adds a public hostname for each app marked public: true and creates its proxied CNAME record. Routes you added by hand are kept.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• cloudflared is a small Go program. It needs no open port: it dials out to Cloudflare and keeps several connections open to nearby Cloudflare data centres.
  • The tunnel is remotely managed: its routes (public hostnames) live in your Cloudflare account, and the container only holds the token. Route changes reach cloudflared without a restart.
  • A visitor's request goes Cloudflare's edge (TLS, firewall rules, DDoS protection) → the tunnel → http://nginx-proxy-manager:80 on the tunnel's own network, homelab-tunnel → the app. Cloudflare holds the public certificate; inside the tunnel the request is plain HTTP to the proxy.
  • The proxy reads the visitor's real address from CF-Connecting-IP, so CrowdSec judges the visitor, not the tunnel. It takes that header only from cloudflared's fixed address on homelab-tunnel (198.18.89.2): a device at home or another app sending it is seen as itself.
  • cloudflared is on homelab-tunnel alone, so the proxy is all it can reach: a route added by hand in Cloudflare's dashboard that points straight at an app (http://jellyfin:8096) no longer works. Point it at http://nginx-proxy-manager:80 with a proxy host for the name instead.
  • ./homelab domain setup writes the routes and the DNS records through the Cloudflare API with CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN. It adds and updates; it never removes routes.

docs.title: Where things live
docs.text:
Nothing is stored on this Mac apart from .env.

What Where Tunnel token TUNNEL_TOKEN in .env, passed to the container's environment Token for domain setup CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN in .env Routes (public hostnames) The tunnel's page under Zero Trust › Networks › Tunnels DNS records Cloudflare dashboard › example.com › DNS: a proxied CNAME per public app to <tunnel id>.cfargotunnel.com Logs Container output only: ./homelab logs cloudflared

docs.title: Everyday use
docs.text:
Mostly nothing: it reconnects by itself after a restart or an outage.

  • Health: Zero Trust › Networks › Tunnels shows the tunnel as Healthy, with the connector's version and the data centres it is connected to.
  • Publish an app: add public: true to its x-homelab block and run ./homelab domain setup.
  • Unpublish an app: remove the flag, then delete its route on the tunnel's page and its DNS record by hand.
  • Traffic: the zone's Analytics and Security pages in the Cloudflare dashboard show visitors and what Cloudflare blocked.

docs.title: Connects to
docs.text:
• Every route ends at Nginx Proxy Manager, so CrowdSec bans apply to tunnel visitors too.
  • The public apps: Vaultwarden, ntfy (once its token exists), Immich, Paperless-ngx, Navidrome, Feishin, Audiobookshelf, Calibre-Web, Komga, and Nextcloud once it is installed. The generated list is in Inventory.
  • .env: TUNNEL_TOKEN, CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN (Zone:Read and DNS:Edit on the zone, Cloudflare Tunnel:Edit on the account), and HOMELAB_DOMAIN.
  • The watchdog's public checks alert through ntfy on tunnel-watchdog.
  • Tailscale is the private way in for apps that should not be public. The zone settings are in Networking.

docs.title: Tinkering ideas
docs.text:
• Security › WAF › Custom rules: block countries you never visit from. Use Block, not a challenge: the native apps cannot answer challenges (Decisions, ADR-0005).
  • Notifications in the Cloudflare dashboard: add a tunnel health alert, so you also get an email when the tunnel goes down.
  • Look at the zone's Analytics now and then to see which public apps get traffic and from where.
  • Run ./homelab domain setup without --apply: it shows the plan and asks before it changes anything.

docs.title: Useful commands
docs.text:
dig against 1.1.1.1 shows what the internet sees (Cloudflare's addresses, not 192.168.1.10), and the curl request takes the same path as a visitor's when run away from home.

./homelab logs cloudflared -f
./homelab compose cloudflared restart cloudflared
./homelab compose cloudflared exec cloudflared cloudflared --version
./homelab domain setup
./homelab watchdog
dig +short passwords.example.com @1.1.1.1
curl -sI https://passwords.example.com

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• Cloudflare One docs (Tunnel is part of it)
  • cloudflared on GitHub
  • Image on Docker Hub

docs.title: Backup
docs.text: Nothing local: the tunnel's configuration lives in Cloudflare, and the token is in .env (Homelab Secrets job).

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Fix Cloudflare error 1033 The tunnel is not connected. ./homelab logs cloudflared; check TUNNEL_TOKEN Cloudflare 502 Proxy Manager is down, or the route does not point at http://nginx-proxy-manager:80 Proxy Manager's default page No proxy host for that hostname. ./homelab domain setup Too many redirects The proxy host does not trust forwarded proto. ./homelab domain setup Token lost Copy it again from the tunnel's page (or create a new tunnel) and rerun ./homelab domain setup

The watchdog checks every public hostname every 15 minutes and alerts tunnel-watchdog.

docs.title: Nginx Proxy Manager
docs.text:
The front door: every request, from the LAN or through the Cloudflare Tunnel, enters here. It terminates TLS and forwards to the app by service name. The image is built locally with CrowdSec's bouncer inside.

Service nginx-proxy-manager in compose/network.yaml (project homelab_network) Image Built locally from dockerfiles/npm-crowdsec Category Network Starts with ./homelab up Yes (./homelab up) Address https://npm.example.com (LAN, through Nginx Proxy Manager) On this machine http://localhost:8181 (NPM_ADMIN_PORT) Data data/appdata/nginx-proxy-manager/data → /datadata/appdata/nginx-proxy-manager/letsencrypt → /etc/letsencryptnpm-logs (volume) → /data/logs Database dump Daily by ./homelab backup into recovery-staging/databases/nginx-proxy-manager Updates Built locally: ./homelab update nginx-proxy-manager rebuilds it. Carries the CrowdSec bouncer; pulling the upstream image would silently drop it

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
• One entry point on ports 80 and 443 for every hostname.
  • TLS with a wildcard certificate for *.example.com (Let's Encrypt, Cloudflare DNS challenge).
  • Enforces CrowdSec's decisions on every request before it reaches an app.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. The first start creates the automation account from NPM_API_EMAIL and NPM_API_PASSWORD. There is no default login.
  2. Sign in at http://localhost:8181 with that account (Sign-in details on its page in Status shows the email and copies the password). Under Users, add a personal administrator and turn on 2FA for it. Leave 2FA off on the automation account; the CLI signs in with it.
  3. ./homelab domain setup --ssl issues the certificate and creates a proxy host for every app.
  4. For a proxy host made by hand: scheme http, forward host is the service name, port is the container port, the wildcard certificate, Force SSL, HTTP/2, websockets, Block common exploits, and trust upstream forwarded proto headers on.

The image: dockerfiles/npm-crowdsec adds lua-cs-bouncer and lua-resty-http to jc21/nginx-proxy-manager. At start, homelab-init.sh writes the bouncer configuration from CROWDSEC_API_URL and CROWDSEC_API_KEY, and creates /data/nginx/custom/server_proxy.conf (real_ip_header CF-Connecting-IP) if it is missing. To update, set NPM_VERSION and run ./homelab update nginx-proxy-manager; never pull the upstream image.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Two parts in one container: OpenResty (nginx with Lua) does the proxying on ports 80 and 443, and a Node.js app serves the admin UI and its API on port 81 (8181 on this Mac).
  • The admin app keeps hosts, certificates, users, and settings in SQLite (/data/database.sqlite), writes one nginx config file per host, and reloads nginx. Hand edits to those files are lost the next time the host is saved; use the host's Advanced tab or /data/nginx/custom/ instead.
  • Certificates come from Let's Encrypt through certbot. The wildcard uses the Cloudflare DNS challenge, and Proxy Manager renews it before it expires.
  • Requests go to apps by service name on the homelab network (http://<service>:<port>), and to native Jellyfin through host.docker.internal.
  • The Lua bouncer checks every request against CrowdSec's decisions (refreshed every 10 seconds) and asks CrowdSec's AppSec component (http://crowdsec:7422, virtual-patching rules only) about it. If CrowdSec does not answer, requests go through (fail open).
  • Access and error logs go to /data/logs (the npm-logs volume), which CrowdSec reads.

docs.title: Where things live
docs.text: What Where Settings database (hosts, users, certificates) data/appdata/nginx-proxy-manager/data/database.sqlite → /data/database.sqlite Generated config, one file per proxy host data/appdata/nginx-proxy-manager/data/nginx/proxy_host/<id>.conf → /data/nginx/proxy_host/ Snippets included in every host data/appdata/nginx-proxy-manager/data/nginx/custom/ → /data/nginx/custom/ (server_proxy.conf sets CF-Connecting-IP) Certificates and certbot state data/appdata/nginx-proxy-manager/letsencrypt → /etc/letsencrypt (live/npm-<id>/) Access and error logs npm-logs volume → /data/logs (proxy-host-<id>_access.log, proxy-host-<id>_error.log) CrowdSec bouncer settings /etc/crowdsec/bouncers/crowdsec-openresty-bouncer.conf, written from .env at every start Bouncer hook into nginx /etc/nginx/conf.d/crowdsec_openresty.conf, from dockerfiles/npm-crowdsec

docs.title: Everyday use
docs.text:
• Hosts › Proxy Hosts: every hostname with its target and certificate. The menu on each row edits, disables, or deletes it; ./homelab domain setup keeps the apps' hosts in line.
  • SSL Certificates: the wildcard's expiry date, and Renew Now from its menu if a renewal failed.
  • Access Lists: require a username and password, or allow only some addresses, then pick the list on a host's Details tab.
  • Users: your administrator (2FA on) and the automation account (leave it as .env says).
  • Audit Log: who changed what in the UI, and when.
  • Settings › Default Site: what an unknown hostname shows.

docs.title: Connects to
docs.text:
• LAN requests arrive by name through AdGuard Home; public requests come from Cloudflare Tunnel to http://nginx-proxy-manager:80.
  • CrowdSec reads its logs, and its bouncer enforces CrowdSec's bans with CROWDSEC_BOUNCER_KEY (passed in as CROWDSEC_API_KEY).
  • .env: NPM_API_EMAIL and NPM_API_PASSWORD (the automation account the CLI signs in with), NPM_VERSION (the upstream version the image builds on), NPM_HTTP_PORT, NPM_HTTPS_PORT, NPM_ADMIN_PORT, LAN_BIND_IP, and CLOUDFLARE_API_TOKEN for the wildcard's DNS challenge.
  • The nightly updates leave it alone (built locally). Uptime Kuma checks http://nginx-proxy-manager:81.
  • In home mode (no domain) it is not used: Tailscale serves the apps.

docs.title: Tinkering ideas
docs.text:
• Settings › Default Site: answer unknown hostnames with a 404 page instead of the welcome page, so scanners learn less.
  • Access Lists: put a password in front of an app that has no login of its own. ./homelab domain setup keeps access lists, custom locations, and the Advanced tab when it updates a host.
  • A host's Advanced tab: per-host nginx directives, such as client_max_body_size for large uploads or extra security headers.
  • Hosts › Redirection Hosts: send a short name, such as pw.example.com, to the real address.
  • Run the ban test in Runbooks and look at the 403 page the bouncer serves.
  • Tail one host's access log (below) to see who visits and which paths scanners try.

docs.title: Useful commands
docs.text:
nginx -t checks the generated config without changing anything. Proxy host ids are in the file names under /data/nginx/proxy_host.

./homelab logs nginx-proxy-manager -f
./homelab compose nginx-proxy-manager restart nginx-proxy-manager
./homelab compose nginx-proxy-manager exec nginx-proxy-manager nginx -t
./homelab compose nginx-proxy-manager exec nginx-proxy-manager ls /data/nginx/proxy_host
./homelab compose nginx-proxy-manager exec nginx-proxy-manager tail -f /data/logs/proxy-host-1_access.log
./homelab compose nginx-proxy-manager exec nginx-proxy-manager grep -E '^(ENABLED|API_URL|MODE)=' /etc/crowdsec/bouncers/crowdsec-openresty-bouncer.conf
./homelab update nginx-proxy-manager
./homelab domain setup --ssl

docs.title: API
docs.text:
• The admin UI is built on a JSON API at http://localhost:8181/api; ./homelab domain setup uses it.
  • Get a token by posting the automation account (NPM_API_EMAIL, NPM_API_PASSWORD) to /api/tokens, then send it as Authorization: Bearer <token>:
curl -s -X POST http://localhost:8181/api/tokens -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"identity":"homelab@example.com","secret":"<NPM_API_PASSWORD>"}'
curl -s http://localhost:8181/api/nginx/proxy-hosts -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>'
  • There is no separate API reference site; the request shapes are in the source repo's backend folder.

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• Nginx Proxy Manager docs
  • Source on GitHub
  • Upstream image on Docker Hub (the base of dockerfiles/npm-crowdsec)
  • CrowdSec Lua bouncer

docs.title: Backup
docs.text: data/appdata/nginx-proxy-manager (settings database, proxy hosts, certificates) is in the Homelab AppData job. Logs live in the npm-logs volume and are not backed up. Everything except hand-made hosts can also be recreated with ./homelab domain setup --ssl.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Fix 502 Bad Gateway The app is stopped or not on the homelab network. ./homelab status; check the forward host is the service name Too many redirects through the tunnel Trust forwarded proto is off on that host. Rerun ./homelab domain setup Proxy Manager's default page for a hostname No proxy host for it. ./homelab domain setup homelab-init: CROWDSEC_API_KEY is empty in the logs Set CROWDSEC_BOUNCER_KEY and ./homelab update nginx-proxy-manager Bans not enforced Status › Fix it reconnects the proxy to CrowdSec. cscli bouncers list must show a recent pull; see CrowdSec CLI says the login was rejected The automation account was changed in the UI. Make the UI match .env again Certificate did not renew The Cloudflare token expired or lost DNS:Edit. Renew from SSL Certificates once fixed

docs.title: Speedtest Tracker
docs.text:
Measures the internet connection on a schedule and keeps the history.

Service speedtest-tracker in compose/network.yaml (project homelab_network) Image lscr.io/linuxserver/speedtest-tracker:latest Category Network Starts with ./homelab up No: optional, ./homelab install speedtest-tracker Address https://speedtest.example.com (LAN, through Nginx Proxy Manager) On this machine http://localhost:8765 (SPEEDTEST_PORT) Data data/appdata/speedtest-tracker → /config Updates Nightly at 4 AM, with a copy of its data first

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Runs a speed test every six hours (SPEEDTEST_SCHEDULE) and keeps the history, so slowdowns and outages on the home connection are on record, not a feeling.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. ./homelab install speedtest-tracker (its SPEEDTEST_APP_KEY is generated).
  2. Open it and sign in with the default account admin@example.com / password, then change both under the profile.
  3. Optionally, under Settings › Notifications, send failed or slow tests to ntfy with the publishers' token.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• A Laravel (PHP) web app with a Filament admin interface, packaged by LinuxServer.io with nginx and PHP in one container.
  • On the SPEEDTEST_SCHEDULE cron (every six hours by default), its scheduler runs Ookla's Speedtest CLI inside the container and stores the result: download, upload, ping, jitter, packet loss, and the server used.
  • Results and settings are in SQLite (DB_CONNECTION: sqlite) in its /config folder.
  • APP_KEY (SPEEDTEST_APP_KEY) encrypts its sessions and stored secrets; APP_URL is its https address.
  • The test runs from the container over this Mac's connection, so anything that slows the Mac's connection (a VPN, a big download) shows in the results.

docs.title: Where things live
docs.text: What Where Results and settings database data/appdata/speedtest-tracker → /config (database.sqlite) Schedule and key SPEEDTEST_SCHEDULE, SPEEDTEST_APP_KEY in .env Logs Container output: ./homelab logs speedtest-tracker

docs.title: Everyday use
docs.text:
• Dashboard: charts of recent download, upload, and ping, with the latest result on top.
  • Results: every test with its server and numbers; open one for the details.
  • Run a test now from the button at the top of the dashboard.
  • Settings › Notifications: where alerts to ntfy are set up (see Setup).

docs.title: Connects to
docs.text:
• Optional alerts to ntfy at http://ntfy:80 with the publishers' token (NTFY_PUBLISH_TOKEN). The token may only write to the granted topics, so pick one of those.
  • Uptime Kuma can watch it at http://speedtest-tracker:80.
  • .env: SPEEDTEST_PORT, SPEEDTEST_APP_KEY, SPEEDTEST_SCHEDULE, TZ (shown times), and HOMELAB_DOMAIN (its address).

docs.title: Tinkering ideas
docs.text:
• Test more often: set SPEEDTEST_SCHEDULE to 0 * * * * (hourly) in .env and run ./homelab update speedtest-tracker.
  • Pin the test server, so results compare like with like: add SPEEDTEST_SERVERS (Ookla server ids) to its environment in compose/network.yaml.
  • Keep the database small with PRUNE_RESULTS_OLDER_THAN (days) in its environment.
  • Set notification thresholds, so ntfy hears only about slow or failed tests rather than every result.
  • Add the Speedtest Tracker widget to Homepage; Homepage's widget docs say what it needs.

docs.title: Useful commands
docs.text:
Laravel's artisan lists the app's own maintenance commands.

./homelab logs speedtest-tracker -f

docs.title: Tailscale
docs.text:
Reach the home network from anywhere, privately, without opening router ports.

Service tailscale in compose/network.yaml (project homelab_network) Image tailscale/tailscale:latest Category Network Starts with ./homelab up No: optional, ./homelab install tailscale Data data/appdata/tailscale → /var/lib/tailscale Updates Nightly at 4 AM, with a copy of its data first

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Private access to the whole home network from anywhere: phones and laptops on your tailnet reach the proxy, AdGuard, and every app's address as if they were at home. It is a subnet router, so nothing else needs Tailscale installed, and no router ports are opened. Admin apps that stay off the public tunnel (Nginx Proxy Manager, AdGuard, Duplicati) become reachable this way.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
These steps make it a subnet router for the home network, which a homelab with a domain uses. In Home mode (the default), follow Home mode below instead.

  1. Check TAILSCALE_ROUTES matches the home network (for example 192.168.1.0/24).
  2. ./homelab install tailscale, then ./homelab tailnet login: it opens Tailscale's sign-in page in the browser (make a free account there if you have none) and carries on once you signed in. No auth key is needed; one in TAILSCALE_AUTHKEY (login.tailscale.com, Settings, Keys) signs it in without the browser instead.
  3. In the Tailscale admin, open the homelab machine › Edit route settings, and approve the subnet route.
  4. DNS › Nameservers › Add nameserver › Custom: 192.168.1.10, restricted to the domain example.com (split DNS), so the app names resolve through AdGuard away from home.
  5. Install Tailscale on the phone and sign in; with mobile data, https://npm.example.com should open.

docs.title: Home mode (no domain)
docs.text:
