With HOMELAB_DOMAIN empty (the default), Tailscale gives every app its https address instead of the domain, AdGuard rewrites, Cloudflare, and the tunnel:

  1. In the Tailscale admin, turn on DNS › MagicDNS and HTTPS Certificates.
  2. Setup › Addresses on your tailnet (or ./homelab install tailscale then ./homelab tailnet setup). The first time, it opens Tailscale's sign-in page and waits until you signed in.
  3. Each app is at https://homelab.<tailnet>.ts.net:<its port>, e.g. Vaultwarden at :8087. Status shows the addresses; they open on any device signed in to the same tailnet, at home or away. Nothing is published to the internet.

How it works: homelab tailnet setup writes data/appdata/tailscale/serve.json (TS_SERVE_CONFIG), one HTTPS listener per running app's port, forwarding to the app's container on the homelab network (host.docker.internal for native apps like Jellyfin), and saves the machine's tailnet name in TAILSCALE_HOST. Tailscale fetches a Let's Encrypt certificate for the name on first use, so the first visit can take a few seconds. Apps that need to know their own address (Vaultwarden, Paperless-ngx, Karakeep, MoneyMatter, Pocket ID, ntfy, and a few more) get the tailnet one in their *_URL setting and are restarted with it, so sign-in and links work. Every install reruns it, so new apps get an address by themselves. TAILNET_ADMIN_APPS=false keeps the admin apps (the proxy, AdGuard, Duplicati, Dozzle) off the tailnet, so only this machine opens them. Setting a domain later and running Set up the domain clears those settings again. ./homelab doctor warns when the tailnet has no HTTPS certificates.

Useful commands:

./homelab compose tailscale exec tailscale tailscale status
./homelab compose tailscale exec tailscale tailscale serve status
./homelab compose tailscale exec tailscale tailscale cert homelab.<tailnet>.ts.net

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• tailscaled (Go) runs in userspace networking mode (TS_USERSPACE): WireGuard runs inside the process, so it needs no kernel module or extra privileges.
  • It signs in to Tailscale's coordination server once, through the sign-in page homelab tailnet login opens (or with TAILSCALE_AUTHKEY), then keeps its identity in its state folder. Devices connect to it directly when they can, and through Tailscale's relays (DERP) when they cannot; traffic is end-to-end encrypted either way.
  • As a subnet router it advertises TAILSCALE_ROUTES (192.168.1.0/24): your devices send traffic for that range to this container, which forwards it onto the home network.
  • TS_ACCEPT_DNS=false keeps the container on Docker's DNS, so service names still resolve for it.
  • In home mode, its HTTPS listeners come from serve.json (see above).

docs.title: Where things live
docs.text: What Where Machine identity and keys data/appdata/tailscale → /var/lib/tailscale (tailscaled.state) Home-mode listeners /var/lib/tailscale/serve.json (TS_SERVE_CONFIG) Certificates for the tailnet name /var/lib/tailscale/certs/ Control socket /var/run/tailscale/tailscaled.sock (TS_SOCKET) Optional auth key, routes, tailnet name TAILSCALE_AUTHKEY, TAILSCALE_ROUTES, TAILSCALE_HOST in .env

docs.title: Everyday use
docs.text:
• The Tailscale app on iPhone, iPad, Android, Mac, and Windows: turn it on away from home, and the home addresses work as if you were there.
  • Settings › Phones › Devices on your tailnet in the app: every device on the tailnet, whether it is online or when it was last seen (one unseen for a month is marked, in case it is lost), and Remove…, which opens that device in the admin console: a device cannot be removed from another device, so removing is done there.
  • Admin console (login.tailscale.com) › Machines: which devices are online, the homelab machine's routes, and renaming or removing devices.
  • Admin console › Users: invite family members to the tailnet.
  • ./homelab doctor checks that it is logged in and its route is approved.

docs.title: Connects to
docs.text:
• Reaches Nginx Proxy Manager and every app's address on the LAN, and uses AdGuard Home (192.168.1.10) as the split-DNS nameserver for example.com.
  • The way in for apps that stay off the tunnel: AdGuard Home, Duplicati, Pocket ID, Uptime Kuma.
  • The private alternative to Cloudflare Tunnel. In home mode it replaces the domain, AdGuard's rewrite, the proxy, and the tunnel.
  • .env: TAILSCALE_AUTHKEY (optional), TAILSCALE_ROUTES, TAILSCALE_HOST, and HOMELAB_DOMAIN (empty means home mode).

docs.title: Tinkering ideas
docs.text:
• Admin console › Machines › homelab › Disable key expiry, so the Mac does not drop off the tailnet when its key expires (every 180 days by default).
  • Make it an exit node: set TAILSCALE_EXTRA_ARGS=--advertise-exit-node in .env, run homelab install tailscale --apply, approve it in the admin, and choose it in the phone's app to browse through home on public Wi-Fi.
  • Run the tailnet yourself: with your own Headscale server, set TAILSCALE_EXTRA_ARGS=--login-server=https://<your Headscale> and an auth key from it in TAILSCALE_AUTHKEY. Headscale gives out no HTTPS certificates, so Home mode's https addresses do not open there; a domain does.
  • Admin console › Access controls: limit which users or devices may use the 192.168.1.0/24 route.
  • In the iPhone app's settings, turn on VPN On Demand so it connects by itself when you leave home Wi-Fi.
  • tailscale netcheck (below): which relay is nearest and whether direct connections are possible from here.

docs.title: Useful commands
docs.text:
These add to the home-mode commands above. tailscale ping shows whether a device is reached directly or through a relay.

./homelab logs tailscale -f
./homelab compose tailscale restart tailscale
./homelab compose tailscale exec tailscale tailscale ip -4
./homelab compose tailscale exec tailscale tailscale netcheck
./homelab compose tailscale exec tailscale tailscale ping <device>
./homelab tailnet setup
./homelab doctor

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• Tailscale docs, including Tailscale in Docker and subnet routers
  • Source on GitHub
  • Image on Docker Hub

docs.title: Backup
docs.text: data/appdata/tailscale holds the machine's identity and is covered by the AppData job. Without it, the machine signs in again (./homelab tailnet login).

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Routes do nothing: the route was not approved in the admin, or TAILSCALE_ROUTES does not match the network; ./homelab doctor says which, and whether Tailscale is still logged in.
  • Names do not resolve away from home: the split-DNS nameserver is missing; addresses like 192.168.1.10 still work.

docs.title: CrowdSec
docs.text:
Reads Nginx Proxy Manager's logs, recognises attacks (scans, brute force, exploit attempts), and bans the source. The ban is enforced by the bouncer inside the proxy image, for LAN and tunnel traffic alike. It also pulls CrowdSec's community blocklist.

Service crowdsec in compose/security.yaml (project homelab_security) Image crowdsecurity/crowdsec:latest Category Security Starts with ./homelab up Yes (./homelab up) Data data/appdata/crowdsec/config → /etc/crowdsecdata/appdata/crowdsec/data → /var/lib/crowdsec/dataconfig/crowdsec/acquis.yaml, read-only → /etc/crowdsec/acquis.d/nginx-proxy-manager.yamlconfig/crowdsec/appsec.yaml, read-only → /etc/crowdsec/acquis.d/appsec.yamlnpm-logs (volume), read-only → /var/log/npm Updates Nightly at 4 AM, with a copy of its data first

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
• Detection: the crowdsecurity/nginx-proxy-manager collection parses the proxy's access and error logs.
  • Enforcement: the proxy's Lua bouncer pulls decisions every 10 seconds and answers banned addresses with 403.
  • Intelligence: the community blocklist bans known-bad addresses before they try anything.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
Nothing to do by hand:

  • CROWDSEC_BOUNCER_KEY registers the proxy's bouncer (BOUNCER_KEY_nginx_proxy_manager) when CrowdSec starts, and the proxy uses the same key.
  • The proxy's logs reach CrowdSec through the npm-logs volume; config/crowdsec/acquis.yaml tells it where to look.
  • Optional: set CROWDSEC_ENROLL_KEY (app.crowdsec.net › Engines › Add) to see alerts in the CrowdSec console.

Check it works:

./homelab compose crowdsec exec crowdsec cscli bouncers list   # nginx_proxy_manager (or nginx_proxy_manager@<address>), recent last pull
./homelab compose crowdsec exec crowdsec cscli metrics         # lines read from /var/log/npm

./homelab doctor reads the bouncer list for you ("the proxy's bouncer pulled decisions 8 seconds ago"), and the watchdog alerts when the bouncer is missing, revoked, or has not pulled for 5 minutes. Since CrowdSec 1.6.4, a proxy that comes back with a new address (after an update recreates its container) is listed a second time as nginx_proxy_manager@<address>, and its pulls go there while the first entry stops moving: doctor, the watchdog, and Protection read every entry under that name, so the proxy counts as pulling while any of them is.

Then run the ban test in Runbooks: the app's Status screen lists it under Protection (as a manual ban) within a minute.

If the bouncer stopped pulling: Status › Fix it (or ./homelab fix) reconnects the proxy to CrowdSec; it shows the plan first, and both restart for a moment. ./homelab logs nginx-proxy-manager shows CrowdSec errors; a 403 there means CrowdSec no longer accepts the key (its database kept an older registration). Fix it removes every nginx_proxy_manager entry, the @<address> ones too. By hand, remove the old registrations and let CrowdSec register the current key again:

./homelab compose crowdsec exec crowdsec cscli bouncers delete nginx_proxy_manager
./homelab compose crowdsec exec crowdsec cscli bouncers delete nginx_proxy_manager@<address>   # each one bouncers list shows
./homelab restart crowdsec

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• One Go program with two halves. The agent tails logs, parses each line, and runs scenarios (for example, "too many 404s from one address in a short time"). The Local API (LAPI, port 8080 on the homelab network) stores the resulting alerts and decisions and serves them to bouncers.
  • Acquisition files say what to read: acquis.yaml (the proxy's logs in /var/log/npm) and appsec.yaml (the AppSec listener on port 7422, which the proxy's bouncer asks about each request). AppSec loads only the crowdsecurity/virtual-patching rules (exploits of known vulnerabilities), which rarely touch normal traffic; if it is down, requests go through.
  • Hub collections installed at start (COLLECTIONS) say what to detect: crowdsecurity/nginx-proxy-manager (log parsers and HTTP scenarios) and crowdsecurity/appsec-virtual-patching (rules for known vulnerabilities).
  • When a scenario fires, profiles.yaml turns the alert into a decision, by default a 4-hour ban of the address.
  • It shares its alerts (address and scenario) with CrowdSec's central API and gets the community blocklist back.
  • Alerts and decisions are kept in SQLite. The default crowdsecurity/whitelists parser skips private addresses.

docs.title: Where things live
docs.text: What Where Main configuration data/appdata/crowdsec/config → /etc/crowdsec (config.yaml) What a ban is (type, duration) /etc/crowdsec/profiles.yaml Installed collections, parsers, scenarios /etc/crowdsec/collections/, parsers/, scenarios/ (linked into /etc/crowdsec/hub/) Credentials (local API, central API) /etc/crowdsec/local_api_credentials.yaml, /etc/crowdsec/online_api_credentials.yaml Alerts and decisions database data/appdata/crowdsec/data → /var/lib/crowdsec/data/crowdsec.db Log sources config/crowdsec/acquis.yaml and config/crowdsec/appsec.yaml → /etc/crowdsec/acquis.d/ (read-only) The proxy's logs npm-logs volume → /var/log/npm (read-only)

docs.title: Everyday use
docs.text:
• cscli decisions list: who is banned now, why, and for how long.
  • cscli alerts list: what was detected, including attempts that did not lead to a ban.
  • The app's Status screen › Protection and ./homelab doctor show whether the bouncer is pulling.
  • With CROWDSEC_ENROLL_KEY set, app.crowdsec.net shows alerts on a map and the engine's health.
  • The weekly check in Monitoring includes a look at the decisions.

docs.title: Connects to
docs.text:
• Reads Nginx Proxy Manager's logs, and the bouncer inside that image enforces the decisions. Tunnel visitors from Cloudflare Tunnel are judged by their real address (CF-Connecting-IP).
  • .env: CROWDSEC_BOUNCER_KEY (the same key on both sides) and CROWDSEC_ENROLL_KEY (optional console).
  • The watchdog's bouncer checks alert through ntfy.

docs.title: Tinkering ideas
docs.text:
• Ask why a log line did or did not trigger: cscli explain --file /var/log/npm/<file> --type nginx-proxy-manager.
  • Change the ban length in /etc/crowdsec/profiles.yaml (duration: 4h) and restart CrowdSec.
  • Send new bans to ntfy with the HTTP notification plugin (/etc/crowdsec/notifications/http.yaml, then notifications: in profiles.yaml), using the publishers' token and a granted topic.
  • Enroll in the console (CROWDSEC_ENROLL_KEY) and subscribe the engine to extra blocklists there.
  • Whitelist a trusted outside address (a relative's house, an office) with your own file in /etc/crowdsec/parsers/s02-enrich/.
  • Look at cscli metrics after a week to see which scenarios fire most.

docs.title: Useful commands
docs.text:
cscli runs inside the container. The decisions add line bans a documentation address for 5 minutes, which is a safe way to see a decision appear.

./homelab logs crowdsec -f
./homelab compose crowdsec restart crowdsec
./homelab compose crowdsec exec crowdsec cscli metrics
./homelab compose crowdsec exec crowdsec cscli alerts list
./homelab compose crowdsec exec crowdsec cscli decisions list
./homelab compose crowdsec exec crowdsec cscli decisions add --ip 203.0.113.7 --duration 5m
./homelab compose crowdsec exec crowdsec cscli collections list
./homelab compose crowdsec exec crowdsec cscli hub update
./homelab compose crowdsec exec crowdsec cscli capi status

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• CrowdSec docs
  • Source on GitHub
  • Image on Docker Hub
  • The proxy's Lua bouncer

docs.title: Backup
docs.text: data/appdata/crowdsec (configuration, local database of decisions and alerts) is in the Homelab AppData job. If lost, CrowdSec starts fresh and re-downloads the blocklist.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Fix Bouncer stopped pulling, or Status › Protection says the proxy is not connected Status › Fix it reconnects it (./homelab fix) Bouncer missing from cscli bouncers list CROWDSEC_BOUNCER_KEY was empty when CrowdSec first started. Set it, then ./homelab update crowdsec nginx-proxy-manager Metrics show no lines read The proxy is not writing to npm-logs, or acquis.yaml is not mounted. ./homelab compose network config and the logs Someone legitimate was banned cscli decisions list, then cscli decisions delete --ip <address> A LAN device is never banned Expected: private addresses are whitelisted

docs.title: Frigate
docs.text:
Cameras recorded on this machine, with person, car, and animal detection.

Service frigate in stacks/frigate/compose.yaml (project homelab_frigate) Image ghcr.io/blakeblackshear/frigate:0.18.2 Category Security Starts with ./homelab up No: optional, ./homelab install frigate Address https://cameras.example.com (LAN, through Nginx Proxy Manager) On this machine http://localhost:8971 (FRIGATE_PORT) Depends on frigate-mqtt Helpers frigate-mqtt docker.io/library/eclipse-mosquitto:2 Data appdata/frigate → /config/Volumes/Media/frigate → /media/frigate Database dump Daily by ./homelab backup into recovery-staging/databases/frigate Updates By hand. A new version can change the settings file and migrate the database; set FRIGATE_VERSION to a newer release after reading its notes, then ./homelab update frigate

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
Records your cameras on this machine and watches them for people, cars, and animals, so you get "a person at the front door" instead of every leaf that moves. Nothing goes to a vendor's cloud: no subscription, and the footage stays home. With Home Assistant, its detections become sensors, camera views, and phone notifications.

It is heavy and optional: decoding video and running detection keeps the processor busy around the clock, about one core for each camera without a detector chip.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. Find each camera's stream address (RTSP) in its manual or app, usually rtsp://user:password@<camera address>:554/<path>. Cameras that only work through a vendor's cloud app cannot be used.
  2. ./homelab install frigate (it brings its event broker). Recordings go to frigate on the media drive, or to the folder in FRIGATE_RECORDINGS if you add that setting to .env.
  3. Sign in: on its first start Frigate makes the account admin with a random password, written in its log: ./homelab logs frigate | grep -i password. Change it under your account once signed in.
  4. Add the cameras: open the configuration editor in Frigate's settings, replace the example front_door camera's address with yours, set enabled: true, then save and restart from the editor. Each further camera is another entry under cameras.
  5. To keep recordings, add to each camera (or once at the top level): 
    record:
  enabled: true
    and choose how long to keep them in its settings. A camera recording all the time at 4 Mbit/s fills about 43 GB a day.
  6. Pair it with Home Assistant (below).

docs.title: Pairing with Home Assistant
docs.text:
1. In Home Assistant: Settings › Devices & services › Add integration › MQTT. Broker frigate-mqtt, port 1883, username frigate, password FRIGATE_MQTT_PASSWORD from Settings (Show).
  2. Install the Frigate integration. It is not built in: add HACS to Home Assistant, then search HACS for Frigate and install it, and restart Home Assistant.
  3. Add integration › Frigate, with the URL http://frigate:5000 (Frigate by its name inside Docker; that port needs no sign-in and is not reachable from outside Docker).
  4. Each camera appears as a device with its live view, a sensor for each kind of object, and the latest snapshot; automations can notify your phone on a person, with the picture.

docs.title: How much it takes, on each system
docs.text:
• Processor: each camera's stream is decoded all the time, and detection runs on the moving parts. On the processor alone, plan on one core for each 720p camera at 5 frames a second.
  • Shared memory: shm_size in stacks/frigate/compose.yaml is 512 MB, enough for several 720p cameras. Raise it if the log says Bus error.
  • A detector chip (a Coral, or a graphics chip) makes detection several times faster:
  • Mac: containers cannot reach USB devices or Apple's graphics, so it runs on the processor.
  • Windows: an NVIDIA graphics card works through WSL 2, with the -tensorrt image; a USB Coral cannot be passed through.
  • Linux: a USB Coral, Intel graphics (OpenVINO), AMD graphics (the -rocm image), or NVIDIA (the -tensorrt image, with NVIDIA's container toolkit) can all be passed through (Tinkering ideas).
  • SteamOS: its AMD graphics can be passed through like on Linux, with the -rocm image.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• One container runs Frigate: FFmpeg reads each camera, a motion check finds what changed, and the detector looks for objects there. Recordings and snapshots are written to /media/frigate.
  • frigate-mqtt (Mosquitto) is the stack's event broker: Frigate publishes each detection there, and Home Assistant listens. It lets only the frigate account in, with FRIGATE_MQTT_PASSWORD.
  • Port 8971 is its page and API with sign-in (the one the proxy and http://localhost:8971 use). Port 5000, without sign-in, stays inside Docker for Home Assistant.
  • Events, reviews, and the users are in a SQLite database, frigate.db, next to config.yml.

docs.title: Where things live
docs.text: What Where Settings appdata/frigate/config.yml Events, reviews, users appdata/frigate/frigate.db Recordings, clips, snapshots <MEDIA_ROOT>/frigate, or FRIGATE_RECORDINGS Secrets FRIGATE_MQTT_PASSWORD in .env; the admin password in its database

docs.title: Everyday use
docs.text:
• Review: the home page lists what it saw, by camera, as short clips; mark them reviewed as you go.
  • Explore: search past detections by object, camera, and time.
  • Zones and masks: draw where a person matters (the path to the door) and what to ignore (a busy street, a waving tree), in each camera's settings.
  • On the phone: through Home Assistant's app, or open https://cameras.example.com at home and over Tailscale.

docs.title: Connects to
docs.text:
• Home Assistant: sensors, camera views, and notifications (Pairing, above).
  • The media drive: recordings, alongside the films; homelab doctor warns when it fills.
  • .env: FRIGATE_PORT (default 8971), FRIGATE_VERSION, FRIGATE_MQTT_PASSWORD, FRIGATE_RECORDINGS.

docs.title: Tinkering ideas
docs.text:
• A USB Coral (Linux): add devices: ["/dev/bus/usb:/dev/bus/usb"] to frigate in stacks/frigate/compose.yaml and, in config.yml, detectors: { coral: { type: edgetpu, device: usb } }.
  • Intel graphics (Linux, SteamOS on Intel): add devices: ["/dev/dri:/dev/dri"] and an openvino detector with device: GPU; AMD graphics need the -rocm image (set the image tag to ${FRIGATE_VERSION}-rocm).
  • Face and licence-plate recognition: built into Frigate, switched on in its settings; both run better with a detector chip.

docs.title: Useful commands
docs.text:
./homelab logs frigate -f
./homelab compose frigate restart frigate
./homelab compose frigate exec frigate curl -s http://127.0.0.1:5000/api/stats
./homelab update frigate          # after changing FRIGATE_VERSION

docs.title: API
docs.text:
• Sign in: POST /api/login with {"user":"admin","password":…} on port 8971 (it sets a cookie), or use port 5000 from another container (no sign-in).
  • Base URL: http://localhost:8971/api on this machine, https://cameras.example.com/api on the LAN.
  • Useful calls: GET /api/stats (each camera's frames per second), GET /api/events, GET /api/<camera>/latest.jpg.
  • The reference is in Frigate's documentation.

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• frigate.video and its documentation
  • GitHub: blakeblackshear/frigate and the Home Assistant integration

docs.title: Backup
docs.text: ./homelab backup copies frigate.db nightly into recovery-staging/databases/frigate, and Duplicati takes it off-site with the rest; config.yml is in appdata/frigate, with the apps' folders. Recordings are on the media drive and are not backed up: they are kept for the days you set and then deleted.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• A camera shows nothing: check its address in VLC first; in Frigate's log, Connection refused or 401 means the address or the camera's password is wrong.
  • Bus error, or Frigate restarting: raise shm_size in stacks/frigate/compose.yaml, then ./homelab up.
  • The processor is always busy: lower each camera's detect size and fps (5 is enough), add motion masks, or add a detector chip where the system allows it.
  • Home Assistant shows no events: its MQTT integration must use frigate-mqtt and the frigate account; Frigate's log says MQTT connected when its own side works.

docs.title: Pocket ID
docs.text:
One sign-in with passkeys for the household's apps (OpenID Connect)

Service pocket-id in compose/security.yaml (project homelab_security) Image ghcr.io/pocket-id/pocket-id:v2 Category Security Starts with ./homelab up No: optional, ./homelab install pocket-id Address https://id.example.com (LAN, through Nginx Proxy Manager) On this machine http://localhost:1411 (POCKET_ID_PORT) Data data/appdata/pocket-id → /app/data Updates Nightly at 4 AM, with a copy of its data first Also known as sso, oidc, passkeys

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: One sign-in for the household, with passkeys (Face ID, Touch ID, or a security key) instead of a password per app. ./homelab sso setup makes it the sign-in of Karakeep, Open WebUI, Paperless-ngx, Mealie, and Vikunja by itself, and makes Immich's client with the steps to paste it. Other apps with OpenID Connect (Audiobookshelf) are connected by hand.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. ./homelab install pocket-id and open /setup on its https address: https://<TAILSCALE_HOST>:1411/setup in Home mode, or https://id.example.com/setup with a domain (passkeys need the https address, not localhost).
  2. Create the admin account and register a passkey.
  3. Users › add each person, then send them the sign-up link it makes so they register their own passkey.
  4. ./homelab sso setup (it needs a domain; see below): for each app it supports that runs here, it makes an OIDC client through Pocket ID's API (POCKET_ID_API_KEY, its STATIC_API_KEY) and writes the app's sign-in settings to data/sso/<app>.env, which the app's service reads, then restarts the app. ./homelab sso shows which are connected.
  5. Any other app: OIDC Clients › Add, name it, set the callback URL from the app's own SSO settings, and copy the client ID and secret into the app.

The apps' containers reach id.example.com through Nginx Proxy Manager on this Mac whatever their DNS says (SSO_HOST, mapped to the host in each of their services). In Home mode they cannot reach the tailnet address from inside a container, so single sign-on needs Set up the domain.

POCKET_ID_ENCRYPTION_KEY in .env protects Pocket ID's signing keys. It is backed up with .env (Secrets job); losing it means everyone registers their passkeys again.

docs.title: Away from home
docs.text: In Home mode (the default), Pocket ID is on the tailnet: it opens at home and away on every device signed in to Tailscale. With a domain, it is on the home network only: install Tailscale to reach it from anywhere, or, to publish it through the tunnel, add public: true to its x-homelab block and run ./homelab domain setup again.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• One Go program serves the web UI and the OpenID Connect endpoints on port 1411. It is a sign-in provider only, and passkeys are the only way to sign in: there are no passwords.
  • An app sends you to Pocket ID, you confirm with a passkey, and Pocket ID sends you back with a code; the app then trades the code for your name, email, and groups.
  • Users, passkeys, OIDC clients, and the audit log are in a SQLite database under /app/data. ENCRYPTION_KEY (POCKET_ID_ENCRYPTION_KEY) encrypts its signing keys.
  • APP_URL is https://id.example.com. Passkeys are bound to that name, which is why localhost cannot sign in.
  • TRUST_PROXY=true takes the client's address from the proxy's headers, so the audit log shows real addresses.

docs.title: Where things live
docs.text: What Where Database (users, passkeys, clients, audit log) and uploaded images data/appdata/pocket-id → /app/data Key that encrypts the signing keys POCKET_ID_ENCRYPTION_KEY in .env What apps read to configure themselves https://id.example.com/.well-known/openid-configuration

docs.title: Everyday use
docs.text:
• My Account: your name and email, and your passkeys. Add a second passkey (another device or a security key) so a lost phone does not lock you out.
  • Users: ./homelab person add "Anna Smith" --email anna@example.com adds someone, with a one-time link to add their passkey and a welcome page listing their apps (data/people/anna.html); ./homelab person password anna gives them a new password in Jellyfin and Navidrome, which have their own; ./homelab person remove anna turns their sign-in off. In Pocket ID itself: send sign-up links, and make a one-time sign-in link for someone who lost their passkey.
  • User Groups: group people (adults, kids) to decide who may use which app.
  • OIDC Clients: one per connected app, with its callback URL, client ID, and secret.
  • Audit log: recent sign-ins with device and address.

docs.title: Connects to
docs.text:
• Apps with OpenID Connect sign-in, among them Immich, Paperless-ngx, Karakeep, Vikunja, Open WebUI, Grocy, Mealie, and Audiobookshelf. Each gets a client ID and secret, and the issuer URL https://id.example.com.
  • Reached through Nginx Proxy Manager at home and Tailscale away.
  • .env: POCKET_ID_ENCRYPTION_KEY, POCKET_ID_PORT, and HOMELAB_DOMAIN (its address).

docs.title: Tinkering ideas
docs.text:
• Connect Immich first (Administration › Settings › Authentication Settings › OAuth): it shows the whole flow, including mobile sign-in.
  • Limit an OIDC client to a user group, so only the adults can sign in to Paperless-ngx.
  • Add custom claims to a user or group for apps that expect extra fields.
  • Save a passkey in Bitwarden (Vaultwarden) as a second one that follows you across devices.
  • Set up email in the application settings, so people get a message when their account signs in from a new device.
  • Make an API key in the admin settings to script adding users.

docs.title: Useful commands
docs.text:
If every admin passkey is lost, one-time-access-token makes a one-time sign-in link for that user. The curl line shows the discovery document apps read.

./homelab logs pocket-id -f
./homelab compose pocket-id restart pocket-id
./homelab compose pocket-id exec pocket-id /app/pocket-id one-time-access-token <username>
curl -s http://localhost:1411/.well-known/openid-configuration

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• Pocket ID docs
  • Source on GitHub
  • Image on GitHub Container Registry

docs.title: Backup
docs.text: The database and keys are in data/appdata/pocket-id, covered by the AppData job.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• "Passkeys are not supported": open it through https://id.example.com; passkeys need HTTPS on the real name.
  • Changing the domain: passkeys are tied to id.example.com. After moving to another domain, everyone registers again.

docs.title: Uptime Kuma
docs.text:
Watches every app from inside the Docker network and sends ntfy alerts when one stops answering.

Service uptime-kuma in compose/security.yaml (project homelab_security) Image louislam/uptime-kuma:2 Category Security Starts with ./homelab up Yes (./homelab up) Address https://uptime.example.com (LAN, through Nginx Proxy Manager) On this machine http://localhost:3001 (UPTIME_KUMA_PORT) Data data/appdata/uptime-kuma → /app/data Database dump Daily by ./homelab backup into recovery-staging/databases/uptime-kuma Updates Nightly at 4 AM, with a copy of its data first

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
• One page that shows whether everything is up, with history.
  • Down and up alerts on the uptime-kuma topic.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. Open http://localhost:3001 and create the admin account (store it in Vaultwarden).
  2. Settings › Notifications › Setup Notification › ntfy: server URL http://ntfy:80, topic uptime-kuma, priority 4, authentication method Access token with NTFY_PUBLISH_TOKEN from .env (after ./homelab notify setup). Turn on "Default enabled" so new monitors use it.
  3. Create the monitors in Monitoring. Use service names and container ports (http://paperless:8000), not localhost.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• A Node.js server with a Vue web UI. The page talks to the server over a websocket (Socket.IO), not a REST API, which is why monitors cannot be created by script here.
  • Each monitor runs inside the server on its own interval (60 seconds by default) from the homelab network, so it reaches apps by service name.
  • Monitors, results, and settings are in SQLite (kuma.db), dumped daily. Version 2 can also use MariaDB; this homelab uses SQLite.
  • When a monitor changes state (down after its retries, or up again), it sends the notifications attached to it: here, ntfy on uptime-kuma.
  • History is kept for 180 days by default (Settings › Monitor History).

docs.title: Where things live
docs.text: What Where Database (monitors, history, settings) data/appdata/uptime-kuma → /app/data/kuma.db Uploaded status-page logos /app/data/upload/ Daily database dump recovery-staging/databases/uptime-kuma

docs.title: Everyday use
docs.text:
• Dashboard: every monitor with its recent up and down bars; open one for response times and events.
  • Add New Monitor: HTTP(s), HTTP(s) keyword, TCP port, ping, DNS, push, and more.
  • Maintenance: schedule a window so planned downtime does not alert.
  • Status Pages: a read-only page for the family that shows what is up.
  • Settings › Notifications: the ntfy notification from Setup.
  • On a phone, the web page works; add it to the home screen.

docs.title: Connects to
docs.text:
• Alerts go to ntfy at http://ntfy:80, topic uptime-kuma, with NTFY_PUBLISH_TOKEN.
  • Watches every app (Monitoring has the list), including Nginx Proxy Manager, AdGuard Home (web and DNS), Vaultwarden, and native Jellyfin through host.docker.internal.
  • The watchdog covers the same apps; Uptime Kuma adds history and status pages.
  • .env: UPTIME_KUMA_PORT and NTFY_PUBLISH_TOKEN.

docs.title: Tinkering ideas
docs.text:
• Push monitor: Add New Monitor › Push gives a URL; have a script call it when it finishes, and Uptime Kuma alerts when the calls stop.
  • Keyword monitor: check that a page contains a word, which catches an app that answers 200 with an error page.
  • On an HTTPS monitor of https://npm.example.com, turn on certificate expiry notification to hear about a failed renewal early.
  • Build a status page and show it on Homepage with Homepage's Uptime Kuma widget.
  • Settings › Security: turn on two-factor authentication for the admin account.
  • Tags on monitors to group them by category.

docs.title: Useful commands
docs.text:
reset-password asks for a new admin password if you lose it. The curl inside the container tests a target exactly as a monitor sees it.

./homelab logs uptime-kuma -f
./homelab compose uptime-kuma restart uptime-kuma
./homelab compose uptime-kuma exec uptime-kuma npm run reset-password
./homelab compose uptime-kuma exec uptime-kuma curl -sI http://paperless:8000
curl -s "http://localhost:3001/api/push/<push token>?status=up&msg=OK"

docs.title: API
docs.text:
There is no API for creating monitors. What there is:

  • Push: http://localhost:3001/api/push/<token>; the token is on the push monitor's page.
  • Badges: /api/badge/<monitor id>/status and /api/badge/<monitor id>/uptime, for monitors on a public status page.
  • Metrics: /metrics in Prometheus format, with an API key from Settings › API Keys as the basic-auth password.

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• Uptime Kuma wiki
  • Source on GitHub
  • Image on Docker Hub

docs.title: Backup
docs.text: data/appdata/uptime-kuma (monitors, history, settings) is in the Homelab AppData job.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Fix A monitor using localhost is always down Inside the container, localhost is Uptime Kuma itself. Use the service name Jellyfin monitor down Use http://host.docker.internal:8096/health No alerts arrive ./homelab notify setup grants uptime-kuma; check the notification uses NTFY_PUBLISH_TOKEN, then use its Test button

docs.title: Vaultwarden
docs.text:
The household password manager. It speaks the Bitwarden protocol, so the official Bitwarden apps and browser extensions work with it. It also holds every homelab credential.

Service vaultwarden in compose/security.yaml (project homelab_security) Image vaultwarden/server:latest Category Security Starts with ./homelab up Yes (./homelab up) Address https://passwords.example.com (LAN and public, through the Cloudflare Tunnel) On this machine http://localhost:8087 (VAULTWARDEN_PORT) Data data/appdata/vaultwarden → /data Database dump Daily by ./homelab backup into recovery-staging/databases/vaultwarden Updates Nightly at 4 AM, with a copy of its data first

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
• Passwords, 2FA codes, and secure notes for the family, synced to every device.
  • The homelab's own credentials, as homelab - <service> <credential>.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. Open sign-ups for a while: Setup › Open sign-ups for 10 minutes, or ./homelab signups open (--for 30m for longer).
  2. Create each family account at https://<TAILSCALE_HOST>:8087 in Home mode, or https://passwords.example.com with a domain.
  3. Sign-ups close by themselves when the time is up (or ./homelab signups close now). By hand instead: VAULTWARDEN_SIGNUPS_ALLOWED=true, ./homelab update vaultwarden, and back to false afterwards; ./homelab doctor warns while sign-ups are open.
  4. Turn on two-step login for every account.
  5. In the Bitwarden apps, choose Self-hosted and enter that same address.

Keep an offline copy of your master password: every other credential, including the backup passphrases, is in here.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• A Rust server that speaks the Bitwarden client API, so the official Bitwarden apps work with it. It also serves the Bitwarden web vault.
  • Everything is encrypted on your devices with a key derived from the master password. The server stores only the encrypted vault and cannot read it, which is also why a lost master password cannot be reset.
  • Data is a SQLite database (/data/db.sqlite3), plus attachments and Sends on disk and an RSA key that signs sign-in tokens.
  • DOMAIN (https://passwords.example.com) is used for links and for passkey two-step login, so it must match the address you use.
  • Clients get live updates over a websocket on the same port, through the proxy (websockets are on in its proxy host).
  • No admin page (ADMIN_TOKEN is not set) and no email (no SMTP settings), so features that send email, such as emergency access, do not work as is.

docs.title: Where things live
docs.text: What Where Database (accounts, encrypted vaults, organizations) data/appdata/vaultwarden → /data/db.sqlite3 File attachments /data/attachments/ Sends with files /data/sends/ Key that signs sign-in tokens /data/rsa_key.pem Website icon cache /data/icon_cache/ Daily database dump recovery-staging/databases/vaultwarden

docs.title: Everyday use
docs.text:
• Apps: Bitwarden for iPhone and Android (turn it on as the AutoFill provider in the phone's settings), the browser extension, and the desktop app. In each: Self-hosted, server https://passwords.example.com.
  • Browser extension shortcut: Cmd+Shift+L (Ctrl+Shift+L elsewhere) fills the login for the current page.
  • Generator: strong passwords and passphrases, in every app and the web vault.
  • Account settings › Security › Two-step login: an authenticator app or a passkey for each account.
  • Send: share a password or file with a link that expires.
  • Organizations: a shared family vault with collections.
  • Export vault: in the web vault's Tools, for the encrypted extra copy in Backup.

docs.title: Connects to
docs.text:
• Public through Cloudflare Tunnel and Nginx Proxy Manager, so the apps sync away from home; CrowdSec watches the proxy in front of it.
  • Holds the homelab's own credentials, including Duplicati's backup passphrases and the admin logins of Uptime Kuma and the others.
  • Uptime Kuma checks http://vaultwarden:80/alive.
  • .env: VAULTWARDEN_PORT, VAULTWARDEN_SIGNUPS_ALLOWED, and HOMELAB_DOMAIN (its DOMAIN). ./homelab doctor warns while sign-ups are open.

docs.title: Tinkering ideas
docs.text:
• Create a "Family" organization with collections (Wi-Fi, streaming, utilities) and move shared logins into it.
  • Run the web vault's Reports for reused, weak, and exposed passwords, and fix the worst ones.
  • Store website passkeys in Bitwarden; the browser extension and phone app offer to save them.
  • Use Send instead of a chat message to share a one-off password, with an expiry and an access limit.
  • Install the Bitwarden CLI (bw) on this Mac for scripted lookups and exports (commands below).
  • Turn on the "unlock with biometrics" option in each app, so the master password is typed less often but stays strong.

docs.title: Useful commands
docs.text:
/alive answers when the server is up. The two bw lines point the Bitwarden CLI at this server and sign in.

./homelab logs vaultwarden -f
./homelab compose vaultwarden restart vaultwarden
./homelab compose vaultwarden exec vaultwarden /vaultwarden --version
./homelab compose vaultwarden exec vaultwarden ls -la /data
./homelab update vaultwarden
curl -s http://localhost:8087/alive
bw config server https://passwords.example.com
bw login

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• Vaultwarden wiki
  • Source on GitHub
  • Image on Docker Hub
  • Bitwarden help for the apps

docs.title: Backup
docs.text:
data/appdata/vaultwarden (the SQLite database, attachments, keys) is in the Homelab AppData job. Each Bitwarden app also keeps an encrypted offline copy of its vault. Export the vault (encrypted) now and then as an extra copy.

Also keep a monthly password-protected export in recovery-staging/secrets: Backups has the steps, and the nightly backup reminds you.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Fix The web vault says it needs a secure context Open it through https://passwords... (or http://localhost:8087 on the Mac), not by IP Apps fail to sync from outside The tunnel or proxy is down. ./homelab watchdog Sign-up page missing Sign-ups are closed, as intended. Open them briefly as in Setup

docs.title: ntfy
docs.text:
The homelab's notification server. Every alert, from the nightly updates, Duplicati, Uptime Kuma, and the watchdog, arrives on your phone through it.

Service ntfy in compose/security.yaml (project homelab_security) Image binwiederhier/ntfy:latest Category Security Starts with ./homelab up Yes (./homelab up) Address https://ntfy.example.com (LAN and public, through the Cloudflare Tunnel) On this machine http://localhost:9293 (NTFY_PORT) Data data/appdata/ntfy/cache → /var/cache/ntfydata/appdata/ntfy/lib → /var/lib/ntfy Database dump Daily by ./homelab backup into recovery-staging/databases/ntfy Updates Nightly at 4 AM, with a copy of its data first

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
• Push notifications, self-hosted: messages stay on the Mac. The iPhone app is woken through ntfy.sh, which only sees a message ID.
  • Five topics: watchtower, duplicati-alerts, uptime-kuma, tunnel-watchdog, reminders.

Access is deny-all: nobody can read or publish unless granted.

Away from home. The services publish with an access token, not anonymously, so ntfy can be public: ./homelab domain setup publishes it through the tunnel once ./homelab notify setup has made that token. Until then it is LAN-only, and the phone gets alerts only on home Wi-Fi. See Known Issues, ISSUE-0011 (fixed, to verify).

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. ./homelab notify setup lets the services publish (write-only, as user homelab with NTFY_PUBLISH_TOKEN) to exactly these topics and removes anonymous write access. It also creates homelab-reader for the desktop app and phone for the phone (read-only; its password is NTFY_PHONE_PASSWORD).
  2. Optionally, create your own user and let it read every topic:
./homelab compose ntfy exec ntfy ntfy user add <name>
./homelab compose ntfy exec ntfy ntfy access <name> '*' read-only
  1. In the ntfy iPhone app, Settings › Users: add server https://<TAILSCALE_HOST>:9293 in Home mode, or https://ntfy.example.com with a domain, with user phone (or your own), and subscribe to the topics.
  2. With a domain, ./homelab domain setup publishes ntfy through the tunnel. In Home mode the phone reaches it over Tailscale.
  3. ./homelab notify test watchtower and check the phone.

A new alert topic must be added to the list in internal/notify and granted with ./homelab notify setup, or its messages are refused.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• One Go program. Publishing is an HTTP POST or PUT to /<topic>; subscribing is a long-lived HTTP, websocket, or JSON stream on the same topic.
  • Messages are kept in a SQLite cache (cache.db) for 12 hours, so a phone that was offline catches up.
  • Users, access grants, and tokens are in user.db. With NTFY_AUTH_DEFAULT_ACCESS=deny-all, a topic is closed to anyone without a grant.
  • The iPhone app can only be woken by Apple's push service, so ntfy sends a poll request (the message ID only) to ntfy.sh (NTFY_UPSTREAM_BASE_URL), which wakes the app; the app then fetches the message from this server. What ntfy.sh (and Apple) learn: that a message arrived and when, its ID, and a SHA-256 hash of this server's address and the topic, from this computer's internet address. Never the message's words, title, or buttons, and never the topic's name.
  • NTFY_BEHIND_PROXY=true takes the client's address from the proxy's headers.
  • Accounts made by ./homelab notify setup: homelab publishes (write-only, NTFY_PUBLISH_TOKEN), homelab-reader reads for the desktop app (NTFY_READ_TOKEN), and phone reads for the phone app (NTFY_PHONE_PASSWORD).

docs.title: Where things live
docs.text: What Where Message cache data/appdata/ntfy/cache → /var/cache/ntfy/cache.db Users, grants, tokens data/appdata/ntfy/lib → /var/lib/ntfy/user.db Server settings The NTFY_* environment in compose/security.yaml (no server.yml is mounted) Daily dump of user.db recovery-staging/databases/ntfy The list of alert topics internal/notify (Topics)

docs.title: Everyday use
docs.text:
• The phone app: notifications, each topic's history, and muting a topic for a while.
  • The web app: open https://ntfy.example.com, sign in, subscribe to topics, and allow browser notifications for alerts on a computer.
  • The desktop app: Status shows the last 12 hours of alerts, and the menu bar shows the newest one.
  • ./homelab notify test <topic> sends a test message.

docs.title: Connects to
docs.text:
• Publishers: the nightly updates (watchtower), Duplicati (duplicati-alerts), Uptime Kuma (uptime-kuma), the watchdog (tunnel-watchdog), and Wallos and Changedetection.io (reminders).
  • Published through Cloudflare Tunnel once the publishers' token exists.
  • .env: NTFY_PORT, NTFY_PUBLISH_TOKEN, NTFY_PUBLISH_AUTH, NTFY_READ_TOKEN, NTFY_PHONE_PASSWORD, DESKTOP_ALERTS, and HEARTBEAT_URL (the outside check for when ntfy itself is down; see Monitoring).

docs.title: Tinkering ideas
docs.text:
• Headers change how a message looks: Priority: 5 for a loud alert, Tags: warning for an emoji, Click: https://uptime.example.com to open a page when tapped.
  • Scheduled delivery: an At: tomorrow 9am or Delay: 30m header holds a message until then.
  • Action buttons: an Actions: header adds up to three buttons, such as one that opens a URL.
  • A personal topic for your own scripts or iPhone Shortcuts: grant your user with ntfy access <name> <topic> rw, and give the script its own token with ntfy token add <name>.
  • Keep the web app open in a browser tab as a desktop notifier.

docs.title: Useful commands
docs.text:
ntfy access with no arguments lists every grant. The publish example uses the publishers' token, so it only works on the granted topics.

./homelab logs ntfy -f
./homelab compose ntfy restart ntfy
./homelab compose ntfy exec ntfy ntfy user list
./homelab compose ntfy exec ntfy ntfy access
./homelab compose ntfy exec ntfy ntfy token list
./homelab notify test watchtower
curl -s http://localhost:9293/v1/health
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer <NTFY_PUBLISH_TOKEN>" -H "Title: Hello" -H "Priority: 4" -d "Test from this Mac" http://localhost:9293/watchtower

docs.title: API
docs.text:
• Tokens: NTFY_PUBLISH_TOKEN (write) and NTFY_READ_TOKEN (read) in .env, or a new one from ntfy token add <user>. Send as Authorization: Bearer <token>.
  • Base URL: http://localhost:9293 on this Mac, http://ntfy:80 from containers, https://ntfy.example.com elsewhere.
  • Example, the last 12 hours of one topic: curl -s -H "Authorization: Bearer <NTFY_READ_TOKEN>" "http://localhost:9293/uptime-kuma/json?poll=1&since=12h".
  • Docs: publishing and subscribing.

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• ntfy docs
  • Source on GitHub
  • Image on Docker Hub

docs.title: Backup
docs.text: data/appdata/ntfy (users, grants, message cache) is in the Homelab AppData job.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Fix Services get 403 when publishing The topic is not granted. ./homelab notify setup Phone gets nothing at home The phone's user lacks read access, or the phone's DNS is not 192.168.1.10 Phone gets nothing away from home ntfy is not published yet. ./homelab notify setup, then ./homelab domain setup (see Purpose) Health check failing ./homelab logs ntfy

docs.title: Beszel agent
docs.text:
Reads this machine and its containers for Beszel.

Service beszel-agent in stacks/beszel/compose.yaml (project homelab_beszel) Image docker.io/henrygd/beszel-agent:0.21.1 Category System Starts with ./homelab up No: optional, ./homelab install beszel-agent Updates By hand. It holds the Docker socket; set BESZEL_AGENT_VERSION to a newer release after reading its notes (keep it near Beszel's own version), then ./homelab update beszel-agent Needs in .env BESZEL_AGENT_KEY

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Reads this machine and its containers for Beszel: CPU, memory, disks, network, temperatures, and each container's share.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text: It starts once BESZEL_AGENT_KEY is set: Beszel's note, Setup.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• A small Go program on this machine's network (network_mode: host), listening on BESZEL_AGENT_PORT (45876) for the hub, which signs in with its SSH key; the agent only answers that key.
  • It reads the containers through Docker's socket, read-only. On the host's network it cannot reach the socket proxy the other readers use by name.
  • With Docker Desktop or OrbStack, "this machine" is the runtime's Linux VM (Beszel's note).

docs.title: Where things live
docs.text: What Where The hub's key it accepts BESZEL_AGENT_KEY in .env

docs.title: Everyday use
docs.text: Nothing to do: Beszel shows what it reads.

docs.title: Connects to
docs.text: • Beszel, which reads it.

docs.title: Tinkering ideas
docs.text: • EXTRA_FILESYSTEMS (in Beszel's documentation) adds the media drive as its own disk on the graphs.

docs.title: Useful commands
docs.text: ./homelab logs beszel-agent -f

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text: • Beszel's agent documentation

docs.title: Backup
docs.text: Nothing of its own; its key is in .env.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: • It restarts again and again: BESZEL_AGENT_KEY is empty or not a key; copy it from Beszel's Add System.

docs.title: Beszel
docs.text:
How this machine and its apps are doing over time, with alerts.

Service beszel in stacks/beszel/compose.yaml (project homelab_beszel) Image docker.io/henrygd/beszel:latest Category System Starts with ./homelab up No: optional, ./homelab install beszel Address https://monitor.example.com (LAN, through Nginx Proxy Manager) On this machine http://localhost:8090 (BESZEL_PORT) Data appdata/beszel → /beszel_data Database dump Daily by ./homelab backup into recovery-staging/databases/beszel Updates Nightly at 4 AM, with a copy of its data first

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: How this machine and its apps are doing over time: CPU, memory, disk use and speed, network, temperatures, and each container's share, as graphs over hours, days, and weeks. Alerts (by email, or through ntfy with a webhook) when the machine runs hot, a disk fills, or it stops answering. Status shows now; Beszel shows the trend.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. ./homelab install beszel. Its first account is made on its first start from BESZEL_EMAIL and BESZEL_PASSWORD (Sign-in details on its page in Status shows the email and copies the password).
  2. Open it, Add System, and copy the Public Key it shows into Settings as BESZEL_AGENT_KEY. Then ./homelab install beszel-agent.
  3. Back in Add System: name it after this machine, host host.docker.internal, port 45876 (BESZEL_AGENT_PORT), and add it. It turns green within a minute.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• The hub is a Go app with PocketBase (its database, data.db, in appdata/beszel). It keeps the history and the alerts, and connects to each agent over SSH with its own key.
  • The agent (beszel-agent) runs on this machine's network and reads the machine's counters, and each container's through Docker's socket (read-only). The hub reaches it at host.docker.internal.
  • What the agent sees depends on the runtime: on Linux and SteamOS the machine itself; with Docker Desktop (Windows) or OrbStack (macOS), the runtime's Linux VM, so CPU and memory are the VM's share and the Mac's or PC's own sensors are not there. Its containers are the homelab's either way.

docs.title: Where things live
docs.text: What Where History, systems, alerts, accounts appdata/beszel/data.db → /beszel_data The hub's SSH key appdata/beszel/id_ed25519 Settings BESZEL_EMAIL, BESZEL_PASSWORD, BESZEL_AGENT_KEY, BESZEL_PORT, BESZEL_AGENT_PORT, BESZEL_URL in .env

docs.title: Everyday use
docs.text:
• The dashboard: each system with its CPU, memory, and disk now; click one for its graphs over time and each container's.
  • Alerts: the bell on a system sets limits (CPU, memory, disk, temperature, down); Settings › Notifications says where they go.
  • Other machines: run its agent on another computer (Beszel's site has a one-line install) and add it the same way.

docs.title: Connects to
docs.text:
• ntfy: Settings › Notifications › add ntfy:// with the homelab's topic, for alerts on the phone.
  • Uptime Kuma watches that each app answers; Beszel watches the machine under them.
  • Beszel agent, which it reads.

docs.title: Tinkering ideas
docs.text:
• Alert when the media drive is over 90% full.
  • Add the other computers at home (a NAS, a desktop) to see them all on one page.

docs.title: Useful commands
docs.text:
./homelab logs beszel -f
./homelab logs beszel-agent -f
./homelab compose beszel ps

docs.title: API
docs.text: PocketBase's REST API: POST /api/collections/users/auth-with-password for a token, then GET /api/collections/systems/records with Authorization: <token>. See Beszel's documentation.

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• beszel.dev
  • GitHub: henrygd/beszel

docs.title: Backup
docs.text: ./homelab backup copies data.db nightly (SQLite, checked) into recovery-staging/databases/beszel, and Duplicati takes it off-site. The hub's key in appdata/beszel goes with the Homelab Stack Data job; without it, add the key to the agent again (Setup, step 2).

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• The system stays red: BESZEL_AGENT_KEY does not match the hub's key (copy it again from Add System), or the agent is not running (./homelab status).
  • No temperatures: the runtime's VM has no sensors (macOS, Windows), or the machine does not expose them.

docs.title: Dozzle
docs.text:
Live logs of every container, in the browser.

Service dozzle in compose/system.yaml (project homelab_system) Image amir20/dozzle:latest Category System Starts with ./homelab up No: optional, ./homelab install dozzle Address this computer only: it has no sign-in of its own, so it gets no tailnet or domain address On this machine http://localhost:9998 (DOZZLE_PORT) Depends on docker-socket-proxy Helpers docker-socket-proxy ghcr.io/tecnativa/docker-socket-proxy:v0.5.0 Updates Nightly at 4 AM, with a copy of its data first

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: Live logs from every container in the browser, with search and filters. The first stop when an app misbehaves, instead of ./homelab logs in a terminal.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. ./homelab install dozzle (it brings the read-only Docker socket proxy with it).
  2. Open it at http://localhost:9998, on this computer only: there is no account, so it gets no tailnet or domain address (Connects to, below).
  3. Anyone who can open it reads every container's log, including the line where Nginx Proxy Manager printed its first account's password on its first start. If others use this computer, change that password in the NPM UI and put the new one in NPM_API_PASSWORD.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• A single Go program that serves the web page and streams each container's log to it as lines are written.
  • It reads containers and logs from the Docker engine through docker-socket-proxy (DOCKER_HOST: tcp://docker-socket-proxy:2375), which answers reads only (containers, their logs and settings, engine info), so Dozzle cannot start, stop, or change anything. Reads include every container's settings, passwords among them, so the proxy is on a network of its own that only Dozzle, Homarr, and Homepage join, not the one every app shares.
  • It stores nothing. The history it shows is what Docker still keeps: every service here logs with the json-file driver, at most 3 files of 10 MB per container, so older lines of a busy container roll off.
  • Anonymous usage reporting is off (DOZZLE_NO_ANALYTICS).

docs.title: Everyday use
docs.text:
• Pick a container in the left column; containers are grouped by Compose project (homelab_media, homelab_immich, and so on).
  • Type in the search box above a log to filter its lines, and use the level filter (error, warning, info) for apps that write levelled logs.
  • Open a second container beside the first to follow two at once, for example Sonarr and qBittorrent during a download.
  • Press ⌘K to jump to a container by name.
  • Download a log from the toolbar to attach it to a bug report.

docs.title: Connects to
docs.text:
• Shares docker-socket-proxy with Homarr, and with Homepage if you give it container status.
  • Opened on this computer only (an app's page on Status › its log › Dozzle, or http://localhost:9998): it has no sign-in of its own and logs can hold secrets, so it gets no address on the tailnet or the domain (Security, L1). A proxy host or tailnet address made before this change goes away the next time ./homelab domain setup or ./homelab tailnet setup runs.
  • Pairs with Uptime Kuma: Kuma says something is down, Dozzle shows why.
  • .env: DOZZLE_PORT.

docs.title: Tinkering ideas
docs.text:
• Show only some containers with DOZZLE_FILTER in its environment, for example label=com.docker.compose.project=homelab_media.
  • Give a container a friendlier name or group with the labels dev.dozzle.name and dev.dozzle.group on its service.
  • Add a sign-in: DOZZLE_AUTH_PROVIDER: simple with a users.yml in a /data volume (see the authentication page of its docs).
  • Leave container actions off: the socket proxy is read-only on purpose, and DOZZLE_ENABLE_ACTIONS would also need write access to the engine.

docs.title: Useful commands
docs.text:
Its logs, the socket proxy it depends on, its own health check, a restart, and whether the page answers:

./homelab logs dozzle -f
./homelab status docker-socket-proxy
./homelab compose dozzle exec dozzle /dozzle healthcheck
./homelab compose dozzle restart dozzle
curl -sI http://localhost:9998

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• Docs: https://dozzle.dev/
  • Source and image: https://github.com/amir20/dozzle

docs.title: Backup
docs.text: Nothing to back up: Dozzle keeps no data.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: • No containers listed: the socket proxy is not running; ./homelab install docker-socket-proxy or reinstall Dozzle.

docs.title: Duplicati
docs.text:
Encrypted, versioned, deduplicated backups of everything that matters, written to the Proton Drive folder on the Mac.

Service duplicati in compose/system.yaml (project homelab_system) Image lscr.io/linuxserver/duplicati:latest Category System Starts with ./homelab up Yes (./homelab up) Address https://backups.example.com (LAN, through Nginx Proxy Manager) On this machine http://localhost:8200 (DUPLICATI_PORT) Data data/appdata/duplicati → /configdata/appdata, read-only → /source/appdataappdata, read-only → /source/homelab-appdatastacks, read-only → /source/stacks~/.local/share/jellyfin, read-only → /source/jellyfin/Volumes/Media/photos, read-only → /source/immich/Volumes/Media/Books, read-only → /source/calibredata/sync, read-only → /source/syncrecovery-staging → /stagingbackups → /destination Updates Nightly at 4 AM, with a copy of its data first

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text:
• Off-site copies of settings, documents, photos, database dumps, and .env.
  • Versions, so a mistake from last week can still be undone.

Sources are mounted read-only; restores go to /staging/... and are copied back by hand.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. Pick where the backups go: Setup › Backups leave this machine (Use Proton Drive, another synced cloud folder, or an external drive), or ./homelab duplicati destination. It sets BACKUP_DESTINATION and recreates Duplicati so it sees the folder at /destination.
  2. Setup › Create the backup jobs (or ./homelab duplicati setup) makes every job in Automation through Duplicati's API: the sources, a folder each under /destination, AES-256 with the passphrases in .env, smart retention, the schedules, and the alerts to ntfy. It runs the small jobs once straight away, and leaves a job that already exists (by name) as it is.
  3. Copy DUPLICATI_SECRETS_PASSPHRASE (Settings › Copy) into Vaultwarden and onto the recovery kit (Backups › Recovery kit): it opens the Secrets job, which holds every other passphrase.
  4. To look inside, sign in at http://localhost:8200 with DUPLICATI_PASSWORD: Sign-in details on its page in Status copies it.

By hand instead: in Duplicati, add a job per row of the table in Automation, with a Local folder destination /destination/<folder>, AES-256, the container paths from Backups as sources, the schedule listed, and Smart backup retention. send-http-url and send-http-level are set for every job as default options by Set up the alert token.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Duplicati 2 is a .NET app with a web UI and its own scheduler; this image is LinuxServer's build of it.
  • A job splits its sources into blocks, stores each block once (deduplication), packs them into compressed volumes, encrypts each with AES-256, and writes three kinds of files: dblock (data), dindex (index), and dlist (one per version).
  • Each job keeps a local SQLite database in /config that describes what is at the destination. It makes backups fast and can be rebuilt from the destination (Database › Repair or Recreate).
  • The server's settings and job definitions are in Duplicati-server.sqlite; the secrets in it are encrypted with SETTINGS_ENCRYPTION_KEY (DUPLICATI_SETTINGS_KEY).
  • Live databases are never copied directly: ./homelab backup dumps them at 03:30 into recovery-staging, and the Homelab Databases job reads them from /staging at 05:00.
  • The destination is a plain folder (/destination); the Proton Drive app on this Mac uploads it.

docs.title: Where things live
docs.text: What Where Server settings and job definitions data/appdata/duplicati/Duplicati-server.sqlite (/config) Each job's local database data/appdata/duplicati/<random name>.sqlite Backup files BACKUP_DESTINATION/<job folder> (/destination/...): photos, databases, secrets, appdata, stack-data, infrastructure, jellyfin, calibre Database dumps and volume archives recovery-staging/databases/, recovery-staging/volumes/ (/staging/...) Copy of .env for the Secrets job recovery-staging/secrets/ Sources, read-only /source/appdata, /source/homelab-appdata, /source/stacks, /source/jellyfin, /source/immich, /source/calibre, /source/sync

docs.title: Everyday use
docs.text:
• The home page lists each job with its last and next run; Run now starts one at once.
  • Restore: Restore › pick the job › pick a version (date) › tick files › restore to a folder under /staging, never to the original location.
  • A job's menu has Show log (each run's result and warnings), Verify files (checks the destination against the local database), and Export.
  • From the terminal, ./homelab duplicati jobs shows every job's last run, next run, size, and last error.

docs.title: Connects to
docs.text:
• Warnings and errors go to ntfy on the duplicati-alerts topic; ./homelab duplicati setup sets that for every job.
  • The passphrases (DUPLICATI_PASSPHRASE, DUPLICATI_SECRETS_PASSPHRASE) and exported job files belong in Vaultwarden.
  • Backs up Immich's library (IMMICH_UPLOAD_LOCATION), native Jellyfin's data (JELLYFIN_DATA_DIR), and the Books folder under MEDIA_ROOT that Calibre-Web uses.
  • The dumps come from the PostgreSQL containers and the SQLite apps marked dump: in their compose files.
  • .env: DUPLICATI_PORT, DUPLICATI_PASSWORD (sign-in), DUPLICATI_SETTINGS_KEY, BACKUP_DESTINATION.

docs.title: Tinkering ideas
docs.text:
• Add a second destination for the small, critical jobs (Secrets, Databases): an external drive, or a cloud backend such as Backblaze B2 or S3, so one copy does not depend on Proton Drive.
  • Tune retention: in a job's options, a custom retention such as 1W:1D,4W:1W,12M:1M keeps dailies for a week, weeklies for a month, and monthlies for a year.
  • Add filters (job › Edit › Source data › Filters) to skip caches and logs that bloat the AppData job.
  • Raise the advanced option backup-test-samples so each run checks more files at the destination.
  • Run ./homelab restore-test --auto once a month: it restores a sample and compares it with the live files.
  • Back up Syncthing's SYNC_ROOT: it is not mounted here, so add a read-only volume to the service first.

docs.title: Useful commands
docs.text:
Job status, the first-time job setup, the database dumps (preview, then for real), a restore test, an alert test, the logs, and the latest dumps:

./homelab duplicati jobs
./homelab duplicati setup
./homelab backup
./homelab backup --apply
./homelab restore-test --auto
./homelab notify test duplicati-alerts
./homelab logs duplicati -f
./homelab compose duplicati restart duplicati
ls -lh recovery-staging/databases/*

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• Docs: https://docs.duplicati.com/
  • Source: https://github.com/duplicati/duplicati
  • Image: https://docs.linuxserver.io/images/docker-duplicati/ and https://github.com/linuxserver/docker-duplicati

docs.title: Backup
docs.text: Its own settings (data/appdata/duplicati) are in the Homelab AppData job, and the exported job files are in Vaultwarden. If both are lost, any job can be rebuilt from Proton Drive with its passphrase (Restore › Direct restore from backup files). When the whole machine is lost, ./homelab rebuild <backup folder> restores every job from its files alone with Duplicati's own command line, then makes the jobs again here (Disaster Recovery).

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Fix Destination not found Proton Drive is not running, or BACKUP_DESTINATION is wrong. ./homelab doctor Restore fails on permissions In the restore wizard, turn off restoring permissions "Local database is out of sync" Database › Repair. If that fails, Recreate Job never alerts ./homelab notify setup grants the duplicati-alerts topic

docs.title: Homarr
docs.text:
A dashboard with live container status: one page of links to every app, with which ones are running.

Service homarr in compose/system.yaml (project homelab_system) Image ghcr.io/homarr-labs/homarr:latest Category System Starts with ./homelab up No: optional, ./homelab install homarr Address https://homarr.example.com (LAN, through Nginx Proxy Manager) On this machine http://localhost:7575 (HOMARR_PORT) Depends on docker-socket-proxy Helpers docker-socket-proxy ghcr.io/tecnativa/docker-socket-proxy:v0.5.0 Data data/appdata/homarr → /appdata Database dump Daily by ./homelab backup into recovery-staging/databases/homarr Updates Nightly at 4 AM, with a copy of its data first

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: A start page for the family and a quick status view for the administrator.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. ./homelab install homarr (it brings Docker Socket Proxy with it); with a domain, then ./homelab domain setup.
  2. Open https://<TAILSCALE_HOST>:7575 in Home mode, or https://homarr.example.com with a domain, and create the admin account.
  3. Add apps by their public addresses. Container status comes from docker-socket-proxy (read-only), already configured.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• Homarr 1.x is a TypeScript (Next.js) app. Boards, apps, users, and integrations are in a SQLite database at /appdata/db/db.sqlite; the secrets in it (integration API keys and passwords) are encrypted with SECRET_ENCRYPTION_KEY.
  • A task runner in the same container polls integrations and pings apps on a schedule, so widgets and status dots stay current.
  • Container status comes from the Docker engine through docker-socket-proxy (DOCKER_HOSTNAMES and DOCKER_PORTS in the compose file), read-only.
  • ./homelab backup copies the database every day into recovery-staging/databases/homarr.

docs.title: Where things live
docs.text: What Where Everything Homarr keeps data/appdata/homarr → /appdata Database data/appdata/homarr/db/db.sqlite (/appdata/db/db.sqlite) Daily copies recovery-staging/databases/homarr/homarr-YYYYMMDD-HHMMSS.sqlite.gz

docs.title: Everyday use
docs.text:
• Open a board and switch to edit mode to add apps and widgets, move and resize them, then save.
  • Management (from the user menu) holds apps, boards, integrations, users and groups, and settings.
  • An app tile can show a status dot from a ping of its address.
  • Choose a home board for everyone, or give each person their own board.

docs.title: Connects to
docs.text:
• Shares docker-socket-proxy with Dozzle.
  • An alternative to Homepage; run one or the other.
  • Integrations take API keys from apps here, such as Sonarr, Radarr, Prowlarr, qBittorrent, Jellyfin, AdGuard Home, and Home Assistant. Each integration form lists what it needs.
  • Sign-in through Pocket ID works over OIDC (the AUTH_PROVIDERS and AUTH_OIDC_* environment variables in Homarr's docs).
  • .env: HOMARR_PORT, HOMARR_SECRET_ENCRYPTION_KEY.

docs.title: Tinkering ideas
docs.text:
• Add the calendar widget with the Sonarr and Radarr integrations to see upcoming episodes and films.
  • Add the DNS widget with the AdGuard Home integration for today's queries and blocks.
  • Add a media server widget with the Jellyfin integration to see who is watching.
  • Show a Home Assistant entity (a temperature, a door) on the family board.
  • Make a family board with only the household apps, and an admin board with the system ones.
  • Sign in with Pocket ID instead of a Homarr password.

docs.title: Useful commands
docs.text:
Its logs, a restart, the socket proxy it reads, a fresh database copy, the saved copies, and whether the page answers:

./homelab logs homarr -f
./homelab compose homarr restart homarr
./homelab status docker-socket-proxy
./homelab backup --apply
ls -lh recovery-staging/databases/homarr
curl -sI http://localhost:7575

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• Docs: https://homarr.dev/
  • Source and image: https://github.com/homarr-labs/homarr

docs.title: Backup
docs.text: data/appdata/homarr (boards, users, its database) is in the Homelab AppData job. HOMARR_SECRET_ENCRYPTION_KEY in .env is needed to read it back.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: If container status is empty, check ./homelab status docker-socket-proxy.

docs.title: Homepage
docs.text:
A fast, static dashboard configured with YAML files: links, bookmarks, and service widgets.

Service homepage in compose/system.yaml (project homelab_system) Image ghcr.io/gethomepage/homepage:latest Category System Starts with ./homelab up No: optional, ./homelab install homepage Address https://homepage.example.com (LAN, through Nginx Proxy Manager) On this machine http://localhost:3000 (HOMEPAGE_PORT) Data data/appdata/homepage → /app/config Updates Nightly at 4 AM, with a copy of its data first

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: A start page for the household: one address with every app on it, kept up to date by the homelab. An alternative to Homarr, whose page you arrange by hand. Install one or the other.

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. ./homelab install homepage and open https://<TAILSCALE_HOST>:3000 in Home mode, or https://homepage.example.com with a domain (after ./homelab domain setup).
  2. The homelab writes services.yaml for you: every running app with its https:// address, its icon, and what it does, grouped like Choose apps. It is rewritten after each install, start, stop, or removal (or with ./homelab homepage), so the page always matches what runs.
  3. To keep your own list instead, delete the file's first line (the marker); from then on the homelab leaves services.yaml alone. bookmarks.yaml and widgets.yaml are always yours.
  4. For container status, install docker-socket-proxy and add it in docker.yaml as host: docker-socket-proxy, port: 2375.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• A Next.js app with no database and no accounts: the page is built from YAML files in /app/config.
  • Service widgets call each app's API from the Homepage server, not from your browser, so API keys in the YAML never reach the page.
  • ./homelab homepage writes services.yaml from the apps that run, with a marker on its first line; without the marker it leaves the file alone.
  • With people in the household (./homelab person add), each gets a tab with only the apps they use, at https://homepage.<domain>/#anna, and every app moves to an Everything tab. That needs Homepage's layout, so the homelab writes settings.yaml too, with the same marker; a settings.yaml of your own is left alone (the tabs then show as groups on one page). ./homelab person apps anna immich-server mealie chooses a person's apps.
  • Most edits show on the next page reload; restart it if one does not.
  • HOMEPAGE_ALLOWED_HOSTS lists the host names it answers to.

docs.title: Where things live
docs.text: What Where Config folder data/appdata/homepage → /app/config App list (written by the homelab) services.yaml Your links bookmarks.yaml Info widgets along the top widgets.yaml Title, theme, layout (the people's tabs; written by the homelab while it has the marker) settings.yaml Docker hosts for container status docker.yaml Your own styles and scripts custom.css, custom.js Log logs/homepage.log

docs.title: Everyday use
docs.text:
• Start typing anywhere on the page to search apps and bookmarks (Quick Launch); Enter opens the first match.
  • Edit the YAML files in data/appdata/homepage with any editor, then reload the page.
  • Set the page title, theme, and colour in settings.yaml (title, theme, color).

docs.title: Connects to
docs.text:
• Each tile links to the address Status shows: https://<TAILSCALE_HOST>:<port> in Home mode, or https://<subdomain>.example.com behind Nginx Proxy Manager with a domain.
  • An alternative to Homarr; run one or the other.
  • Container status uses docker-socket-proxy (shared with Dozzle). Homepage matches containers by name, and Compose names them <project>-<service>-1, for example homelab_system-duplicati-1.
  • Service widgets exist for many apps here, such as Immich, Paperless-ngx, Sonarr, Radarr, AdGuard Home, and Uptime Kuma. Each needs that app's API key in a widget: block, so keep your own services.yaml (remove the marker) to use them.
  • .env: HOMEPAGE_PORT and HOMELAB_DOMAIN, which make up HOMEPAGE_ALLOWED_HOSTS.

docs.title: Tinkering ideas
docs.text:
• Add the resources (CPU, memory, disk), datetime, and search widgets to widgets.yaml.
  • Add an openmeteo weather widget with your town's coordinates.
  • Add siteMonitor: <url> to a service to show its response time.
  • Turn on container status: a docker.yaml entry, then server: and container: on each service.
  • Group the family's links (school, bills, utilities) in bookmarks.yaml.
  • Change how groups are laid out (columns, rows) under layout: in settings.yaml.

docs.title: Useful commands
docs.text:
Rewrite the app list, follow the logs, restart, check whether services.yaml still has the homelab's marker, read Homepage's own log, and check the page answers:

./homelab homepage
./homelab logs homepage -f
./homelab compose homepage restart homepage
head -1 data/appdata/homepage/services.yaml
tail -f data/appdata/homepage/logs/homepage.log
curl -sI http://localhost:3000

docs.title: Learn more
docs.text:
• Docs, including every widget: https://gethomepage.dev/
  • Source and image: https://github.com/gethomepage/homepage

docs.title: Backup
docs.text: data/appdata/homepage is in the Homelab AppData job.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: "Host validation failed": open it at https://homepage.example.com, https://<TAILSCALE_HOST>:3000, or http://localhost:3000, the hosts in HOMEPAGE_ALLOWED_HOSTS.

docs.title: Kopia
docs.text:
A second, independent backup beside Duplicati, to another drive.

Service kopia in compose/system.yaml (project homelab_system) Image kopia/kopia:0.23.1 Category System Starts with ./homelab up No: optional, ./homelab install kopia Address https://kopia.example.com (LAN, through Nginx Proxy Manager) On this machine http://localhost:51515 (KOPIA_PORT) Data config/kopia/start.sh, read-only → /homelab/start.shdata/appdata/kopia/config → /app/configdata/kopia/cache → /app/cachedata/kopia/logs → /app/logsdata/appdata, read-only → /source/appdataappdata, read-only → /source/homelab-appdatastacks, read-only → /source/stacks~/.local/share/jellyfin, read-only → /source/jellyfin/Volumes/Media/photos, read-only → /source/immich/Volumes/Media/Books, read-only → /source/calibrerecovery-staging → /stagingbackups-kopia → /repository Updates By hand. A backup engine reads and writes every copy you keep; set KOPIA_VERSION to a newer release after reading its notes, then ./homelab update kopia

docs.title: Purpose
docs.text: A second backup of the homelab, made by different software into a different place. Duplicati stays the main backup and the one that goes off-site; Kopia keeps another copy, usually on a second drive. If Duplicati's copy or its own database breaks, Kopia's is still there (ADR-0019).

docs.title: Setup
docs.text:
1. ./homelab install kopia. On its first start it makes the repository at KOPIA_REPOSITORY, encrypted with KOPIA_PASSWORD, and schedules each folder for 3:45 every night. Left as it is, that is backups-kopia in the homelab folder, on the same drive as everything else.
  2. Choose where its copies go: Setup's step A second copy with Kopia offers one button per drive plugged in (then the cloud drives), each making a Homelab Kopia folder there. It never offers the drive with Duplicati's backups or the media. Or ./homelab kopia repository /Volumes/Spare/Homelab\ Kopia, or any folder in Settings › KOPIA_REPOSITORY. Kopia starts again on the new folder. Once done, the step also says how Kopia's last restore test went (homelab restore-test --auto --engine kopia), or that none has run yet.
  3. Keep KOPIA_PASSWORD outside this machine, with DUPLICATI_SECRETS_PASSPHRASE (Vaultwarden and the recovery kit): without it, nothing in the repository can be read.
  4. Open it to see the snapshots: the user is admin, and Sign-in details on its page in Status copies the password (KOPIA_SERVER_PASSWORD).

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
• config/kopia/start.sh runs at each start: it connects to the repository at KOPIA_REPOSITORY (making it the first time), and when KOPIA_REPOSITORY now points at another folder, it disconnects first and connects to the repository there, or makes one. It knows which by the ID in the repository's own file, kept in data/appdata/kopia/config/homelab-repository.id. It sets the 3:45 schedule and zstd compression for each folder that is there, then starts Kopia's server with its web page. The snapshots belong to homelab@homelab on every machine, so a moved homelab finds its own.
  • It runs as your account (PUID, PGID), like Duplicati, so what it restores is yours to read and copy back. It starts as root only to hand its own folders (settings, cache, logs, the repository) to that account, including anything a command run as root left in them.
